Microsoft 365 for Managers

A complete course · Basics to pro

Learn Microsoft 365 the way an analyst actually uses it

Fourteen modules, twelve capstone projects, and a live Excel formula lab wired to a real-looking retail dataset. Written for business students who will be asked, in their first week on the job, to "just pull that number and put it on a slide."

See how M365 runs a company Start Module 01 Open the Formula Lab

What this is

Every job description for a business analyst, a management trainee or an operations associate says "proficient in MS Office". Nobody is ever tested on Office. They are tested on whether they can take a 6,000-row export, get a clean number out of it in twenty minutes, and explain it to someone senior without a fuss. That is a narrower skill than "Office" and a far more valuable one, and this course teaches exactly that.

So it starts where the work starts. Excel gets half the modules, because Excel is where the number comes from: formulas, lookups, PivotTables, Power Query, charts, and the modelling tools that finance teams live in. Word, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams get the rest, taught as what they are on the job: the ways a number becomes a decision. Forms, Lists, Planner and Power Automate come last, because once you can produce the number you'll want the routine to run itself.

Everything runs against Novamart, a fictional Indian omnichannel retailer with 13 stores, 500 customers, 3,000 orders and a lead export that somebody clearly filled in by hand. It is the same company, and the same rows, as the SQL for Managers course, so if you have done that one you already know the data. If you haven't, you'll know it well by Module 03.

Why a manager cares

The gap between "I know Excel" and "I can answer that by 3:30" is where most first-year careers stall. The people who move fast are not the ones who know the most functions. They know a dozen well, they know which one the question needs, and they know how to check that the answer is right before anyone else does.

The path, end to end

Work through it in order and you go from never having made an Excel Table to building a linked management dashboard, cleaning a CRM export with Power Query, and automating the weekly report with a flow. Each module runs 45 to 90 minutes and ends with exercises the site checks for you.

LevelModulesWhat you can do at the end
Foundations 01 Workspace, 02 Excel foundations, 03 Formulas, 04 Lookups, 05 PivotTables Find any file, keep one version of it, and answer any single-sheet question: totals by anything, a lookup across sheets, a pivot with a slicer.
Intermediate 06 Power Query, 07 Dashboards, 08 Word, 09 PowerPoint, 10 Outlook & Teams Clean a messy export once and refresh it forever, build a one-page dashboard, write the memo and the deck that carry the number, and run the meeting where it lands.
Advanced 11 Forms, Lists, Planner, 12 Power Automate, 13 Modelling, 14 Copilot & career Capture data at source, automate the routine, build a what-if model with a Data Model behind it, use Copilot without trusting it blindly, and pass the assessment test.
Build Twelve capstone projects Finish three and you have a portfolio: a workbook, a deck or document, a named stakeholder, a trap you caught, and a recommendation.

The workbook you'll be working in

Novamart sells electronics, fashion, home goods, beauty, sports gear and groceries through 12 stores and Novamart.in, from January 2024 to August 2026. The data is generated, but it behaves. Revenue spikes around Diwali, the Kochi store opens in April 2024 and drags every "by store" average down for a year, the app channel appears in 2025, roughly one order in fourteen gets cancelled, and the lead-form export has the same person in it three times with three spellings of Bengaluru.

Thirteen sheets, laid out the way a real export would be: one row per order line in Sales, one row per order in Orders, lookup sheets for Stores, Products and Customers, monthly Targets, Employees, Returns, Inventory, NPS responses, and the deliberately awful Leads. Every formula on every page runs against these sheets in your browser, and the Formula Lab lets you browse them column by column.

You can also download the whole thing as a real workbook, files/novamart-m365.xlsx, with each sheet already formatted as an Excel Table. The capstones and the Power Query and PivotTable modules expect you to open it in Excel itself, because some things (Power Query, Solver, the Data Model) only exist on the desktop.

Note

The Lab speaks Excel 365: dynamic arrays spill, XLOOKUP, FILTER, UNIQUE and LET all work, dates are serial numbers, and TODAY() is pinned to 31 August 2026 so every answer on the site is reproducible. Anything Excel 2016 or Google Sheets does differently is flagged in the module where it matters.

What you need

A Microsoft 365 account. Your university almost certainly gives you one (the same login as your college email), and it includes the desktop apps, OneDrive and Teams. If you only have Excel for the web, you can do Modules 01 to 05, 07 and 08 to 12 fully; Power Query (06), Solver and the Data Model (13) need the desktop version of Excel on Windows. A Mac runs most of it; the module pages say where it doesn't.

No add-ins, no sample files to hunt for, no account to create for this site. Your progress, your theme and whatever you last typed in the Lab are kept in this browser.

How to use this site

  • Press / anywhere to search every module, formula and capstone.
  • Every formula block has a Run button. Press it. Then change something and press it again; predicting what breaks is the fastest way to learn.
  • Exercises have a Write your answer box that checks your formula's result against the solution's, so you can try before you peek.
  • Mark modules complete at the bottom of each page. The rail on the left keeps count.
  • The cheat sheet is designed to be printed. Keep it beside you for a month, then stop needing it.

About this course

Built by the DGU AI Cell at DBS Global University for BBA and MBA (Business Analytics) students, as the sibling of SQL for Managers. Videos and articles linked from each module are free, public resources from Microsoft and independent trainers; every link was checked when the course was published. Novamart, its stores, its people and its numbers are fictional.

Orientation · Start here

How Microsoft 365 actually runs a company

Before you learn a single ribbon path, it helps to see where the path leads. This page is the map: where a company's numbers are captured, which file they land in, who opens that file, what they build from it, and how the result reaches a meeting on Monday and a to-do list by Tuesday. Almost every step is a Microsoft 365 app. Very few of them are the app you think.

  • You'll be able to point at any number in a board deck and describe the path it took from a till in Kochi or a Forms survey to that slide.
  • You'll know which apps a CEO opens daily, which a store manager opens weekly, and which an analyst lives in.
  • You'll recognise the five shapes of work Microsoft 365 answers in every business, and which module teaches each.
  • You'll know what Microsoft 365 cannot do, so you stop treating a workbook as a database and an inbox as a project plan.

A number that lives in six places

Thursday, 4:40 pm

Meera Krishnan wants one figure before she leaves: August delivered revenue against target, by region, with Kochi called out. She asked Nandini. Nandini asked Vikram. Vikram has just asked you, and he wants it as a slide, not a spreadsheet, because it goes into Monday's review deck. The POS export for August arrived in a shared mailbox as twelve CSVs, one per store. The online numbers are in a different file Sameer's team drops into SharePoint. Targets are in a workbook Arjun's team owns. You have until 6.

The number exists. All of it. It sits in fourteen files across three folders, and every one of those files is inside Microsoft 365 already. Nobody needs to buy anything or call IT. The only question is whether the person holding the request can get from those files to one honest sentence on a slide in eighty minutes.

In most companies the honest answer is no. The analyst opens each CSV, copies rows into a master sheet, writes a fresh SUM, screenshots a chart into PowerPoint, and mails the deck as an attachment. Next month it happens again from scratch. Six months in, three versions of "the scorecard" circulate and the CFO's one shows a different total from the COO's. Nobody was careless. The work was never wired together.

Microsoft 365 is the wiring. Not magic, and not one app: a set of apps that share the same files, the same identity and the same cloud, so that a Forms response can become an Excel row can become a chart can become a slide can become a task without anyone re-typing anything. Below is the machinery, drawn once so that every module afterwards has a place to sit.

For the record, the figure Meera wants comes to ₹12.5 lakh delivered in August 2026 against a ₹16.3 lakh target across the thirteen stores, about 77%. You will build that whole chain yourself by Module 07.

The map

Walk it left to right

Start at the far left, with the things that capture data without anyone meaning to. A till in T. Nagar closes at 9:30 pm and the POS system drops a CSV into a shared mailbox. A customer in Dehradun taps 9 on an NPS form her phone showed her after delivery. Priya's CRM lets her export leads, and the export is a mess: DELHI, New Delhi and Delhi in the same column, dates in three formats. The ERP spits out GST invoices monthly. Meta and Google let you download spend as CSV. None of these people is doing analysis. They are doing their job, and the data is a by-product.

Every one of those exports has to land somewhere, and where it lands is the first decision that matters. OneDrive is yours: drafts, scratch files, the thing you are not ready to show. SharePoint is the team's: a document library with a folder per month that Vikram, Nandini and Arjun can all open. Teams "Files" is SharePoint wearing a different jacket, which is why a file you drop into the Analytics channel shows up in the SharePoint site too. Module 01 spends an hour on this, because the single most common failure in a new analyst's first month is a workbook that lives on a laptop and gets mailed around as Scorecard_FINAL_v2 (1).xlsx.

Now the wide box in the middle. Excel is the only place on the map where you type formulas, and the order inside it is the order you will learn it in. Power Query connects to the folder of twelve CSVs, trims and fixes and stacks them, and loads the result as a Table. Nobody copies a row. Next month you press Refresh and August becomes September. The Table is the thing formulas and PivotTables point at: one header row, one record per row, no merged cells, no blank rows, and it grows on its own. On top of the Table sit the summaries: a PivotTable for revenue by region, a SUMIFS for the one number Meera asked for, an XLOOKUP that pulls each store's target alongside its actual. And on top of those, a chart, whose title is the finding, not the topic.

Look right of Excel. The chart becomes a slide in a PowerPoint deck, pasted as a linked object so a refresh in Excel refreshes the slide. The clean-up you had to do to the CRM export becomes a two-page Word memo to Priya with a table of what changed and why. The dashboard is a one-page Excel sheet with slicers that Nandini opens on her own on Tuesday without asking anyone. Three outputs, three readers, three different amounts of your time. A good analyst spends most of it on the one that gets a decision.

The last column is where the numbers meet people. Monday, 9:30, the review runs in Teams. The deck is shared from SharePoint, not attached. Meera decides Kochi gets a festive promotion budget. That decision goes out in an Outlook mail whose first line is the ask and whose subject line says what it is about, and it lands as three tasks in Planner with names and dates on them. By Wednesday somebody has ticked one off, and Nandini can see that without asking.

Then the dashed line. Power Automate makes the loop run without you: each new NPS response gets appended to the Excel Table and posted into the store's Teams channel; every Monday at 8 a flow reads the Table of orders stuck in Processing and mails Nandini a summary. Thirteen orders are in Processing right now. Next week you will not be the one who counts them. And across all of it sits Copilot, which will draft, summarise and suggest in every app on the map, and which has never once checked whether a number is right. That is your job, and Module 14 shows you how to do it in thirty seconds.

Why a manager cares

When a number in the Monday deck looks wrong, "it's an Excel issue" is not a diagnosis. Seeing the chain lets you ask better questions: did the Power Query refresh run? Is the PivotTable pointing at the old range? Is the slide linked to the right workbook, or a copy someone saved to their desktop in June? Three different failures, three different two-minute fixes, and the only way to pick the right one is to know the map.

Who uses what at Novamart

Every one of the 85 employees has the same licence, and nobody uses the same six apps the same way. That matters for you twice: once because you build things for these people and should know what they will open, and once because the depth you need in each app depends on which of these desks you are heading for.

Note

Look at the "Never" column for the people above you. Nobody there will ever open Power Query, and every one of them will read a PivotTable you built. So the test of your work is not whether the query is elegant. It is whether Nandini can flip a slicer on Tuesday without calling you.

What the wiring replaces

The attachment way

Monday: twelve store CSVs arrive by mail. You open each, copy the rows into Master_Aug.xlsx on your desktop, and fix the Kochi file by hand because its columns are in a different order.

Tuesday: you write the SUMs, screenshot two charts into a deck, and mail Review_Aug_v1.pptx to Vikram.

Tuesday, 6 pm: Vikram replies with edits. You make them and send v2. Nandini has already forwarded v1 to the store managers.

Wednesday: Arjun's team spots that returns were included. v3 goes out. Three decks now exist with three totals.

Next month: all of it again, from the first CSV.

The linked way

Monday, 10:02: the CSVs are in the SharePoint folder your Power Query points at. Data ▸ Refresh All. The Table grows by August; the Kochi column order is handled by a step you wrote in April.

10:06: the PivotTable and the SUMIFS cells update. The chart's title still reads "Delivered revenue by region against target" because you wrote it that way.

10:09: the deck is linked to the workbook. Open, refresh links, read every slide once. Post the SharePoint link in the Analytics channel.

10:15: Vikram comments on slide 4 in the same file. You fix it in place. There is one deck, and it is the current one.

Caveat, and it is not a small one: this works only if somebody agreed what "revenue" means and the Status filter is part of that definition. Linked files with a disputed definition produce one deck that everybody argues about instead of three. Module 05 is where the definition gets written down.

The five shapes of work Microsoft 365 answers

Strip away the department and almost every request that reaches an analyst is one of five shapes. Retail, a bank, a hospital chain, a D2C brand: same five. Each of the Excel ones below runs against the Novamart workbook, so press Run and read the result. The other two are worked in their modules, because there is no formula for a good email.

Summarise

How much, how many, by what. The manager's question nine times out of ten. The trick is never the SUM; it is the filter and the window. Module 03 teaches the formula version, Module 05 the PivotTable version, and you will use both in the same afternoon.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2026-08")

₹12,48,348, or ₹12.5 lakh, which is the number Meera was waiting for on Thursday. Drop the Status criterion and you get every cancelled and returned line too, which is how two decks end up disagreeing.

=COUNTIFS(Orders!G:G,"Cancelled")/COUNTA(Orders!A2:A3001)

7.3%, so roughly one order in fourteen. Format that cell as a percentage and it is a KPI tile; put it beside last month's and it is a story.

Look up

What goes with this key. The store's region, the product's cost, the campaign's budget, the employee's manager. Most business data is split across sheets that share an ID, and the lookup is how you stitch them. Module 04 is entirely this shape.

=TEXT(XLOOKUP("Novamart MG Road Kochi",Stores!B:B,Stores!G:G),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

10-Apr-2024, which is why Kochi has no 2024 Q1 in any comparison and why a naive year-on-year growth figure for it is meaningless. A lookup is how you know the caveat before Nandini asks.

Clean

Make the export usable. The CRM dump, the twelve POS files, the ad-platform CSV with a currency symbol in the number column. Cleaning is half of most analyst jobs and almost never appears in the job description. Module 02 gives you the hand tools, Module 06 gives you the machine that does it on refresh.

=COUNTA(Leads!A2:A151)-ROWS(UNIQUE(LOWER(TRIM(Leads!C2:C151))))

21 of the 150 leads are the same person typed twice, once with a trailing space or a capital letter. Priya's "150 new leads" is 129. Nobody lied; the export did.

=UNIQUE(Leads!E2:E151)

Fifteen spellings for about six cities, including Hyd, BLR, Bombay and Bengaluru with a space on the end. A PivotTable on this column is fifteen rows of nonsense until it is cleaned, and Power Query cleans it once.

Communicate

Turn the number into a decision somebody else can make. This is the shape most analysts underrate and most managers judge you on. It lives in Word, PowerPoint and Outlook and Teams, and the rule is the same in all three: the first line is the finding, the rest is the support.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")
    /SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-11")-1

14.4% up. That is not a chart title yet. "November 2025 delivered ₹11.7 lakh, 14% ahead of last Diwali, with the app doing most of the growth" is a chart title, and it is the whole slide. Module 09 spends an hour on writing that sentence.

Automate

Do it without me. Anything you have done three Mondays in a row is a candidate. Module 11 covers capturing and tracking, Module 12 the flows that connect them. The formula that turns 400 survey responses into one score is a good test of whether a routine is ready to be automated: if you can write it once and it is right every week, hand it to a flow.

=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9")/COUNTA(NPS!A2:A401)
    -COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6")/COUNTA(NPS!A2:A401)

0.105, so an NPS of about +10: 164 promoters, 122 detractors, 400 responses. Once the Form feeds the Table through a flow, this cell updates itself every time a customer taps a number, and the Teams post that quotes it goes out at 8 am without you.

Five shapes. Fourteen modules that teach you to do them accurately, on messy data, at speed, in the app the reader will open, and to defend the result when Arjun pushes back.

What Microsoft 365 cannot do

Be clear about the boundary, because a lot of training material is not.

  • Excel is not a database. A sheet holds 1,048,576 rows and slows down long before that. The Sales sheet is 6,314 lines and behaves; the real POS system at a twelve-store chain writes that many lines a week. Excel is where you analyse a cut of the data, not where the data lives. When the cut stops fitting, the answer is a database and a query, which is what the SQL course exists for.
  • A workbook is not a system of record. The ERP owns the invoice. The CRM owns the lead. Your Leads_clean.xlsx is a snapshot that was true at 4 pm on Thursday, and if Priya fixes a phone number in the CRM on Friday your file does not know. Clean in Excel, report from Excel, but fix at the source or the fix evaporates on the next export.
  • Version history is not version control. OneDrive keeps old copies of a file and will restore one. It will not show you which cell changed, who changed a formula, or let two people merge their edits. For a model that many people touch, that means one owner, a change log sheet, and discipline. For code, it means Git, which is a different world.
  • It does not do statistics beyond the basics. An average, a percentile, a correlation, a linear trend, fine. Regression with diagnostics, significance testing, seasonality models, anything with a confidence interval you would defend in front of a statistician: Python, R or a proper package. Pull and shape the data in Excel, model it elsewhere.
  • Copilot does not check anything. It writes a plausible formula, a plausible summary, a plausible deck. Plausible is not the same as right, and in Excel the gap is usually a wrong range or a missing status filter. Every Copilot number gets a SUMIFS beside it before it leaves your desk.
  • Power Automate is not an integration platform. It moves a row, sends a mail, asks for an approval. It will not reconcile two systems with different IDs, process 50,000 records an hour, or recover gracefully when the CSV has an extra column. When a flow grows past twenty steps, something upstream should have been fixed instead.
  • Nothing here decides what matters. A PivotTable will happily summarise gross revenue when the business should be watching contribution after returns, and the ₹8.4 lakh of approved refunds in the Returns sheet will sit there unread. Choosing the metric is a management act. The pivot is the easy part afterwards.
  • An inbox is not a project plan, and a chat is not a decision. If the Kochi promotion budget was agreed in a Teams thread and never became a Planner task with a name and a date, it did not happen. Module 10 and Module 11 are largely about moving things out of the inbox into places where they can be seen and finished.

Watch out

The most expensive mistake in this whole stack is a beautiful workbook answering a question nobody asked. Before you build anything, say the question out loud in one sentence and get the person who asked to nod at it. "August delivered revenue by region against target, Kochi flagged" took Meera ten seconds to confirm and saved you an evening.

Novamart's head office, Gurugram. Nothing exotic happens, and every hour touches a different box on the map.

Notice how little of it is clever. One refresh, one pivot, one lookup, done carefully and checked twice. The hard part is knowing which box you are in and refusing to send a number you have not looked at.

Orientation · Choose your path

Four routes into Microsoft 365, and how to pick yours

Fourteen modules sit on this site. You almost certainly do not need all fourteen, and not in the order an IT trainer would teach them. Pick the route that matches the desk you are walking towards, and this becomes a six-week habit instead of an abandoned tab.

  • You'll choose a route that matches your role rather than the internet's default "Excel full course".
  • You'll know which modules to study, in what order, roughly how many hours each takes, and which ones you can skip without guilt.
  • You'll have a plan for one weekend and a plan for one semester, whichever you actually have.
  • You'll have scored yourself against ten plain statements and know which module to open first.

Why the route matters

Most Microsoft 365 training was written for someone who will administer it. That person needs licensing in week one, SharePoint permissions in week two, and a Power Automate connector reference by week four. A perfectly good curriculum for that job.

Now put a future brand manager on it. She wants to know whether last Diwali's Meta campaign brought back customers, and by week two she is reading about sensitivity labels. She quits. The ribbon was never her problem; two weeks of study had answered none of her questions.

So the four routes below are different routes, not one route at four speeds. They start together, because everyone needs a Table, a SUMIFS, a lookup and a PivotTable, and then they separate. One route skips Power Query entirely. Another spends a third of its time on Word and PowerPoint. A third goes deep on flows and What-If because nobody else in the company will.

Pro habit

Pick a route by the request you most often get at work, in an internship or in a case competition, not by the title you want in five years. You can take a second route later, and the second pass is far faster than the first.

The four routes at a glance

Pick one

Route 1 · about 8 hours

The decision-maker

You will read what others build and sign off on it. Enough Excel to check a number, enough PowerPoint to judge a deck, enough Outlook and Teams to run a week. Meera's and Nandini's route.

 Route 2 · all fourteen

The analyst

The default if you are aiming at a business, marketing, finance or operations analyst role. Every module, in order, with the capstones. Vikram's team's route, and the one the assessment test assumes.

 Route 3 · about 14 hours

The consultant / project person

You will meet a new client's mess every few weeks and leave behind a deck, a document and a plan. Heavy on Power Query, Word, PowerPoint and Planner; light on automation.

 Route 4 · about 14 hours

The founder / operator

You are the analyst, the ops head and the IT department. Dashboards, Forms, flows and What-If, so the business runs on a Sunday without you opening a laptop.

Route 1 · The decision-maker

Who it is for. Managers who live inside workbooks and decks somebody else built. Future brand managers, category heads, store operations leads, anyone on a general-management track, anyone joining the family business. You are not becoming an analyst, only ceasing to be at the mercy of one. Meera reads the scorecard on her phone and asks why Kochi is red; that is the standard.

05 · PivotTablesRefresh a pivot, flip a slicer, change SUM to COUNT, and know what one row of the source means before quoting a total.1.25
07 · Charts and dashboards (skim)Read a chart honestly. Ask for an axis that starts at zero and a title that says what changed.0.75
09 · PowerPointThe storyline and the action title. You will judge decks for the rest of your career; learn what a good one looks like from the inside.1.25
10 · Outlook and TeamsEmail that gets replies, invites with agendas, when a Teams thread beats a mail. This is the module that changes your week fastest.1
14 · Copilot (first half)Recap a meeting, draft a reply, and check the number Copilot gave you with one SUMIFS before repeating it.0.5

What you skip and why. Power Query, Word, Forms and Lists, Power Automate, modelling. All useful, none needed to verify a number, run a meeting or ask a sharper question. Come back to Module 06 the first time you find yourself pasting CSVs together two months running.

How long. About eight hours, so three weeks at three hours, with Modules 09 and 10 sharing week three.

What you can do at the end. Open the scorecard behind a slide and check the headline yourself. Brief an analyst with the grain, the filter and the date window, so the first attempt is right. Notice when two decks in one meeting have defined revenue differently. Send an email that gets a reply the same day.

Capstone and next step. From the capstones page, take 01 · Store Performance Scorecard, because it makes you build the thing you will spend years reading. After that the next skill is not more Excel; it is getting your team to write its metric definitions down and put its files in one library.

Route 2 · The analyst

Who it is for. The default, and the right choice if you are aiming at business analyst, marketing analyst, FP&A, operations analyst, research associate, or any first job with "analyst" in the description. Take this one if you are unsure. It is the route the assessment test in Module 14 assumes you took.

05 · PivotTablesThe manager's summary machine, and the idea of grain, which explains more wrong numbers than anything else here.1.25

Interview preparation. Every module ends with an "On the job" section: an assessment-test callout and three interview questions with model answers. Read each when you finish the module, then again cold a month later, out loud. Do not save them for the week before placements.

How long. About seventeen hours of pages, which with exercises and capstones becomes ten to twelve weeks at three to four hours. The twelve-week plan further down is written for this route.

What you can do at the end. Take a vague request from Nandini, find the grain it needs, refresh the query, build the pivot, put one chart with one sentence on a slide, share it from SharePoint, and defend the number when Arjun asks whether returns are netted. That is the job.

Capstones and next step. Do three from the capstones page with different shapes: 03 · CRM Lead Clean-up, 04 · Management Dashboard and 11 · Workforce Analytics, and put all three somewhere public. After this course, add SQL as a reader, then Power BI as a builder, then enough statistics to know when a gap between two months is noise.

Why a manager cares

Analyst assessment tests rarely reward memorised shortcuts. They hand you a workbook you have never seen and forty-five minutes, and watch what you do first. Candidates who convert the range to a Table and check what one row means before writing a formula finish, and the others run out of time.

Route 3 · The consultant / project person

Who it is for. Consulting, strategy, transformation, corporate development, programme management, anyone who meets a new client's data every few weeks and leaves behind a deck, a document and a plan. Breadth beats depth here, and the deliverable is always something a stranger has to read without you in the room.

ModuleWhy it is on this routeHours
01 to 05 · the foundationsWorkspace, Tables, SUMIFS, XLOOKUP, PivotTables. Non-negotiable; the client's data will arrive as six workbooks and you have to summarise them by Friday.5.75
06 · Power QueryThe most-used module on this route. Every engagement starts with an export that has to be profiled, cleaned and stacked, and the client will send a new one next week.1.5
07 · Charts and dashboards (skim)Chart choice and formatting only. You build charts for slides, not dashboards that live on.0.5
08 · WordStyles, TOC, Track Changes, compare. Client reports and SOPs are Word, and a document with hand-made headings is a document that cannot be reviewed.1
09 · PowerPointThe storyline, the slide master, linked charts. Two thirds of what a client sees of your work is this module.1.25
10 · Outlook and TeamsRunning a steering committee week: invites, agendas, follow-ups that land, and a channel the client actually reads.1
11 · Forms, Lists and PlannerPlanner for the workplan, Forms for the stakeholder survey, Lists for the issue log.1
13 · Excel modellingScenario Manager, Data Tables, Goal Seek and model hygiene. The base, best and worst case is the slide the client remembers.1.5

What you skip and why. Power Automate and the certification half of Module 14. On a six-week engagement you rarely build a flow that outlives you; you need to know whether the client's revenue table double-counts returns. If a project wants a flow, Module 12 is two evenings.

How long. About fourteen hours, so six weeks at two and a half hours.

What you can do at the end. Dropped into a client's SharePoint on Monday, you produce a defensible revenue cut by Wednesday, a ten-slide storyline by Friday, and a one-page Word note listing everything wrong with their data. The note is often what they remember.

Capstones and next step. From the capstones page, take 08 · Festive Season Review deck first, then 10 · Budget vs Actual Variance Model, then 12 · Project Launch Hub. Afterwards, learn enough SQL to read the client's warehouse, and practise turning any pivot into one slide with one message.

Watch out

The fastest way to lose a client's trust is a number from a sheet you never profiled. Before any analysis: row count, date range, blanks in the columns you need, distinct values of every category column. In Power Query that is Column profile, and it takes ten minutes every time.

Route 4 · The founder / operator

Who it is for. Founders, operations leads, anyone running a small business or a unit inside a big one where you are the analyst, the ops head and the IT department at once. A D2C brand with three people, a family distribution business moving off paper, a college incubation project that suddenly has customers. Nobody will build your dashboard for you.

01 to 05 · the foundationsYou will set up the SharePoint library, the naming rule and the first Tables yourself, and everyone who joins later inherits them. Get them right once.5.75
06 · Power QueryThe payment-gateway export, the marketplace settlement file and the courier CSV, stacked and cleaned on refresh. This is where your evenings come back.1.5
07 · Charts and dashboardsThe one page you look at every morning: revenue, orders, cancellations, stock. Dynamic arrays and slicers make it refresh itself.1.5
09 · PowerPoint (skim)The storyline section only. You will pitch, and the SCQA shape works on an investor as well as on a CEO.0.5
10 · Outlook and TeamsChannels instead of WhatsApp groups, a weekly review with an agenda, and Bookings for the customer calls.1

12 · Power AutomateNew order to Excel row to Teams post, an approval for discounts, a Monday-morning summary mail. The work that does itself, so you can sell.1.25
13 · Excel modellingGoal Seek for the price that hits break-even, Scenario Manager for the fundraising deck, Solver for the reorder quantity, PMT for the equipment loan.1.5

What you skip and why. Word beyond a template, and certification. You need a working invoice template, not a styled forty-page SOP, and no investor asks about MOS. When you hire your first ops person, hand them Module 08 and the SOP capstone.

How long. About fourteen hours, six to seven weeks, with Module 12 deserving two of them because your first flow will fail on a blank row and you should learn why.

What you can do at the end. Run the business from one SharePoint site: orders captured by a Form, stock in a Table that a flow updates, a dashboard that is right at 8 am without anyone touching it, and a model that tells you what a 10% discount does to the month. Above all, no Orders_FINAL_v7.xlsx on anybody's laptop.

Capstones and next step. From the capstones page, take 07 · Customer Feedback Pipeline, then 06 · Inventory Reorder Model, then 05 · Campaign ROI Tracker. Next comes a real database when the Table passes a hundred thousand rows, and the unglamorous pair every owner needs: a backup you have tested, and sharing permissions so the intern cannot open the salary sheet.

If you have one weekend

The assessment test is on Monday. You have used Excel for a mark sheet and nothing else. Twelve hours across Saturday and Sunday will not make you an analyst, but they will get you through the four things every test asks for: a SUMIFS with criteria, an XLOOKUP, a PivotTable, and a chart with a sensible title. Do the exercises; skip the "Watch and read" sections entirely.

Pro habit

In the test itself, the first ninety seconds decide most of the marks. Convert the range to a Table, look at ten rows, say out loud what one row is, check whether the dates are dates. Then start typing. Candidates who start with the formula spend the last ten minutes wondering why the total is text.

Three to four hours a week: twenty minutes on five days plus one longer session at the weekend. Written for the Analyst route; the other three cut rows from it rather than reordering them.

Score yourself first

Ten statements. Answer each one honestly with yes or no, and be strict: "yes" means you could do it right now, in a workbook you have never seen, with somebody watching. Each "no" points at a module.

#Can you, right now…If no, open
1Say where a given file lives (OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams), share it as an edit link that expires, and restore last Tuesday's version?Module 01
2Turn a range into a Table with Ctrl+T, explain why the PivotTable wants one, and fix a column of numbers stored as text?Module 02
3Write a SUMIFS for delivered revenue between two dates without looking up the criteria syntax?Module 03
4Write an XLOOKUP that returns "not found" instead of #N/A, and a slab lookup for GST rates that needs a sorted table?Module 04
5Build a PivotTable showing % of column with a slicer, and say what one row of its source represents before quoting the total?Module 05
6Clean a messy export so that next month's file cleans itself when you press Refresh?Module 06
7Make a chart whose title is the finding, whose axis starts at zero, and a conditional-formatting rule that flags stores below target?Module 07
8Build a Word document whose table of contents updates itself, and write a slide title that is a sentence with a verb and a number?Module 08, Module 09
9Write an email whose first line is the ask, send a meeting invite with an agenda, and set up a Form whose responses land in Excel?Module 10, Module 11
10Build a flow that posts to Teams when a Form is submitted, and use Goal Seek to find the discount that hits a target?Module 12, Module 13

Count the noes. Eight or more, take your route from the top and do not skip Module 02 however dull it looks. Four to seven, start at the first no and work forward. Three or fewer, go straight to the mock assessment test in Module 14 and let it tell you which one was a lie. Anyone who said no to 3 or 5 is not ready for an analyst test yet, whatever the other answers say.

How to actually study this

Nobody fails at Excel because the ribbon defeats them. They fail because they watched six hours of video on one Sunday, typed nothing, and never opened the workbook again. A few habits fix that.

Twenty minutes a day beats four hours on Saturday
Daily contact keeps the shortcuts in your hands; a marathon feels productive and has evaporated by Wednesday. With twenty minutes, build one pivot rather than read three pages.
Type the formula, do not copy it
Copying teaches you only that the formula works. Typing drags you past every comma, quote and dollar sign. You will make errors, and the errors are the lesson.
Break every example you read
Change one thing and predict the result before you press Enter. Remove the Status criterion. Swap the pivot's rows and columns. Delete a step in Power Query. Predict, run, compare. Worth more than a second course.
Keep your own workbook of patterns
One file, one sheet per pattern: the date-range SUMIFS, the XLOOKUP with a fallback, the UNIQUE plus SUMIFS summary, the NPS formula. Every working analyst has one. The cheat sheet seeds yours.
Redo last week's exercises cold
Each Monday, before the new module, solve two of last week's exercises in a blank workbook with the solutions closed. It feels like backtracking. It is what makes any of this survive past the exam.
Practising with no company data
The Formula Lab runs the whole Novamart workbook in your browser, so invent questions: which city has the worst return rate, which campaign months went flat, how many employees each manager has. When you want a second dataset, export anything you own, your own bank statement, a college fee sheet, and treat it the same way.

One more, which sounds soft and is not. Explain a pivot out loud to somebody who has never opened one. If you cannot say in plain words what one row of the summary represents, Nandini will find the hole before you do.

Start

With a route chosen, start at Module 01, whichever route it is, because forty-five minutes on where files live saves a semester of FINAL_v2. If you skipped the orientation, the map page shows where all of this sits inside a company. And if you want to see whether the Lab is real before committing, open the Formula Lab and type =COUNTIFS(Orders!G:G,"Cancelled"). It says 219. Now you know something about Novamart that Meera had to ask for.

Level 1 · Module 01 · about 45 min

The M365 workspace: OneDrive, SharePoint, sharing and versions

Before you build a single PivotTable you have to know where the file lives, who can open it, and how to get last Tuesday's version back when someone pastes over the wrong column. Most "the numbers changed" arguments at Novamart are not Excel problems. They are two people editing two copies of the same workbook. This module fixes that on day one.

  • You'll explain what Microsoft 365 is made of (apps, cloud storage, one identity) and why a work account behaves differently from a personal one.
  • You'll decide, for any file, whether it belongs in OneDrive, a SharePoint library or a Teams channel, and say who can see it there.
  • You'll share a file with the right link type (people in Novamart, specific people, anyone), the right permission (view or edit) and an expiry when it matters.
  • You'll use AutoSave and version history to recover an earlier version of a workbook in under a minute.
  • You'll name and file documents so that 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v03.xlsx is the only kind of name in the library, and Final_FINAL2.xlsx never appears.
  • You'll set up a SharePoint document library for a monthly review, with folders, naming and a sharing rule that a new joiner can follow without asking.

Concept

Monday, 9:10 am, your first day

Vikram Shah sends you a Teams message: "Welcome. The store scorecard for August is in the Analytics site, folder 02_Monthly-Review. Nandini says the Kochi number is wrong on the version she got by email on Friday. Find out which version is right and share the correct one with her by 11." You have a laptop, a work account, and no idea where "the Analytics site" is.

Microsoft 365 is three things bolted together. The apps you know (Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams). A cloud where files live (OneDrive for your files, SharePoint for the team's). And one identity, you@novamart.in, that signs you into all of it and decides what you may open. Take away the cloud and the identity and you're back to 2009: files on a laptop, attachments in email, six copies of the truth.

The identity part matters more than it looks. A personal Microsoft account (@outlook.com, the one you made for Xbox) and a work account (issued by Novamart's IT) look the same at the sign-in box and are completely different underneath. The work account belongs to the company. IT can reset it, wipe a lost laptop, and see what was shared with whom. It carries multi-factor authentication (MFA), which is why the Authenticator app on your phone buzzes every time you sign in from a new device. That buzz is not a nuisance to switch off. It is the thing that stops a stolen password from opening the salary sheet.

Files have three possible homes, and the home decides who can see the file without anyone doing anything.

Read the diagram left to right and you have the whole habit. Start a draft in OneDrive if you like. The moment a second person needs it, move it to the team library, because a file in OneDrive is a file in your desk drawer, and when you go on leave the drawer goes with you. Vikram's scorecard is in the Analytics site's library. Nandini's email attachment is a photocopy of a version from Friday, and that is the real cause of the "wrong Kochi number".

Why a manager cares

Nandini runs 12 stores and gets forty attachments a week. When two of them are "the August scorecard" with different totals, she stops trusting both, and the analyst who sent them. One file, one place, one link is a reputation issue before it is a tidiness issue. It is also a security one: the Employees sheet has 85 salaries in it, and a share link to "anyone" is a leak waiting for a forwarded email.

How it works

Three homes, one rule each

HomeWho owns itDefault visibilityPut hereDon't put here
OneDriveYouOnly youdrafts, scratch analysis, personal notes, a copy you are experimenting onthe team's only copy of anything
SharePoint site libraryThe site (a team or department)Everyone with access to the sitethe working copy of reports, models, SOPs, templatesprivate HR notes, unless the library is locked down
Teams channel ▸ FilesThe team (it is a SharePoint library)All channel membersfiles people are actively discussing in that channelanything that needs a folder structure deeper than two levels
Teams chat attachmentYour OneDrive (a share link is created)The people in the chata quick file for one personanything the team will need to find next month

The last row surprises people. When you drop a file into a one-to-one chat, Teams puts it in a folder called Microsoft Teams Chat Files in your OneDrive and shares it with the other person. It is still your file. Leave the company and the link dies.

AutoSave and version history

A file in OneDrive or SharePoint saves itself every few seconds. The toggle at the top-left of Excel says AutoSave On. There is no Ctrl+S to forget any more, and also no "don't save" escape hatch when you've broken something. Version history is the escape hatch. Every save is kept as a version, with who and when, for as long as the file exists (SharePoint keeps 500 major versions by default).

  1. File ▸ Info ▸ Version History. A pane opens on the right listing every version, newest first, with the editor's name and a timestamp. In the browser it is the file's three-dot menu ▸ Version history.
  2. Click a version. Excel opens it read-only in a second window with a yellow bar. Nothing has changed yet. Look at the Kochi cell.
  3. Restore on the yellow bar makes that version the current one. The version you replaced is kept too, as a new entry, so restoring is never destructive.
  4. Or copy what you need from the old window into the current file and close it. Use this when only one range went wrong.

Pro habit

Before a big edit on a shared workbook (pasting a new month of data, changing a formula in a column), open File ▸ Info ▸ Version History and note the time. If the edit goes wrong you already know which version to go back to. Thirty seconds, and it has saved more analysts than any backup.

Sharing links: the three questions

Click Share at the top-right of any Office app, or right-click the file ▸ Share in OneDrive or SharePoint. Before you press Send, answer three questions. Who. What they may do. For how long.

Link typeWho can open itUse it forRisk
People in Novamart with the linkAnyone signed in with a Novamart account who has the linkinternal working files; the default for most team sharingthe link can be forwarded internally, so not for salary or personal data
People with existing accessWhoever already has permission; the link grants nothing newpointing a colleague to a file in a library they are already innone; if they can't open it, they weren't meant to
Specific peopleOnly the names you type, inside or outside Novamartconfidential files; anything going to a vendor, auditor or the CAthe least; forwarded links don't work for others
Anyone with the linkAnyone at all, no sign-inpublic material like a brochure PDF, if IT allows it at allthe most; most companies switch it off

Under the link type sit two switches. Can view versus Can edit, and for the "specific people" and "anyone" links, an expiry date and an optional password. A view link to Nandini is enough for a scorecard she reads. An edit link to Rohan is right for a buying plan he fills in. An external link to the auditors should expire the day after they need it.

"Copy link" versus "Attach"

Outlook and Teams both offer two ways to send a file. Attach a copy takes a snapshot of the file right now and mails it. The recipient edits their snapshot; you edit the original; by Friday there are two Augusts. Share a link (Outlook calls it "Share link", Teams shows a cloud icon next to the file) points at the one file in its home. Everyone opens the same thing and sees each other's edits. The only good reasons to attach are a recipient outside Novamart with no account, or a frozen record you want to keep as sent (the signed GST invoice, the final board pack). Everything else is a link.

Co-authoring

With the file in OneDrive or SharePoint and AutoSave on, several people can edit at once. You see coloured cell borders with initials in Excel, coloured cursors in Word, and a small avatar list at the top-right. Changes appear in a second or two. Co-authoring works in the browser and in the desktop apps, with three limits worth knowing. A workbook with a password, a legacy .xls, or a sheet someone has "protected" will kick everyone into read-only. Some features (Data Validation edits, macros, Power Query refresh) are desktop-only and can block others while you use them. And two people typing in the same cell get the last save, not a merge, so agree who owns which sheet.

Web versus desktop

TaskExcel for the webExcel desktop
Open, read, filter, comment, small editsfine, and faster to open from a linkfine
PivotTables, most formulas, charts, conditional formattingworks, with a smaller ribbonfull
Power Query, Power Pivot, Solver, macros, Camera toolnot available (Power Query is view-only)desktop only
Files over ~100 MB, workbooks with 50+ sheetsslow or refuses to openfine
Co-authoringbest; always sees the latestworks with AutoSave on

The practical habit: open from the link, and if you find yourself reaching for a feature the web ribbon doesn't have, click Editing ▸ Open in Desktop App. Same file, same AutoSave, no download.

Office.com and Search

Go to office.com (or microsoft365.com, same place) and sign in with the work account. That page is the launcher: every app on the left, your recent files in the middle, and files shared with you in a tab. When a colleague says "I shared it with you" and you can't see the email, the Shared tab on that page finds it. The search box at the top searches file names and contents across OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams and Outlook at once. Typing Kochi scorecard finds the workbook even if the file name says neither.

In Teams, the same search box takes /files to jump to your recent files, and in Outlook the search understands from:nandini hasattachments:yes. Module 10 goes deeper into search operators. For now, the rule is that you never scroll through folders looking for a file when a three-word search would find it.

File naming: the Novamart convention

A file name has to answer three questions when it shows up in a search result, an email, or a folder listing sorted by name: which period, what it is, which version. Dates go first so files sort in time order. Words are joined with hyphens, sections with underscores, and the version has two digits so v10 sorts after v09.

PartFormatExampleWhy
PeriodYYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD2026-08sorts chronologically; unambiguous, unlike 08-26
WhatWords-With-HyphensStore-Scorecardreadable in a URL; no spaces turning into %20
VersionvNNv03two digits sort correctly; bump on every shared change
Status (optional)DRAFT or FINAL2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v03_FINAL.xlsxonly one file per period may be FINAL; never FINAL2
Whole namePeriod_What_vNN.ext2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v03.xlsxevery question answered before the file is opened

Excel can build the prefix for you, which is handy when a report is generated every month from the same workbook. The as-of date in the Lab is 31 Aug 2026.

=TEXT(MAX(Sales!B:B),"yyyy-mm")&"_Store-Scorecard_v01.xlsx"

It returns 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v01.xlsx, which is exactly what the August file should be called. Paste it into the Save As box.

=TEXT(TODAY(),"yyyy-mm-dd")&"_Analytics-Weekly-Notes.docx"

2026-08-31_Analytics-Weekly-Notes.docx. Meeting notes get the full date because there is one per week; monthly packs get the month.

Folder discipline

Two levels of folders, numbered so they sort in the order people use them, and never more than about a dozen files in a folder before you ask whether it needs splitting. The Analytics library at Novamart looks like this.

FolderWhat goes inRule
01_Data-Exports/raw POS and CRM exports, one subfolder per monthnever edited; copy out, never type in
02_Monthly-Review/the scorecard, the pack, the notes, one subfolder per monthone FINAL per month
03_Models/budget model, reorder modelversioned; FINAL copies pinned at the top
04_Templates/blank scorecard, slide master, SOP templateopen, Save As elsewhere, never edit the template by accident
05_Reference/store list, product master, holiday calendarno period in the name; one owner per file
99_Archive/anything older than two yearsmove, don't delete; search still finds it

Raw exports in 01_ are read-only by convention: you copy a file out of it, you never type into it. That single rule is what makes "where did this number come from?" answerable six months later.

The vocabulary IT will use at you

Tenant
Novamart's whole Microsoft 365 account: every user, site and mailbox under novamart.in. "It's a tenant setting" means IT decides, not you.
Site
A SharePoint workspace for a team or a purpose (the Analytics site, the HR site). Every Team in Teams has a site behind it.
Document library
A folder-like container inside a site, with version history and permissions. "Documents" is the default one; a site can have several.
Sync
The OneDrive client on your laptop keeping a local copy of a library or folder in File Explorer. Handy offline; the source of every "-Laptop-01" duplicate.
Recycle Bin
Deleted files sit in the site's Recycle Bin for 93 days and can be restored by anyone with access. Deleting is rarely final; overwriting without version history is.
Manage access
The panel on any file or folder that lists every link and every person who can open it, and lets you remove them.

The habit, before and after

Before

  • Scorecard saved on the laptop's Desktop, emailed to three people on Friday.
  • Rohan edits his copy; Nandini annotates hers; Arjun forwards his to the CA.
  • Monday: three Augusts, one argument, no way to tell who changed Kochi.
  • File names: scorecard aug.xlsx, Scorecard_Aug_final_FINAL2.xlsx.

After

  • One file in 02_Monthly-Review/2026-08/, AutoSave on.
  • One view link in the channel post; Arjun's CA gets a specific-people link that expires.
  • Monday: one August; version history shows who changed what, and restore takes a minute.
  • File name: 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v04_FINAL.xlsx, and everyone can guess September's.

Application: the Analytics team's review library

Monday, 9:40 am

Vikram adds: "While you're at it, the site is a mess. Set the monthly-review folder up properly so that Nandini, Arjun and Priya get one link each month and stop asking for attachments." Here is how you do it, from an empty library to the first shared link, in about twenty minutes.

Build the library

  1. Teams ▸ Strategy & Analytics team ▸ General channel ▸ Files tab ▸ Open in SharePoint. The Files tab opens as a normal SharePoint document library in the browser, with the full ribbon. Everything you do here shows up in Teams too, because it is the same folder.
  2. + New ▸ Folder, six times, with the numbered names from the structure above. Numbers first so the folders sort in working order rather than alphabetically.
  3. Inside 02_Monthly-Review, + New ▸ Folder for 2026-08. One subfolder per month means the library will still be usable in 2028.
  4. Upload ▸ Files the current scorecard into 2026-08 and rename it in place (three dots ▸ Rename) to 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v03.xlsx. Renaming in SharePoint keeps the version history; downloading, renaming and re-uploading throws it away.
  5. Three dots on the file ▸ Details. The details pane shows who last modified it and when. Compare with the timestamp on the email Nandini received on Friday. If the library copy is newer, the email is the stale one.
  6. Library ▸ Settings (gear) ▸ Library settings ▸ Versioning settings. Confirm major versions are on. Leave "require check out" off; check-out blocks co-authoring and the team will hate it.
  7. Pin the library in Teams: Files tab ▸ + Add cloud storage is not it. Instead, in the channel, click + on the tab strip ▸ SharePoint ▸ Document library ▸ pick it. Now the review folder is a tab the whole team sees.

Version history rescue: the Kochi number

You open 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v03.xlsx from the library. The Kochi revenue cell says ₹4,12,000. The email copy from Friday says ₹9,86,000. Which is right, and who changed it? Version history answers in four clicks.

  1. File ▸ Info ▸ Version History. The pane lists eleven versions since Thursday. Three are by Rohan on Friday evening, after the email went out.
  2. Click the version from Friday 3:15 pm (the one just before Rohan's edits). It opens in a second window with the yellow bar. Kochi says ₹9,86,000. So Rohan's later edits changed it.
  3. Click Rohan's first edit. Kochi says ₹4,12,000, and the Products sheet has a new column. He pasted a filtered product list over the store totals and didn't notice the store column shift. Not malice, a Friday 6 pm paste.
  4. Restore the 3:15 pm version. Excel keeps Rohan's version as a newer entry in the list, so nothing he added is lost. Message him: "Restored the scorecard to Friday 3:15; your product list is in version 12 if you need it."
  5. Bump the file name to v04 (three dots ▸ Rename) so that anyone who saved a link to v03 still gets the corrected file, since links follow the file through a rename in SharePoint, and the name tells the story.

The whole rescue takes two minutes. Without version history it is a Monday spent reconciling two spreadsheets and a difficult conversation with Rohan about a mistake you can't prove.

Share it right

  1. Select the file ▸ Share. The share box opens with the default link type shown under the names field. At Novamart it is "People in Novamart with the link, can edit".
  2. Click the link settings ▸ People in Novamart with the link ▸ untick Allow editing ▸ Apply. Nandini, Arjun and Priya read the scorecard; they don't type into it. View-only stops a stray keystroke in a leadership meeting from becoming a version to rescue.
  3. Copy link. Paste it into the Teams channel post that announces the pack. One post, one link, three readers. Next month, same folder, same post, new link.
  4. For Arjun's CA firm, a separate share: Specific people ▸ their email ▸ Can view ▸ Set expiration date ▸ 30 September. The auditors get exactly one file for exactly one month.

Check the workbook you just shared

A share is only as good as the file behind it. Two quick checks in the Lab tell you the scorecard's data source is what it claims to be.

=COUNTA(Stores!B:B)-1

13, twelve physical stores plus Novamart.in. If the scorecard shows eleven rows, someone has filtered the wrong store out.

=TEXT(XLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:C,Stores!G:G),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

10-Apr-2024, which is why Kochi has no like-for-like comparison before that month, and why its "growth" looks absurd in any chart that starts in January 2024. Module 04 explains the XLOOKUP; here it is just a check.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askWhere it lives · how it is shared
Finance (Arjun)"The budget model, and the auditors need last year's."Finance site ▸ 03_Models; auditors get a specific-people, view-only link with a 30-day expiry
Store ops (Nandini)"Every store manager fills in the weekly audit."one workbook in the Operations library, edit link to the 12 store managers, one sheet per store; co-authoring handles Tuesday morning
Marketing (Priya)"The lead export from the CRM, every Monday."01_Data-Exports/2026-08/, never edited; the cleaned version is a separate file in 02_
HR (Kavita)"Salary revisions for the appraisal cycle."HR private site; specific people only; never a Teams chat attachment, never "people in Novamart"
Merchandising (Rohan)"The Diwali buying plan, all three buyers on it at once."Merch library, edit link to the team; agree one buyer per category sheet to avoid overwrites
Digital (Sameer)"App download numbers for the board, as a PDF."export the chart page to PDF, that is a frozen record, and attach it; keep the workbook linked
You (Analytics)"Try a new layout for the scorecard."OneDrive, as 2026-09_Store-Scorecard_v01_DRAFT.xlsx; move to the library when Vikram says yes

Kavita's row is the one to memorise. Personal data (salaries, phone numbers, the Leads sheet with 150 emails) never gets an organisation-wide link. If in doubt, share to a named person and set the link to view. The Customers sheet has 500 names with phone numbers and birth years; that is enough to be a privacy incident if it ends up in a public link.

Sameer's row is the one exception to "never attach". A board pack is a record of what was said at a moment in time. Exporting it to PDF and attaching that is correct, because you want the version to freeze. The live workbook stays linked for anyone who wants to dig.

Practice

These are tasks, not formulas. Do them in your own tenant if you have one (a university M365 account works), or write out the click-path and the decision. The solution says what good looks like.

Exercise 1 · Where does it live?

For each file, name the home (OneDrive, SharePoint library, Teams channel Files, or "don't store it there") and give one reason. (a) Your half-finished attempt at a new NPS chart. (b) The store list every report looks up. (c) The August lead export from the CRM. (d) Kavita's salary revision sheet. (e) The agenda for Thursday's channel discussion about Kochi.

Hint

Ask "who needs it next, and will they still need it after I leave?"

What good looks like
  • (a) OneDrive. It is a draft nobody else needs yet. Move it when Vikram wants to see it.
  • (b) Analytics library, 05_Reference. Every report links to it, so it needs one permanent home that outlives you.
  • (c) Analytics library, 01_Data-Exports/2026-08/, read-only by convention. Raw exports are evidence.
  • (d) HR's own site with restricted permissions, shared to specific people only. Not the Analytics library, not Teams, not OneDrive.
  • (e) The Strategy & Analytics channel's Files tab. It belongs with the conversation.

Exercise 2 · Pick the link

Priya asks you to share the cleaned Leads workbook with her, her two CRM executives, and a freelance email designer who works from a Gmail address. What link type, what permission, what expiry, and is there anything you should change in the file first?

Hint

The Leads sheet has 150 names, emails and phone numbers. Who outside Novamart needs those?

What good looks like

Two shares, not one. The internal three get a "specific people" link (not "people in Novamart", because it is personal data), can edit if they are going to work in it, no expiry. The freelancer almost certainly does not need 150 phone numbers to design an email; make a copy with the contact columns removed, share that as specific people, view only, with a 14-day expiry. If Priya insists the freelancer needs the full file, ask why, then set an expiry and view-only anyway.

Exercise 3 · Rename the pile

A folder contains these files. Rename them into the Novamart convention and say which one you would archive or delete: scorecard aug.xlsx, Scorecard_Aug_final.xlsx, Scorecard_Aug_final_FINAL2.xlsx, Copy of Scorecard_Aug_final.xlsx, store list.xlsx, notes 28 aug.docx.

Hint

Open each one and check the modified date in Details before you decide which is the real latest.

What good looks like
  • 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v01.xlsx, _v02.xlsx, _v03_FINAL.xlsx for the three scorecards, in modified-date order after checking their contents. The "Copy of" file is either identical to one of them (delete) or a fork (rename to _v04_DRAFT and ask whose it is).
  • Store-List.xlsx in 05_Reference. No period, because it is a master list, not a monthly file.
  • 2026-08-28_Monthly-Review-Notes.docx. Full date, because notes are per meeting.
  • Only one file may carry FINAL. If a later change is needed, it becomes v04_FINAL and v03 loses the suffix.

Exercise 4 · The rescue

At 10:05 on Tuesday a store manager reports that the weekly audit workbook now shows every store's stock as zero. It was fine at 9:30. Write the click-path to find out what happened and put it right without losing any audit entries typed after 9:30.

Hint

Restoring keeps the newer version in the list. Compare before you restore.

What good looks like
  1. File ▸ Info ▸ Version History; find the versions between 9:30 and 10:05 and note who saved each.
  2. Open the 9:30 version read-only. Stock is fine. Open the first version where stock is zero; the editor's name is your answer (probably a fill-down or a paste over the column).
  3. Don't restore yet. Open the current version alongside and copy any audit rows typed after the breaking version into a scratch sheet.
  4. Restore the last good version, paste the rescued rows back in, save.
  5. Message the editor without blame, and add a note to the audit sheet's header row about which column is calculated.

Exercise 5 · Stop the attachment

Nandini replies to your link: "Can you just attach it? Links never open on my phone." Write the two-line reply that keeps the file linked and solves her real problem.

Hint

Her real problem is sign-in on the phone, not the link.

What good looks like

"The link opens in the Teams or Excel app on your phone once you're signed in with your Novamart account; I've pinged IT to check your phone is set up. Sending a copy would mean two Augusts again, which is how Friday's Kochi mix-up happened." Then follow up with IT so it actually gets fixed. The attachment is the easy yes that creates next month's problem.

Exercise 6 · The first-week search

You need the deck from the last festive-season review, presented in November 2025, and nobody remembers the file name. List three searches, in order, that would find it, and where you would run each.

Hint

Search contents, not just names. Filter by type and date.

What good looks like
  • office.com search: festive review, filter Type to PowerPoint, sort by modified date, look for November 2025.
  • Teams search: festive in the Strategy & Analytics team, Files tab of results, which finds anything posted in a channel.
  • SharePoint Analytics site search: Diwali OR festive filetype:pptx, then browse 02_Monthly-Review/2025-11/ if the convention was followed.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

"Anyone with the link" plus "Can edit" on a workbook with the Customers sheet in it is the single worst thing you can do in your first month. The link works for whoever the email is forwarded to, forever, with no sign-in and no record of who opened it. Most tenants block the option. If yours doesn't, act as if it did.

Watch out

Sync conflicts. If you use the OneDrive sync client on your laptop and edit a synced file while offline, the desktop copy and the cloud copy can diverge; OneDrive then creates Scorecard-Laptop-01.xlsx next to the original. When you see a file with your machine's name in it, don't delete either: open both, decide, merge, then delete the extra.

  • One file, one home, one link. If you are about to press Attach, ask what the recipient will do with the file. Read it: link. Keep it as a record: PDF, then attach. Edit it: link with edit.
  • Move, don't copy. Copying a file from OneDrive to the library leaves the OneDrive one behind, and someone will edit it. Use Move to in the file's menu. Version history travels with it.
  • Rename in place. Download, rename, upload loses version history and creates a second file. The three-dot menu has Rename.
  • Bump the version when you share, not when you save. AutoSave makes hundreds of saves. The vNN in the name changes when someone else has seen the file and the content moved on.
  • Raw exports are read-only. Nobody types into 01_Data-Exports. Copy out, clean, save in 02_. Six months later, you can prove what the CRM said.
  • FINAL means final. There is no FINAL2, no FINAL-revised, no FINAL (1). If the final changes, the version number goes up and the old file loses the word.
  • Check who has access before you share the folder. Sharing a folder shares every file in it, now and later. Sharing the file is usually what you meant.
  • Stop sharing when the reason ends. The file's Manage access panel lists every link and person. The auditors leave in September; their link should too.

Pro habit

Once a week, open Manage access on the three or four files you share most and read the list. It takes a minute. You will find a link to an intern who left in June, and you will remove it before anyone asks why it was there.

On the job

Nobody tests OneDrive in an assessment. Everybody notices in the first week when a new analyst emails attachments, and everybody notices in the first month when the new analyst is the one who found Friday's version in thirty seconds. This module is the difference between "who is that?" and "ask the new person, they know where everything is."

First 90 days

Onboarding week at any company that runs on M365 looks the same. Day 1: account, MFA, laptop, OneDrive sync. Day 2: added to the team's sites and channels, and you cannot find anything. Day 3: you find the library, read the folder names, and work out which files are live. By Friday you should be able to answer "where is the latest X?" for your team's five most-used files without asking. Do that and you have earned the right to be given real work in week two.

In the assessment test

Some analyst assessments are delivered as a shared workbook in the company's tenant with a one-hour edit link. The first thing they see is whether you opened the link or asked for an attachment. The second is whether you saved a copy to your own OneDrive and worked on that (wrong: they can't see it) or worked in the shared file (right: they can watch you build it and version history shows your method).

Interview question: "What's the difference between OneDrive and SharePoint?"
OneDrive is personal cloud storage tied to one account; files there are private unless shared, and they go when the account goes. SharePoint is team storage organised into sites and document libraries; files belong to the site, everyone with site access can see them, and they stay when people leave. Teams channel files are SharePoint underneath. The rule I use is draft in OneDrive, move to SharePoint the moment someone else needs it.
Interview question: "A colleague overwrote a shared workbook. What do you do?"
Open version history from File ▸ Info, find the last good version by timestamp and editor, open it read-only to confirm, then restore it. Restoring keeps the overwritten version in the list, so nothing is lost. Then I'd copy across anything useful from the newer version and let the colleague know without making it a blame conversation.
Interview question: "How would you share a confidential file with an external auditor?"
A "specific people" link to their named email, view-only unless they must edit, with an expiry date set to the end of the engagement, and I'd check the file doesn't contain columns they don't need, such as phone numbers or salaries. Never an "anyone" link, never an attachment of the live workbook, and I'd remove the access from Manage access once the audit closes.

Quick check

1. You upload the August scorecard to the General channel's Files tab in Teams. Who can open it, with no further sharing?

A channel's Files tab is a folder in the team's SharePoint site, so team members already have access. Nobody outside the team does.

2. Arjun's external CA firm needs the budget model for the audit. Which link?

Option a doesn't work for outsiders; b works for anyone who receives a forward. Specific people, view, expiry is the pattern for anything leaving the company.

3. You restore a version from Friday 3:15 pm. What happens to the version that was current a moment ago?

Restore is never destructive. The replaced version is kept, so you can go back to it if the restore was wrong.

4. Which file name follows the Novamart convention?

Period first so files sort by time, hyphens inside a part, underscores between parts, two-digit version, FINAL only once.
