Level 1 · Module 02 · about 60 min

Excel foundations: cells, Tables and clean data

Every formula you will ever write sits on top of a grid, and the grid has rules. A number that is secretly text adds up to zero. A merged cell breaks a sort. A blank row ends a Table. This module is about making the sheet trustworthy before you ask it a single question, and about moving around 6,314 rows without touching the mouse.

  • You'll tell a number from a text-that-looks-like-a-number in one glance, and fix a column of them in one move.
  • You'll format money the Indian way (₹2,71,69,185), percentages and dates, and know that a date is a number wearing a costume.
  • You'll turn any range into an Excel Table with Ctrl+T and explain, in one sentence each, four reasons an analyst never works without one.
  • You'll recognise untidy data (merged headers, subtotals in the middle, two facts in one cell) and describe the tidy version.
  • You'll count rows, blanks and problems in a sheet with COUNTA, ROWS, COUNTBLANK and COUNTIF before you trust a single total.
  • You'll use twelve keyboard shortcuts without thinking, which is the visible difference between a beginner and an analyst in a test.

Concept

Tuesday, 2:15 pm

Priya Nair forwards the CRM export: "150 leads from the August campaigns. How many can we actually email, and why does my count change every time I sort?" You open Leads. Names in capitals, names with two spaces, emails without an @, cities spelt four ways, dates typed as text in three formats. The count changes because the sheet isn't a table yet. It is a pile.

A worksheet is a grid of cells. Each cell has an address (C7: column C, row 7), holds one value, and that value has a type: a number, a piece of text, a date (which is a number), a TRUE/FALSE, or an error. Excel decides the type when you type, and it decides quietly. Type 1299 and you get a number. Paste 1299 from a web page with an invisible space after it and you get text. The two look identical until you add them up.

The grid doesn't care what you put where. That freedom is why Excel works for a mark sheet, a budget and a wedding guest list, and it is also why a sheet built for reading (a title across the top, a blank row, subtotals every ten rows) is useless for analysis. Analysis needs the other shape, the one a database would use: one header row, one record per row, one fact per cell, nothing else on the sheet. People call it tidy data. Excel calls it a Table, and gives you a button for it.

Why a manager cares

Priya's "how many can we email" is a thirty-second question on a tidy sheet and a two-hour one on a messy sheet, and the two-hour answer is usually wrong. Every downstream tool in this course (SUMIFS in Module 03, PivotTables in Module 05, Power Query in Module 06) assumes the tidy shape. An analyst who can't get data into that shape is an analyst who is stuck before the analysis starts. A manager who can recognise the messy shape stops asking for numbers the sheet can't give.

How it works

Addresses and the Name Box

The white box to the left of the formula bar is the Name Box. It shows the address of the selected cell, and it accepts addresses: type P6315 and press Enter and you are there. Type Sales!P2:P6315 and that whole range is selected. Type P:P and the whole column is. Those three spellings are the three kinds of reference you will use all course: a cell, a bounded range, a whole column. Whole columns (Sales!P:P) are the habit for teaching formulas because they keep working when rows are added; bounded ranges are for when you mean exactly those rows.

Number or text? The green triangle

Excel right-aligns numbers and left-aligns text by default, and puts a small green triangle in the top-left corner of a cell holding a number stored as text. That triangle is the most useful warning in the program. A column of them means every SUM over it is wrong.

You can test a value's type in the Lab. Quotation marks make Excel treat something as text, which is what a CSV import does to a whole column.

=ISTEXT("1299")

TRUE. It looks like a number and it isn't one.

=VALUE("1,299")

1299, a real number, comma removed. VALUE also handles " 1299 " with spaces. It does not handle "₹1,299"; for that, SUBSTITUTE the symbol out first, which Module 03 covers.

Note

Excel is lenient in arithmetic: ="1299"+1 returns 1300 because the + forces a conversion. SUM is not lenient; it skips text. That is why a column of text-numbers gives a plausible-looking SUM that is just too small, which is worse than an error.

Number formats: the same value, dressed differently

Ctrl+1 opens Format Cells. A format changes how a value is displayed and nothing else; the cell still holds 27169184.8 however many commas you add. The Indian grouping (lakh, crore) needs a custom format because Excel's default is the Western thousands grouping.

You wantFormat code27169184.8 shows asWhere
Indian rupees, no decimals₹#,##,##0₹2,71,69,185Custom
Indian grouping, two decimals#,##,##0.002,71,69,184.80Custom
In lakhno format code does this cleanlyhelper cell =value/100000 formatted 0.0" L" shows 271.7 La helper column, so the raw value survives
Percentage, one decimal0.0%0.0731 shows 7.3%Number ▸ Percentage
Date, unambiguousdd-mmm-yyyy46265 shows 31-Aug-2026Custom
Date, Indian shortdd/mm/yyyy31/08/2026Custom
Month bucketyyyy-mm2026-08Custom; sorts correctly as text too
Negative in brackets, red#,##,##0;[Red](#,##,##0)(4,12,000)Custom; finance packs

The last number in the date row is the whole secret of dates. 31 Aug 2026 is serial number 46,265: days since 1 Jan 1900. That is why you can subtract two dates and get days, and why a date typed as text ("31/08/2026") can't be subtracted at all. TEXT() applies a format inside a formula, which the Lab uses to show dates readably.

=MAX(Sales!B:B)

46265. Unformatted, that is the last order date. Wrap it:

=TEXT(MAX(Sales!B:B),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

31-Aug-2026, the dataset's as-of date. In a real sheet you'd leave the cell as a number and set the format with Ctrl+1; TEXT is for when the result has to be a string, like a chart title or a file name.

Fill handle and Flash Fill

  1. Select the cell with the formula ▸ double-click the small square at its bottom-right corner. The formula fills down to the bottom of the adjacent data. Dragging works too, but double-click is the analyst's move on 6,314 rows.
  2. Type the first result you want in the column next to the data ▸ Data ▸ Data Tools ▸ Flash Fill (or Ctrl+E). Type Mohit Rao next to MOHIT RAO, press Ctrl+E, and Excel fills the column with its guess at the pattern. It is a guess: check ten rows before you trust it. Flash Fill pastes values, not formulas, so it won't update when the source changes; for anything repeated monthly, use a formula or Power Query instead.

Sort and filter

  1. Click one cell inside the data ▸ Data ▸ Sort & Filter ▸ Sort. One cell, not a column. Excel extends the selection to the whole block and keeps rows together. Selecting a single column and sorting it is how a lead's email ends up next to somebody else's name; Excel warns you, and the warning is right.
  2. Add Level for a second key: Region, then LineRevenue largest to smallest. Tick My data has headers, which is why one header row and no title row matter.
  3. Data ▸ Sort & Filter ▸ Filter (or Ctrl+Shift+L) puts a dropdown on every header. Filters hide rows; they never delete them. The status bar at the bottom says "27 of 150 records found", which is a count you can quote.
  4. Clear the filter before sharing. A filtered sheet with a SUM at the bottom shows the unfiltered total, and the next reader will believe the visible rows add up to it. SUBTOTAL(109, …) respects filters; plain SUM doesn't.

Freeze panes

  1. Click the cell below and to the right of what you want frozen ▸ View ▸ Window ▸ Freeze Panes ▸ Freeze Panes. Click B2 to freeze the header row and the ID column. On Sales, freeze C2 to keep OrderID and OrderDate visible while you scroll to Payment in column R.
  2. Freeze Top Row is the one-click version when only the header matters. Unfreeze Panes appears in the same menu once something is frozen.

Excel Tables: Ctrl+T and why it matters

Click a cell in the data and press Ctrl+T. Tick "My table has headers". That is all. What you get is not formatting; it is a named object Excel understands as a set of records, and four things change.

What a Table gives youWhat it means on Monday
A name (Table Design ▸ Properties ▸ Table Name: call it tblSales)formulas, PivotTables and Power Query refer to tblSales, not Sales!A1:R6315
Auto-expandpaste September's rows under August and every formula, pivot and chart that uses the Table includes them, with no range edits
Structured references[@Qty]*[@UnitPrice] reads like English and fills the whole column the moment you press Enter
Total Row (Table Design ▸ Total Row)a dropdown per column with Sum, Count, Average that respects filters, because it uses SUBTOTAL
Banded rows, filter buttons, headers that replace the column letters when you scrollreadable at 6,314 rows without freezing anything

Structured references are the part that looks strange the first week and indispensable the second. The Lab can't run them, because they refer to a Table in your own workbook, so they carry the "syntax" badge here.

=[@Qty]*[@UnitPrice]*(1-[@DiscountPct]/100)

[@Qty] means "the Qty column, this row". Press Enter once and the whole column fills, and stays filled as rows are added.

=SUM(tblSales[LineRevenue])

Whole-column references (Sales!P:P) do the same job on a plain range, and they are what this site's Lab runs. The Table version is safer in a real workbook because it can't accidentally include a stray number typed under the data.

=SUBTOTAL(109,tblSales[LineRevenue])

109 means "sum, ignoring hidden rows". Filter the Table to Kochi and the Total Row shows Kochi's total. A plain SUM would keep showing ₹2.72 crore.

=COUNTA(tblLeads[Email])

The header row is excluded automatically, so no -1. Compare with the plain-range version in the Application section, where the header is counted and subtracted.

Pro habit

Rename the Table the moment you create it. Table1, Table2, Table7 in a workbook six months old is a puzzle; tblSales, tblStores, tblTargets is a data model. The tbl prefix is a convention, not a rule, but everyone who reads your formulas will thank you for it.

Data hygiene: the rules a Table enforces

  • One header row, in row 1 of the data. No title above it, no units row below it. Put the title in the sheet name or a cell far to the right.
  • One record per row. An order line is a row. A store-month target is a row. A region heading is not a row; it's a column value.
  • One fact per cell. "Hyd / Bengaluru" is two cities. "₹1,299 (incl. GST)" is a number and a note. Split them.
  • No merged cells. Merging breaks sort, filter, Tables and every formula that fills down. Use Center Across Selection in Format Cells ▸ Alignment if you want the look.
  • No blank rows or columns inside the data. A blank row is where Ctrl+A and Ctrl+T think the data ends.
  • No totals inside the data. A TOTAL row in the middle gets summed with everything else the moment someone writes a SUM over the column. Totals live in the Total Row or a separate sheet.
  • Consistent types down a column. Dates as dates, not "2026-08-19 14:28" as text in one row and a real date in the next. Numbers as numbers.

Paste Special, Find & Replace, Go To Special

  1. Copy ▸ right-click ▸ Paste Special ▸ Values (or Ctrl+Alt+V, then V). Replaces formulas with their results. Do this on a copy before you send a sheet to someone who shouldn't see the source, and never on the original.
  2. Paste Special ▸ Transpose flips rows to columns. A twelve-column month strip becomes a twelve-row list, which is the tidy shape.
  3. Home ▸ Editing ▸ Find & Select ▸ Replace (Ctrl+H). Replace Hyd with Hyderabad, but tick Match entire cell contents or you will also turn "Hyderabad" into "Hyderabadabad". Wildcards work: *gmail.com finds every Gmail address.
  4. Find & Select ▸ Go To Special ▸ Blanks selects every empty cell in the range. Type a value and press Ctrl+Enter to fill all of them at once. Go To Special ▸ Formulas / Constants tells you which cells are typed and which are calculated, which is how you audit a model you didn't build.

Named ranges

Select a cell or range, type a name in the Name Box, press Enter. GSTRate for a cell holding 0.18 means a formula reads =Price*GSTRate instead of =B4*$H$2. Formulas ▸ Defined Names ▸ Name Manager lists them all. Names are for assumptions, thresholds and rates: things that appear in many formulas and will change. Tables already name your data, so you rarely need a named range for a data block.

The shortcuts that make you look like you've done this before

KeysDoesWhen
Ctrl+↓ / ↑ / → / ←jump to the edge of the data blockget to row 6315 in one keystroke; find the first blank in a column (it stops before it)
Ctrl+Shift+↓ (and the others)select from here to the edgeselect a whole column of data without the header
Ctrl+Aselect the current data block; twice for the sheetbefore Ctrl+T, to see what Excel thinks the block is
Ctrl+Tmake a Tablethe first thing you do to any imported data
Ctrl+1Format Cellsnumber formats, alignment, Center Across Selection
F2edit the cell in place, with references colouredreading someone else's formula
F4cycle A1 → $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 while editing; otherwise repeat last actionlocking a reference before you fill down (Module 04 leans on this)

Ctrl+Shift+Lfilter buttons on/offand off again before you share
Ctrl+;today's date as a valuedate-stamping a note; it doesn't update, unlike TODAY()

Ctrl+EFlash Filla one-off reshaping of text

Application: sizing up the workbook before you trust it

Before you answer Priya, you answer a duller question: what is actually in these sheets? Eight checks, each a one-line formula, each one you'd run on any file that lands in your inbox. The Lab runs them against the Novamart workbook.

How big is it, and what is one row?

COUNTA counts non-empty cells. Over a whole column it counts the header too, hence the -1.

=COUNTA(Sales!A:A)-1

6,314 order lines. The spec says 6,314; the sheet says 6,314. First check passed.

=ROWS(Sales!A2:A6315)

6,314 again. ROWS counts cells in the range whether or not they hold anything, so it only agrees with COUNTA when there are no blanks. When the two disagree, you have gaps to find.

=ROWS(UNIQUE(Sales!A2:A6315))

3,000. One row is an order line, not an order; an order with three products is three rows. Say that out loud before you count "orders" from this sheet, because 6,314 is not the number of orders and someone will quote it as if it were.

Are the numbers numbers?

COUNT counts only numeric cells. Compared with COUNTA, it tells you how many cells in a column are text.

=COUNT(Sales!B:B)

6,314. Every date is a real date (a serial number). COUNTA(Sales!B:B) gives 6,315, one more, because the header "OrderDate" is text. Now the same test on the CRM export.

=COUNT(Leads!G2:G151)

Zero. All 150 "dates" in CreatedAt are text: 13/07/2026, 2026-07-20, 21-Aug-2026, even 2026-08-19 14:28. You can't sort them, subtract them or group them by month until they are converted, which is Module 06's worked example. For today, you know not to trust any "leads by week" chart built from this sheet.

The total, and the total dressed up

=SUM(Sales!P:P)

27,169,184.8. Correct and unreadable. Nobody in a meeting can parse eight digits.

=TEXT(SUM(Sales!P:P),"₹#,##,##0")

₹2,71,69,185, which a manager reads instantly as "two crore seventy-two lakh". Note it includes cancelled and returned lines; the delivered-only figure is ₹2,37,44,826 and needs SUMIFS from Module 03. Whenever you quote a revenue number, say which one it is.

=TEXT(MIN(Sales!B:B),"dd-mmm-yyyy")&" to "&TEXT(MAX(Sales!B:B),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

01-Jan-2024 to 31-Aug-2026. Thirty-two months. Any "annual" comparison that includes 2026 is comparing eight months with twelve, and you now know that before the CFO does.

Blanks: missing, or meaningful?

COUNTBLANK needs a bounded range; over a whole column it would count a million empty rows.

=COUNTBLANK(Sales!F2:F6315)

3,448 blanks. Alarming until you check what they are.

=COUNTIF(Sales!G:G,"Online")+COUNTIF(Sales!G:G,"App")

3,448. Exactly the blanks. Region is empty for every online and app order because Novamart.in has no region, so the blank is a meaning, not a mistake. Write that in a note on the sheet; the next analyst will otherwise "fix" it. On the Customers sheet the blanks are the other kind.

=COUNTBLANK(Customers!C2:C501)

33 of 500 customers can't be emailed, whatever Priya's campaign says.

=COUNTBLANK(Customers!L2:L501)

221. Blank Tier means "not in the programme", which is the biggest group. A PivotTable will show it as "(blank)"; you'll want to relabel it.

The Leads sheet: finding the mess before you fix it

Priya's export. Row count first, then the four faults you saw on opening it: spacing, capitals, broken emails, city spellings.

=COUNTA(Leads!A:A)-1

150, as she said.

=COUNTIF(Leads!B:B,"*  *")

13 names with two spaces in a row, the kind that makes "Mohit Rao" and "Mohit Rao" two different people to a filter. The criterion is two spaces between the wildcards. Leading and trailing spaces need TRIM to catch.

=SUMPRODUCT(--(Leads!B2:B151<>TRIM(Leads!B2:B151)))

36 names carry extra spaces somewhere. TRIM collapses runs of spaces and strips the ends; the comparison is TRUE where it changed something, and -- turns TRUE into 1 so SUMPRODUCT can add them. That double-minus trick appears all over analyst workbooks.

=COUNTIF(Leads!C:C,"*@*")

128 of 150. Seven are blank; the rest are typos like joseph.gupta21outlook.com.

=COUNTIFS(Leads!C2:C151,"<>",Leads!C2:C151,"<>*@*")

15 typed-but-broken addresses. Bounded ranges here, because the whole column would count the header "Email" as a non-blank without an @. So Priya's real answer: 128 emailable, before deduplication. Mohit Rao appears twice with the same address in different capitalisation.

=ROWS(UNIQUE(Leads!E2:E151))

15 distinct values for what should be six cities. Look at them:

=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,UNIQUE(Leads!E2:E151))

New Delhi, DELHI, PUNE, Hyderabad, Dehra Dun, Hyd, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Mumbai (with a trailing space), Bombay, Dehradun, Bengaluru (trailing space), Bangalore, BLR, bangalore. UNIQUE ignores case, so "pune" and "PUNE" are already one; trailing spaces and synonyms are not.

=ROWS(UNIQUE(UPPER(TRIM(Leads!E2:E151))))

12. Three spellings were spacing. The other six (New Delhi, Hyd, Dehra Dun, Bombay, Bangalore, BLR) are synonyms for cities already in the list, and no function fixes those; a lookup table does, in Module 04, or a Replace Values step in Power Query.

=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,UNIQUE(Leads!F2:F151))

referral, web form, Walk-in, Event, Instagram, Facebook, FB. Six real sources, one of them written two ways. A PivotTable on this column shows seven rows and Priya's Facebook number is split in two.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askFoundation skill
Marketing (Priya)"How many leads can we actually email?"COUNTA, COUNTIF with wildcards, then a Table with filters
Finance (Arjun)"Why does the revenue column sum to zero in the export?"green triangle; Convert to Number; COUNT vs COUNTA
HR (Kavita)"Current headcount, and the payroll bill."COUNTBLANK on ExitDate; SUM with Indian format
Store ops (Nandini)"Freeze the store name so I can scroll the months."Freeze Panes at B2; a Table so headers stay visible anyway
Merchandising (Rohan)"How many products are live?"COUNTIF on a TRUE/FALSE column
Digital (Sameer)"Flip this month-across-columns export into a list."Paste Special ▸ Transpose, then Ctrl+T
Analytics (Vikram)"Every file you build starts as a Table named tblSomething."Ctrl+T, Table Design ▸ Table Name

Kavita's two, because a blank in ExitDate means "still here", which is the one time a blank is the answer you want.

=COUNTBLANK(Employees!H2:H86)

78 of 85 rows are current staff; seven have left. Headcount is 78, and any "average salary" over all 85 rows is wrong by seven leavers.

=TEXT(SUM(Employees!I:I),"₹#,##,##0")

₹92,90,000 a month across all 85 rows, leavers included. The current-staff figure needs SUMIFS on ExitDate being blank, which is the first thing you'll build in Module 03. For now the lesson is that SUM over a column sums every row, and a column that includes history overstates the present.

=COUNTIF(Products!I:I,TRUE)

68 of 72 products are active. The four inactive ones still have sales history, which is why the Sales sheet has products the Products sheet says aren't sold.

Practice

Each answer is one formula. Before you write it, say what one row of the sheet is and whether you need the header excluded.

Exercise 1 · How many orders?

Using the Orders sheet (one row per order), count the orders. Not the lines.

Hint

COUNTA over the ID column, minus the header.

Show solution 
=COUNTA(Orders!A:A)-1

3,000, matching the UNIQUE count of OrderID on Sales. When two sheets agree on a grain, you can start to trust both.

Exercise 2 · Customers with no phone

How many of the 500 customers have a blank Phone?

Hint

COUNTBLANK needs a bounded range: rows 2 to 501.

Show solution 
=COUNTBLANK(Customers!D2:D501)

51. Together with the 33 missing emails, Priya's "reach everyone" campaign can't reach about a tenth of the base by any channel.

Exercise 3 · Leads with no status

How many leads on the Leads sheet have an empty Status? (These are the ones nobody has touched.)

Hint

Same shape as exercise 2, column H, rows 2 to 151.

Show solution 
=COUNTBLANK(Leads!H2:H151)

28 untouched leads out of 150. That is the list Priya's team should be calling this afternoon, and it took one formula to produce.

Exercise 4 · The dearest thing we sell

Return the highest unit price on Sales, formatted with Indian grouping and no currency symbol.

Hint

MAX inside TEXT with the format #,##,##0.

Show solution 
=TEXT(MAX(Sales!N:N),"#,##,##0")

84,990, a 55-inch TV. Without TEXT the cell shows 84990, which is fine in a sheet with the format set, and unreadable in a message.

Exercise 5 · Phones in the +91 format

How many lead phone numbers start with +91? (The rest start with 0, or a bare digit, or are blank, and someone will have to standardise them.)

Hint

COUNTIF with a wildcard after the prefix.

Show solution 
=COUNTIF(Leads!D:D,"+91*")

68 of 150. Another 33 start with a 0, and 10 are blank. Three formats for one field is the definition of a column that needs a clean-up step, not a formula.

Exercise 6 · Distinct names, cleaned

How many distinct lead names are there once you trim the spaces and standardise the case with PROPER? Compare with the raw count of 132.

Hint

ROWS(UNIQUE(PROPER(TRIM(…)))), bounded to rows 2 to 151.

Show solution 
=ROWS(UNIQUE(PROPER(TRIM(Leads!B2:B151))))

123. Nine "different" people were the same person with different spacing. Duplicates by email would find more; that is the Power Query dedupe in Capstone 03.

Exercise 7 · Dates typed with slashes

How many CreatedAt values on Leads are in the dd/mm/yyyy style, meaning they contain a slash?

Hint

A wildcard on either side of the slash.

Show solution 
=COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"*/*")

41. Another 59 are ISO yyyy-mm-dd, 19 are dd-mmm-yyyy, and 31 carry a time. Four formats in one column, all text. Now you can explain to Priya why "leads by week" has never worked.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

A SUM that is too small is worse than an error. An error stops you. A column with 200 text-numbers among 6,000 real ones gives a total that looks right, goes on a slide, and is 3% low. Run COUNT against COUNTA on every numeric column of every file you receive. If they differ by more than the header, find out why before you add anything up.

Watch out

Sorting a selection instead of a block. Select column B, sort it, and every email is now next to the wrong name, silently, with AutoSave already saving it. Click one cell and let Excel choose the block, or better, sort inside a Table where it can't go wrong. If it has already happened: Ctrl+Z immediately, or version history from Module 01.

  • Ctrl+T first, always. Any data you receive becomes a Table before you touch it. Name it. Everything after that is easier.
  • Formats change the look, never the value. ₹2,71,69,185 and 27169184.8 are the same cell. If a number "changes" when you format it, it was text.
  • Blanks have meanings; find out which. Blank Region means online. Blank ExitDate means current. Blank Email means unreachable. Write the meaning in a note before someone fills them in.
  • Never type over an export. Raw data stays raw. Clean-up happens in a copy, a helper column, or Power Query, so that you can show your working.
  • Flash Fill is a one-off. It produces values, not logic. Fine for a Tuesday afternoon; wrong for a monthly report.
  • Clear filters before you send. A filtered sheet with a SUM at the bottom is a trap for the reader. Use the Table's Total Row if you want a filter-aware total.
  • Merged cells are for print layouts, and only the last sheet. Center Across Selection gives the same look without breaking sort, fill or Tables.
  • Keep hands on the keyboard. Ctrl+↓ is 6,314 rows in one press. Scrolling is the tell of someone who has not done this before.

Pro habit

Add a sheet called README at the front of any workbook you share. Five lines: where the data came from, the as-of date, what one row is, which blanks mean what, and what the version number is. The person reading it in six months is usually you.

On the job

Assessment tests for analyst roles rarely ask "what is a Table". They hand you a messy export and forty-five minutes, and they watch. The examiner sees whether your first move is Ctrl+T or a mouse drag to select 6,000 rows. Both get to the answer. Only one says you've done this before.

In the assessment test

A typical opener: "Here is a sales export. Tell us the total revenue and the number of orders." The trap is in the export. The revenue column has 150 text-numbers (from a CSV), and the file has one row per line, not per order. Candidates who write =SUM(P:P) and =COUNTA(A:A)-1 get two wrong answers in under a minute. Candidates who run COUNT against COUNTA, convert the column, and count UNIQUE order IDs get two right ones in five. The five-minute candidate gets the job. Then it is Ctrl+T, Ctrl+1 to format the total in rupees, and Freeze Panes so the examiner can read it over your shoulder.

First 90 days

The shortcuts are the habit to build in week one, because nobody will teach you them later. Pick four a day. Day one: Ctrl+Arrow, Ctrl+Shift+Arrow, Ctrl+T, Ctrl+1. Day two: F2, F4, Alt+=, Ctrl+Shift+L. Day three: Ctrl+Page Down, Ctrl+;, Ctrl+Alt+V, Alt ribbon keys. By the end of the month Vikram will hand you the raw exports instead of the cleaned ones, which is the promotion that doesn't come with a title.

Interview question: "What is an Excel Table and why would you use one?"
A Table is a named range that Excel treats as a set of records: one header row and one record per row. It auto-expands when you add data, so formulas, PivotTables and Power Query built on it pick up new rows without editing ranges. It gives structured references like tblSales[LineRevenue] that read clearly, a Total Row that respects filters, and filter buttons and banding for free. I make any imported data a Table before I do anything else.
Interview question: "A column of numbers sums to zero. What's wrong and how do you fix it?"
The numbers are stored as text, usually from a CSV or copied web page: left-aligned with a green triangle, and COUNT returns far fewer than COUNTA. Fix by selecting the column and choosing Convert to Number from the warning icon, or Data ▸ Text to Columns ▸ Finish, or a helper column with VALUE(). Then I'd check the source so it doesn't happen next month.
Interview question: "What does 'tidy data' mean and why does it matter in Excel?"
One header row, one record per row, one value per cell, no merged cells, no blank rows or subtotals inside the data. It matters because every analysis tool in Excel (sort, filter, Tables, PivotTables, Power Query) assumes that shape. A sheet laid out for reading, with a title row and regional sub-headings, has to be reshaped before it can be analysed, and reshaping is where most of the time goes.

Quick check

1. COUNTA(Sales!P:P) returns 6,315 and COUNT(Sales!P:P) returns 6,100. What does that tell you?

COUNTA counts anything non-empty; COUNT counts numbers only. The gap, less one for the header, is the number of text cells, and a SUM over the column is missing all of them.

2. You apply the format ₹#,##,##0 to a cell holding 27169184.8. What is in the cell now?

Formats change the display only. Formulas that reference the cell still see the full value, decimals included.

3. You paste September's rows directly under a Table named tblSales. Which is true?

Auto-expand is the main reason to use a Table. A plain range reference like P2:P6315 would have stopped at the old last row.

4. Which of these is NOT a tidy-data problem?

A blank that means something (online orders have no region) is data. Heading rows and two values in one cell are structure problems that break sort, filter and pivots.

Level 1 · Module 03 · about 90 min

Formulas that run a business: SUMIFS, IF and friends

Most of what a manager asks for on a Thursday afternoon is one number with two or three conditions on it: delivered revenue, this month, for the South stores. Excel has one function for that shape, and once SUMIFS and its cousins are in your hands, the Monday review pack stops being a copy-paste job and becomes a sheet that refreshes itself. This module also fixes the two things that break beginner formulas: references that move when you copy them, and errors nobody reads.

  • You'll read any formula as three ingredients (references, operators, functions) and predict what happens when it is copied to the next row.
  • You'll write SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS with date ranges, "not equal", wildcards and blanks as criteria.
  • You'll make a cell decide something with IF, IFS, AND and OR, and know when a nested IF is the wrong tool.
  • You'll clean names, emails and phone numbers with the text functions, and build month buckets and working-day counts with the date functions.
  • You'll recognise the five error values on sight, trap the ones that are expected with IFERROR, and step through a broken formula with Evaluate Formula.

Concept

Thursday, 4:40 pm

Nandini Rao has the Monday review at 9:30 and a message for Vikram's team: "Delivered revenue for August against target, by region, plus cancellations. And last year's August next to it." Vikram forwards it to you with one line: "Build it so we never build it again." The Sales sheet has 6,314 order lines. Nobody is going to filter and add those by hand every month.

A formula is a sentence Excel evaluates. It starts with =, and everything after that is one of three things. A reference points at data (Sales!P:P, B2, $F$1). An operator combines values (+ - * / ^ for arithmetic, & for gluing text, = <> > < >= <= for comparisons). A function is a named machine that takes arguments in brackets and returns one thing (SUMIFS(...), TEXT(...), IF(...)). Every formula on this site, however long, is just those three ingredients nested inside each other.

The order matters. Excel works out percentages first, then ^, then * and /, then + and -, then &, then comparisons. So =1+2*3^2 is 19, not 81 and not 27. Brackets override everything, and the habit that saves you from a bad slide is to bracket any division: =SUM(Sales!P:P)/(COUNTA(Sales!A:A)-1) is the average line, ₹4,303. Drop the brackets and you get ₹4,301, because the minus happens after the division. Close enough to go unnoticed, wrong enough to matter when it is a discount rate.

Where beginners get stuck is not the functions. It is that they type a formula for one row, copy it down, and the copies point at the wrong cells. That is the relative-reference behaviour: =B2*F1 in row 2 becomes =B3*F2 in row 3, because Excel remembers the offset, not the address. Usually that is what you want. When it isn't, you lock the reference with dollar signs, and the keyboard for that is F4 while your cursor is on the reference. The How-it-works section has the picture.

Why a manager cares

A review pack built on SUMIFS against the raw Sales sheet is a report that refreshes when the data does. Paste next month's export, and every number on the summary tab is right before you have finished your chai. Built with filters and manual sums, the same pack takes an afternoon a month and is wrong one month in four. Analysts get judged on the second kind; they get promoted on the first.

How it works

Relative and absolute references

Rohan's merchandising team keeps GST at 18% in cell F1 and prices in column B. The formula for the tax-inclusive price of the first product is =B2*(1+F1). Copy it down and row 3 reads =B3*(1+F2). F2 is empty, so every product after the first is priced at exactly its ex-GST price and nobody notices until the invoice bounces.

Whole-column references like Sales!P:P sidestep most of this, because there is nothing to slide: the column is the column. That is why the teaching formulas on this site use them. In your own workbooks the even better habit is an Excel Table (Module 02) and structured references, which read like English and grow with the data.

=SUMIFS(Sales[LineRevenue], Sales[Channel], "App", Sales[Status], "Delivered")

The IFS family and its criteria syntax

SUMIF, COUNTIF and AVERAGEIF take one condition. Their plural cousins take any number, and the arguments are in a different order: the plural versions put the sum range first. Use the plural ones always, even for one condition; you will add a second condition within the week, and you will not have to rewrite.

=SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...)
=COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...)
=AVERAGEIFS(average_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...)
=MAXIFS(max_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...)      MINIFS is the same shape

The criterion is a small language of its own. A bare value means "equals". Anything else is written as text, and if the comparison involves a cell or a function, you glue the operator to it with &.

You want rows where…CriterionNotes
Channel is App"App"Case does not matter: "app" matches too.
Status is anything but Cancelled"<>Cancelled"Operator and value inside one string.
Revenue above ₹10,000">10000"Also ">=", "<", "<=".
Date on or after 1 Aug 2026">="&DATE(2026,8,1)Never type the date inside the quotes; build it with DATE or point at a cell and glue with &.
Revenue above the number in cell H2">"&H2Same glue pattern for any cell.
Product name contains "Smartphone""*Smartphone*"* is any run of characters, ? exactly one. Text only.
Month is Oct, Nov or Dec 2025"2025-1?"The Month column is text, so wildcards work on it.
Region is blank (online lines)""Two quotes, nothing between them.
Region is not blank (store lines)"<>"The opposite of the row above.
Approved is TRUETRUELogical values go bare, no quotes.
The name has a literal * or ? in it"~*"Tilde escapes the wildcard in Excel. The Lab does not support the tilde; test it on the desktop.

Deciding with IF

IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) is the whole of it. The test is any comparison; the values can be numbers, text, or more formulas. Three outcomes used to mean an IF inside an IF. IFS reads top to bottom and stops at the first true test, so the last pair is usually TRUE, "everything else". AND and OR combine tests and go inside the IF.

=IF(actual >= target, "On target", "Below target")
=IFS(ratio >= 1, "Green", ratio >= 0.9, "Amber", TRUE, "Red")
=IF(AND(ratio >= 1, cancels < 30), "Green", "Amber")
=IF(OR(cancels > 30, returns > 30), "Check ops", "OK")

The text and date toolkits

You will not memorise these. You will look them up for a month, and then one day you won't need to. The two tables are the ones worth bookmarking.

Text functionDoesExample on " MOHIT rao "
TRIM(t)Removes leading, trailing and doubled spaces"MOHIT rao"
PROPER(t) / UPPER / LOWERChanges case"Mohit Rao"
LEN(t)Number of characters, spaces included11
LEFT(t,n) / RIGHT(t,n) / MID(t,start,n)Cuts a fixed number of charactersRIGHT(phone,10) keeps the mobile number
TEXTBEFORE(t,d) / TEXTAFTER(t,d)Cuts at a delimiterTEXTAFTER(email,"@") is the domain
SUBSTITUTE(t,old,new)Replaces every occurrence of a piece of textSUBSTITUTE(phone," ","") drops spaces
TEXTJOIN(d,ignore_empty,range)Glues a range into one string with a delimiter"Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru"
TEXT(value,format)Turns a number or date into formatted textTEXT(1248348,"#,##,##0") is 12,48,348
VALUE(t)Turns text that looks like a number into a numberVALUE("1,234") is 1234
Date functionDoesWith TODAY() = 31 Aug 2026
TODAY()Today's date as a serial number; recalculates every day46265
DATE(y,m,d)Builds a date from parts; the only safe way to write one in a formulaDATE(2026,8,1)
YEAR(d) / MONTH(d) / DAY(d)Pulls one part out2026, 8, 31
EOMONTH(d,n)Last day of the month n months away; +1 gives the first of the nextEOMONTH(TODAY(),-1)+1 is 1 Aug 2026
EDATE(d,n)Same day, n months awayEDATE(TODAY(),-12) is 31 Aug 2025
DATEDIF(start,end,"Y"|"M"|"D")Whole years, months or days between two datesKochi store: 28 months old
NETWORKDAYS(start,end,[holidays])Working days, weekends and listed holidays excludedSeptember 2026 has 22
WORKDAY(start,n,[holidays])The date n working days later; deadlines5 working days on: 7 Sep 2026
TEXT(d,"yyyy-mm")A month bucket you can group and match on"2026-08"

That last row is how the Month column on the Sales sheet was made in the first place, and it is the pattern for any bucket you need: a year, a quarter, a week.

=TEXT(Sales!B2,"yyyy-mm")
=YEAR(Sales!B2)&"-Q"&ROUNDUP(MONTH(Sales!B2)/3,0)

"2024-01" and "2024-Q1" for order 10001, placed on 11 January 2024. The quarter trick divides the month by three and rounds up: months 1 to 3 give 1, months 4 to 6 give 2, and so on.

Reading errors instead of hiding them

ErrorExcel is telling youFirst thing to check
#N/A"Not available": a lookup found nothing.Is the key spelled the same on both sheets? Trailing space? Number stored as text? (Module 04)
#VALUE!Wrong type: text where a number was needed, or ranges of different sizes.Green triangles in the column. "12,499" with a comma is text. Dates typed as text.
#DIV/0!Divided by zero or by an empty cell.An average over a group that has no rows yet. New store, new month.
#REF!The cell this formula pointed at was deleted.Someone deleted a row or a column. Undo, or fix the reference. There is no other cure.
#NAME?Excel does not recognise a name.Misspelt function, missing quotes around text, or a named range that does not exist on this workbook.
#SPILL!A dynamic array wanted to spill into cells that are not empty.Clear the cells below or to the right (Module 07).

IFERROR(formula, fallback) replaces any error with something friendlier. Use it when the error is expected: a store with no sales this month dividing by a zero count. Do not wrap a whole sheet in it to make the red go away; a #REF! you have hidden is a wrong number you have signed off.

When a long formula returns something odd, click the cell and use Formulas ▸ Formula Auditing ▸ Evaluate Formula. Each press of Evaluate replaces one piece with its value, inside out, so you watch the number appear. Quicker: select any part of a formula in the formula bar and press F9 to see what that part returns. Press Esc afterwards, or you will have replaced the formula with the value.

Application: the Monday review pack

The totals, and what "revenue" means

Start with the biggest number and the question it forces. SUM over the whole LineRevenue column adds every line whether it was delivered, cancelled or returned.

=SUM(Sales!P:P)

₹2.72 crore, but that includes ₹34 lakh of lines that were cancelled or sent back. Arjun's finance definition of revenue is delivered lines only, and one criterion pair gets you there.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹2,37,44,826, about 87% of the gross figure. Write the definition in a footnote on the slide, every time. Half of "your number doesn't match mine" is two people using two definitions of the same word.

Counting is a different question from summing, and the count function you use decides what you are counting. COUNTA counts non-empty cells, so minus one for the header it is the number of lines.

=COUNTA(Sales!A:A)-1
=COUNTIFS(Sales!Q:Q,"Cancelled")

6,314 lines, 449 cancelled, which is 7.1%: the "one in fourteen" Nandini keeps quoting. Note that this is lines, not orders; the Orders sheet says 219 of 3,000 orders (7.3%). Both are true, and you need to say which one you mean.

This month against target

The Month column holds text like 2026-08, so August is one equality criterion. Add Status and you have the headline.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹12,48,348. The same number from the real date column, for the day the Month column isn't there:

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,
    Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2026,8,1),
    Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31),
    Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

Identical, ₹12,48,348, and this version is the one you will use on a raw export. Two criteria on the same column is how you say "between". The target for the month is on the Targets sheet, one row per store, so it is a SUMIFS too.

=SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08")

₹16.3 lakh. Now the cell can say something instead of just showing a number. The text is built with & and TEXT, and the format string #,##,##0 gives Indian comma grouping.

=IF(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")>=SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08"),
    "On target",
    "Short by ₹"&TEXT(SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08")-SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),"#,##,##0"))

"Short by ₹3,81,652." That formula repeats the two sums three times, which is the moment to reach for LET: name each piece once, then use the names.

=LET(actual,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
    target,SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08"),
    IFS(actual/target>=1,"Green", actual/target>=0.9,"Amber", TRUE,"Red"))

Red. Attainment is 76.6%, well below the 90% amber line. The nested-IF version of the same decision is IF(r>=1,"Green",IF(r>=0.9,"Amber","Red")); it works, but by the fourth outcome the closing brackets are unreadable, and IFS exists so you never write it.

Last year next to it

"Same month last year" should not be typed. TODAY() is 31 Aug 2026 in the Lab, EDATE shifts a date by whole months, and TEXT(...,"yyyy-mm") turns the result into the same text the Month column uses.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,TEXT(EDATE(TODAY(),-12),"yyyy-mm"),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹6,89,786 for August 2025. Growth is a division, and TEXT with a percent format makes it readable in a sentence.

=TEXT(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")-1,"0.0%")

81.0% up on last August, which changes the tone of the target conversation: the store is below a stretch target, not shrinking. That pairing, attainment and growth on the same line, is the single most useful row in a review pack.

Cancellations and the online blank

Nandini's third ask is cancellations this month. Count them, count everything, divide, format.

=TEXT(COUNTIFS(Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Cancelled")/COUNTIFS(Sales!C:C,"2026-08"),"0.0%")

10.7%, against 7.1% all-time. That is the number that gets a question in the meeting, so have the 27 cancelled lines ready in a filter. Regional splits hit the online problem next: online lines have no Region, and an empty string as the criterion is how you pick them up.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,"",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,"<>",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹1.29 crore online against ₹1.09 crore in stores. More than half the delivered revenue has no region, so a region chart without an "Online" bar is lying by omission. Sameer will want that split in his own pack, by channel rather than region.

=AVERAGEIFS(Orders!J:J,Orders!F:F,"App",Orders!G:G,"Delivered")

₹9,315 on the app, against ₹9,302 in store and ₹9,148 on the web. App baskets are no smaller than store baskets, which is the point Sameer has been trying to make for a quarter.

Wildcards for product questions

Rohan wants "the smartphone number" and there are four smartphone SKUs. The product name is text, so a wildcard on either side does the work.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!J:J,"*Smartphone*",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹32,59,479 from 145 delivered units. And the festive quarter, using ? to match October, November and December in one criterion:

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-1?",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹34.9 lakh in the three festive months, which is more than the first eight months of 2025 delivered between them. Be careful with ?: it matched exactly what you wanted here because the Month column is zero-padded. On a column with "2025-1" and "2025-10" both present it would not.

Dates: the working-day questions

Dates in Excel are whole numbers counting from 1 Jan 1900, which is why you can subtract them and why a date typed as text breaks everything downstream. TEXT shows a serial as a date; EOMONTH and EDATE walk in months; DATEDIF gives elapsed time in the unit you ask for; NETWORKDAYS skips weekends and any holidays you list.

=TEXT(EOMONTH(TODAY(),-1)+1,"dd-mmm-yyyy")&" to "&TEXT(EOMONTH(TODAY(),0),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

"01-Aug-2026 to 31-Aug-2026". The -1 then +1 is the standard trick for the first of the month: end of last month, plus one day. Months since the Kochi store opened, for the "still ramping up" argument:

=DATEDIF(DATE(2024,4,10),TODAY(),"M")

28 months. And the count of working days in October 2026 with Gandhi Jayanti and Diwali as holidays, for the daily-run-rate target Nandini will set:

=NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2026,10,1),DATE(2026,10,31),{46297;46315})

20 days. The two serials in braces are 2 Oct and 20 Oct 2026; in a real workbook you would point at a holidays list on its own sheet, and the Lab accepts the array of serials. Note that stores trade on Saturdays, so for a retail run rate you would count differently; NETWORKDAYS is the head-office number.

Text: cleaning the lead export

Priya's Leads sheet arrives with names in capitals, emails in mixed case and phone numbers in four formats. The text functions fix one column at a time. Row 2 is MOHIT RAO, mohit.rao84@gmail.com, 08855516267.

=PROPER(TRIM(Leads!B2))
=LOWER(TEXTAFTER(Leads!C2,"@"))
=RIGHT(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(Leads!D2," ",""),"+91",""),10)

"Mohit Rao", "gmail.com", "8855516267". The phone formula strips spaces, strips a country code, and keeps the last ten characters, which handles the leading zero as well. TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER are the modern replacements for the LEFT(x,FIND(" ",x)-1) pattern you will still see in older workbooks; both are worth recognising. TEXTJOIN goes the other way, gluing a list into one cell, and is the fastest way to write a sentence for a slide.

=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,FILTER(Stores!C:C,Stores!E:E="South"))

"Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kochi". The TRUE tells it to skip empty cells.

Rounding and expected errors

ROUND(x, n) rounds to n decimal places, and a negative n rounds to the left of the decimal point, which is how you get "to the nearest thousand". ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN do what they say. Rounding belongs in the presentation layer, not in the calculation: round the number you show, never the number you add up.

=ROUND(AVERAGE(Sales!P:P),-2)

₹4,300. The last piece of the pack is a store-level average that will be asked to cope with a store that has no lines this month. Divide a sum by a zero count and you get #DIV/0!; that is the expected kind of error, so trap it with a meaningful fallback.

=IFERROR(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,"Novamart Guwahati")/COUNTIFS(Sales!D:D,"Novamart Guwahati"),"no lines")

"no lines" instead of a red error in the middle of the pack. Guwahati is on Nandini's expansion list, so that row will exist before the formula does.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askFormula or feature
Finance"Delivered revenue by month against target, with attainment."SUMIFS on Sales and Targets, IFS for the RAG status
Store ops"Cancellation rate this month versus all time."COUNTIFS divided by COUNTIFS, TEXT as a percentage
Marketing / CRM"How many leads have no email, and what share is Gmail?"COUNTBLANK, COUNTIFS with "*@gmail.com"
HR"Current headcount and monthly payroll."COUNTIFS and SUMIFS on a blank ExitDate
Merchandising"Revenue on any Hestia appliance."SUMIFS with "Hestia*"
Customer service"Refunds actually approved, and the average refund for defectives."SUMIFS on a TRUE criterion, AVERAGEIFS
Digital"Revenue from anything that is not a physical store."SUMIFS with "<>Store" on Channel

The HR one. An employee is current when ExitDate is blank, so the criterion is an empty string, and a second pair on EmpID stops the formula counting empty rows below the data.

=COUNTIFS(Employees!H:H,"",Employees!A:A,"<>")
=SUMIFS(Employees!I:I,Employees!H:H,"")

78 people on the books out of 85 ever hired, and ₹89.9 lakh a month in salaries. Kavita's headcount slide is those two cells and a date. Customer service next: the Approved column is a logical value, so the criterion is a bare TRUE.

=SUMIFS(Returns!F:F,Returns!G:G,TRUE)

₹8,43,594 across 239 approved returns; 24 were declined. And Priya's data-quality line for the lead export, which is the first thing Module 06 will fix properly:

=COUNTBLANK(Leads!C2:C151)

Seven of 150 leads cannot be emailed at all. COUNTBLANK wants a bounded range, because on a whole column it would count a million empty cells.

Practice

Type each answer in the box under the title before you look. Every solution is a single formula that returns one value, and the checker compares values, not text, so your criteria can be in any order.

Exercise 1 · Delivered revenue in the South

How much delivered revenue have the four South stores brought in across the whole dataset? Region is on the Sales sheet.

Hint

Two criteria pairs: Region equals South, Status equals Delivered.

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,"South",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹38,60,735, the largest of the four regions; North is ₹33.1 lakh, West ₹27.0 lakh, East ₹10.1 lakh. Online is none of these.

Exercise 2 · Big-ticket lines

How many delivered order lines were worth more than ₹10,000?

Hint

A comparison criterion is text: ">10000". This is a count, so no sum range.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(Sales!P:P,">10000",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

355 lines, about 6.5% of delivered lines. Most of Novamart's tickets are small; the big ones are laptops, phones and appliances.

Exercise 3 · The first half of 2026 by date

Using the OrderDate column (B), not the Month column, find delivered revenue from 1 January 2026 to 30 June 2026 inclusive.

Hint

Two criteria on the same column, each built as ">="&DATE(...) and "<="&DATE(...).

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2026,1,1),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2026,6,30),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹47,01,468 for the half year. If you typed the date inside the quotes, as ">=01/01/2026", Excel would parse it using the machine's locale, and a laptop set to US dates would silently read a different day.

Exercise 4 · Store baskets

What is the average order value of delivered orders placed in a physical store? Use the Orders sheet, where one row is one order.

Hint

AVERAGEIFS puts the average range first. Channel is column F, Status is G, OrderValue is J.

Show solution 
=AVERAGEIFS(Orders!J:J,Orders!F:F,"Store",Orders!G:G,"Delivered")

About ₹9,302. Averaging LineRevenue on the Sales sheet would give you the average line, roughly ₹4,300, a different fact with a similar-sounding name.

Exercise 5 · New joiners

How many current employees (no ExitDate) were hired on or after 1 January 2026?

Hint

HireDate is column G, ExitDate is H. One date comparison, one blank criterion.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(Employees!G:G,">="&DATE(2026,1,1),Employees!H:H,"")

Seven joiners this year still on the books. Kavita's onboarding tracker is this formula with a month bucket.

Exercise 6 · A status cell for cancellations

Write a formula that returns "Check ops" if August 2026 had more than 20 cancelled lines or more than 20 returned lines, and "OK" otherwise.

Hint

IF(OR(test1, test2), ...). Each test is a COUNTIFS on Month and Status.

Show solution 
=IF(OR(COUNTIFS(Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Cancelled")>20,COUNTIFS(Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Returned")>20),"Check ops","OK")

"Check ops": 27 cancellations trip the first test even though returns (14) don't. Put the thresholds in cells rather than in the formula and Nandini can tune them without calling you.

Exercise 7 · A clean first name

From the full name in Leads!B2 (which is MOHIT RAO), return the first name in title case: Mohit.

Hint

TEXTBEFORE with a space as the delimiter, wrapped in PROPER.

Show solution 
=PROPER(TEXTBEFORE(TRIM(Leads!B2)," "))

"Mohit". The TRIM costs nothing and protects you from a leading space, which is the most common reason a name column refuses to split.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

A criterion range and a sum range must be the same height. SUMIFS(Sales!P2:P6315, Sales!Q:Q, "Delivered") mixes a bounded range with a whole column and returns #VALUE!. Whole columns everywhere, or bounded ranges everywhere. Never both in one formula.

Watch out

Numbers stored as text add up to zero. If SUM over a column that is clearly full of rupees returns 0 or a suspiciously small figure, look for the green triangle in the corner of the cells. Select the column, Data ▸ Data Tools ▸ Text to Columns ▸ Finish converts it in one go. This is the single most common reason a fresh export "doesn't add up".

Pro habit

Put every assumption in a cell and point at it. The threshold, the GST rate, the month you are reporting on, the store name. A formula that reads "2026-08" has to be edited in twelve places next month; one that reads $B$1 is changed once. It also lets a manager change the month themselves, which is most of what "self-service" means.

  • Say the definition before the number. Delivered only? Lines or orders? Including GST? Write it in the cell next to the number, and it will end up in the footnote where it belongs.
  • Build dates with DATE, never type them into criteria. ">="&DATE(2026,8,1) works on every machine. ">=1/8/2026" is August in Gurugram and January in Boston.
  • Glue with &, then read the string back. If a criterion misbehaves, put the ">="&DATE(...) part in a spare cell on its own and look at what it produces. Half the time the operator has a space after it.
  • One IFERROR, close to the expected error. Wrap the division, not the whole formula. If the error moves, you want to see it.
  • Use F9 on a piece before you trust the whole. Highlight the inner SUMIFS, press F9, read the value, press Esc. Faster than Evaluate Formula, and it works in the formula bar of any cell.
  • Percentages are numbers. 18% is 0.18. =100*18% is 18; =100*(1+18%) is 118. Keep the cell as a number formatted as a percentage, and never store "18%" as text.
  • Round for the eye, not for the sum. A column of ROUNDed values summed will not match the rounded total. Round the total.

On the job

In the assessment test

Analyst tests almost always contain a "sum of X where Y and Z" task, usually with a date range and a wildcard hiding in it, and a "flag rows where…" task that wants an IF with AND. The examiner is checking three things: that you used SUMIFS rather than filters and a calculator, that your date criteria are built rather than typed, and that the formula in row 2 still works in row 200 because you locked the right references. Being able to explain a #VALUE! in the sample file is a bonus point most candidates miss.

First 90 days

Your first real deliverable will be a monthly pack somebody else used to build by hand. The win is not the pack; it is the second month, when you paste the new export and everything updates. Spend the first month getting the definitions agreed with the people who read it, and putting the assumptions in cells they can see.

"What is the difference between a relative and an absolute reference?"
A relative reference like B2 is stored as an offset, so it shifts when the formula is copied to another cell. An absolute reference like $B$2 is pinned to that cell wherever the formula goes. Mixed references (B$2, $B2) pin only the row or only the column, which is what you use to fill a two-way table from one formula.
"When would you use SUMIFS instead of a PivotTable?"
When the output has to sit in a fixed layout, feed another formula, or refresh without a click. A pivot is faster for exploring and for a one-off summary, but it does not live inside a model, and it has to be refreshed by hand. In practice a review pack uses both: a pivot to find the story, SUMIFS to report it.
"How would you sum sales between two dates?"
Two criteria on the same date column inside one SUMIFS: ">="&start and "<="&end, where start and end are cells or DATE() calls. The operator is text and the date is glued on with the ampersand, so Excel never has to guess a date format.

Quick check

1. Cell C2 holds =B2*F1 and you copy it to C3. What does C3 contain?

Both references are relative, so both shift by one row. To keep F1 fixed you need $F$1, or at least F$1.

2. Which criterion sums rows dated on or after the date in cell H1?

Inside quotes, H1 is the two letters H and 1. The operator stays in the string and the cell is glued on with &.

3. =SUM(Sales!P:P) returns 0 on a column full of rupee amounts. Most likely cause?

SUM ignores text. Numbers pasted from a system export often arrive as text; look for green triangles and convert them.

4. A store's average line value shows #DIV/0! in a month it had no sales. The right fix is…

The error is expected and local, so trap it locally with a meaningful fallback. Blanket IFERROR hides real mistakes elsewhere, and 0 is a wrong average, not a missing one.
