Level 1 · Module 04 · about 75 min

Lookups: XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH and data validation

Business data never arrives on one sheet. Orders carry a StoreID, the store's name and region live on another tab, the target is on a third, and the manager wants all of it in one row. A lookup is the formula that walks from a key on one sheet to a value on another, and it is the most-tested Excel skill in analyst interviews. This module teaches the modern one, keeps the old one for the day you inherit a 2014 workbook, and closes with the dropdowns that stop bad keys getting typed in the first place.

  • You'll write XLOOKUP with all six arguments and know what each one changes: the not-found text, the four match modes, and searching from the bottom.
  • You'll pull a whole row back in one formula, look up on two keys at once, and do a two-way lookup by row and column header.
  • You'll band a number into a slab (commission tiers, loyalty tiers) with an approximate match on a sorted table, and know why the table must be sorted.
  • You'll read and fix a VLOOKUP, and explain its four traps in an interview without notes.
  • You'll reconcile two lists (which customers have never ordered? which store has no target?) with COUNTIFS and FILTER.
  • You'll build a data-validation dropdown with an input message and an error alert, so the keys people type are keys that exist.

Concept

Tuesday, 11:10 am

Arjun Mehta wants the August store scorecard to show, for every store, its region, its target, its delivered revenue and a "% of target" column. The Sales sheet has the store name but no target. Targets has the target but no region. Stores has the region. Three sheets, one row per store on the scorecard, and it has to be right by the finance call at 3. Vikram's note: "Lookups. No copy-paste."

A lookup does one thing. It takes a key you have, finds it in a column somewhere else, and gives you back whatever is sitting in the same row of another column. "Kochi" goes in, the City column of the Stores sheet is scanned, row 13 matches, and the Store column of row 13 comes out: Novamart MG Road Kochi. That is the whole mechanism. Everything else in this module is about what happens when the key is missing, when it appears twice, when you want a band instead of an exact match, or when you want three columns back instead of one.

Three functions do this in Excel. VLOOKUP is from 1985 and has four design flaws you will be asked about in interviews. INDEX with MATCH is the 2000s workaround: two functions that together avoid the flaws. XLOOKUP arrived in 2019 and is the one to write today; it is in every Microsoft 365 build your employer runs. Learn XLOOKUP first, INDEX/MATCH second, and VLOOKUP well enough to read it.

Why a manager cares

Every join between two lists in a company is a lookup: order to customer, employee to manager, SKU to cost, store to target. When the lookup is wrong, the report is wrong in a way that looks fine: the Kochi row shows a region, just the wrong one. Managers cannot see that from the slide. The analyst who can say "I reconciled the two lists first; 91 registered customers have never ordered and 23 store-months have a target but no sales" is the one whose numbers get trusted.

How it works

XLOOKUP, all six arguments

Two details that matter. The lookup_array and return_array are separate ranges, so the return column can be to the left of the key column, on another sheet, or several columns wide. And the match is not case-sensitive: "kochi" finds Kochi. A trailing space is a different story: "Kochi " finds nothing, which is why the second thing to check on a #N/A is TRIM.

INDEX and MATCH

MATCH(key, column, 0) returns the position of the key in the column: "Kochi" is the 13th cell of Stores!C:C because the header is cell 1. INDEX(column, position) returns the value at that position. Put one inside the other and you have a lookup that can return from any column, in either direction, with the same speed as XLOOKUP. It still wins in two situations: a workbook that has to open in Excel 2016 or in LibreOffice, and a two-way lookup where MATCH on the header row reads more clearly than a nested XLOOKUP. The 0 in MATCH means exact; leave it out and you get an approximate match on a sorted list, the same trap as VLOOKUP's.

=INDEX(return_column, MATCH(key, key_column, 0))
=INDEX(whole_table, MATCH(row_key, first_column, 0), MATCH(column_header, header_row, 0))
=XMATCH(key, key_column)                              MATCH with XLOOKUP's match and search modes; exact by default

VLOOKUP and its four traps

VLOOKUP(key, table, col_index_num, [range_lookup]) searches the first column of the table for the key and returns the value from the column numbered col_index_num, counting the first column as 1. It still works, and it is in a million workbooks, so you need to read it. Its problems are structural.

TrapWhat goes wrongExampleXLOOKUP fix
The key must be the first columnYou can't look up a city and return the StoreID sitting to its left without rearranging the sheet.VLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!A:H,2,FALSE) is #N/A: column A holds ids, not cities.lookup_array and return_array are independent.
The column number is a numberInsert a column inside the table and every col_index_num now points one column to the left of where it should.VLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:H,6,FALSE) returns SqFt today; add a column between and it returns Opened.You name the return column; inserts do not move it.
Approximate match is the defaultLeave off the fourth argument and VLOOKUP assumes the first column is sorted and returns the nearest smaller key. No error, wrong answer.VLOOKUP(1045,Products!A:G,2) returns "Munchly Trail Mix 500g" for a product that does not exist.Exact match is the default.
No "not found" and no "search from last"Every VLOOKUP needs an IFERROR wrapper, and it can only ever find the first match.Latest order for a store needs a helper column or a sort.if_not_found and search_mode -1 are built in.
 
=VLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:H,6,FALSE)

5500 square feet. Column C is the first column of the table you gave it, so City is column 1 and SqFt is column 6. When you inherit one of these, the first thing to do is check for the FALSE. The second is to count the columns.

Inherited

=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A2,Stores!$B$1:$H$14,4,FALSE),"")

Key in column B of a fixed range, region as "column 4", an IFERROR that hides every kind of failure as a blank, and a range that stops at row 14 so the next store never gets a region.

Rewritten

=XLOOKUP(TRIM(A2),Stores!B:B,Stores!E:E,"No store")

Whole columns, the return column named, a trimmed key, and a not-found text that says what happened rather than pretending nothing did.

IFERROR and IFNA patterns

Three ways to handle a missing key, from bluntest to most precise. IFERROR catches every error, including a #REF! that means the sheet is broken. IFNA catches only #N/A, which is the one a lookup produces when the key is absent. XLOOKUP's own fourth argument is narrower again, because it only fires on a miss and never on a broken reference.

=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(1045,Products!A:G,2,FALSE),"Unknown product")     any error becomes text
=IFNA(XLOOKUP(1045,Products!A:A,Products!B:B),"Unknown product")   only #N/A becomes text
=XLOOKUP(1045,Products!A:A,Products!B:B,"Unknown product")         built in; other errors still show
=IFNA(XLOOKUP(1045,Products!A:A,Products!B:B),"Unknown product")

"Unknown product". Use IFNA when you are wrapping an old VLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH; use the fourth argument when you are writing XLOOKUP fresh.

Which lookup, when

You want…UseBecause
One value for one keyXLOOKUPExact by default, any direction, not-found built in.
The same, in Excel 2016 or Google Sheets without XLOOKUPINDEX/MATCHWorks everywhere; same flexibility.
Row and column both chosen by nameINDEX(MATCH, MATCH)Reads as "row, column"; nested XLOOKUP is the alternative.
A band or slab for a numberXLOOKUP … ,-1 or VLOOKUP … ,TRUEApproximate match on a sorted threshold column.
A total, not a rowSUMIFSA lookup returns one row; a key that appears many times needs a sum.
Every row that matches, not just the firstFILTERLookups stop at the first hit; FILTER returns them all (Module 07).
The position, not the valueXMATCHFor INDEX, for conditional formatting, for "which column is this".
Reading someone else's workbookVLOOKUPYou do not write it; you know how to read and fix it.
Key
The value you look up with. It has to be unique on the side you are looking into, or the lookup returns the first match and hides the rest.
Exact match
The key must equal a value in the lookup column. Case is ignored; spaces and type are not.
Approximate match
The key is placed between two thresholds of a sorted column and the nearer one (smaller for -1, larger for 1) is chosen. Slabs, bands, brackets.
Composite key
Two or more columns glued into one text key so a single lookup can match on both, like store & month.
Orphan
A key on one list with no partner on the other. Finding orphans is reconciliation, and it comes before joining.

Data validation: stop the bad key at the door

Half of all #N/A errors come from a human typing "Kochi Store" into a cell that feeds a lookup. Data validation turns the cell into a dropdown of keys that exist, and it is a five-click setup.

  1. Select the input cells, then Data ▸ Data Tools ▸ Data Validation. The dialog opens on the Settings tab.
  2. Allow ▸ List, Source ▸ =Stores!$B$2:$B$14. Point at the column of valid values on the reference sheet. If Stores is an Excel Table, =INDIRECT("Stores[Store]") keeps the list growing with the Table. Leave "In-cell dropdown" ticked.
  3. Input Message tab. Title "Store", message "Pick from the list; names must match the Stores sheet exactly." This appears as a tooltip when the cell is selected, and it is the cheapest documentation you will ever write.
  4. Error Alert tab ▸ Style. Stop refuses anything not on the list. Warning asks "continue?". Information just tells them. For a lookup key, Stop.
  5. Test it. Type "Guwahati" in the cell. If Stop is set you cannot. Pick from the arrow instead, then watch the lookup next to it update.

Dependent dropdowns, where choosing a Category in A2 limits the SubCategory list in B2, use INDIRECT on named ranges: name each category's list of subcategories after the category, then set the second cell's Source to a formula that turns the chosen text into that name. The Lab does not run INDIRECT, so this one is reference syntax.

=INDIRECT(SUBSTITUTE(A2," ","_"))

Lists are the common case, but the Allow box has other useful settings, and the custom formula one is where you stop duplicates and out-of-range dates before they exist.

AllowUse it forExample rule
ListKeys that must match a reference sheet: store, category, statusSource =Stores!$B$2:$B$14
Whole numberRatings, quantities, countsbetween 1 and 5
DecimalDiscounts, percentagesbetween 0 and 0.5
DateOrder dates, hire datesgreater than or equal to =DATE(2024,1,1), less than or equal to =TODAY()
Text lengthMobile numbers, PIN codes, GSTINsequal to 10 for a mobile, 15 for a GSTIN
CustomAnything you can write as a formula that returns TRUE=COUNTIF($A:$A,A2)=1 refuses a duplicate id

Data ▸ Data Tools ▸ Data Validation ▸ Circle Invalid Data draws red rings round every cell that breaks its rule, including cells filled before the rule existed. Run it on an inherited sheet before you run anything else; it is the fastest audit you will find.

Application: the Monday review pack

One key in, one value out

Arjun's scorecard starts with the region for each store. City is on the Sales sheet, Region is on Stores, and the walk is city to region.

=XLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:C,Stores!E:E)

South. Replace "Kochi" with a cell reference, copy down, and the whole column fills. Now the missing-key case: Guwahati is on the expansion list but not on the Stores sheet yet.

=XLOOKUP("Guwahati",Stores!C:C,Stores!B:B,"No store")

"No store" instead of #N/A. Use this when a miss is expected and you want the sheet to read cleanly; leave it off when a miss means something is wrong upstream and you want to see it. A pack full of "No store" is a pack nobody looks at.

Several columns at once

The return_array can be more than one column, and the answer spills across as many cells. StoreID 12, the whole row from Store to SqFt:

=XLOOKUP(12,Stores!A:A,Stores!B:H)

Name, city, state, region, type, opening date as a serial, 5,500 sq ft. In a scorecard you rarely want them all, and CHOOSECOLS lets you pick the ones you do, in the order you want them.

=XLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:C,CHOOSECOLS(Stores!A:H,2,5,8))

Three cells, one formula, and if someone inserts a column in Stores the formula still points at the right ones because it names them by position inside a range you control.

Wildcards and searching from the bottom

Match mode 2 turns on wildcards. You know the store name ends in Kochi but not the exact prefix:

=TEXT(XLOOKUP("*Kochi",Stores!B:B,Stores!G:G,,2),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

10-Apr-2024. The two commas with nothing between them skip if_not_found. Search mode -1 starts from the last row, which on a sheet sorted by date is how you get "most recent". The Sales sheet is in order-id order, so the first match for Kochi is its first ever line and the last match is its latest.

=TEXT(XLOOKUP("Novamart MG Road Kochi",Sales!D:D,Sales!B:B),"dd-mmm-yyyy")
=TEXT(XLOOKUP("Novamart MG Road Kochi",Sales!D:D,Sales!B:B,,0,-1),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

28-Apr-2024 and 11-Aug-2026. Two-and-a-bit years of trading with no helper column and no sort. Before XLOOKUP, "last transaction per customer" was a MAXIFS or a pivot; now it is a sixth argument.

Chaining lookups across sheets

Orders has a CustomerID; the name is on Customers. Two hops means one lookup inside another: the inner one finds the id, the outer one turns the id into a name.

=XLOOKUP(XLOOKUP(10001,Orders!A:A,Orders!C:C),Customers!A:A,Customers!B:B)

Vivek Sheikh. The same idea feeds a lookup into a SUMIFS from Module 03: the city is what the manager types, the store name is what the Sales sheet needs.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,XLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:C,Stores!B:B),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹2,55,305 delivered at Kochi across its life. Change the city in one cell and every number on the store page follows.

Two-way lookups

Arjun wants "SqFt for Kochi" where both the row and the column are chosen by name. This is where INDEX/MATCH reads best: one MATCH finds the row, one finds the column, INDEX picks the intersection.

=INDEX(Stores!A:H,MATCH("Kochi",Stores!C:C,0),MATCH("SqFt",Stores!1:1,0))

5500. The XLOOKUP version nests one lookup inside the other: the inner one returns the whole row for Kochi, the outer one picks the SqFt column from it.

=XLOOKUP("SqFt",Stores!1:1,XLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:C,Stores!A:H))

Same 5500. Both are right; pick the one your colleague will be able to read at 6 pm. XMATCH on its own is useful when the position is the answer: which column is SqFt, or which row is the Kothrud store.

=XMATCH("SqFt",Stores!1:1)
=XMATCH("*Kothrud",Stores!B:B,2)

8 and 8: SqFt is the eighth column, and Kothrud is the eighth row including the header, so StoreID 7. The position is what you feed to INDEX, or to a conditional-format rule that highlights the matched row.

Two keys at once

Targets has one row per store per month, so the key is store and month. The trick is to glue both keys with & in the lookup_value and glue both columns in the lookup_array; XLOOKUP compares the pairs.

=XLOOKUP("Novamart Connaught Place"&"2026-08",Targets!B:B&Targets!C:C,Targets!D:D)

₹1,30,000. That is the cell that makes the "% of target" column possible: delivered revenue for the store and month, divided by this.

=TEXT(
    SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,"Novamart Connaught Place",Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
    / XLOOKUP("Novamart Connaught Place"&"2026-08",Targets!B:B&Targets!C:C,Targets!D:D),
    "0.0%")

94.7%. Copy that across thirteen stores and Arjun has his scorecard. VLOOKUP cannot do a two-key lookup at all without a helper column that concatenates the keys on the Targets sheet; that is the fifth trap, if you want one.

The other way to write a multi-key lookup is to look for the number 1 in a column you build on the fly: each comparison is TRUE or FALSE, multiplying them gives 1 only where both are TRUE, and XLOOKUP finds the first 1. The same idea gives you a lookup on any condition, not just equality.

=XLOOKUP(1,(Targets!B2:B414="Novamart Koramangala")*(Targets!C2:C414="2026-08"),Targets!D2:D414)
=XLOOKUP(1,(Employees!C2:C86="Marketing")*(Employees!H2:H86=""),Employees!B2:B86)
=XLOOKUP(TRUE,Stores!H2:H14<6000,Stores!B2:B14)

₹50,000 for Koramangala, Simran Mehta for Marketing, and Rajpur Road at 5,000 sq ft. Bounded ranges here, because a comparison against a whole column would build a million-row array for nothing. And the classic "which row holds the biggest value" is a lookup where the key is a MAX:

=XLOOKUP(MAX(Sales!P:P),Sales!P:P,Sales!J:J)

Orbit Book 15 Laptop (i7/16GB), a ₹2,71,968 line: four laptops to a small-business customer at Banjara Hills. If two lines tied for the maximum you would only see the first, which is the standing caveat on every lookup in this module.

The scorecard row, assembled

Arjun's sheet has the store name in column A and one formula per column after it. Every one is a lookup or a SUMIFS keyed on $A2, so the row copies down thirteen times and the month sits in one cell, $B$1, that he can change himself.

ColumnFormula in row 2Note
B Region=XLOOKUP($A2,Stores!B:B,Stores!E:E,"Online")The online store has a blank region; the not-found text labels it.
C Target=XLOOKUP($A2&$B$1,Targets!B:B&Targets!C:C,Targets!D:D,0)Composite key; 0 when a new store has no target yet.
D Delivered=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,$A2,Sales!C:C,$B$1,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")Module 03. Total, not lookup, because a store has many lines.
E % of target=IF(C2=0,"n/a",D2/C2)Guard the division; the 23 empty store-months live here.
F Commission=XLOOKUP(D2,Slabs!A:A,Slabs!B:B,,-1)Slab table on its own sheet, sorted ascending, starting at 0.

The same row as one sentence, with LET naming each piece so the formula reads top to bottom. This is the shape of a "headline" cell on a dashboard.

=LET(store,"Novamart Andheri West",
    region,XLOOKUP(store,Stores!B:B,Stores!E:E),
    target,XLOOKUP(store&"2026-08",Targets!B:B&Targets!C:C,Targets!D:D),
    actual,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,store,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
    store&" ("&region&"): ₹"&TEXT(actual,"#,##,##0")&" of ₹"&TEXT(target,"#,##,##0")&", "&TEXT(actual/target,"0%"))

"Novamart Andheri West (West): ₹49,434 of ₹70,000, 71%". Swap the store name for a cell with a validation dropdown on it and Nandini can page through the stores without touching a formula.

Bands and slabs: approximate match

Priya's loyalty tiers are Bronze up to ₹50,000 of lifetime spend, Silver to ₹2,00,000, Gold above. Nobody's spend is exactly ₹50,000, so an exact match finds nothing; what you want is "the largest threshold that is not more than the spend". That is match_mode -1, and the thresholds must be sorted ascending. The table can be a range, or it can be typed in as an array constant, with ; between rows.

=XLOOKUP(65000,{0;50000;200000},{"Bronze";"Silver";"Gold"},,-1)

Silver. Feed in a real customer's delivered spend and the tier computes itself:

=XLOOKUP(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!H:H,"Vivek Sheikh",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
    {0;50000;200000},
    {"Bronze";"Silver";"Gold"},,-1)

Gold, on ₹4,54,630 across 38 orders. The VLOOKUP form of the same slab uses a two-column array constant with , between columns and TRUE for approximate:

=VLOOKUP(65000,{0,"Bronze";50000,"Silver";200000,"Gold"},2,TRUE)

Silver again. This is the one place VLOOKUP's default is what you want, and the one place a sorted table is not optional. Nandini's store-manager incentive works the same way: 2% of delivered revenue above ₹50,000 in the month, 4% above ₹1,00,000, 6% above ₹1,50,000.

=XLOOKUP(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,"Novamart Connaught Place",Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
    {0;50000;100000;150000},
    {0;0.02;0.04;0.06},,-1)

4%, on ₹1,23,126 of delivered revenue. Match mode 1 is the mirror image, "exact or next larger", for shipping-weight bands and the like where you round up to the band above.

Lookups that return arrays

The lookup_value can be a whole column. XLOOKUP then returns one answer per key, spilled down, which is a full join in one cell.

=XLOOKUP({"Kochi";"Pune";"Guwahati"},Stores!C:C,Stores!B:B,"No store")

Three rows: the two store names and "No store". Point the first argument at Targets!A2:A414 instead and you have the region for every target row without copying anything down.

Keys have types. StoreID is a number on the Stores sheet, and a "13" that arrived as text from a CSV will never match it, even though it looks identical.

=XLOOKUP("13",Stores!A:A,Stores!B:B,"text key, no match")

"text key, no match". Wrap the key in VALUE(), or convert the column with Text to Columns, and it becomes Novamart.in (Online). This is the cause of more mystery #N/As than anything else.

Reconciling two lists

Before you trust any join, ask which keys on one side have no partner on the other. COUNTIFS counts how often each key appears in the other list; zero means orphan. For one row, the pattern you would copy down:

=COUNTIFS(Orders!C:C,Customers!A6)

Zero: customer 5 has never ordered. As a spilled list of every such customer, wrapped in ROWS to count them:

=ROWS(FILTER(Customers!B2:B501,COUNTIFS(Orders!C:C,Customers!A2:A501)=0))

91 of 500, which is Priya's re-activation list for the festive campaign. Drop the ROWS to see the names. The other direction, Targets against Stores, is where the Kochi opening date shows up:

=FILTER(Stores!B2:B14,COUNTIFS(Targets!A:A,Stores!A2:A14,Targets!C:C,"2024-01")=0,"all 13 have a target")

Only Kochi, which opened in April 2024, so its first target is April. And the version Arjun actually asked for, target rows that have no sales lines at all in that month:

=FILTER(Targets!B2:B414&" "&Targets!C2:C414,
    COUNTIFS(Sales!D:D,Targets!B2:B414,Sales!C:C,Targets!C2:C414)=0,
    "none")

23 store-months, mostly the small North and South stores in quiet months. Each of those is a #DIV/0! waiting to happen on the scorecard, and knowing the list in advance is what lets you wrap exactly those cells and no others.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askFormula or feature
Finance"Target next to actual for every store and month."Two-key XLOOKUP on store & month
HR"Manager's name on every employee row, not the ManagerID."Nested XLOOKUP on the Employees sheet itself
Marketing"Campaign name and dates for each tagged order."XLOOKUP on CampaignID; COUNTIFS for attribution counts
Merchandising"Unit cost and list price for a product name, margin per unit."XLOOKUP returning two columns from Products
Store ops"Latest restock date per product per store."XLOOKUP with search_mode -1 on Inventory
CRM"Loyalty tier from lifetime spend."Slab lookup with match_mode -1
Data entry"Stop people typing store names that don't exist."Data validation list from Stores

The HR one. ManagerID points back into the same sheet, so the inner lookup reads the manager's id and the outer one reads that id's name.

=XLOOKUP(XLOOKUP(20,Employees!A:A,Employees!K:K),Employees!A:A,Employees!B:B)

Dev Rawat. Kavita's org chart is this formula copied down 85 rows. Marketing next: an order tagged with CampaignID 8 needs the campaign's name and dates, and Priya wants to know how many orders the tag actually caught.

=XLOOKUP(8,Campaigns!A:A,Campaigns!B:B)
    &": "&TEXT(XLOOKUP(8,Campaigns!A:A,Campaigns!E:E),"dd-mmm")
    &" to "&TEXT(XLOOKUP(8,Campaigns!A:A,Campaigns!F:F),"dd-mmm-yyyy")
=COUNTIFS(Orders!E:E,8)

"Big Diwali Dhamaka 2025: 10-Oct to 25-Oct-2025", and 15 tagged orders against a ₹60 lakh TV budget. That is not a campaign result; it is an attribution problem, and finding it is the job. Rohan's margin question is a two-column return: unit cost and list price side by side, and the difference is the gross margin per unit.

=XLOOKUP("Nimbus Fold Smartphone",Products!B:B,Products!G:G)
    -XLOOKUP("Nimbus Fold Smartphone",Products!B:B,Products!F:F)

₹12,999.80 per unit, about 20% of the ₹64,999 list price. Two lookups on the same key is fine at this size; on a 50,000-row sheet you would look up once with a two-column return_array and subtract the spilled cells.

Practice

Each answer is one formula that returns one value. Say the walk out loud before you type: "the key is X, it lives in column Y of sheet Z, I want column W back."

Exercise 1 · Region by city

Which region is the Chennai store in? Use XLOOKUP against the Stores sheet.

Hint

City is column C, Region is column E.

Show solution 
=XLOOKUP("Chennai",Stores!C:C,Stores!E:E)

South. Note that the key column is C, not A: with VLOOKUP you would have had to give it Stores!C:E and column 3.

Exercise 2 · List price with INDEX/MATCH

What is the list price of ProductID 104? Write it with INDEX and MATCH, not XLOOKUP.

Hint

MATCH finds the row of 104 in Products!A:A with a 0 for exact; INDEX reads that row of Products!G:G.

Show solution 
=INDEX(Products!G:G,MATCH(104,Products!A:A,0))

₹64,999: the Nimbus Fold. Forget the 0 and MATCH switches to approximate mode, which on an id column that happens to be sorted gives the right answer today and the wrong one the day a product is deleted.

Exercise 3 · Two-way lookup by header

Return the Kochi store's opening date as text in dd-mmm-yyyy format, finding the column by its header "Opened" rather than by letter.

Hint

INDEX over Stores!A:H, MATCH "Kochi" in column C for the row, MATCH "Opened" in row 1 for the column, then TEXT.

Show solution 
=TEXT(INDEX(Stores!A:H,MATCH("Kochi",Stores!C:C,0),MATCH("Opened",Stores!1:1,0)),"dd-mmm-yyyy")

10-Apr-2024. The nested-XLOOKUP form, XLOOKUP("Opened",Stores!1:1,XLOOKUP("Kochi",Stores!C:C,Stores!A:H)), returns the same serial.

Exercise 4 · Two keys

What was the target for Novamart Andheri West in August 2026? Targets has the store name in column B and the month in column C.

Hint

Glue the two keys with & on both sides of the lookup: name&month against Targets!B:B&Targets!C:C.

Show solution 
=XLOOKUP("Novamart Andheri West"&"2026-08",Targets!B:B&Targets!C:C,Targets!D:D)

₹70,000, against ₹49,434 delivered that month. A SUMIFS on Targets with two criteria gives the same number and is what you would use if a store-month could have two target rows.

Exercise 5 · A tier from a slab

Using the tier thresholds ₹0 Bronze, ₹50,000 Silver, ₹2,00,000 Gold, what tier does Rajesh Chopra's delivered spend earn him? His lines are on the Sales sheet under Customer.

Hint

Inner SUMIFS for the spend, outer XLOOKUP with match_mode -1 against the array constants.

Show solution 
=XLOOKUP(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!H:H,"Rajesh Chopra",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
    {0;50000;200000},
    {"Bronze";"Silver";"Gold"},,-1)

Bronze, on ₹7,860 of delivered spend. The first threshold has to be 0, or anyone below ₹50,000 gets #N/A.

Exercise 6 · The re-activation list, counted

How many customers on the Customers sheet have no order on the Orders sheet? Return the count, not the names.

Hint

COUNTIFS(Orders!C:C, Customers!A2:A501) gives one count per customer; FILTER keeps the zeros; ROWS counts what is left. Bounded ranges, because the header would otherwise be a "customer".

Show solution 
=ROWS(FILTER(Customers!A2:A501,COUNTIFS(Orders!C:C,Customers!A2:A501)=0))

91. SUM(--(COUNTIFS(...)=0)) is the older idiom for the same count and is worth recognising: the double minus turns TRUE/FALSE into 1/0.

Exercise 7 · Most recent, without sorting

What is the OrderID of the last delivered line on the Sales sheet? The sheet is in OrderID order, so "last" means "search from the bottom".

Hint

Match mode 0, search mode -1: the last two arguments are ,0,-1.

Show solution 
=XLOOKUP("Delivered",Sales!Q:Q,Sales!A:A,,0,-1)

Order 13000, the final order in the file. Swap Sales!A:A for Sales!B:B inside TEXT and you get its date, 20-Aug-2026.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

An approximate match on an unsorted table returns an answer, and the answer is wrong. VLOOKUP with TRUE, MATCH without the 0, and XLOOKUP with -1 or 1 all assume the lookup column goes up. Sort the slab table ascending, put the smallest threshold first, and start it at zero.

Watch out

Duplicates in the key column are silent. If two rows of Targets carried the same store and month, XLOOKUP would return the first and never mention the second. Before you rely on a column as a key, check ROWS(UNIQUE(range)) against ROWS(range); when they differ, the lookup should be a SUMIFS, or the source needs fixing.

Pro habit

Reconcile before you join. One COUNTIFS per key, filtered to the zeros, on both sides. It takes two minutes and it is the difference between "the numbers tie" and "the numbers look fine". Put the two orphan lists on a Checks tab and leave them there; the next person will thank you.

  • Trim the key. A trailing space from a CSV export is invisible and fatal. XLOOKUP(TRIM(A2), ...) costs nothing.
  • Match the type. Text "13" is not number 13. Look for left-aligned numbers and green triangles in the key column; VALUE() or Text to Columns fixes them.
  • Prefer the whole column or the whole Table. Stores!C:C or Stores[City]. A bounded C2:C14 silently stops covering the Guwahati row when it is added.
  • Don't wrap in IFERROR by reflex. IFNA is narrower and catches only the not-found case; XLOOKUP's fourth argument is narrower still. A #REF! hiding under IFERROR is a lie in the pack.
  • Return several columns in one lookup. One XLOOKUP with B:H beats seven XLOOKUPs on the same key; it is faster and there is one place to fix.
  • Name the slab table. A named range TierSlabs beats an array constant typed into twelve formulas. Array constants are for teaching and for one-off checks.
  • Validation on inputs, lookups on outputs. If the key is typed by a person, give the cell a dropdown. Then the lookup never sees a key that does not exist.

On the job

In the assessment test

The lookup task is the one the examiner watches. Typically: "bring the region and target onto the sales sheet and compute % of target". The tell-tales of a strong candidate are an XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH rather than VLOOKUP with a hard-coded column number, a deliberate choice about what to show when the key is missing, and a quick check that the key column has no duplicates. A slab question (commission, grade bands, tax brackets) appears in about a third of tests and is the one most candidates get wrong, because they try to do it with nested IFs.

First 90 days

You will inherit a workbook with thirty VLOOKUPs, half of them missing the FALSE. Don't rewrite them on day one. Add a Checks tab, reconcile the keys, and fix the ones the reconciliation catches. Rewrite to XLOOKUP when you have a reason to touch the sheet anyway, and say why in the commit message, which in Excel means the version history comment.

"What are the differences between VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP?"
XLOOKUP takes the lookup column and return column as separate ranges, so it can return from the left and does not break when columns are inserted. It defaults to exact match, has a built-in not-found value, can search from the last row, supports wildcards and approximate match in either direction, and can return several columns at once. VLOOKUP needs the key in the first column, a column number, an explicit FALSE, and an IFERROR wrapper.
"How would you do a lookup on two criteria?"
Concatenate the keys on both sides: XLOOKUP(key1&key2, col1&col2, return). The alternative is XLOOKUP(1, (col1=key1)*(col2=key2), return), which multiplies two TRUE/FALSE arrays into 1s and 0s and looks for the first 1. If the result should be a total rather than a single row, it is a SUMIFS, not a lookup.
"Why does my VLOOKUP return #N/A when I can see the value in the table?"
Almost always one of three: a trailing or leading space in one of the two cells, a number stored as text on one side and a real number on the other, or the key not being in the first column of the table range given to VLOOKUP. Check with LEN, with ISNUMBER, and by reading the range.

Quick check

1. =VLOOKUP(1045,Products!A:G,2) returns "Munchly Trail Mix 500g", but there is no product 1045. Why?

Without FALSE, VLOOKUP assumes a sorted first column and returns the nearest smaller key, which is product 172, the last row. Always write the FALSE, or use XLOOKUP.

2. You need the target for a store and a month from a sheet with one row per store-month. Which works?

Gluing the keys on both sides makes a single composite key. Options a and b match the store only and return its first month's target every time.

3. For a commission slab (0, 50,000, 1,00,000, 1,50,000) which XLOOKUP match_mode finds the right band for ₹1,23,126?

A slab is "the highest threshold you have crossed", so you want the next smaller item: 1,00,000, the 4% band. Mode 1 would give 1,50,000, a band the store has not reached.

4. Your XLOOKUP on StoreID returns #N/A for every row, though the ids look identical on both sheets. First thing to check?

"Every row fails" is the signature of a type mismatch, usually a CSV import storing ids as text. XLOOKUP is happy to return from the left, and Excel recalculates on its own.

Level 1 · Module 05 · about 75 min

PivotTables: the manager's summary machine

Nobody in a review meeting wants 6,314 rows. They want twelve. A PivotTable turns the whole Sales sheet into "revenue by region and channel" in four drags, and then answers the follow-up question in one more. It is also the fastest way to produce a wrong number with total confidence, so this module teaches the machine and the formula that checks it.

  • You'll say the grain of a PivotTable before you build it, and know why "count of OrderID" on the Sales sheet is not the number of orders.
  • You'll drive the Fields pane: Rows, Columns, Values and Filters, and switch a value from SUM to COUNT to AVERAGE without rebuilding anything.
  • You'll use Show Values As for % of column, % of parent, running totals and year-on-year difference, and group dates into months, quarters and years.
  • You'll add slicers and a timeline, sort, apply a Top 10 filter, and lay the pivot out in tabular form so it can feed further analysis.
  • You'll reproduce every pivot with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and UNIQUE, so you can prove a number before it goes on a slide.

Concept

Thursday, 4:40 pm

Nandini Rao's message lands while you're packing up: "For Monday I need revenue by region and channel, the Diwali months for both years, and top ten products. Also, why does the region chart Vikram sent me have a blank slice?" Vikram is on leave until Tuesday. The Sales sheet has 6,314 rows. You have a PivotTable and, if you're careful, an hour.

The Sales sheet is one row per order line. Order 10004 is two rows because Amit Gill bought a pressure cooker and a pair of sneakers in one visit. That is the sheet's grain, and every number you build from it inherits it. Sum the revenue column and you get the right total, because each line's revenue is only on its own row. Count the OrderID column and you get 6,314, which is the number of lines, not the 3,000 orders Nandini means when she says "orders".

A PivotTable does exactly one thing: it sorts rows into buckets by the values you name, then collapses each bucket into one number. Put Channel in Rows and LineRevenue in Values and you get three rows: App, Online, Store. Add Region to Columns and each of those three splits again. If you've written SQL, this is GROUP BY with a drag-and-drop front end; the SQL for Managers module on GROUP BY is the same lesson in another language.

Why a manager cares

Every number on the Monday pack is an aggregate over some grain. A pivot lets a manager ask "and by store?" and get an answer in the meeting instead of on Wednesday. It also lets a trainee report 6,314 "orders" to a CFO who knows there were 3,000, and that is the last analysis that trainee presents unsupervised. Learn the tool and learn the check.

How it works

Start from a Table, never from a plain range. Ctrl+T on the Sales sheet, name it tblSales in Table Design ▸ Properties ▸ Table Name, and every pivot built on it picks up new rows on Refresh. A pivot on A1:R6315 silently ignores row 6,316 forever.

  1. Click inside tblSales, then Insert ▸ Tables ▸ PivotTable ▸ From Table/Range. The dialog already shows the Table name. Choose New Worksheet. A blank pivot appears on the left and the PivotTable Fields pane on the right.
  2. Drag Channel to Rows. Three labels appear: App, Online, Store, sorted A to Z. Nothing else yet, because there's no value to compute.
  3. Drag LineRevenue to Values. It becomes "Sum of LineRevenue" because the column is numeric. Drag a text column such as Customer there and it becomes "Count of Customer", which is why counts sneak into pivots that were meant to sum.
  4. Drag Region to Columns and Status to Filters. The pivot is now a grid, with a Status dropdown above it. Pick Delivered and every cell recomputes.
  5. Right-click any number ▸ Number Format ▸ Custom ▸ [>=10000000]₹##\,##\,##0;[>=100000]₹##\,##0;₹#,##0. Format inside the pivot, not the cells, or the format vanishes on Refresh.

What each area does

AreaFormula twinPut hereDon't put here
Rowsthe first criteria in SUMIFS; the list from UNIQUEStore, Region, Category, Month: anything with 3 to 40 distinct valuesOrderID or Customer on their own, unless you want a 500-row list
Columnsthe second criteria, across the pageChannel, Year, Status: two to six valuesProduct: the pivot becomes wider than the screen
ValuesSUM, COUNT, AVERAGE, MAX of a columnLineRevenue, Qty, Refunda text column when you mean a sum; it will count
Filtersan extra criteria pair applied to everythingStatus, Segmentthe field you also have in Rows; use a slicer instead

Summarise by, and Show Values As

Click the small arrow on "Sum of LineRevenue" ▸ Value Field Settings. The first tab picks the aggregate. The second, Show Values As, keeps the aggregate and changes what is displayed, which is where half the "insight" on a slide comes from.

Show Values AsWhat it showsThe question it answersFormula twin
% of Column Totaleach row as a share of the column's grand total"What share of revenue is Electronics?"SUMIFS(…)/SUM(…)
% of Parent Row Totala child row as a share of its parent row"Within the Store channel, how much is North?"SUMIFS(…two criteria…)/SUMIFS(…one criterion…)
Running Total Incumulative sum down a base field, usually Month"Where are we year-to-date?"SUMIFS(…,Month,"<="&m)
Difference From / % Difference Fromthis row minus a base item, usually the previous year"How did Diwali 2025 compare with 2024?"SUMIFS(2025)-SUMIFS(2024)
Rank Largest to Smallest1, 2, 3 … by value"Which store is fourth?"SORTBY(…,-1)

Grouping dates

  1. Drag OrderDate to Rows. Excel 365 auto-groups it into Years ▸ Quarters ▸ OrderDate and adds the helper fields to the list. If it doesn't, right-click any date ▸ Group.
  2. In the Grouping dialog tick Months, Quarters and Years together. Ticking Months alone stacks January 2024 on top of January 2025. Years plus Months keeps them apart.
  3. Drag Years to Columns and leave Months in Rows. That is the year-on-year grid Arjun asks for every quarter, built in ten seconds.

Slicers and a timeline

  1. Click inside the pivot ▸ PivotTable Analyze ▸ Filter ▸ Insert Slicer ▸ tick Channel and Status. Two button panels appear. Ctrl+click selects several buttons; the funnel icon clears.
  2. PivotTable Analyze ▸ Filter ▸ Insert Timeline ▸ OrderDate. A date bar appears. Switch its level from Months to Quarters with the dropdown on the right, drag across Oct to Dec 2025.
  3. Right-click a slicer ▸ Report Connections. Tick every pivot on the sheet. One click now filters the whole dashboard, which is the entire trick behind Module 07.

Reading a pivot from a formula: GETPIVOTDATA

Type = in a cell and click a pivot value, and Excel writes this instead of =B5:

=GETPIVOTDATA("LineRevenue",$A$3,"Channel","App")

It looks alarming and is a gift. It fetches "the LineRevenue value for Channel = App from the pivot anchored at A3", and keeps fetching the right cell after the pivot is re-sorted, filtered or grows a row. Cover sheets that read from pivots should use it. If you'd rather have plain references while you explore, turn it off under PivotTable Analyze ▸ PivotTable ▸ Options ▸ Generate GetPivotData. The Lab doesn't run it, because there is no pivot to point at.

Layout for further analysis

The default Compact layout stacks Region and Channel in one column with indents. Pretty on screen, useless as a source for a lookup. Switch it under Design ▸ Layout ▸ Report Layout ▸ Show in Tabular Form and then Repeat All Item Labels. Now every row carries its own Region and its own Channel, and XLOOKUP or a second pivot can read it. Turn off subtotals (Design ▸ Layout ▸ Subtotals ▸ Do Not Show) for the same reason.

Application: the Monday review pack

Each pivot below comes with the formula that gives the same number. Build the pivot in Excel, run the formula in the Lab, and don't put anything on Nandini's slide until they agree.

Pivot 1 · Revenue by Channel

Channel in Rows, LineRevenue in Values. Three rows. The App row is the one Sameer Joshi will quote, so check it first.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App")

₹54,92,081, about a fifth of everything, which is why Sameer wants the app budget doubled. The whole pivot in one formula: UNIQUE makes the Rows area, SUMIFS with that list as its criterion makes the Values area, HSTACK glues them side by side.

=LET(k,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!G2:G6315)),
    HSTACK(k,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,k)))

Store ₹1.24 crore, Online ₹92.9 lakh, App ₹54.9 lakh, total ₹2.72 crore. Same three rows the pivot shows, in the same order. Excel 365 also has a GROUPBY function that does this in one call; the Lab doesn't run it, so the UNIQUE + SUMIFS pair is the version you can check anywhere.

=GROUPBY(Sales!G2:G6315,Sales!P2:P6315,SUM)

Pivot 2 · "Orders" by Channel, and the grain trap

Drag OrderID to Values. It says "Count of OrderID" and shows 6,314 in the grand total. That is lines. The formula makes the mistake visible:

=COUNTA(Sales!A:A)-1

6,314, minus one for the header. Now the number Nandini means:

=ROWS(UNIQUE(Sales!A2:A6315))

3,000 orders. A plain pivot cannot do this. The fix in Excel is to tick Add this data to the Data Model when you insert the pivot; Value Field Settings then offers Distinct Count. Per channel, the formula version filters first and counts the distinct ids after:

=ROWS(UNIQUE(FILTER(Sales!A2:A6315,Sales!G2:G6315="App")))

577 App orders, from 1,262 App lines. The Orders sheet is one row per order, so it is the independent check: =COUNTIFS(Orders!F:F,"App") also gives 577. When two sheets at different grains agree, you can stop worrying.

=LET(k,SORT(UNIQUE(Orders!F2:F3001)),
    HSTACK(k,COUNTIFS(Orders!F:F,k)))

App 577, Online 1,041, Store 1,382. Store still wins on orders as well as on rupees.

Pivot 3 · Average of what?

Switch LineRevenue to AVERAGE and the pivot reports ₹4,303. That's the average line. The average order, which is what "average basket" means in a retail review, is revenue divided by orders:

=SUM(Sales!P:P)/ROWS(UNIQUE(Sales!A2:A6315))

₹9,056, more than double. =AVERAGE(Orders!J:J) returns the same ₹9,056 because OrderValue is already at order grain. Whenever a pivot shows an average, ask "average per what?".

Pivot 4 · Region by Channel, and the blank slice

Region in Rows, Channel in Columns, LineRevenue in Values. Four regions plus a fifth row labelled "(blank)". Nandini's blank slice is that row. Online and App orders have no store, so the Stores sheet has no region for Novamart.in, and the Sales sheet inherits the blank.

=LET(r,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!F2:F6315)),
    HSTACK(r,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,r,Sales!G:G,"Store"),
             SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,r,Sales!G:G,"Online"),
             SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,r,Sales!G:G,"App")))

South stores lead with ₹43.1 lakh, North ₹37.8 lakh, West ₹32.3 lakh, East ₹10.8 lakh. The blank row carries ₹92.9 lakh of Online and ₹54.9 lakh of App, and nothing in the Store column. The size of that row:

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,"")

₹1.48 crore, 54% of all revenue. It isn't a bug and it isn't small. The fix is a label, not a deletion: in Power Query (Module 06) replace the blank with "Online", or add a column =IF([@Region]="","Online",[@Region]) to the Table. Never filter the blank out and present the rest as "revenue by region".

Pivot 5 · % of Column Total

Category in Rows, LineRevenue in Values twice. Leave the first as a sum; set the second to Show Values As ▸ % of Column Total. The formula is the sum divided by the whole.

=LET(k,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!K2:K6315)),
    HSTACK(k,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,k),
             SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,k)/SUM(Sales!P:P)))

Electronics is 46% of revenue on ₹1.25 crore; Home & Kitchen 20%, Fashion 17%, Sports 9%, Beauty 5%, Grocery under 3%. Format the third column as a percentage in the Lab with TEXT(…,"0.0%") if you want it to read like the pivot.

Pivot 6 · % of Parent Row Total

Channel in Rows, Region nested under it, Show Values As ▸ % of Parent Row Total. Each region now reads as a share of its channel, not of the company. For North within Store:

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,"North",Sales!G:G,"Store")/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Store")

30.5%. South is 34.8% of Store. Against the company total, North is only 13.9%, which is the number you'd get from % of Column Total. Same cell, two honest percentages, and the slide has to say which one it is.

Pivot 7 · Group dates into years and quarters

OrderDate in Rows, grouped by Years. The Month column on the Sales sheet is text like 2025-10, so a wildcard does the year in one criterion.

=LET(y,{2024;2025;2026},
    HSTACK(y,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,y&"*")))

₹90.5 lakh in 2024, ₹1.03 crore in 2025 (up 13%), ₹78.7 lakh in the first eight months of 2026, already on pace to beat 2025. Quarters need real dates and a date range, which is what the pivot does behind the Group dialog:

=LET(q,{"2025-01";"2025-04";"2025-07";"2025-10"},
    HSTACK(q,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&DATEVALUE(q&"-01"),
                      Sales!B:B,"<"&EDATE(DATEVALUE(q&"-01"),3))))

Q1 ₹17.6 lakh, Q2 ₹21.5 lakh, Q3 ₹24.1 lakh, Q4 ₹39.2 lakh. The festive quarter is 38% of the year. Notice the pattern ">="&start and "<"&next_start: the upper bound is exclusive, so nothing at midnight on the boundary gets counted twice.

Pivot 8 · Running total

Month in Rows, LineRevenue twice, the second one Show Values As ▸ Running Total In ▸ Month. Because Month is YYYY-MM text, "less than or equal to this month" works as a text comparison and gives the cumulative figure.

=LET(m,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!C2:C6315)),
    HSTACK(m,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,m),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"<="&m)))

Thirty-two rows. By March 2024 the running total is ₹21.9 lakh; by December 2025 it is ₹1.93 crore; the last row equals the grand total, which is the check. A running total that doesn't end on the grand total has a sort problem.

Pivot 9 · Difference From: the Diwali months

Years in Columns, Months in Rows, Show Values As ▸ % Difference From ▸ Years ▸ (previous). Diwali fell on 1 November in 2024 and on 20 October in 2025, and the pivot shows it.

=LET(m,{"2024-10";"2024-11";"2025-10";"2025-11"},
    HSTACK(m,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,m)))

October went from ₹6.6 lakh to ₹11.4 lakh, up 74%. November went from ₹12.1 lakh to ₹12.7 lakh, up 5%. Read as a pair, the festive spend moved two weeks earlier; read as single rows, "October is up 74%" is true and misleading. This is the number Meera Krishnan will ask about, so put the two months side by side.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10")/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-10")-1

0.74, which the pivot formats as 74.2%.

Pivot 10 · Slicer plus timeline

Channel slicer on App, Status slicer on Delivered, timeline dragged across Jan to Aug 2026. Every slicer button and every timeline segment is one more criteria pair:

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",
    Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2026,1,1),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31))

₹13.5 lakh of delivered App revenue this year, from 187 orders. If your pivot shows a different figure, one slicer is still holding a selection you can't see; the funnel icon clears it.

Pivot 11 · Top 10 products

Product in Rows, LineRevenue in Values, then right-click a product ▸ Filter ▸ Top 10. Sort largest to smallest with the same right-click menu. In formulas, group first, then sort by the value, then take ten.

=LET(p,UNIQUE(Sales!J2:J6315),v,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!J:J,p),
    TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(p,v),v,-1),10))

Two laptops top the list at ₹25.1 lakh and ₹24.6 lakh each, then the Voltra X1 smartphone at ₹12.7 lakh. Eight of the ten are Electronics, which is Rohan Desai's whole buying argument in one table.

Pivot 12 · Calculated fields, and why they lie about averages

PivotTable Analyze ▸ Calculations ▸ Fields, Items & Sets ▸ Calculated Field lets you type = LineRevenue / Qty and get "average selling price" per row. It works, because it sums each column first and divides after. What doesn't work is dragging UnitPrice to Values as AVERAGE and calling that the selling price: that averages the list prices of lines, ignoring quantity and discount.

=LET(k,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!K2:K6315)),
    HSTACK(k,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,k)/SUMIFS(Sales!M:M,Sales!K:K,k),
             AVERAGEIFS(Sales!N:N,Sales!K:K,k)))

Electronics: ₹8,288 realised per unit against an average unit price of ₹8,902, a 7% discount effect the second column can't see. Calculated fields handle ratios of sums fine and fall apart on anything else (distinct counts, ratios across two tables, last year's value). That is what measures in the Data Model are for; Module 13 builds them.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askPivot setupFormula twin
Finance"Revenue by month and year, with year-on-year change."Months in Rows, Years in Columns, % Difference FromSUMIFS on Month with two criteria
Marketing"Which segment is growing?"Segment in Rows, Years in Columns, % of Column TotalSUMIFS(…)/SUMIFS(year)
Operations"Returns by reason: how many, how much."Reason in Rows, Count of ReturnID and Sum of RefundCOUNTIF + SUMIFS on Returns
HR"Headcount and average salary by department, current staff only."Department in Rows, Count of EmpID, Average of MonthlySalary, filter ExitDate = blankCOUNTIFS + AVERAGEIFS with ""
Merchandising"Top 10 products, Electronics only."Product in Rows, Category slicer, Top 10 filterTAKE(SORTBY(…))
Digital"Orders per payment method as a share."Payment in Rows, Count of OrderID on the Orders sheet, % of Column TotalCOUNTIFS(…)/COUNTA(…)

The HR one, with the exit-date filter as a blank criterion. Kavita Iyer wants people who are still here, so ExitDate must be empty.

=LET(d,SORT(UNIQUE(Employees!C2:C86)),
    HSTACK(d,COUNTIFS(Employees!C:C,d,Employees!H:H,""),
             AVERAGEIFS(Employees!I:I,Employees!C:C,d,Employees!H:H,"")))

Sales & Store Operations is 39 of the 78 current employees at an average of ₹79,269 a month; Technology & Data is 12 people at ₹1.67 lakh. The Executive Office row averages two salaries, one of them the CEO's, which is why an average with a count of 2 should never go on a slide without the count.

The operations one. Reason in Rows, two values.

=LET(r,SORT(UNIQUE(Returns!E2:E264)),
    HSTACK(r,COUNTIF(Returns!E:E,r),SUMIFS(Returns!F:F,Returns!E:E,r)))

Defective leads on both counts: 89 returns and ₹3.16 lakh refunded. "Changed mind" is second by count (61) and "Wrong item" third (50), which is a warehouse conversation, not a product one.

Practice

Formula exercises are checked in the Lab. Task exercises are done in Excel on files/novamart-m365.xlsx; compare your pivot with the formula in the solution before you trust it.

Exercise 1 · Small Business share

Priya Nair wants the Small Business segment's share of total revenue, as a fraction, the way a % of Column Total pivot would show it.

Hint

One SUMIFS on Segment (column I) divided by the grand total.

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!I:I,"Small Business")/SUM(Sales!P:P)

0.215, so about 21% of revenue on ₹58.4 lakh. Consumer is 60%, Corporate 19%.

Exercise 2 · Build the Region × Channel pivot properly

On the Sales sheet, make a Table called tblSales, build the Region-by-Channel revenue pivot, add a Status slicer, and switch to tabular layout with repeated labels. Then relabel the blank region.

Hint

The blank can't be renamed inside the pivot. Add a column to the Table and pivot on that instead.

What good looks like

The pivot sits on its own sheet, reads from tblSales, and has:

  • Rows = RegionLabel (a new Table column, =IF([@Region]="","Online",[@Region])), Columns = Channel, Values = Sum of LineRevenue formatted in ₹.
  • A Status slicer set to Delivered, with the selection visible in the slicer, not hidden in the Filters area.
  • Tabular layout, repeated labels, subtotals off, so a lookup can read it.
  • With the slicer on Delivered, the Online row showing ₹82.9 lakh under Online and ₹45.7 lakh under App, the Store column empty for it, and a grand total of ₹2.37 crore. Clear the slicer and the grand total returns to ₹2.72 crore.

Exercise 3 · Orders in October 2025

How many distinct orders were placed in October 2025? Not lines, orders. Month is text in column C.

Hint

FILTER the OrderID column on Month, then UNIQUE, then ROWS.

Show solution 
=ROWS(UNIQUE(FILTER(Sales!A2:A6315,Sales!C2:C6315="2025-10")))

146 orders, from 314 lines. A pivot with Count of OrderID would have said 314.

Exercise 4 · The festive quarter's share of 2025

What fraction of 2025 revenue came in October to December 2025? Use date criteria on OrderDate, not the Month text.

Hint

Two SUMIFS, each with a ">="&DATE(…) and a "<="&DATE(…) pair.

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2025,12,31))/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,1,1),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2025,12,31))

0.382. Three months carried 38% of the year, which is the reason the festive-season deck in Module 09 exists.

Exercise 5 · Quarterly trend with a timeline and a PivotChart

Build a pivot of revenue by quarter across all three years, add a timeline on OrderDate, and turn it into a PivotChart Nandini can read without a legend.

Hint

Group OrderDate by Quarters and Years together. PivotTable Analyze ▸ Tools ▸ PivotChart, clustered column.

What good looks like
  • Rows show Years and Quarters nested (2024 ▸ Qtr1 … 2026 ▸ Qtr3), not eleven unlabelled quarters.
  • The timeline is set to Quarters and connected to the pivot; sliding it to Q4 2025 shows ₹39.2 lakh.
  • The PivotChart has a title that states the finding ("Q4 is 38% of 2025 revenue"), one colour, and the field buttons hidden (PivotChart Analyze ▸ Show/Hide ▸ Field Buttons).
  • The chart moves with the timeline, which is the demo to give in the meeting.

Exercise 6 · Kochi in 2025

The Kochi store opened on 10 April 2024. What was its revenue in calendar 2025? Store names are in column D; the Kochi store is "Novamart MG Road Kochi".

Hint

Two criteria: Store and a wildcard on Month, "2025*".

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,"Novamart MG Road Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2025*")

₹1,21,708, the smallest store by a distance and double its partial 2024. In a pivot this is one cell of Store by Years; a Store slicer set to Kochi gets you there faster.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

"Count of OrderID" on the Sales sheet counts lines. Every table in this course that has one row per line (Sales, Inventory, Returns by line) will do this to you. Either count on the sheet whose grain matches the question (Orders), or use the Data Model and Distinct Count, or run ROWS(UNIQUE(…)) as the check. Say the grain out loud before you drag.

Watch out

A pivot is a snapshot. Paste 200 new rows under the source and the pivot shows the old numbers until you press Refresh, and if the source was a plain range rather than a Table, Refresh won't even see the new rows. Right-click ▸ PivotTable Options ▸ Data ▸ Refresh data when opening the file for anything that leaves your laptop.

Pro habit

Two sheets per analysis: the pivot sheet, laid out in tabular form and never touched by hand, and a presentation sheet that reads from it with GETPIVOTDATA and carries the formatting. When the pivot re-sorts, the presentation sheet still shows the right cell. When Vikram asks how a number was built, you can show him the pivot instead of remembering.

  • The blank bucket is real data. "(blank)" in Region is ₹1.48 crore of online business. Label it in the source, never filter it away and call the remainder "all regions".
  • Averages of averages. Average of UnitPrice is not the selling price, and Average of a monthly average is not the yearly average. Sum first, divide once.
  • Show Values As changes the display, not the aggregate. A % of Column Total pivot still sums under the hood. If you need the rupees too, drag the field into Values a second time.
  • Grouping by Months alone merges years. Tick Years with it, or every January is three Januaries added together.
  • Slicers remember. A slicer scrolled out of view is still filtering. Check the funnel icons before you read any number aloud.
  • Calculated fields are for ratios of sums. Anything else, a distinct count, a value from last year, a ratio across two tables, needs a measure in the Data Model. Module 13.
  • Recommended PivotTables is a starting point, not a finished analysis. It picks aggregates by data type, so it will count text and sum anything numeric, including OrderID.

On the job

In the assessment test

Almost every analyst screening test has one pivot task, usually "summarise revenue by X and Y and tell us the top three". The graders look at three things: did you start from a Table, did you check the grand total against a SUM, and did you notice the blank or duplicate that they planted. The formula twin is your proof; write it next to the pivot and label it "check".

First 90 days

Your first recurring deliverable will be a pack somebody else built, with pivots on plain ranges that stopped growing in March. Rebuild it on Tables, add a refresh-on-open, and put a check cell (=SUM(tblSales[LineRevenue]) next to the pivot's grand total) on every sheet. That is a week of quiet work that makes you the person whose numbers tie.

Interview question: "What is a PivotTable and when would you not use one?"
A PivotTable groups a table by one or more columns and aggregates a value per group, interactively. I'd not use one when the result has to feed further formulas (a Table with SUMIFS or a dynamic array is stabler), when I need a distinct count without the Data Model, or when the logic has to be reviewed line by line, because a pivot hides its definition in menus.
Interview question: "Your pivot says 6,314 orders and finance says 3,000. Who is right?"
Both, for different grains. My source is one row per order line, so Count of OrderID counts lines. Finance counts order headers. I'd switch to Distinct Count via the Data Model or count on the orders table, and I'd write the grain in the slide footnote.
Interview question: "How do you make sure a PivotTable stays current?"
Build it on an Excel Table so new rows are inside the source range, set Refresh on open in PivotTable Options, and keep a check cell that sums the source column next to the grand total. If the two differ, the pivot is stale or the source range was a fixed reference.

Quick check

1. You drag Customer to Values on the Sales sheet. What does the pivot show?

Text fields default to COUNT, and COUNT counts rows, so a customer with three lines counts three times. Distinct Count needs the Data Model.

2. Which Show Values As option answers "what is North's share of the Store channel", with Channel above Region in Rows?

% of Parent Row Total divides each child (Region) by its parent (Channel). % of Column Total would divide by the company total instead.

3. The pivot's grand total is ₹2.72 crore but =SUM(Sales!P:P) returns a bigger number. Most likely cause?

A pivot only sees its source range. New rows outside a plain range are invisible until you change the source; a Table would have grown with them.

4. What does =GETPIVOTDATA("LineRevenue",$A$3,"Channel","App") return after the pivot is re-sorted so App moves from row 5 to row 7?

GETPIVOTDATA looks the value up by field and item, not by address. That is the reason to use it on any sheet that reads from a pivot.

Watch and read
