Level 2 · Module 06 · about 90 min

Power Query: clean once, refresh forever

Every month somebody at Novamart opens twelve store exports, pastes them under each other, fixes the same broken dates by hand and prays the pivot still points at the right rows. Power Query is the end of that. You record the clean-up once, as a list of steps, and from then on the work is one click: Refresh. This module builds that recording on the ugliest sheet in the workbook.

  • You'll load a Table, a CSV, a whole folder of files or a SharePoint list into the Power Query editor and read its four panes.
  • You'll trim, case, split, replace, fill down, remove duplicates and change types, with every step visible in Applied Steps and reversible.
  • You'll unpivot a wide monthly sheet into tidy rows, and merge or append two queries, choosing the right join kind.
  • You'll clean the Leads export end to end: 150 rows, five phone formats, four date formats, three spellings of Bengaluru, and twenty duplicates.
  • You'll verify every step with a formula in the Lab, so "cleaned" means a number you can defend, not a feeling.

Concept

Thursday, 4:50 pm

Priya Nair forwards a spreadsheet: 150 leads from the web form, Instagram, two events and the store walk-in register. "CRM import by tonight please, and sales will start calling tomorrow. Oh, and we get this export every Thursday from now on." The CRM bills per contact. You open the file. Mohit Rao is in it twice, once in capitals. Bengaluru is spelled three ways. The dates come in four flavours, and fifteen emails have no @ sign.

You could fix this with formulas, and Module 03 taught you enough TRIM, PROPER and SUBSTITUTE to do it. Next Thursday you'd do it again. The Thursday after that, the intern would do it, differently. A formula clean-up lives in cells; it is only as repeatable as the person copying it.

Power Query moves the clean-up out of the cells and into a recipe. You point it at a source, you click through the fixes, and each click becomes a step in a list. The output lands on a sheet as a Table. When the source changes, Data ▸ Queries & Connections ▸ Refresh All re-runs the recipe from the top. The raw data is never edited, which means you can always go back, and the recipe is readable by the next person, which means it survives you.

Why a manager cares

A duplicate lead is two salespeople phoning the same person on the same afternoon. A bad email is a bounce, and enough bounces get the sending domain throttled. A dashboard that needs an hour of manual prep every Monday is a dashboard that gets skipped the week it matters. Power Query turns "clean the data" from a chore someone does into a process the file does. That is the difference between an analyst and a very fast clerk.

How it works

Get Data: where the source can live

SourceRibbon pathUse it forWatch
A Table in this workbookData ▸ Get & Transform Data ▸ From Table/Rangethe Leads sheet, anything you already havea plain range gets converted to a Table on the way in; name it first
CSV or text fileData ▸ Get Data ▸ From File ▸ From Text/CSVPOS exports, bank statements, the CRM dumpcheck the delimiter and the encoding in the preview; ₹ breaks in the wrong encoding
Another workbookFrom File ▸ From Excel Workbookthe finance team's monthly filepick the Table, not the sheet, so a stray note in Z1 doesn't become a column
A folderFrom File ▸ From Folder ▸ Combine & Transformtwelve store files with the same layoutone file with a renamed column breaks the combine; the error names the file
SharePoint / OneDriveFrom File ▸ From SharePoint Folder, or paste the file's URL into From Excel Workbookanything the team editsuse the site URL, not the browser URL with ?web=1 on the end
The webFrom Other Sources ▸ From Weban RBI rate table, a public price listtables change shape without warning; keep a copy of last month's

The transformation catalogue

Almost every clean-up you'll ever do is one of these, and each is one click plus a dialog. The M code that appears in the formula bar is the same function every time, which is how you learn M without meaning to.

StepRibbon pathWhat it doesM function behind it
Remove top rows / blank rows / errorsHome ▸ Reduce Rows ▸ Remove Rowsdrops report titles, empty spacer rows, rows that failed a type changeTable.Skip, Table.SelectRows
Choose / remove columnsHome ▸ Manage Columnskeeps only what the output needsTable.SelectColumns
Split columnTransform ▸ Text Column ▸ Split Column by delimiter, by number of characters, by digit-to-non-digit"Rao, Mohit" into two; "2026-08-19 14:28" into date and timeTable.SplitColumn
Trim / Clean / FormatTransform ▸ Text Column ▸ Formatstrips spaces, non-printing characters; lowercase, UPPERCASE, Capitalize Each WordText.Trim, Text.Clean, Text.Proper
Replace valuesTransform ▸ Any Column ▸ Replace Values"FB" to "Facebook"; "@@" to "@"; null to "Unknown"Table.ReplaceValue
Fill downTransform ▸ Any Column ▸ Fill ▸ Downfills the blanks under a merged-cell header with the value aboveTable.FillDown
Change type, with localethe type icon ▸ Using Locale…turns text into dates and numbers, telling it which country wrote themTable.TransformColumnTypes(…, "en-IN")
Conditional / custom columnAdd Column ▸ Generalan IF without cells; any expression on the rowTable.AddColumn
Group byTransform ▸ Table ▸ Group Bya pivot that outputs a tableTable.Group
UnpivotTransform ▸ Any Column ▸ Unpivot Columnswide monthly columns into long rowsTable.UnpivotOtherColumns
PivotTransform ▸ Any Column ▸ Pivot Columnthe reverse, for a report layoutTable.Pivot
Merge / AppendHome ▸ Combinejoins two queries side by side / stacks themTable.NestedJoin, Table.Combine
Remove duplicatesHome ▸ Reduce Rows ▸ Remove Rows ▸ Remove Duplicateskeeps the first row per selected column(s)Table.Distinct

Unpivot: the feature that pays for the course

Rohan Desai's category targets arrive as one row per store and one column per month, because that is how a human types a budget. Every formula and every pivot wants one row per store per month. Unpivot does the conversion in one click and, unlike copy-paste-transpose, does it again next month when a thirteenth column appears.

= Table.UnpivotOtherColumns(Source, {"Store"}, "Month", "Target")

The Targets sheet in the Lab is already the "after" shape: 13 stores × 32 months, 413 rows, one Target per row. That is what makes =SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2025-10") possible.

Merge and Append: two queries into one

Append stacks rows: twelve store files with the same columns become one long table (that is what Combine Files does for a folder). Merge joins columns: Leads gets a clean CityName column by looking up each raw spelling in a small mapping table. Merge asks which join kind you want, and the answer decides which rows survive.

Close & Load To

OptionWhat you getPick it when
Tablea Table on a new or existing sheetpeople will read it, or a pivot will sit on it
Only Create Connectionnothing on a sheet; the query exists and other queries can reference itit's an intermediate step (the raw import, the CityMap)
Add this data to the Data Modelthe table goes into Power Pivotyou want Distinct Count in a pivot or DAX measures (Module 13)
PivotTable Reportan empty pivot on the query, no Tablethe raw rows are too many to keep on a sheet

Change your mind later with Data ▸ Queries & Connections, right-click the query ▸ Load To…. A parameter (Home ▸ Manage Parameters) holds a value like the folder path or the reporting month, so the query survives being moved to another laptop: change one cell, refresh, done.

A taste of M

Every query is a small program in the M language. Home ▸ Advanced Editor shows it. You'll rarely write it from scratch; you'll edit one step in the formula bar when the dialog can't express what you want. Read it as a list of named steps, each built from the one before:

let
    Source      = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="tblLeads"]}[Content],
    Trimmed     = Table.TransformColumns(Source, {{"FullName", Text.Trim, type text}, {"Email", Text.Trim, type text}}),
    Lowercased  = Table.TransformColumns(Trimmed, {{"Email", Text.Lower, type text}}),
    Cased       = Table.TransformColumns(Lowercased, {{"FullName", Text.Proper, type text}})
in
    Cased

Three things to know. Step names with spaces are written #"Changed Type". M is case-sensitive: text.lower is an error. And null is what a blank cell becomes, so "replace null with…" is a thing you'll type often.

Excel vs Power BI

The same engine, the same editor, the same M. Power Query in Power BI Desktop has a few more connectors and the output goes to a data model rather than a sheet. A query you build here for Priya's leads pastes into Power BI unchanged via the Advanced Editor. Learn it once.

Application: clean the Leads sheet end to end

The routine is fixed and the order matters: profile, standardise, dedupe, validate, load. Dedupe before lowercasing the emails and Mohit Rao stays twice. This is the Excel twin of the SQL data-quality module, which cleans the same file in SQL; the steps line up one for one.

Profile before you touch anything

Run these in the Lab. They are the "before" numbers, and every one gets a matching "after" once the query is built.

=COUNTA(Leads!A:A)-1

150 rows. Now the blanks per column: three names, seven emails, ten phones, twenty-eight statuses.

=HSTACK(COUNTBLANK(Leads!B2:B151),COUNTBLANK(Leads!C2:C151),COUNTBLANK(Leads!D2:D151),COUNTBLANK(Leads!H2:H151))

Nobody is missing both an email and a phone, so every row is reachable. Next, the invisible problem: leading and trailing spaces. LEN of the cell against LEN of its trimmed self counts the padded ones.

=SUMPRODUCT(--(LEN(Leads!B2:B151)<>LEN(TRIM(Leads!B2:B151))))

36 of 147 names are padded, 10 emails and 14 cities too. A padded "Mumbai " is a different value from "Mumbai" to a pivot, a lookup and a CRM. The -- turns TRUE/FALSE into 1/0 so SUMPRODUCT can add them.

=HSTACK(ROWS(UNIQUE(Leads!C2:C151)),ROWS(UNIQUE(LOWER(TRIM(Leads!C2:C151)))))

133 distinct values as typed; 129 once you lowercase and trim, one of which is the blank. So 128 real distinct addresses among 143 filled cells: fifteen rows are email duplicates that exact matching would have missed by four.

=COUNTIF(Leads!C:C,"*@*")

128 of the 143 filled emails have an @. The other fifteen are addresses like joseph.gupta21outlook.com, one character from real. And six have two:

=COUNTIF(Leads!C:C,"*@@*")

Cities and sources next. Twelve spellings of six cities, seven of six sources.

=LET(u,SORT(UNIQUE(TRIM(Leads!E2:E151))),HSTACK(u,COUNTIF(TRIM(Leads!E2:E151),u)))

Bangalore 8, Bengaluru 7, BLR 6. Bombay 2 next to Mumbai 20. Hyd 8. Dehra Dun 14 and Dehradun 13. Delhi 19 and New Delhi 7. Five of the six cities have an alias; only Pune was typed one way, and even that came as PUNE, Pune and pune.

Phones come five ways. Wildcards count each shape: +91 with spaces, +91-, a leading zero, a hyphen in the middle, ten bare digits.

=HSTACK(COUNTIF(Leads!D:D,"+91 *"),COUNTIF(Leads!D:D,"+91-*"),COUNTIF(Leads!D:D,"0??????????"),COUNTIF(Leads!D:D,"?????-?????"),COUNTIF(Leads!D:D,"??????????"))

55, 13, 33, 12 and 27: 140 phones, 140 accounted for. Strip the plus, the hyphen and the space and keep the last ten characters, and the formats collapse:

=ROWS(UNIQUE(RIGHT(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(Leads!D2:D151,"+",""),"-","")," ",""),10)))-1

120 distinct numbers from 140 filled cells (the −1 removes the blank). Twenty rows share a phone with another row. Ayesha Kapoor, rows 15 to 17, is in there three times with two phone formats and one blank.

Last, the dates. Column G is text in four shapes, and the shape is visible at character 3 and character 5:

=HSTACK(SUMPRODUCT(--(MID(Leads!G2:G151,3,1)="/")),
    SUMPRODUCT(--(MID(Leads!G2:G151,5,1)="-"),--(LEN(Leads!G2:G151)=10)),
    SUMPRODUCT(--(MID(Leads!G2:G151,5,1)="-"),--(LEN(Leads!G2:G151)>10)),
    SUMPRODUCT(--(MID(Leads!G2:G151,3,1)="-")))

41 like 13/07/2026, 59 like 2026-07-20, 31 like 2026-08-19 14:28, 19 like 21-Aug-2026. Four systems, one column. Twelve of the slash dates have a day of 12 or less, which means an American parser would read 04/05/2026 as April 5th and not complain. Hold that thought for the locale step.

Step 1 · Load and undo the guess

  1. Click in the Leads sheet ▸ Ctrl+T ▸ Table Design ▸ Table Name: tblLeads. Then Data ▸ From Table/Range. The editor opens with two steps already in Applied Steps: Source and Changed Type.
  2. Click Changed Type and look at CreatedAt. Excel guessed a type for every column from the first 200 rows. If your Windows locale is English (US), it tried to read the slash dates as mm/dd and either produced errors or April 5th. Delete the step with the ✕ or reopen it with ⚙ and set CreatedAt back to Text. Types are set deliberately, at the end.
  3. Rename the query Leads_Clean in Query Settings. Names with spaces work but you'll type #"Leads Clean" in M forever after.

Step 2 · Standardise text

  1. Select FullName, Email, City, Source ▸ Transform ▸ Format ▸ Trim, then Format ▸ Clean. Trim removes the padding; Clean removes line breaks and other non-printing characters that copy-paste from web forms leaves behind.
  2. Select FullName ▸ Format ▸ Capitalize Each Word. Select Email ▸ Format ▸ lowercase. MOHIT RAO becomes Mohit Rao; the 22 all-caps emails match their lowercase twins. Do this before any duplicate check.
  3. Select Source ▸ Format ▸ Capitalize Each Word, then Replace Values: "Fb" → "Facebook". Seven source labels become six.
= Table.TransformColumns(#"Changed Type", {{"FullName", Text.Trim, type text}, {"Email", Text.Trim, type text}, {"City", Text.Trim, type text}, {"Source", Text.Trim, type text}})
= Table.TransformColumns(#"Trimmed Text", {{"FullName", Text.Proper, type text}, {"Email", Text.Lower, type text}, {"Source", Text.Proper, type text}})
= Table.ReplaceValue(#"Capitalized Each Word", "Fb", "Facebook", Replacer.ReplaceValue, {"Source"})

The Lab check for the Source step, using PROPER and a single IF to mirror the replace:

=LET(s,PROPER(TRIM(Leads!F2:F151)),m,IF(s="Fb","Facebook",s),u,SORT(UNIQUE(m)),HSTACK(u,COUNTIF(m,u)))

Web Form 38, Referral 31, Instagram 26, Facebook 25, Walk-In 18, Event 12. Six rows, 150 leads. Note PROPER capitalises after a hyphen, so it's "Walk-In"; Capitalize Each Word does the same. Fix it with one more Replace Value if the CRM is fussy.

Step 3 · Cities through a mapping table

You could do six Replace Values. A mapping table is better because Priya's team can add "Blore" to it next month without opening the query. Put a two-column Table on a sheet called CityMap: Variant (bangalore, blr, bombay, hyd, new delhi, dehra dun, plus the six correct names in lowercase) and CityName (Bengaluru, Bengaluru, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Delhi, Dehradun, …). Load it as a connection only.

  1. In Leads_Clean, Add Column ▸ Custom Column: Text.Lower([City]), name it CityKey. The merge will be case-sensitive, so both sides must agree.
  2. Home ▸ Combine ▸ Merge Queries ▸ CityMap, match CityKey to Variant, Join Kind: Left Outer. The dialog reports "The selection matches 150 of 150 rows". If it says 136, a spelling is missing from the map; switch to Left Anti for a second to see which.
  3. Click the expand icon on the new CityMap column ▸ tick CityName only ▸ untick "Use original column name as prefix". Then remove City and CityKey. Twelve spellings are now six names.
= Table.NestedJoin(#"Added CityKey", {"CityKey"}, CityMap, {"Variant"}, "CityMap", JoinKind.LeftOuter)
= Table.ExpandTableColumn(#"Merged Queries", "CityMap", {"CityName"}, {"CityName"})

The Lab twin is a nested IF doing the map's job. Same six buckets, same counts, so the merge is right:

=LET(c,LOWER(TRIM(Leads!E2:E151)),
    m,IF((c="bangalore")+(c="blr"),"Bengaluru",IF(c="bombay","Mumbai",IF(c="hyd","Hyderabad",
        IF(c="new delhi","Delhi",IF(c="dehra dun","Dehradun",PROPER(c)))))),
    u,SORT(UNIQUE(m)),HSTACK(u,COUNTIF(m,u)))

Hyderabad 28, Dehradun 27, Delhi 26, Pune 26, Mumbai 22, Bengaluru 21. Six rows adding to 150. Before mapping, "Mumbai" alone showed 20 and the Bengaluru three were 8, 7 and 6; nobody would have believed Bengaluru was the smallest market, and they'd have been right not to.

Step 4 · Phones to ten digits

  1. Add Column ▸ Custom Column, name Phone10: Text.End(Text.Remove([Phone], {"+", "-", " "}), 10). Text.Remove deletes every listed character; Text.End keeps the last ten, which drops both the 91 and the leading zero.
  2. Keep the original Phone column. Normalising throws information away (a country code, a formatting a rep chose). The CRM gets Phone10; the raw column stays for the audit.

The Lab check is the formula from the profile: 120 distinct numbers. If your query's Phone10 column has 121 distinct values, one row had a character you didn't remove; look for a dot or a bracket.

Step 5 · Emails: repair one thing, flag the rest

  1. Select Email ▸ Replace Values: "@@" → "@". Six rows fixed. That's the only repair you can do without guessing.
  2. Add Column ▸ Custom Column, EmailOK: Text.Contains([Email], "@") and Text.Contains([Email], "."). A TRUE/FALSE column. The fifteen addresses with no @ get FALSE and stay in the file; sales can fix "joseph.gupta21outlook.com" in a thirty-second call, which is cheaper than losing the lead.
=COUNTIFS(Leads!C2:C151,"?*",Leads!C2:C151,"<>*@*")

15. The first criterion, "?*", means "at least one character", so blanks aren't counted as broken. Quarantine beats deletion: a flagged row can be fixed, counted and reported; a deleted one leaves no trace.

Step 6 · Dates, using locale

  1. Add Column ▸ Custom Column, CreatedDate: Text.BeforeDelimiter([CreatedAt], " "). That strips the time off the 31 timestamp rows and leaves the other 119 untouched (no delimiter, whole text returned).
  2. Click the ABC icon on CreatedDate ▸ Using Locale… ▸ Data Type: Date, Locale: English (India). Not plain "Date". With the Indian locale, 13/07/2026 is 13 July, 04/05/2026 is 4 May, 2026-07-20 is ISO and 21-Aug-2026 is a named month; all four shapes parse.
  3. Home ▸ Remove Rows ▸ Remove Errors is NOT the next step. Instead, sort by CreatedDate and look at the top: if there are error rows, a fifth format slipped in. There aren't. Then Add Column ▸ Date ▸ Month ▸ Start of Month for the reporting bucket.
= Table.TransformColumnTypes(#"Added CreatedDate", {{"CreatedDate", type date}}, "en-IN")

The Lab can parse the same four shapes with a nested IF on the separator position and DATEVALUE, which doubles as the check on the query's month counts:

=LET(g,Leads!G2:G151,
    iso,IF(MID(g,3,1)="/",RIGHT(g,4)&"-"&MID(g,4,2)&"-"&LEFT(g,2),
        IF(MID(g,3,1)="-",TEXT(DATEVALUE(g),"yyyy-mm-dd"),LEFT(g,10))),
    m,LEFT(iso,7),u,SORT(UNIQUE(m)),HSTACK(u,COUNTIF(m,u)))

May 39, June 43, July 38, August 30: 150 leads, four months, none unparsed. If your Power Query month column disagrees, the locale step is wrong, and the giveaway is a lead dated in the wrong month because 04/05 flipped.

Step 7 · One survivor per person

Which rows are the same person? Same ten-digit phone, or, when the phone is blank, same normalised email. Build that key, decide which copy wins, keep it.

  1. Add Column ▸ Custom Column, PersonKey: if [Phone10] <> null then [Phone10] else [Email]. Phone first because it survives the broken-email problem: Ayesha's first row has a bad email and a good phone.
  2. Sort by EmailOK descending, then CreatedDate descending. This is the survivor rule: a valid email beats a broken one, then newest wins. Write the rule in a note next to the query.
  3. Select PersonKey ▸ Home ▸ Remove Rows ▸ Remove Duplicates. Remove Duplicates keeps the first row per key, and "first" is the sort order you just set. In M, wrap the sorted table in Table.Buffer first, or the engine may dedupe before it sorts.
= Table.Distinct(Table.Buffer(Table.Sort(#"Added PersonKey", {{"EmailOK", Order.Descending}, {"CreatedDate", Order.Descending}})), {"PersonKey"})

The Lab can count what should be left:

=LET(p,RIGHT(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(Leads!D2:D151,"+",""),"-","")," ",""),10),
    e,LOWER(TRIM(Leads!C2:C151)),k,IF(p<>"",p,e),ROWS(UNIQUE(k)))

130. From 150 rows to 130 people: twenty duplicates, which at CRM prices is not a rounding error. The key isn't perfect. Someone with a blank phone on one row and a broken email on the other slips through as two people; say so in the hand-over note rather than pretending.

Step 8 · Statuses, then load

  1. Select Status ▸ Replace Values: null → "New". Twenty-eight blanks. Priya's rule: an untouched lead is New. Ask before you assume; a blank might mean "do not call".
  2. Set final types: LeadID whole number, everything else text, CreatedDate date, EmailOK true/false. Now, at the end, when you know what each column holds.
  3. Home ▸ Close & Load To ▸ Table ▸ New worksheet. Name the sheet Leads_Clean. Next Thursday: paste the new export over tblLeads, Data ▸ Refresh All, done.
=LET(h,SORT(UNIQUE(Leads!H2:H151)),HSTACK(h,COUNTIF(Leads!H2:H151,h)))

Contacted 35, Lost 31, New 29, Qualified 27, blank 28. After the fill New is 57, and after the dedupe every count drops a little; the total must be 130.

Watch out

Remove Duplicates on a column that has blanks treats every blank as the same value and keeps one of them. Dedupe on Email alone and six of the seven no-email leads disappear. That's why the key falls back to something, and why you count before and after.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe messy inputThe queryThe step that matters
Marketingweekly lead export, five sourcesthis module's Leads_Cleanmerge to a mapping table, dedupe on a key
Financebudget typed as one column per monthTargets in tidy formUnpivot Other Columns
Operationstwelve store stock files, one per store, same layoutone Inventory tableFrom Folder ▸ Combine Files
MerchandisingSales lines without costmargin by productmerge to Products on ProductID, Left Outer, expand UnitCost
HRemployee master with merged-cell department headersa flat Employees tableFill Down on Department
Digitalapp event log, 200,000 rowsdaily summaryGroup By date, count rows; load to the Data Model

The merchandising one is a Left Outer merge, and in the Lab it's an XLOOKUP. Revenue for one product from Sales, its cost from Products:

=HSTACK(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!J:J,"Orbit Wireless Mouse"),XLOOKUP("Orbit Wireless Mouse",Products!B:B,Products!F:F))

₹2.03 lakh of revenue on a ₹431.52 unit cost. In Power Query the same lookup happens for all 6,314 lines in one merge step, and a Group By on Product gives Rohan margin by SKU without a single formula on the sheet.

The finance one is already done for you: the Targets sheet is 413 rows, one per store per month, which is what a wide sheet becomes after unpivot.

=HSTACK(COUNTA(Targets!A:A)-1,ROWS(UNIQUE(Targets!B2:B414)),ROWS(UNIQUE(Targets!C2:C414)))

413 rows, 13 stores, 32 months. 13 × 32 is 416, so three store-months have no target: Kochi opened in April 2024. A tidy table makes that gap countable; a wide one hides it in three empty cells.

Practice

Task exercises are done in Excel on files/novamart-m365.xlsx. Formula exercises are checked in the Lab, and each one is the "after" count for a query step, so do them in pairs.

Exercise 1 · Broken emails to flag

How many leads have an email that is present but has no @ sign? These are the rows your EmailOK column marks FALSE, and the call list for sales.

Hint

COUNTIFS with two criteria on the same bounded range: "?*" for non-blank, "<>*@*" for no @.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(Leads!C2:C151,"?*",Leads!C2:C151,"<>*@*")

15, all missing exactly the @ before the domain. All but one have a phone, so this is a call list, not a delete list.

Exercise 2 · Standardise Source in Power Query

Load tblLeads into the editor and make the Source column read Web Form, Referral, Instagram, Facebook, Walk-in, Event, with nothing else. Then add a Group By that counts leads per source.

Hint

Trim, Capitalize Each Word, Replace Values for "Fb", and one more Replace for "Walk-In". Group By on the same query via Reference so the clean list stays intact.

What good looks like
  • Applied Steps reads Source ▸ Trimmed Text ▸ Capitalized Each Word ▸ Replaced Fb ▸ Replaced Walk-In, each with a name that says what it did.
  • A second query, Leads_BySource, created with right-click ▸ Reference, with one Group By step: Source, Count Rows.
  • Six rows: Web Form 38, Referral 31, Instagram 26, Facebook 25, Walk-in 18, Event 12. Total 150.
  • Both queries refresh without error after you type "fb " (with a trailing space) into a new row of tblLeads.

Exercise 3 · Distinct phones after normalising

How many distinct phone numbers are there once every phone is reduced to its last ten digits? Don't count the blank.

Hint

Three nested SUBSTITUTEs remove +, - and the space; RIGHT(…,10); UNIQUE; ROWS; subtract one for the blank.

Show solution 
=ROWS(UNIQUE(RIGHT(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(Leads!D2:D151,"+",""),"-","")," ",""),10)))-1

120, from 140 filled phones. Your Phone10 column in the query should show the same 120 in the column distribution (View ▸ Column Distribution).

Exercise 4 · Parse the dates with the right locale

In the editor, turn CreatedAt into a real Date column that parses all 150 rows, then add a month column and group by it. Compare with the Lab's month counts.

Hint

Strip the time with Text.BeforeDelimiter first. Then Change Type ▸ Using Locale ▸ Date ▸ English (India). Plain Change Type uses your machine's locale, which may be wrong.

What good looks like
  • No error rows after the type change (Home ▸ Keep Rows ▸ Keep Errors shows an empty table).
  • A Month column from Add Column ▸ Date ▸ Month ▸ Start of Month, typed as Date.
  • Group By Month, Count Rows: 1 May 39, 1 June 43, 1 July 38, 1 August 30.
  • Lead 9, dated 04/05/2026, sits in May, not April. That single row is the locale test.

Exercise 5 · Leads created in July, across all formats

Without parsing anything, count the leads created in July 2026 by matching the three text shapes July can take in column G. The result should match the July row from Exercise 4.

Hint

Three COUNTIFs added together: "2026-07*", "??/07/2026", "??-Jul-2026".

Show solution 
=COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"2026-07*")+COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"??/07/2026")+COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"??-Jul-2026")

38, same as the query. The first pattern catches both the plain ISO dates and the timestamps, because * matches nothing or anything.

Exercise 6 · Merge the city map and prove nothing was missed

Build the CityMap table, merge it into the leads query, expand CityName, and then prove that every row found a match. Finally, add a new spelling ("Blore") to a lead and to the map, and refresh.

Hint

Do the merge twice: once Left Outer for the real query, once Left Anti in a throwaway query. The anti-join should have zero rows.

What good looks like
  • CityMap is a Table with lowercase Variant values and loaded as Connection Only; the merge key on the leads side is Text.Lower(Text.Trim([City])).
  • The Left Outer merge dialog says 150 of 150 rows match; after expanding, no null in CityName.
  • A Left Anti query on the same keys returns an empty table. Before you added "dehra dun" to the map it returned 14 rows.
  • Group By CityName gives Hyderabad 28, Dehradun 27, Delhi 26, Pune 26, Mumbai 22, Bengaluru 21.
  • After adding "Blore" on both sides and pressing Refresh All, the Bengaluru count is 22 and nothing else changed.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

The automatic Changed Type step is the most expensive line in Power Query. It guesses from 200 rows, in your laptop's locale. On an Indian date column it either errors on 13/07/2026 or, worse, silently reads 04/05/2026 as April 5th and nothing looks wrong until the month chart does. Delete the guess, type the column yourself at the end, and use Using Locale for any date that came from a human.

Watch out

The preview shows 1,000 rows. Column Quality, Column Distribution and "matches 150 of 150" are computed on what's loaded, and on a big source that's a sample. Turn on View ▸ Column profiling based on entire data set before you trust a distinct count, or check it on the loaded Table with ROWS(UNIQUE(…)).

Pro habit

Rename every step as you go (right-click ▸ Rename): "Replaced @@ in Email" beats "Replaced Value2". Keep the raw import as its own connection-only query and build the clean one by Reference. Load a tiny Checks table next to the output: rows in, rows out, duplicates removed, rows flagged. When the numbers move next Thursday, the Checks table tells you before Priya does.

  • Steps are ordered, and order is logic. Trim and lowercase before you dedupe. Fix @@ before you test for @. Strip the time before you parse the date.
  • Remove Duplicates keeps the first row it sees. Sort first, buffer, then dedupe, and write the survivor rule down.
  • Case matters in a merge. "Mumbai" and "mumbai" don't match. Lowercase both keys, or use a fuzzy merge only after reading what it decided.
  • Null is not an empty string. A cell that was blank arrives as null; one that held two spaces arrives as " " until Trim. Replace both if you want a clean "Unknown".
  • Query folding is real but not your problem yet. Against a database, Power Query pushes steps back to the server when it can; against a sheet, it can't. Filter early anyway; it's the habit that scales.
  • A moved file breaks Source. Put the folder path in a parameter, or better, point the query at SharePoint so the path never changes.
  • Privacy levels will ask. When a query combines a local file and a web source, Excel asks about privacy levels once. Answer Organizational for both, or the merge won't run.

On the job

In the assessment test

The clean-up task is where candidates separate. You get a sheet with padded text, mixed dates and duplicates, and 20 minutes. The formula-only candidate fixes half. The Power Query candidate loads it, trims, cases, types with a locale, dedupes on a sensible key, and, this is the part graders mark, writes a count of rows in and rows out next to the result. Say your survivor rule out loud if it's an interview; "I kept the newest row with a valid email" is a sentence hiring managers remember.

First 90 days

Find the pack that takes someone three hours on the first of every month. Rebuild its inputs as queries: From Folder for the store files, a merge for the product master, an unpivot for the budget. Hand it back as one Refresh All. Nobody will thank you for the M code. Everybody will notice the pack now lands on the 1st at 10 am.

Interview question: "What is Power Query and how is it different from formulas?"
Power Query is Excel's import-and-transform tool: it records a sequence of steps against a source and reruns them on refresh, producing a Table. Formulas recalculate on the sheet, cell by cell; queries run once as a pipeline, keep the raw data untouched, and handle shape changes like new files or columns that formulas can't.
Interview question: "How would you dedupe a lead list with no unique ID?"
Normalise first: trim, lowercase the email, strip the phone to ten digits. Build one key per person, phone if present else email. Sort so the row I want to keep is first, buffer, then Remove Duplicates on the key. And I count rows before and after so I can say how many were removed and why.
Interview question: "When would you use Unpivot?"
Whenever a sheet has data in its column headers: months, years, regions, product names across the top. Unpivot turns each header into a value in a new column, giving one row per entity per period, which is the only shape SUMIFS, PivotTables and Power BI want. The reverse, Pivot Column, is for presenting, not analysing.

Quick check

1. Applied Steps reads: Source, Removed Duplicates on Email, Lowercased Email. What's wrong?

Steps run top to bottom. Normalise (trim, case) first, then dedupe; drag the step up in Applied Steps to fix it.

2. Which merge kind lists the Leads rows whose city spelling is NOT in your CityMap table?

Left Anti keeps only the left-side rows with no match. It's the exceptions report; Left Outer keeps everything and puts null where there's no match.

3. Your CreatedAt column parses 29 of 41 slash dates as errors and the other 12 as valid. Most likely cause?

04/05/2026 parses as April 5th in en-US; 13/07/2026 can't. Redo the step with Using Locale ▸ English (India).

4. Priya's team adds 40 rows to the source Table next Thursday. What do you do?

That is the whole point. The steps are the recipe; refresh reruns it on the new source. The checks tell you whether anything unexpected came in.
