Level 2 · Module 07 · about 90 min

Charts, conditional formatting and dashboards

A manager reads a dashboard in eight seconds and then asks one question. This module is about making those eight seconds count: the right chart for the question, formatting that points at the number that matters, and a sheet of dynamic-array formulas underneath so the whole page refreshes itself when next month's data lands.

  • You'll pick the chart from the question (compare, trend, share, relationship) and say why a pie with eight slices is a mistake.
  • You'll format a chart the way an analyst does: title as the takeaway, axis at zero, one colour plus one highlight, labels on the bars.
  • You'll write conditional-formatting rules driven by formulas, such as colouring every store that missed target.
  • You'll build a dashboard engine from UNIQUE, SORTBY, FILTER, SEQUENCE and TAKE so the summary tables rebuild themselves.
  • You'll lay out a one-page dashboard: KPI tiles, trend, breakdown, table, slicers, and get it onto a slide and onto paper.

Concept

Thursday, 4:40 pm

Nandini Rao, the COO, forwards you a workbook with fourteen sheets and one line: "I need this on one page for the Monday review. Which stores missed target in July, what's the trend, what's growing. Don't make me scroll." The workbook has a 3-D pie chart on the first sheet. It has eight slices.

A chart is a sentence with a picture attached. "Kochi missed target by 62%" is a sentence. "Store revenue" is not, and a chart titled "Store revenue" leaves the reader to write the sentence themselves, which they will do wrong or not at all. So before you touch Insert ▸ Charts, write the sentence. Then pick the chart that makes the sentence obvious in two seconds.

Four questions cover nearly everything a manager asks. How do these compare? is a bar chart, sorted. How has it changed? is a line. How does actual sit against target? is a column with a target line, or a table with conditional formatting. What share does each part have? is a stacked bar, or a pie only when there are two or three parts. Relationships between two measures ("do discounts drive volume?") are scatter plots, and they are rarer in a review pack than textbooks suggest.

Why a manager cares

Nandini has twelve store managers, one hour, and a decision to make about the Kochi rent renewal. A dashboard that shows the July miss in red, the trend since opening, and the Kochi number next to the other Standard-format stores gets the decision made in that hour. A workbook with fourteen sheets and a 3-D pie gets a follow-up meeting. Your job is to remove the follow-up meeting.

How it works

The bad chart and the good chart

Nandini's inherited pie is below on the left, redrawn faithfully. Eight slices, 3-D tilt, a legend you have to cross-reference, and the biggest slice looks bigger than it is because it's at the front. On the right is the same data as a sorted bar. One colour, one highlight, the number on every bar, and the title says what to conclude.

Chart formatting rules that matter

Excel's default chart is not wrong so much as undecided. Every rule below is a decision the default leaves to you, and in an assessment test the grader checks for most of them.

RuleWhere in ExcelWhy
Title is the takeaway, not the subjectClick the title, type the sentence; or type = and click a cell that holds the sentence"Kochi missed target by 62%" beats "Revenue vs target". A linked title updates with the data.
Value axis starts at zero (bars and columns)Double-click axis ▸ Axis Options ▸ Bounds ▸ Minimum = 0A bar's length is the value. Start at 60% and a 5% gap looks like a collapse.
Sort bars largest firstSort the source table, or use SORTBY in the engine sheetAlphabetical order asks the reader to rank; sorted order does it for them.
One colour, one highlightSelect series ▸ Fill ▸ grey; click the one bar ▸ Fill ▸ accentColour means "look here". Six colours mean nothing.
Direct labels, no legendChart Elements (+) ▸ Data Labels ▸ Outside End; delete LegendThe eye shouldn't travel to a key and back.
Gridlines light or goneChart Elements ▸ untick Gridlines, or format them 25% greyLabels on bars make gridlines redundant.
Horizontal bars for long namesInsert ▸ Charts ▸ Bar (not Column)"Novamart Connaught Place" won't fit under a column without a 45° tilt.
Months as text in YYYY-MM or MMM-YYSource column already formatted; axis type = TextDate axes add phantom gaps and reformat on their own.
Source and definition in a footnoteInsert ▸ Text Box under the chart, 9 pt"Delivered lines only, excl. GST" ends the "your number is different" argument.
No 3-D, no shadows, no gradientChart Styles ▸ the plain one; Format ▸ Effects ▸ noneDepth and shine change perceived size. Nothing else.

Sparklines: a chart in a cell

A store table with twelve rows wants twelve tiny trend lines, not twelve charts. Insert ▸ Sparklines ▸ Line, data range = the twelve monthly columns for that row, location = the cell at the end of the row. Fill down and each row gets its own line. Tick Sparkline ▸ Show ▸ High Point and Markers and Diwali shows as a dot. Sparklines share an axis only if you set Axis ▸ Same for All Sparklines; the default lets each row scale itself, which makes Kochi's ₹4,000 wobble look like Connaught Place's ₹1.2 lakh swing.

Conditional formatting: formatting that reads the data

Three built-in kinds do most of the work. Data bars turn a column of numbers into an in-cell bar chart (Home ▸ Conditional Formatting ▸ Data Bars). Colour scales shade a block from low to high, good for a store-by-month grid. Icon sets put a traffic light next to attainment; set the thresholds by number, not percentile, or the icons move every month.

The fourth kind is the one that matters: Use a formula to determine which cells to format. You write a logical test for the top-left cell of the selection, and Excel copies that test down and across exactly like a fill handle would. So the anchoring rules from Module 03 apply. Select A2:R6315 on Sales and write:

=$P2>10000

Read it as "for the cell I'm standing in, look at column P of my row." The $ locks the column so every cell in the row tests P, not its own column. The row number is relative so row 3 tests P3. The formula is written for the active cell (A2, the one Excel shows in white when the range is selected) and stretched to the rest. If you select the range from the bottom up, the active cell is A6315 and you must write $P6315, which is why people say "my rule is off by one". Select top-down.

=$Q2="Cancelled"                  'selection A2:R6315 — grey out cancelled lines
=AND($Q2="Delivered",$O2>=20)     'delivered at 20%+ discount: worth a look
=$C2<$D2                          'on a Store · Actual · Target sheet, selection A2:D14 — missed target

The Lab can't run these (they're rules, not results), but you can count what they would colour, which is a good habit before you apply a rule to six thousand rows.

=COUNTIF(Sales!P:P,">10000")

408 lines, about one in fifteen. If that came back as 4,000 you'd know the threshold was wrong before anyone saw a sheet that's mostly orange.

Slicers on a Table

Slicers aren't only for PivotTables. Convert the summary range to a Table (Ctrl+T), then Table Design ▸ Insert Slicer and tick Region or Channel. The slicer filters the Table; a chart built on the Table follows the filter; and the formulas in the engine sheet don't change at all. This is the cheapest interactivity in Excel and the one that impresses in a demo.

Application: Nandini's one-page dashboard

The build has two sheets. Engine holds the formulas below, each one spilling a small table. Dashboard holds charts and tiles that point at those spills. Change the month in one cell on Engine and the whole page moves. Every formula here is against the Lab workbook, so run them.

KPI tiles: one number, one comparison

A tile is a big number and a small comparison. The number is a SUMIFS with the month in a cell (here hard-coded so the Lab can run it).

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹12,48,348 for the month. The comparison beside it is the month-on-month change, and the same formula twice with a division:

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
    /SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-07",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")-1

Up 36.1% on July, which sounds like a great month until the second tile puts it against target.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
    /SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08")

76.6% of a ₹16.3 lakh target. Both facts are true; a good tile shows both so nobody gets to pick the flattering one.

The dynamic-array engine

Old dashboards had a hidden sheet with a hand-typed list of stores and a SUMIFS per row. Add a store and someone had to remember to add the row. Dynamic arrays fix that: one formula produces the list, and the list resizes itself. Start with the distinct values.

=UNIQUE(Sales!G2:G6315)

Three rows spill: Store, Online, App. Wrap it in SORT and you get alphabetical, which is what you want for a slicer list and not what you want for a chart.

=SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!K2:K6315))

Now put a number next to each. SUMIFS accepts the spilled list as its criterion and returns one total per item, so HSTACK can glue the label column and the number column into a two-column table. The third column divides by the total for share.

=LET(ch,UNIQUE(Sales!G2:G6315),
     rev,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,ch,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
     HSTACK(ch,rev,TEXT(rev/SUM(rev),"0.0%")))

Store ₹1.09 crore (45.8%), Online ₹82.9 lakh (34.9%), App ₹45.7 lakh (19.3%). That's the "By channel" bar chart's source, and it will grow a fourth row the day Sameer launches a marketplace channel.

Charts want the biggest bar first. SORTBY sorts one array by another, and -1 means descending. LET keeps you from writing the SUMIFS twice.

=LET(cats,UNIQUE(Sales!K2:K6315),
     rev,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,cats,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
     SORTBY(HSTACK(cats,rev),rev,-1))

Electronics ₹1.11 crore, then Home & Kitchen at ₹48.3 lakh, then a long tail down to Grocery at ₹6.2 lakh. This is the good bar chart from earlier, and it sorted itself.

Rohan's standing question is "top five products". TAKE keeps the first n rows of a spill, so TAKE(SORTBY(...),5) is a top-N in one cell. Products has 72 rows, so the list comes from there and the revenue is looked up from Sales.

=LET(p,Products!B2:B73,
     rev,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!J:J,p,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
     TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(p,rev),rev,-1),5))

Two Orbit laptops at ₹23.7 lakh and ₹21.3 lakh, then the Voltra X1 at ₹11.6 lakh. Change the 5 to -5 and you get the bottom five, which is Rohan's other standing question.

A month spine with SEQUENCE

Trend charts need every month present, including a month with no sales, or the line skips it and lies. Don't take months from the data; generate them. SEQUENCE(12,1,0) is the numbers 0 to 11, EDATE adds that many months to a start date, and TEXT turns the dates into the YYYY-MM strings that match column C.

=TEXT(EDATE(DATE(2025,9,1),SEQUENCE(12,1,0)),"yyyy-mm")

Twelve rows, 2025-09 to 2026-08. Feed that spine to SUMIFS and the trend table writes itself.

=LET(m,TEXT(EDATE(DATE(2025,9,1),SEQUENCE(12,1,0)),"yyyy-mm"),
     HSTACK(m,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,m,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")))

Diwali is visible without a chart: ₹11.7 lakh in November and ₹13.9 lakh in December 2025 against ₹5.7 lakh in April 2026. Point a line chart at this spill (use the # spill reference, =Engine!A2#, as the series) and it extends itself when a thirteenth month appears.

FILTER: the stores that missed

Nandini's actual question was "which stores missed target in July". That's a FILTER: build the store · actual · target table, then keep only the rows where actual is below target. The third argument is what to show when nothing matches, which you must supply or you'll get #CALC! the first month everybody hits target.

=LET(st,Stores!B2:B14,
     act,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,st,Sales!C:C,"2026-07",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
     tgt,SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!B:B,st,Targets!C:C,"2026-07"),
     FILTER(HSTACK(st,act,tgt,TEXT(act/tgt,"0%")),act<tgt,"Every store hit target"))

Twelve of thirteen. Park Street and Rajpur Road at 21%, Novamart.in the closest miss at 96%. Flip the comparison and the fourth tile's "1 of 13" falls out:

=LET(st,Stores!B2:B14,
     act,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,st,Sales!C:C,"2026-07",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
     tgt,SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!B:B,st,Targets!C:C,"2026-07"),
     FILTER(HSTACK(st,act,tgt),act>=tgt,"No store hit target"))

Malviya Nagar, ₹82,908 against ₹80,000. One row. The "No store hit target" fallback is there for August, when the answer is nobody.

Two more for the detail table

Status counts for the footnote, using COUNTIFS the same way:

=HSTACK(UNIQUE(Sales!Q2:Q6315),COUNTIFS(Sales!Q:Q,UNIQUE(Sales!Q2:Q6315)))

5,425 delivered, 449 cancelled, 420 returned, 20 still processing. And the three stores with the worst cancellation rate, which is the kind of row Nandini circles with a pen:

=LET(st,Stores!B2:B14,
     n,COUNTIFS(Sales!D:D,st,Sales!Q:Q,"Cancelled"),
     t,COUNTIFS(Sales!D:D,st),
     TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(st,n,t,TEXT(n/t,"0.0%")),n/t,-1),3))

Malviya Nagar cancels 12.7% of its lines, nearly double the company rate. Same store that hit target. Both facts go on the page.

Getting it onto a slide and onto paper

Copy a chart, then in PowerPoint use Home ▸ Paste ▸ Use Destination Theme & Link Data. The slide's chart now refreshes from the workbook (Chart Design ▸ Refresh Data). Module 09 covers what to do when the theme fights the colours. For a picture of a cell range that stays live, use the Camera tool (add it via File ▸ Options ▸ Quick Access Toolbar ▸ All Commands ▸ Camera): select the range, click Camera, click where the picture goes. The picture updates when the cells do, and it's how the store table travels to the dashboard sheet without merging cells.

  1. Page Layout ▸ Orientation ▸ Landscape. A dashboard is wider than it is tall.
  2. Page Layout ▸ Print Area ▸ Set Print Area. Select the dashboard block first, so the engine sheet's spills never print.
  3. Page Layout ▸ Scale to Fit ▸ Width 1 page, Height 1 page. This is the "don't make me scroll" setting for paper.
  4. View ▸ Page Break Preview. Drag the blue line if a chart is cut. Then Ctrl+P and check the preview before sending the PDF.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askChart or feature
Operations (Nandini)"Which stores missed target, and by how much?"Table with formula rule =$C2<$D2 plus data bars on attainment
Merchandising (Rohan)"Top five and bottom five products this quarter."TAKE(SORTBY()) feeding a sorted bar
Finance (Arjun)"Monthly revenue against target for the board."Column (actual) + line (target) combo on a SEQUENCE month spine
Marketing (Priya)"Is the app share growing?"100% stacked column by year, three series
Digital (Sameer)"Do bigger discounts move more units?"Scatter of DiscountPct vs Qty, trendline, one dot per line
HR (Kavita)"Headcount by department, current staff only."Horizontal bar from UNIQUE + COUNTIFS
Supply chain"What's below reorder level right now?"FILTER on Inventory, icon set on stock cover

Kavita's one. The blank-ExitDate test keeps only current employees, and the list of departments comes from the data so a new department appears on its own.

=LET(d,UNIQUE(Employees!C2:C86),
     HSTACK(d,COUNTIFS(Employees!C:C,d,Employees!H:H,"")))

Sales & Store Operations has 39 of the 78 current staff; Technology & Data is next with 12. A horizontal bar, sorted, with the store-ops bar highlighted, and Kavita's slide is done.

Supply chain's one. How many store-product combinations are below their reorder level today?

=ROWS(FILTER(Inventory!B:D,Inventory!E:E<Inventory!F:F))

235 of 936. A quarter of the inventory grid is flashing, which is either a stock problem or a reorder-level problem, and the dashboard's job is to make someone ask which.

Practice

Each solution is a spill or a number the Lab can check. Before you run one, say what shape you expect: "13 rows, 3 columns" or "one number about ₹12 lakh". If the shape is wrong the formula is wrong.

Exercise 1 · Revenue by region, including the blank

Build the two-column table of delivered revenue by Region straight from the Sales sheet with UNIQUE and SUMIFS. One of the rows will have an empty label. What is it?

Hint

Region is blank for online lines. UNIQUE keeps the blank as a value, and SUMIFS with a blank criterion matches blank cells.

Show solution 
=LET(r,UNIQUE(Sales!F2:F6315),
     HSTACK(r,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,r,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")))

Five rows. The blank row is ₹1.29 crore, more than any region, because it's Novamart.in. On a chart, label it "Online" rather than leaving a bar with no name, and say so in the footnote.

Exercise 2 · Top three physical stores

The three highest-revenue physical stores (exclude Novamart.in) by delivered revenue across the whole dataset, largest first, as a store · revenue table.

Hint

Stores!B2:B13 is the twelve physical stores; row 14 is the online store. Then TAKE(SORTBY(...),3).

Show solution 
=LET(st,Stores!B2:B13,
     rev,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,st,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),
     TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(st,rev),rev,-1),3))

Connaught Place ₹18.3 lakh, Koramangala ₹16.2 lakh, Andheri West ₹15.2 lakh. The three Flagship stores, which is reassuring for whoever chose the format.

Exercise 3 · The 2026 actual-vs-target spine

Generate the eight months of 2026 with SEQUENCE and put delivered revenue and total target beside each: month · actual · target, three columns, eight rows.

Hint

Copy the trend-table pattern, start at DATE(2026,1,1), eight rows, and add a second SUMIFS on Targets inside the HSTACK.

Show solution 
=LET(m,TEXT(EDATE(DATE(2026,1,1),SEQUENCE(8,1,0)),"yyyy-mm"),
     HSTACK(m,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,m,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,m)))

Every month of 2026 is below target; the closest is July at ₹9.2 lakh against ₹11.7 lakh. This spill is exactly what a column-plus-line combo chart wants as its source.

Exercise 4 · Kochi's reorder list

List the products at Novamart MG Road Kochi whose StockOnHand is below ReorderLevel. Product names only.

Hint

Two conditions in a FILTER are multiplied: (cond1)*(cond2). TRUE×TRUE is 1.

Show solution 
=FILTER(Inventory!D:D,(Inventory!B:B="Novamart MG Road Kochi")*(Inventory!E:E<Inventory!F:F))

21 products, from the Voltra X1 to trail mix. Wrap it in ROWS() for the tile, keep the list for the store manager's email.

Exercise 5 · Count what the rule will colour

You're about to apply =AND($P2>10000,$Q2="Delivered") to the Sales sheet. How many rows will turn orange?

Hint

A formula rule with AND is a COUNTIFS with the same conditions.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(Sales!P:P,">10000",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

355 rows. The plain >10000 rule coloured 408, so 53 of the big lines were cancelled or returned, which is itself a number Nandini would want.

Exercise 6 · Festive season, year on year

Priya wants a two-bar chart: delivered revenue for October plus November, 2024 versus 2025. Produce the year · revenue table from an array constant {2024;2025}, without typing the month strings out four times.

Hint

y&"-10" turns 2024 into "2024-10" and works on the whole array. Add two SUMIFS.

Show solution 
=LET(y,{2024;2025},
     HSTACK(y,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,y&"-10",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
             +SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,y&"-11",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")))

₹15.8 lakh in 2024, ₹21.0 lakh in 2025: up a third. Two bars, the 2025 one highlighted, title "Festive revenue grew 33% in 2025". Done.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

A spill needs empty cells below and beside it. Type anything into the space a UNIQUE wants to grow into and the whole formula shows #SPILL!. On an engine sheet, give every spill its own column block with a blank column between, and never put a "Total" row under a spill that can grow. Put totals at the top or in a separate cell with SUM(A2#).

Watch out

Conditional-formatting rules pile up. Every copy-paste of a formatted cell brings its rules along, and after a month a sheet has forty overlapping rules, half of them pointing at $A$1:$A$1. Open Home ▸ Conditional Formatting ▸ Manage Rules ▸ This Worksheet before you send anything and delete what you don't recognise.

Pro habit

Put the month in one cell (say Engine!B1) and make every SUMIFS point at it. Next month, change one cell. In the Lab the month is typed into each formula so it can run standalone; in your workbook it should never be.

  • Write the sentence, then the chart. If you can't write the title as a claim, you don't yet know what the chart is for.
  • Charts on Tables or spills, never on a fixed range. A2:B13 stops at row 13 forever. Table1[Revenue] and A2# grow.
  • Delivered only, and say so. Revenue on a dashboard means delivered lines unless the footnote says otherwise. The 449 cancelled lines are worth ₹17.4 lakh of arguments.
  • Colour scales on a grid, not on a single column. Twelve stores by twelve months as a heat map tells a story; a colour scale on one column is a data bar that's harder to read.
  • Icon-set thresholds by number. The default is percentile, which means the bottom third is always red even in a record month.
  • Test rules with COUNTIFS first. If the count is 0 or 6,000, the rule is wrong.
  • Never merge cells on a dashboard. Use Center Across Selection (Ctrl+1 ▸ Alignment) for a title. Merged cells break sorting, slicers and the Camera tool.

On the job

In the assessment test

Almost every analyst test has one chart task and one conditional-formatting task, and they're graded on decisions, not effort. "Create a chart showing revenue by store" is checked for: right type (bar, sorted), axis at zero, a title that says something, no legend clutter. "Highlight stores below target" is checked for a formula rule, not for cells coloured by hand. Hand-coloured cells are the fastest way to fail that question, because the grader changes a number and watches whether the colour follows.

First 90 days

Week two, someone hands you a dashboard nobody trusts. Don't rebuild it. Add an engine sheet with UNIQUE + SUMIFS spills, point the existing charts at the spills, and put a "Checks" block at the top: spill total versus SUMIFS of the whole sheet, difference should be zero. When the totals tie for three months running, people start trusting the page, and you.

"When would you use a pie chart?"
When there are two or three parts and the point is that one of them dominates: "Store is still nearly half of revenue". For more parts a sorted bar is easier to read because people compare lengths well and angles badly. Never 3-D, because the tilt changes the apparent size of the slices.
"How do you make a dashboard update when new data arrives?"
Keep the raw data in a Table so it grows, drive summaries with dynamic-array formulas such as UNIQUE and SUMIFS or with PivotTables, and point charts at the spill ranges or the pivot rather than at fixed cells. Then a refresh or a paste of new rows moves every number. Hard-coded lists and fixed ranges are what break.
"Explain conditional formatting with a formula."
You select a range and write a logical test for its top-left cell, like =$C2<$D2. Excel applies the test to every cell as if the formula were filled down and across, so the dollar signs decide which column stays fixed. It's how you colour a whole row based on one column, which the built-in rules can't do.

Quick check

1. Rohan wants "revenue by sub-category" for 24 sub-categories. Which chart?

Long labels want horizontal bars; a comparison wants sorting; 24 slices can't be read. The highlight is the sentence.

2. You select A2:D14 top-down and want to colour rows where actual (column C) is below target (column D). Which rule?

Lock the columns so every cell in a row tests C and D of that row; leave the row relative so row 3 tests C3 and D3. Option c tests row 2 for every row; option a drifts across columns.

3. =TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(p,rev),rev,-1),5) returns…

SORTBY with -1 sorts descending, TAKE keeps the first five rows of the result. For the bottom five, TAKE with -5.

4. Your trend line chart skips from 2026-03 to 2026-05. Most likely cause?

Months taken from UNIQUE of the data vanish when a month is empty. Generate the spine with SEQUENCE and EDATE so every month exists, with zero if it must.

Watch and read

VideoTwo Excel Dynamic Array Functions: UNIQUE and SORTTechnology for Teachers and Students · UNIQUE and SORT dynamic array basics VideoIntroduction to Conditional Formatting in ExcelChandoo · conditional formatting fundamentals for dashboards ReadExcel FILTER functionExceljet · extracting matching rows dynamically ReadExcel UNIQUE functionExceljet · pulling distinct values with a dynamic array ReadExcel SEQUENCE functionExceljet · generating number and date sequences dynamically ReadConditional formatting with formulasExceljet (Dave Bruns) · rule-based formatting driven by formulas PracticeAnalyze trends in data using sparklinesMicrosoft Support · step-by-step sparkline creation and customization

Level 2 · Module 08 · about 60 min

Word: documents people actually read

Most business documents are skimmed by someone busy, on a phone, between meetings. Word can make a document that survives that treatment, but only if you stop painting text and start giving it structure. This module is about styles, the review loop and mail merge: the three things that separate a trainee's document from an analyst's.

  • You'll build a document from heading styles so the Navigation pane, the table of contents and Copilot all understand it.
  • You'll add page numbers, headers, footers and section breaks without the document fighting back.
  • You'll bring a table in from Excel the right way, caption it and cross-reference it.
  • You'll run a review loop with Track Changes and Comments, and compare two versions when someone edited a copy.
  • You'll mail-merge 44 personalised letters from an Excel list in under ten minutes, and prepare the list with a formula.
  • You'll save a template, check accessibility, and export a PDF that still has a clickable contents page.

Concept

Tuesday, 11:20 am

Nandini Rao wants a Store Audit SOP on every store manager's desk by Friday. There is an old one: 14 pages, written in 2022, every heading bolded by hand, the contents page typed out and wrong since page 6. "Rebuild it. Numbered procedures, a checklist table, a version box. And I want to comment on it without you retyping my comments." Then Priya Nair walks past: "While you're in Word, the Gold-tier festive letter needs to go to 44 people. By name."

Here is the idea the whole module hangs on. A document has two layers: what the text says, and what the text is. "Store opening checks" is a heading. "Count the float before 9:45" is a numbered step. Word only knows the second layer if you tell it, and you tell it with styles. Once a paragraph is styled Heading 2, Word can list it in the Navigation pane, put it in an automatic table of contents, number it, let a screen reader jump to it, and let Copilot summarise the section under it. Make it bold and 14 pt by hand and Word knows nothing. It's just fat text.

That one decision, styles instead of formatting, is what the old SOP got wrong. Everything else in this module is what you get for free once you get it right.

Before: the 2022 SOP

  • Headings are bold 14 pt Calibri, applied by hand; two are 13 pt by accident.
  • Contents page typed in, wrong from page 6 onwards.
  • Procedure numbers typed as "1)", "2)"; one procedure goes 1, 2, 4.
  • Checklist is tab-aligned text that falls apart on a phone.
  • Reviewed by email: SOP_final_Nandini_v2_FINAL.docx.

After: this module

  • Heading 1 / 2 styles; change the font once, every heading follows.
  • Automatic TOC; F9 rebuilds it; every line is a link in the PDF.
  • Multilevel numbering tied to the styles; move a section, numbers follow.
  • A real table from Excel, header row repeated, captioned "Table 1".
  • One file on SharePoint, Track Changes locked, version history behind it.

Why a manager cares

Nandini will not read 14 pages. She'll open the Navigation pane, click "Closing checks", read that, and comment. If the document has no real headings she has to scroll, and the comments land as a WhatsApp voice note instead. The SOP also gets reprinted every quarter for three years; if its contents page is typed by hand it is wrong by the second reprint. Styles are the difference between a document that costs an hour a quarter to maintain and one that costs a day.

How it works

Styles, not formatting

The Styles gallery sits on Home ▸ Styles. Five styles do ninety percent of the work: Title (once, at the top), Heading 1 (major sections), Heading 2 (subsections), Heading 3 (rarely, and if you need Heading 4 the document needs restructuring), and Normal for body text. Keyboard: Ctrl+Alt+1, 2, 3 for the headings, Ctrl+Shift+N back to Normal. Learn those four and you never touch the mouse for structure.

To change how every Heading 1 looks, don't reformat them one by one. Right-click the style in the gallery, Modify, change the font, size, colour and spacing, and tick "New documents based on this template" if you want it in every future Novamart document. One edit, forty headings. If you have already made a heading look right by hand, select it, right-click the style, and choose Update Heading 1 to Match Selection.

Heading numbering ("2.1 Cash float") comes from Home ▸ Paragraph ▸ Multilevel List, and the trick is to pick a list in the gallery whose preview shows "Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3" next to the numbers. That links the numbering to the styles. Type numbers by hand and they'll be wrong the first time a section moves.

StyleUse it forShortcutWhat it unlocks
TitleThe document name, oncenone (apply from the gallery)Document properties, the PDF title
Heading 1 / 2 / 3Sections and subsectionsCtrl+Alt+1/2/3Navigation pane, TOC, numbering, PDF bookmarks, screen readers, Copilot summaries
NormalBody textCtrl+Shift+NThe base every other style inherits from; change its font and the whole document follows
List Number / List BulletProcedures and checklistsnone; or Ctrl+Shift+L for bulletsContinuous numbering across the document, "restart at 1" per procedure
Caption"Table 3: Closing checks"via References ▸ Insert CaptionCross-references that renumber themselves, a table of figures
Quote / Intense QuotePolicy extracts, exec sign-off textnoneVisually distinct without manual indents

The Navigation pane and the TOC

View ▸ Show ▸ Navigation Pane, or Ctrl+F. The Headings tab shows the outline; drag a heading and its whole section, body text and all, moves with it. This is how you restructure a 20-page document in two minutes. The Pages tab shows thumbnails; the Results tab is search. Once headings exist, the contents page is one click: References ▸ Table of Contents ▸ Automatic Table 1. After you edit, click the table and Update Table ▸ Update entire table, or select everything with Ctrl+A and press F9 to refresh every field in the document, TOC included.

Page numbers, headers, footers and section breaks

Insert ▸ Header & Footer ▸ Page Number ▸ Bottom of Page. Double-click a header to edit it; the Header & Footer tab appears with "Different First Page" (no number on the cover) and "Different Odd & Even Pages" (for printing double-sided). To put the SOP's version and date in the footer, use Insert ▸ Quick Parts ▸ Field and choose SaveDate or FileName; the field updates itself.

Section breaks are the part that trips people up. A page break (Ctrl+Enter) starts a new page. A section break (Layout ▸ Breaks ▸ Section Breaks ▸ Next Page) starts a new page and a new set of rules: its own header, its own page numbering, its own orientation. You need one when the appendix has a landscape table, or when the cover and contents pages should show roman numerals and the body should start at 1. Turn on formatting marks with Ctrl+Shift+8 to see where the breaks are; most "why did my header change on page 7?" problems are an invisible section break with "Link to Previous" switched off.

Tables from Excel

Copy the range in Excel, come to Word, and instead of Ctrl+V right-click and look at the Paste Options icons. They matter.

Paste optionWhat you getWhen to use it
Keep Source FormattingA Word table wearing Excel's fonts and fillsAlmost never; it clashes with the document
Use Destination StylesA Word table in the document's own table styleThe default for anything final. Then apply a table style from Table Design
Link & Use Destination StylesA table that updates when the workbook changes (right-click ▸ Update Link)Monthly packs where the numbers move and the layout doesn't
PictureA static imageWhen the table must not be editable, such as an audit extract in an appendix
Keep Text OnlyTab-separated textWhen you want to rebuild the table in Word from scratch

Once the table is in, Table Layout ▸ Repeat Header Rows so the header prints at the top of every page, and Table Design to pick a style with banded rows. Then caption it: References ▸ Insert Caption, label "Table". In the prose, write "see References ▸ Cross-reference ▸ Table ▸ Only label and number" instead of typing "Table 3", and when you insert a new table before it, the reference renumbers itself when you press F9.

The review loop: Track Changes, Comments, Compare

Reviewing is a loop, not a step. You send a draft, someone changes it, someone else comments, you decide what to keep, and a new version goes out. Word supports each stage as long as everybody stays in the same file on OneDrive or SharePoint (Module 01) rather than emailing copies.

Review ▸ Tracking ▸ Track Changes, or Ctrl+Shift+E. The drop-down under it lets you track "For Everyone" or "Just Mine", and Lock Tracking stops a reviewer from quietly switching it off. Set the markup view to Simple Markup to read the document cleanly with a red bar in the margin, or All Markup to see every change inline. To comment, select the text and press Ctrl+Alt+M; type @Nandini to send her a notification. When the round is done, Review ▸ Changes ▸ Accept ▸ Accept All Changes (or one at a time with Next / Accept), and Resolve each comment thread so the sidebar is clean. Version history in OneDrive (File ▸ Info ▸ Version History) keeps every earlier state, so accepting is not destructive.

Compare is for the case where someone ignored all of that and edited an emailed copy. Review ▸ Compare ▸ Compare, pick the original and the revised file, and Word produces a third document with the differences shown as tracked changes, which you can then accept or reject in the normal way.

Templates and Quick Parts

When the SOP is done, strip its content down to the skeleton (title block, headings, the checklist table's header row, the footer fields) and File ▸ Save As ▸ Word Template (*.dotx). Word puts it in your Custom Office Templates folder and it appears under File ▸ New ▸ Personal. Every future SOP starts from it, styles and all. For smaller reusable pieces, such as the Novamart address block or the standard confidentiality paragraph, select the text and Insert ▸ Quick Parts ▸ Save Selection to Quick Part Gallery. Type the first few letters of its name and press F3 to drop it in.

Find & Replace with wildcards

Ctrl+H, then More ▸ Use wildcards. This is a small regular-expression engine and it saves hours on documents that came from somewhere else.

FindReplaceWhat it fixes
^p^p (no wildcards)^pDouble paragraph marks left by someone pressing Enter twice for spacing
(two spaces) (one space)Double spaces after full stops; run it until it finds nothing
Rs\.? ?([0-9])₹\1"Rs. 500" and "Rs500" become "₹500"; \1 re-inserts what the brackets captured
([0-9]{1,2})/([0-9]{1,2})/([0-9]{4})\1-\2-\3Dates from slashes to dashes, keeping the numbers
<[Ss]tore>outletWhole word only, either case; < and > are word boundaries
Format ▸ Font ▸ Bold, empty Find boxFormat ▸ Style ▸ Heading 2Turn every hand-bolded line into a real Heading 2 in one pass
Style
A named bundle of formatting plus a meaning ("this is a level-2 heading"). Paragraph styles apply to whole paragraphs; character styles (Emphasis, Strong) to selected words.
Field
A placeholder Word computes: page number, date, TOC, caption number, merge field. Grey when you click it; F9 updates it, Alt+F9 shows the code.
Section
A stretch of the document with its own page setup, headers and footers. Created by a section break, not a page break.
Redline
What people call a document with tracked changes showing: insertions underlined, deletions struck through, each in the reviewer's colour.
Main document
The mail-merge letter with merge fields in it, as opposed to the merged output and the data source.

Editor, accessibility, PDF

Review ▸ Editor is the spelling and grammar pass plus clarity, conciseness and formality suggestions; run it once before anything leaves the team, and ignore the suggestions that would change the meaning. Review ▸ Check Accessibility tells you what a screen reader user would hit: images without alt text (right-click an image ▸ View Alt Text), tables without a header row, text that is a heading in looks but not in style. Fixing those is not charity; the same fixes are what make the document work with Copilot and with the Navigation pane. Then File ▸ Export ▸ Create PDF/XPS, and in Options tick "Create bookmarks using Headings" so the PDF gets a clickable outline. File ▸ Save As ▸ PDF does the same with fewer options.

Application: the Store Audit SOP and the Gold letter

Part A · Build the Store Audit SOP

Twelve stores, one audit routine, one document. The structure first, on paper, before Word: Purpose and scope; Roles; Opening checks; Floor and planogram checks; Cash and UPI reconciliation; Closing checks; Escalation; Appendix A the checklist. Seven Heading 1s. Now build it.

  1. File ▸ New ▸ Blank document, then save it straight to the Analytics SharePoint library as 2026-09_Store-Audit-SOP_v01.docx. Naming is from Module 01; AutoSave switches on because the file is in the cloud.
  2. Home ▸ Styles ▸ Title and type "Store Audit SOP". Press Enter, and under it in Normal type one line: "Applies to all 12 Novamart stores. Owner: Nandini Rao, COO." Word drops you back into Normal automatically after a Title or Heading, which is the behaviour you want.
  3. Type the seven section names, one per line, then put the cursor in each and press Ctrl+Alt+1. Open the Navigation pane with Ctrl+F; you should see all seven. If one is missing, it is in Normal, not Heading 1.
  4. Under "Opening checks" add "Cash float", "Planogram", "Systems" and make them Ctrl+Alt+2. Repeat for the other sections. Your outline now has about 20 headings and the document has no body text yet. That's correct. Structure first.
  5. Home ▸ Paragraph ▸ Multilevel List, and pick the gallery entry that shows "1 Heading 1 / 1.1 Heading 2 / 1.1.1 Heading 3". Every heading numbers itself. Drag "Escalation" above "Closing checks" in the Navigation pane and watch the numbers follow.
  6. Write the procedures. Under "2.1 Cash float", type each step and apply Home ▸ Paragraph ▸ Numbering. Right-click the first "1." of the next procedure and choose Restart at 1 so each procedure counts from one. Keep every step an instruction that starts with a verb: "Count the float against the ₹5,000 standard. Record the variance on the sheet. Escalate any variance above ₹200 to the store manager before the store opens."
  7. The checklist table. Build it in Excel first because Excel is better at rows: columns Check · Frequency · Owner · Evidence · Pass/Fail, about 25 rows. Copy, and in Word paste with Use Destination Styles. Then Table Layout ▸ Repeat Header Rows and Table Design ▸ pick a "Grid Table 4" style with banded rows.
  8. Caption it: click in the table, References ▸ Insert Caption, label Table, text "Store audit checklist". In section 1 write "The full checklist is in " and References ▸ Cross-reference ▸ Table ▸ Only label and number. It reads "The full checklist is in Table 1" and will stay right when you add a table before it.
  9. Cover and contents. Put the cursor before the Title, Insert ▸ Cover Page (pick a plain one, delete the subtitle placeholders you don't need). Press Ctrl+Enter after the cover's text, type "Contents" in Heading 1, and References ▸ Table of Contents ▸ Automatic Table 1. Right-click the TOC ▸ Edit Field ▸ Table of Contents ▸ Options if you need to exclude "Contents" itself.
  10. Page numbers: Insert ▸ Page Number ▸ Bottom of Page ▸ Plain Number 2. In the Header & Footer tab tick Different First Page so the cover is clean. Add "Store Audit SOP · v" and a Quick Parts ▸ Field ▸ SaveDate to the footer.
  11. Appendix A holds the checklist in landscape. Put the cursor at the end of section 7, Layout ▸ Breaks ▸ Next Page, then Layout ▸ Orientation ▸ Landscape. Only the appendix turns. Check the footer still shows on the landscape page; if it vanished, double-click the footer and switch Link to Previous on.
  12. Ctrl+A, F9, and choose "Update entire table" when asked. Run Review ▸ Check Accessibility. Turn on Track Changes, lock it, and share the link with Nandini and Vikram with edit access. Message them the link, not the file.

What comes back on Thursday is a document with 30 tracked changes and 11 comments. Walk them with Review ▸ Next. Accept the wording changes, reject the one where Nandini deleted the UPI reconciliation step (and reply in the comment explaining why it stays), resolve each thread, save, and the version history shows v01 (yours) and the reviewed state. Rename the file to _v02 only when it goes to the store managers. Export to PDF with bookmarks. Done in the hour.

Part B · The Gold-tier festive letter, merged from Excel

Mail merge is three things plugged together: a data source (an Excel sheet where each row is one recipient), a main document (the letter with placeholders), and the merge that stamps out one letter per row. The data source is where the work is, and it is Excel work.

Start in the Lab. Priya's rule is "Gold tier, with an email address, and I want the first name in the salutation". How many are we talking about?

=COUNTIF(Customers!L:L,"Gold")

44. Small enough to eyeball every letter after the merge, which you should do anyway the first time. Now the list itself: name, email and city, Gold only, and only rows that have an email. The multiply between the two conditions is how FILTER does AND.

=FILTER(HSTACK(Customers!B2:B501,Customers!C2:C501,Customers!G2:G501),
    (Customers!L2:L501="Gold")*(Customers!C2:C501<>""))

44 rows spill out, so every Gold customer has an email. Priya wants Silver next month, and there the same formula would drop people, because seven Silver customers have no email on file. That's the number to send back to CRM before the merge, not after.

=COUNTIFS(Customers!L:L,"Silver",Customers!C:C,"")

Seven. A merge doesn't warn you; it produces seven letters addressed to nobody. Two more prep columns and the list is ready: the salutation and a display string for the email version. TEXTBEFORE takes everything before the first space, so "Riya Saxena" gives "Dear Riya,". Names in this sheet are already Proper Case, but on a CRM export they often aren't, so the PROPER habit is worth keeping.

="Dear "&TEXTBEFORE(Customers!B2:B6," ")&","
=PROPER(Customers!B2:B6)&" <"&Customers!C2:C6&">"

"Tanvi Gupta <tanvi.gupta@gmail.com>" is the format Outlook accepts when you paste a list into To. Paste the spilled results as values into a new workbook (Paste Special ▸ Values), header row Name · Email · City · Tier · FirstName, save it as GoldList.xlsx, close it. Word can't merge from an open workbook that is mid-edit.

One more list while you are here. Nandini's SOP goes to the 12 store managers with a covering letter, and that list is on the Employees sheet: current store managers and the store each one runs.

=FILTER(HSTACK(Employees!B2:B86,Employees!E2:E86),
    (Employees!D2:D86="Store Manager")*(Employees!H2:H86=""))

Twelve rows, Kritika Sheikh at Connaught Place through Amit Iyer at MG Road Kochi. The blank ExitDate test matters: without it, anyone who left the role would still get a letter.

Last prep question, because the print run goes to stores for hand-delivery: which cities are the Gold customers in? UNIQUE over the filtered city column, joined into one line you can paste into the email to the store managers.

=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,UNIQUE(FILTER(Customers!G2:G501,Customers!L2:L501="Gold")))

Fourteen cities, and only ten of them have a Novamart store: Bhubaneswar, Indore, Guwahati and Chandigarh customers get theirs by post. Sort the recipient list by City in Word and the pile comes off the printer grouped for dispatch.

Now Word.

  1. Mailings ▸ Start Mail Merge ▸ Letters. Nothing visible changes; Word is now in merge mode for this document.
  2. Mailings ▸ Select Recipients ▸ Use an Existing List, pick GoldList.xlsx, choose the "Recipients" sheet, and leave "First row of data contains column headers" ticked. Word reads the header row as field names.
  3. Mailings ▸ Edit Recipient List. Untick anyone who shouldn't get this one, sort by City so the printed pile comes out grouped by store, and use Filter if you'd rather keep everyone in the sheet and filter here. Filtering in Excel first is cleaner because the list is then the audit trail.
  4. Write the letter in Normal style with a Novamart Quick Part for the letterhead. Where the name goes, Mailings ▸ Insert Merge Field ▸ Name. Repeat for City and FirstName. The fields show as «Name». Address Block and Greeting Line are shortcuts that try to guess your columns; with your own FirstName column, the plain field is more predictable.
  5. Make the date a field too: Insert ▸ Date & Time, tick "Update automatically". If the print run slips a day, the letters are still right.
  6. Conditional text. Corporate customers get a different closing line. Mailings ▸ Rules ▸ If…Then…Else, field Segment, "Equal to" Corporate, then the two versions of the sentence. The rule compiles to a field code you can inspect with Alt+F9.
  7. Mailings ▸ Preview Results and step through with the arrows. Read at least five letters end to end. This is where "Dear Riya," next to a Delhi address for a Bhubaneswar customer gets caught. Check a name with an initial and a name with three words.
  8. Mailings ▸ Finish & Merge ▸ Edit Individual Documents ▸ All. Word creates one new document with 44 letters separated by section breaks. Save that as Gold-Letters_2026-09-30.docx, export to PDF, and send to print. Send Email Messages does the same through Outlook using the Email column as the To field, subject line typed once; use it only after a test run to yourself.
  9. Save the main document too. Next month, open it, and Word asks whether to reconnect to the list. Point it at the Silver file and the letter is ready in a minute.
{ MERGEFIELD Name }
{ MERGEFIELD Spend \# "₹#,##0" }
{ IF { MERGEFIELD Segment } = "Corporate" "Your account manager will call to book a slot." "Walk in any time from 10 October." }

The \# switch is how you format a number from Excel inside Word; without it, ₹12,500.00 arrives as 12500. Labels work the same way: Start Mail Merge ▸ Labels, pick the A4 label vendor and product number from the box, insert fields in the first label, then Update Labels to copy the layout to every label on the sheet.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askWord feature that answers it
Operations"Rewrite the store audit SOP and keep it current every quarter."Heading styles, multilevel numbering, automatic TOC, a .dotx template, SaveDate field in the footer
Marketing / CRM"Personalised festive letter to 44 Gold customers, by name and city."Mail merge from an Excel list prepared with FILTER; If…Then…Else for segment-specific lines
Finance"Monthly MIS commentary with the variance table from the workbook."Paste as linked table with destination styles; Update Link before each issue; caption and cross-reference
HR"Offer letters for 9 new sales associates by Monday."Mail merge from the recruitment sheet, \# switch for the salary figure, PDF export per letter
Legal / Procurement"Vendor agreement redlines from three reviewers, in one document."Track Changes locked on, Comments with @mentions, Compare for anyone who edited a copy
Strategy"Two-page brief for the board, clean PDF, accessible."Styles, Editor pass, Check Accessibility, Export to PDF with heading bookmarks
Everyone"Minutes of the Monday review, out within the hour."A minutes template with a Decisions table and an Actions table; Quick Parts for the attendee block

The HR letter and the audit SOP share a data question: who exactly is on the list? Kavita Iyer's policy circular on the new leave rules goes to every current manager, and "manager" is any job title containing the word. The wildcard does the matching, and the blank ExitDate test keeps it to current staff.

=COUNTIFS(Employees!D:D,"*Manager*",Employees!H:H,"")

21 people, from the Analytics Manager to the twelve store managers. Wrap the same criteria in FILTER to get the names and cities, and the circular's merge list is done before Kavita has finished asking.

Practice

Most of these are tasks in Word. Do them in a real document; the "what good looks like" text is the checklist a reviewer would use. The two formula exercises run in the Lab.

Exercise 1 · Rescue the old SOP

Open the 2022 Store Audit SOP (or any long document where the headings are hand-bolded). Without retyping anything, turn every hand-formatted heading into a real Heading 1 or Heading 2, and make the Navigation pane show the full outline.

Hint

Ctrl+H ▸ More ▸ Format. The Find box can search for formatting with no text at all, and the Replace box can apply a style.

What good looks like

Find: empty text, Format ▸ Font ▸ Bold, size 14. Replace: empty text, Format ▸ Style ▸ Heading 1. Replace All. Then the same for bold 12 pt to Heading 2. Then select all and clear the leftover direct formatting with Ctrl+Space on the affected paragraphs if the bold survived.

  • The Navigation pane shows every section, nested correctly.
  • No heading is bold "by hand"; the Styles pane shows Heading 1 or 2 when the cursor is on it.
  • The typed contents page has been deleted and replaced by an automatic TOC.

Exercise 2 · Roman numerals, then 1

The SOP's cover and contents pages should be numbered i and ii; the body should start at page 1 on "Purpose and scope". The cover itself should show no number.

Hint

Two sections. Page Number ▸ Format Page Numbers is per section, and "Link to Previous" is the switch that keeps sections sharing a footer.

What good looks like

Insert a Next Page section break at the end of the contents page. In section 1, Format Page Numbers ▸ i, ii, iii, tick Different First Page for the cover. Double-click the footer of section 2, switch off Link to Previous, Format Page Numbers ▸ 1, 2, 3 ▸ Start at 1.

  • Cover: no number. Contents: ii. First body page: 1.
  • The TOC shows 1 for "Purpose and scope", not 3.
  • Formatting marks (Ctrl+Shift+8) show exactly one section break.

Exercise 3 · The linked variance table

Arjun Mehta's monthly commentary carries a Budget vs Actual table that changes every month while the layout stays the same. Bring the table from Excel into the Word commentary so that next month's refresh is one click, not a re-paste.

Hint

Paste Options has two "Link" choices. Choose the one that uses the document's table style, then find where links are managed under File ▸ Info.

What good looks like

Copy the range in Excel; in Word, Paste Options ▸ Link & Use Destination Styles. Apply a table style, Repeat Header Rows, caption it "Table 1: Budget vs Actual, August 2026". Next month, change the workbook, then in Word right-click the table ▸ Update Link (or File ▸ Info ▸ Edit Links to Files ▸ Update Now).

  • The table takes the document's font, not Excel's.
  • Changing a number in the workbook and updating the link changes it in Word.
  • The caption's number is a field, not typed.

Exercise 4 · Who can actually receive the tier letter?

Priya now wants the festive letter to go to both Gold and Silver customers. How many customers will receive it, counting only those with an email address on file?

Hint

Two COUNTIFS, added. The email test is "<>", meaning not blank.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(Customers!L:L,"Gold",Customers!C:C,"<>")+COUNTIFS(Customers!L:L,"Silver",Customers!C:C,"<>")

111 letters: all 44 Gold and 67 of the 74 Silver. The seven Silver customers without an email go back to CRM as a data fix, not into the print run as blank envelopes.

Exercise 5 · Run the review loop

Share the SOP with two colleagues. One edits with Track Changes on; the other ignores the link, downloads a copy, edits it and emails it back. Bring both sets of changes into the master without losing anything.

Hint

The first reviewer's changes are already in the master. The second reviewer's need Review ▸ Compare.

What good looks like

Walk the first reviewer's changes with Review ▸ Next, Accept or Reject each, reply to and resolve every comment. Then Review ▸ Compare ▸ Compare, original = the master, revised = the emailed copy; Word opens a third document showing the copy's edits as tracked changes. Accept the ones you want there, then copy the revised sections back into the master, or keep the compare result as the new master if it is cleaner.

  • No comment is left unresolved.
  • Version history shows the state before and after each round.
  • File ▸ Info ▸ Inspect Document reports no hidden tracked changes or comments before the PDF is exported.

Exercise 6 · Clean a pasted vendor document

A vendor sent their delivery terms as a document with double spaces after every full stop, "Rs." in six different spellings, and dates as 03/10/2026. Fix all three with Find & Replace, then make the document pass Check Accessibility with zero errors.

Hint

Wildcards on. Brackets capture; \1 reuses. Accessibility errors on tables are usually the missing header row.

What good looks like

Three replaces: two spaces to one (repeat until "0 replacements"); Rs\.? ?([0-9]) to ₹\1; ([0-9]{2})/([0-9]{2})/([0-9]{4}) to \1-\2-\3. Then Review ▸ Check Accessibility: add alt text to the vendor logo, tick Repeat Header Rows on the rates table, restyle the bold lines as Heading 2.

  • Searching for two spaces finds nothing.
  • Every rupee amount starts with ₹ and no "Rs" remains (search to prove it).
  • The Accessibility pane says "No accessibility issues found".

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

Tracked changes and comments travel with the file. A vendor agreement that still carries "can we push them to 45 days? they'll take 30" in a resolved comment is a real thing that has happened to real people. Before any document leaves the company, File ▸ Info ▸ Check for Issues ▸ Inspect Document and remove comments, revisions and document properties, or export to PDF, which drops them. Do this even when you are sure you accepted everything.

Watch out

A mail merge sends exactly what the list says. "riya.saxena@gmai.com" gets a bounced email, "RIYA SAXENA" gets a shouty letter, a blank City field produces "Novamart from 10 October" with two spaces. Preview Results is not optional, and the fixes go into the spreadsheet, never into individual merged letters, or the next merge repeats the mistake.

Pro habit

Write the outline as headings before writing a single body sentence, then write into it. The Navigation pane becomes your plan, the TOC is done, and when Vikram says "move escalation earlier" it is a drag, not an afternoon. The same habit makes Copilot's "summarise this section" useful, because a section exists.

  • Never format by hand what a style could do. If you find yourself selecting text and clicking Bold for the third time, stop and modify the style instead.
  • One file, shared by link. Emailing a .docx forks it. Two forks need Compare; five forks need a weekend.
  • Fields update, typed numbers rot. TOC, captions, cross-references, dates, page numbers: fields. Ctrl+A, F9 before you export.
  • Tables come from Excel. Build rows in Excel, sort and filter there, paste with destination styles. Word's table editor is for small adjustments, not for data entry.
  • Section breaks are rare and deliberate. Three in a 20-page document is normal; fifteen means someone used them as page breaks.
  • The merge list is a data product. Save it, name it, date it. When someone asks who got the letter, the answer is a file, not a memory.

On the job

In the assessment test

Word tasks in an analyst test are short and they test structure: "Here is a six-page document. Apply heading styles, add a table of contents and page numbers, insert this Excel table with a caption, and turn on Track Changes. 15 minutes." The candidates who fail are the ones who bold the headings and type "Contents". Practise the sequence until it is under five minutes: Ctrl+Alt+1 and 2 down the document, References ▸ Table of Contents, Insert ▸ Page Number, paste with destination styles, Insert Caption, Ctrl+Shift+E.

First 90 days

The documents a management trainee is asked to produce in the first month, in the order they usually arrive.

WeekDocumentWhat it needs from this module
1Minutes of the Monday reviewA template with Decisions and Actions tables; out within the hour; shared by link
1–2One-page brief on a question Vikram askedTitle, three Heading 2s (What we found · So what · Next), one linked table, Editor pass
2An SOP or process noteNumbered headings, numbered procedures, a checklist table, a version footer, Track Changes for review
3A letter or circular to many peopleMail merge from a list you prepared with FILTER; Preview Results; PDF per recipient
3–4Commentary for the monthly packLinked Excel tables, captions and cross-references, exported to PDF with bookmarks; feeds Module 09
4A vendor or partner document with redlinesLocked Track Changes, Compare, Inspect Document before it leaves
Interview question: "How would you keep a 40-page policy document maintainable over three years?"
Build it on heading styles with linked multilevel numbering, an automatic TOC, captions and cross-references, so every renumbering is a field update. Keep it in one SharePoint location with version history, review with Track Changes rather than emailed copies, and save the skeleton as a .dotx so the next policy starts consistent.
Interview question: "Walk me through a mail merge, including what can go wrong."
Prepare the list in Excel: one header row, one recipient per row, filtered to exactly who should receive it, with derived columns such as FirstName. Connect it in Word, insert merge fields, add rules for conditional text, Preview Results across several records, then Finish & Merge. The failures are data failures: blank fields, wrong casing, invalid emails, and formatting numbers without the \# switch.
Interview question: "What is the difference between a page break and a section break?"
A page break moves text to the next page and nothing else changes. A section break starts a new section that can carry its own headers, footers, page-number format, margins and orientation. You need a section break for a landscape appendix or for roman-numeral front matter; you need a page break for almost everything else.

Quick check

1. You bold and enlarge every section name by hand. Which of these still works?

The Navigation pane, the TOC, numbering, PDF bookmarks and screen readers all read the style, not the look. Bold text in Normal style is body text to Word.

2. The appendix must be landscape while the rest stays portrait. What do you insert before it?

Orientation is a section property. A page break stays in the same section, so changing orientation there would turn the whole document.

3. A reviewer edited an emailed copy of the SOP instead of the shared file. Fastest way to see exactly what they changed?

Compare recreates the redline between two files as tracked changes. Track Changes only records edits made after it is switched on.

4. In the merged letters, a salary of 45000 should read ₹45,000. Where is the fix?

Mail merge reads the raw value, not Excel's display format. The numeric picture switch on the MERGEFIELD formats it in Word; typing ₹ alone still leaves 45000 without the comma.
