Then build it for real: Capstone 09, Store Audit SOP and mail-merge letters is this module end to end, graded.

Level 2 · Module 09 · about 75 min

PowerPoint: slides that get a decision

A deck is not a document you read out loud. It is an argument, one claim per slide, built so that a CEO with nine minutes reaches the decision you need her to reach. This module teaches the storyline first, the software second, and then builds the ten-slide Festive Season Review that Meera and Nandini will see, with every number pulled from the Novamart workbook.

  • You'll plan a deck as a storyline (situation, complication, question, answer) before opening PowerPoint.
  • You'll write action titles that state the finding, with the number in them, and put one message on each slide.
  • You'll set up a slide master and layouts so that thirty slides share one look and a font change takes ten seconds.
  • You'll bring Excel charts in linked, so the pack refreshes when the workbook does, and know when a table beats a chart.
  • You'll use Designer, Morph, Zoom, sections, speaker notes, Presenter View and rehearsed timings without letting them run the show.
  • You'll pass the "make me three slides by 6" test that every analyst gets in month one.

Concept

Wednesday, 2:05 pm

Vikram forwards a one-line email from Meera Krishnan: "Festive review at Monday's leadership meeting. Ten slides, twenty minutes, I want to leave with a decision on next year's festive budget split." Nandini has added: "And tell me whether Kochi is working." You have the Sales, Orders and Returns sheets, and four days.

Most first decks fail in the same way. They are organised by data: a slide of revenue, a slide of channels, a slide of categories, a slide of returns, each titled with the name of the thing on it. The audience does the analysis in their heads, in real time, and reaches whatever conclusion their mood suggests. Twenty minutes later, no decision.

A deck that gets a decision is organised by argument. Consultants call the shape SCQA, after Barbara Minto: Situation (what everyone agrees on), Complication (what changed or went wrong), Question (the one thing to decide), Answer (your recommendation, stated up front), then the evidence, then the ask. The answer comes early because executives read the first slide and the last slide and skim the middle. Give them the conclusion on slide 2 and the middle becomes proof rather than suspense.

The second idea is the action title. A topic title names the subject: "Revenue by channel". An action title states the finding: "The app nearly doubled at festive; stores grew 6%". A reader who sees only the titles, one per slide, should be able to follow the whole argument. That's the test. Open the Outline view (View ▸ Outline View) and read the titles top to bottom. If they don't make an argument, the deck isn't finished, however good the charts look.

Why a manager cares

Meera has seen a thousand decks. She will read slide 2 and ask a question about slide 7 before you reach it. A storyline deck survives that, because every slide stands alone with its claim in the title and its proof underneath. A data deck falls apart, because the point was going to be made on slide 9. The budget decision she makes on Monday is worth more than the whole Analytics team's salaries for the year; a deck that helps her make it well is the most valuable thing you'll produce this quarter.

How it works

The slide master and layouts

Every slide in a deck sits on a layout, and every layout sits on the slide master. Change the master's font and every slide changes. Put the Novamart logo on the master and it appears everywhere. Put it on a slide by hand and you will be nudging it into place on thirty slides at 11 pm. View ▸ Slide Master opens the hierarchy; the big thumbnail at the top is the master, the smaller ones under it are the layouts.

  1. View ▸ Slide Master. Click the top thumbnail. Slide Master ▸ Background ▸ Fonts ▸ Customize Fonts: one heading font, one body font. Novamart's deck uses Segoe UI for both; a single family is the safe choice.
  2. Slide Master ▸ Background ▸ Colors ▸ Customize Colors. Set Accent 1 to the brand colour and Accent 2 to a grey. Every chart you paste later will pick these up, which is how a deck ends up with one colour and one highlight instead of six.
  3. Drag the logo onto the master, bottom right, small. Insert ▸ Header & Footer, tick Slide number and Footer, type "Novamart · Festive Season Review · Confidential". Apply to All.
  4. Delete the layouts you won't use (right-click ▸ Delete Layout) until five remain: Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content, Section Header, Title Only. Fewer layouts, fewer ways to drift.
  5. On Title and Content, drag the title placeholder to allow two lines; action titles are longer than topic titles. Set it to 24 pt, left-aligned, bold. Body 16 pt minimum; 14 for a table if you must.
  6. Close Master View. From now on, every new slide comes from Home ▸ New Slide ▸ [layout], and if a slide looks wrong, Home ▸ Slides ▸ Reset fixes it.

Save the finished master as a theme (Design ▸ Themes ▸ Save Current Theme) or a template (.potx) so the next deck starts from it. Company decks that look inconsistent are almost always decks where each analyst rebuilt the look by hand.

Action title vs topic title

Writing an action title is a discipline. It has a subject, a verb and usually a number. It fits in two lines at 24 pt, about 90 characters. It is a sentence, not a label, and it is true on its own. "Electronics carried the festive season: +40% to ₹11.0 lakh, 46% of the total" is a title. "Category performance" is a filing label.

Charts from Excel: paste options

Build the chart in Excel (Module 07), copy it, and in PowerPoint right-click and look at the five paste icons. They decide whether the deck updates next month.

Paste optionWhat you getUse it when
Use Destination Theme & Embed WorkbookA chart in the deck's colours with a copy of the workbook inside the .pptxOne-off decks that travel; the file gets bigger and the copy goes stale
Keep Source Formatting & Embed WorkbookSame, in Excel's coloursRarely; it fights the master
Use Destination Theme & Link DataA chart in deck colours that points at the workbook on SharePoint; Chart Design ▸ Refresh Data pulls the new numbersMonthly packs and the festive review: the numbers move, the slide doesn't
Keep Source Formatting & Link DataLinked, Excel coloursWhen the Excel chart was already styled to the brand
PictureA static imageDecks that leave the company, or when the source workbook is confidential

Linked charts break when the workbook moves or is renamed, so keep the pack and its workbook in the same SharePoint folder and manage links under File ▸ Info ▸ Edit Links to Files. Sometimes a table is the honest choice: when the audience will read individual numbers (a budget by channel with owners), when there are more than seven categories, or when the point is the exact figure rather than the shape. Paste as a table with destination styles, 14 pt minimum, right-align numbers, and bold the one row that matters.

The tools that are worth learning, and what each is for

FeatureWhereWhat it's forTrap
DesignerDesign ▸ Designer (appears when you add content)Layout ideas for a title slide or a slide with one image and three bulletsIt ignores your master and over-decorates data slides; use it for the cover, then close it
MorphTransitions ▸ Morph on the second of two slides sharing objectsZooming into the Kochi bar, or moving the same chart while the title changesObjects must be the same object (duplicate the slide, then edit); more than three Morphs and it looks like a screensaver
ZoomInsert ▸ Zoom ▸ Section Zoom / Slide ZoomAn agenda slide that jumps to whichever section Meera asks about firstOnly useful when you present live and expect questions out of order
SectionsRight-click between thumbnails ▸ Add SectionGrouping 10 slides into Context · Evidence · Ask; collapsing them in the thumbnail pane; printing one sectionNone; use them from slide 6 onwards on every deck
Speaker notesView ▸ Notes or the Notes bar under the slideWhat you'll say, the source of each number, the answer to the obvious questionNotes are not a script to read; two or three lines per slide
Presenter ViewSlide Show ▸ Use Presenter View; Alt+F5 to try it on one screenYour notes, the next slide and a timer on your screen; the slide alone on theirsTest the second screen before the meeting, not during it
Rehearse TimingsSlide Show ▸ Rehearse TimingsFinding out that slide 6 takes four minutes and the deck takes 31Don't save the timings as an auto-advance unless it is a kiosk
Align toolsShape Format ▸ Align, and the Smart Guides that appear as you dragThree boxes the same width and evenly spaced in two clicksAlignment by eye is visible from the back of the room
Crop and iconsPicture Format ▸ Crop (also Crop to Shape); Insert ▸ IconsA product photo cropped to the frame; a consistent icon set for the four next stepsStretched images; icons from six different sets
ExportFile ▸ Export ▸ Create PDF / Create a Video / HandoutsThe PDF goes in the pre-read; the video with recorded narration goes to store managers who missed itA PDF loses Morph and Zoom; check that nothing depended on them

Two shortcuts that pay for themselves: Ctrl+D duplicates the selected slide or object, and F5 / Shift+F5 start the show from the beginning or from the current slide. Ctrl+Shift+G ungroups a pasted chart into shapes when you need to recolour one bar and nothing else works, though a linked chart should be recoloured in Excel instead.

Application: the Festive Season Review, slide by slide

Festive at Novamart means October and November: Dhanteras through Diwali to the Bhai Dooj weekend, plus the sale that runs into late November. The workbook's Month column is text, so each two-month window is two SUMIFS added together. Every number below comes from the Lab; the slide title is written after the number, never before.

Before any slide, the storyline on paper. Ten titles, one line each. If the argument doesn't work as ten lines it won't work as ten slides.

#LayoutJob in the storylineAction title (draft, numbers filled in below)
1Title SlideTitleFestive Season Review 2025 · what it tells us about 2026
2Title and ContentAnswerFestive grew 29% to ₹24.1 lakh; the growth came from app and online, so 2026 spend should follow it
3Section HeaderQuestionHow should the 2026 festive budget be split across store, online and app?
4Two ContentEvidence: totalFestive revenue grew 29% to ₹24.1 lakh; October carried it because Diwali moved
5Two ContentEvidence: channelThe app nearly doubled (+96%); stores grew 6% and lost nine points of share
6Two ContentEvidence: categoryElectronics and Home & Kitchen carried the season; Fashion fell 6%
7Two ContentEvidence: KochiKochi grew 46% at festive but is still 1% of the total
8Two ContentEvidence: returnsReturns fell to 6.9% of orders, but "defective" is now nearly half of them
9Title and ContentRecommendationMove a third of festive spend to app and online, and stop defective stock at the door before October
10Title and ContentAskFour decisions today, four owners, first check-in 15 October

Slide 1 · Title

Title Slide layout. "Festive Season Review 2025", subtitle "Strategy & Analytics · Leadership meeting · 29 September 2026 · v03". The version number saves a "which file are we looking at?" on Monday. Nothing else. Let Designer suggest a cover if you like, then close it.

Slide 2 · Executive summary

This is the answer slide. Three short paragraphs, or three numbered lines: what happened, why it matters, what we recommend. It is written last, after the evidence slides exist, and it is the slide Meera will photograph. The numbers in it are the ones the evidence slides prove.

Slide 3 · The question

Section Header layout, one sentence: "How should the 2026 festive budget be split across store, online and app?" It sits alone so the room agrees on what it is deciding before any evidence lands. If Nandini's Kochi question is going to be answered too, add it as a second line, smaller.

Slide 4 · Festive revenue, 2024 vs 2025

Start with the two totals. Order lines of every status, because that is what the stores rang up; the delivered-only view goes in the notes.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-11")
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11")

₹18,65,267 became ₹24,13,539: ₹18.65 lakh to ₹24.14 lakh. The growth as one number, formatted for the title:

=TEXT((SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))
    /(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-11"))-1,"0.0%")

29.4%. Now the part that makes the slide worth having. Someone will ask "which month?", and the monthly view is a trap. October alone looks like a miracle and November alone looks flat, because Diwali sat on the month boundary in 2024 (31 October, with Bhai Dooj on 3 November) and fell on 20 October in 2025. The whole festive fortnight moved into October.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10")/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-10")-1
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11")/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-11")-1

+74% and +5%. Neither is the story; the two-month window is. That's the second line of the title and the first line of the speaker notes. The chart is a clustered column, two bars per month, 2024 in grey, 2025 in the accent colour, data labels on, no legend needed once the title says which is which. Paste it with Use Destination Theme & Link Data.

Two supporting figures for the right-hand text box: orders and average order value, from the Orders sheet where an order is one row.

=COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),Orders!B:B,"<="&DATE(2025,11,30))
=AVERAGEIFS(Orders!J:J,Orders!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),Orders!B:B,"<="&DATE(2025,11,30))

289 orders, up from 240, and ₹8,351 per order, up from ₹7,772. So growth came from more orders (+20%) more than from bigger baskets (+7%). Three bullets on the right: orders +20%, basket +7%, Diwali moved to October.

Slide 5 · By channel

Three channels, two years, one table, built with VSTACK so it comes out as a block you can chart directly. The Lab doesn't spill SUMIFS over an array of criteria, and neither does older Excel, so each channel is written out.

=VSTACK(
    HSTACK("Store",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Store",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Store",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),
                   SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Store",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Store",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("Online",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Online",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Online",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),
                    SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Online",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"Online",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("App",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),
                 SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")))

Store ₹9.85 lakh to ₹10.44 lakh, Online ₹6.10 lakh to ₹8.42 lakh, App ₹2.70 lakh to ₹5.28 lakh. Growth of 6%, 38% and 96%. Share is the number that makes the budget argument, so compute it for the title:

=(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!G:G,"App",Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))
    /(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))

21.9%, from 14.5% a year earlier; stores went from 52.8% to 43.3%, the "nine points of share" in the title. Chart: clustered column by channel, the App 2025 bar in the accent colour and every other bar grey. Right-hand bullets: the shares, and one line on where the marketing budget currently goes (that number comes from Priya, not the workbook; say so in the notes).

Slide 6 · By category

Six categories is the limit for a chart; beyond that it's a table. Same pattern, six rows.

=VSTACK(
    HSTACK("Electronics",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Electronics",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Electronics",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Electronics",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Electronics",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("Home & Kitchen",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Home & Kitchen",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Home & Kitchen",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Home & Kitchen",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Home & Kitchen",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("Fashion",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Fashion",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Fashion",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Fashion",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Fashion",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("Sports & Outdoors",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Sports & Outdoors",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Sports & Outdoors",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Sports & Outdoors",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Sports & Outdoors",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("Beauty & Personal Care",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Beauty & Personal Care",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Beauty & Personal Care",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Beauty & Personal Care",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Beauty & Personal Care",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")),
    HSTACK("Grocery & Gourmet",SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Grocery & Gourmet",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Grocery & Gourmet",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"),SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Grocery & Gourmet",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!K:K,"Grocery & Gourmet",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")))

Electronics ₹7.85 lakh to ₹11.00 lakh (+40%, and 46% of the season on its own). Home & Kitchen ₹3.49 lakh to ₹5.32 lakh (+52%). Fashion ₹3.71 lakh to ₹3.47 lakh, down 6%, the only category that fell. Sports +17%, Beauty +28%, Grocery +26% on small bases. The chart is a horizontal bar, sorted by 2025 value, Fashion's bar in the warning colour. Rohan Desai will want to know why Fashion fell; that's a speaker note ("assortment landed late; Rohan to confirm"), not a claim on the slide.

Slide 7 · The Kochi story

Nandini's question deserves an honest slide, which means two numbers that pull in opposite directions.

=(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!E:E,"Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!E:E,"Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))
    /(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!E:E,"Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!E:E,"Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"))-1
=(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!E:E,"Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!E:E,"Kochi",Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))
    /(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))

+46%, from ₹16,467 to ₹24,097, and 1.0% of the season. Both go in the title, because a slide that says only "+46%" is spin and a slide that says only "1%" is unfair to a store that opened in April 2024. Two big numbers side by side, no chart, and a one-line so-what: "Kochi is growing faster than the chain but from a base too small to move the festive result; judge it on 2026". A Morph from slide 5's channel chart into a single Kochi bar works well here if you want one Morph in the deck.

Slide 8 · Returns

Returns are on their own sheet, one row per return, dated by the return date, so the criteria are real dates rather than the text month. The rate needs a denominator from Orders.

=COUNTIFS(Returns!D:D,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),Returns!D:D,"<="&DATE(2025,11,30))
    /COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),Orders!B:B,"<="&DATE(2025,11,30))
=COUNTIFS(Returns!D:D,">="&DATE(2024,10,1),Returns!D:D,"<="&DATE(2024,11,30))
    /COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&DATE(2024,10,1),Orders!B:B,"<="&DATE(2024,11,30))

6.9% against 8.75%: 20 returns on 289 orders versus 21 on 240. Better, and the refunds tell the same story, ₹70,342 against ₹93,515. Then the reason mix, which is where the operations point hides.

=COUNTIFS(Returns!E:E,"Defective",Returns!D:D,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),Returns!D:D,"<="&DATE(2025,11,30))

Nine of the twenty, up from six of twenty-one the year before, and ₹35,617 of the ₹70,342 refunded. Fewer returns overall, but nearly half are now stock that arrived faulty: two Glow serums, a shampoo, trail mix, baked chips, a candle trio, a perfume, a charger and one ₹27,999 smartphone. That is a buying and inbound-check problem, not a customer problem, and it lands on Rohan Desai's desk before the 2026 stock-up. The link to slide 9: the categories that grew most are the ones being stocked deepest, so a defect rate that holds steady costs more rupees next year. Chart: a stacked bar of reasons, two years, "Defective" highlighted; or a table if the room will want the counts.

Slide 9 · Recommendation

Title and Content layout, and the title is the recommendation: "Move a third of festive spend to app and online, and stop defective stock at the door before October". Under it, three numbered recommendations, each with its evidence slide number in brackets so anyone can check. Nothing new appears on this slide; if you find yourself adding a fact here, it belongs on an evidence slide.

Slide 10 · Next steps

A four-row table: Decision · Owner · By when · Evidence. Sameer Joshi owns the app and online allocation, Priya Nair the Gold-tier early-access campaign, Rohan Desai the inbound quality check on Beauty and Grocery batches, Arjun Mehta the budget line; Nandini chairs the 15 October check-in and carries the Kochi 2026 target. Dates in the same column, first check-in 15 October. This slide is the ask; it is what the meeting produces if it goes well, and it is the slide you send round afterwards as the minutes.

Finishing the deck

  1. View ▸ Outline View. Read the ten titles top to bottom as a paragraph. Fix any title that doesn't move the argument on.
  2. Add sections: right-click between slides 3 and 4 ▸ Add Section "Evidence", and between 8 and 9 "Ask". Rename the first "Context".
  3. Speaker notes on every evidence slide: the formula or sheet the number came from, and the answer to the obvious question. Slide 4's notes say "delivered-only growth is 33%, all-status is 29%; Diwali 31 Oct 2024 vs 20 Oct 2025, so the festive fortnight moved into October".
  4. Slide Show ▸ Rehearse Timings. Talk it through once, out loud. If it's over 16 minutes, the cuts come from slides 6 and 8, never from 2, 9 or 10.
  5. Transitions ▸ Morph on slide 7 if you built the Kochi zoom; nothing on any other slide. Check every chart is linked (File ▸ Info ▸ Edit Links to Files) and that the workbook is in the same folder.
  6. File ▸ Export ▸ Create PDF/XPS for the pre-read; send it Friday morning. Alt+F5 to test Presenter View, then F5 in the room. Keep the .pptx open on the second screen in case Meera asks for the category table on slide 6 to be sorted the other way.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askStoryline shape and PowerPoint feature
Finance"Monthly pack for the leadership meeting, same layout every month."Fixed master and layouts; every chart linked to the pack workbook; Refresh Data on the first of the month; Capstone 02
Marketing"Post-campaign review: did the Diwali preview pay back?"SCQA with the answer on slide 2; a waterfall of spend to revenue; one table of campaign by channel
Operations"Store managers' briefing on the new audit SOP, recorded."Section per SOP chapter; Zoom agenda slide; Record narration; Export as video for those who miss it
HR"Induction deck for the September trainees."Designer for the image-heavy slides; icons for the four values; notes with what the presenter says each time
Merchandising"Category review for Rohan: which SKUs to drop before festive."Tables, not charts, for the 20 SKUs; bold the drop candidates; a single action title per category
Strategy"Three slides for the board on Kochi, by 6 pm."Answer, evidence, ask; numbers from SUMIFS; Title Only layout with one chart; see On the job

The finance pack and the festive review share a rule: the number on the slide must be reproducible from the workbook by someone else. When Arjun asks "delivered only, or everything?", the notes answer it, and the formula is one line.

=(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-10",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"))
    /(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-10",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2024-11",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"))-1

33.1% on delivered lines, against 29.4% on everything. Both true, both in the notes, and the slide says which one it is showing in a footnote in 10 pt. A deck that hides its definition gets caught by the CFO in the first five minutes.

Practice

Four of these are tasks in PowerPoint; the "what good looks like" text is what Vikram would check. Two run in the Lab, because the deck is only as good as its numbers.

Exercise 1 · Rewrite the titles

Here are five topic titles from a trainee's festive deck: "Revenue overview", "Channel performance", "Category analysis", "Kochi store update", "Returns data". Rewrite each as an action title using the numbers from this module, then read the five in a row and check they make an argument.

Hint

Subject, verb, number. Under 90 characters. Each one true on its own.

What good looks like
  • "Festive revenue grew 29% to ₹24.1 lakh, with October carrying it because Diwali moved"
  • "The app nearly doubled (+96%) while stores grew 6% and lost nine points of share"
  • "Electronics and Home & Kitchen drove the season; Fashion was the only category to fall (−6%)"
  • "Kochi grew 46% at festive but is still 1% of the total"
  • "Returns fell to 6.9% of orders, but 'defective' is now nearly half of them"

Read together, they say: we grew, the growth was digital, two categories did the work, Kochi is early, and faulty inbound stock is the risk. That is the argument slide 9 rests on.

Exercise 2 · Build the master

Start a blank deck and set up a Novamart master: one font family, an accent colour and a grey, a logo bottom right, slide numbers and a footer, and exactly five layouts. Then add three slides from three different layouts and confirm that changing the master's heading font changes all three.

Hint

View ▸ Slide Master. Fonts and Colors are under Background. Delete layouts from the thumbnail pane.

What good looks like
  • Slide Master view shows one master and five layouts: Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content, Section Header, Title Only.
  • The logo and footer appear on every content slide without being on any slide individually (click one on a slide; nothing selects).
  • Changing the heading font in the master changes every slide's title.
  • Home ▸ Reset on a slide you deliberately messed up snaps it back.

Exercise 3 · Cancelled lines in the festive window

Slide 4 counts every order line regardless of status. How much festive 2025 line revenue was on lines that ended up Cancelled? (Two months, one status.)

Hint

Same pair of SUMIFS as slide 4, with a third criterion on Sales!Q:Q.

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Cancelled",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Cancelled",Sales!C:C,"2025-11")

₹1,48,191, about 6% of the season. Worth a footnote on slide 4 and a line in the notes; not worth a slide.

Exercise 4 · Link, then refresh

Build the slide 5 channel chart in Excel from the VSTACK block, paste it into the deck linked with the destination theme, then change one number in the workbook and get the slide to show it without re-pasting.

Hint

Paste Options, third icon. Refresh lives on the Chart Design tab.

What good looks like
  • The chart is in the deck's accent colour, not Excel's default blue.
  • Chart Design ▸ Refresh Data pulls the changed value onto the slide.
  • File ▸ Info ▸ Edit Links to Files lists the workbook with its SharePoint path.
  • Only the App 2025 bar is coloured; every other bar is grey, done in Excel so the link survives.

Exercise 5 · December did what?

Meera asks whether the festive lift continued. What was December 2025 line revenue as a percentage of November 2025?

Hint

Two single-month SUMIFS on the text Month column, divided.

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-12")/SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2025-11")

About 119%: December 2025 came in above November, ₹15.07 lakh against ₹12.69 lakh, which is the year-end and wedding season rather than a festive tail. That's a backup slide, not one of the ten.

Exercise 6 · Rehearse, cut, present

Rehearse the ten-slide deck with timings. It must come in under 16 minutes, with speaker notes on every evidence slide, sections named, and a PDF exported. Then present slides 2, 5 and 9 to a colleague in Presenter View and have them ask one hostile question per slide.

Hint

Slide Show ▸ Rehearse Timings shows per-slide time at the end. The hostile questions are almost always "delivered or all?", "what's the base?", and "who owns this?".

What good looks like
  • Rehearse Timings total under 16:00; no evidence slide over 2:30.
  • Every evidence slide's notes name the sheet and the definition (all statuses vs delivered; lines vs orders).
  • Three sections visible in the thumbnail pane; the PDF opens with page 1 as the cover and nothing missing that relied on Morph.
  • The three hostile questions are answered from the notes, not improvised.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

A pasted chart with an embedded workbook carries the whole workbook inside the .pptx, including the Employees sheet with salaries. Anyone who receives the deck can right-click ▸ Edit Data and read it. For anything that leaves the team, link or paste as picture, and run File ▸ Info ▸ Check for Issues ▸ Inspect Document before you send.

Watch out

Growth percentages on small bases. Kochi's +46% is ₹7,630 of extra revenue. Grocery's +26% is ₹13,349. Put the absolute number next to any percentage under ₹1 lakh, or the room will make decisions on rounding noise. The same goes for "October +74%": a true number that tells a false story until you say Diwali moved.

Pro habit

Write the deck backwards. Slide 10 (what you want decided) first, then slide 9 (the recommendation), then the evidence slides that prove it, then slide 2 (the summary of what you just built), then slide 1. Decks written front to back end where the analysis happened to stop; decks written backwards end where the decision is.

  • One message per slide. If the title has an "and" joining two findings, that's two slides, or one finding you haven't chosen between.
  • Titles first, charts second, decoration never. No 3-D, no gradients, no clip art, one accent colour. The master enforces most of this if you let it.
  • Numbers on slides are reproducible. The formula or the pivot that produced each one is in the notes. "Roughly" is not a source.
  • Label the bars, drop the legend. A data label next to the bar beats a legend the eye has to travel to.
  • Sixteen minutes for a twenty-minute slot. Questions are the point of the meeting, not an interruption to the deck.
  • Backup slides after the last slide, in a section called Appendix. The December chart, the delivered-only view, the store-by-store table. Present none of them unless asked.

On the job

First 90 days

Sometime in the first month, at about 4:30 pm, a manager says: "Can you give me three slides on this by 6?" It is a test, and the test is not whether you can use PowerPoint. It is whether you can find the point. The answer is always the same shape: slide 1 says what you found (one sentence, one number), slide 2 shows the evidence (one chart or one table, action title, source in the notes), slide 3 says what you'd do about it and what you need from them. Use the team's master. Ask one clarifying question before you start ("delivered only, or everything?"), and none after. Send at 5:45 with a two-line email that repeats slide 1.

In the assessment test

A PowerPoint task in an analyst test is usually "here is a chart and a paragraph; make a slide". Marks go to the action title, the one-colour highlight, the labelled bars, the source line, and alignment. Marks come off for a topic title, a legend nobody needs, a pie chart with seven slices, and text under 14 pt. Ten minutes is plenty if the storyline habit is already there.

Interview question: "How do you structure a presentation for senior management?"
Answer first. I state the situation and the complication in a slide, the question the meeting exists to decide, then my recommendation on slide 2, with one evidence slide per supporting claim and a final slide of specific asks with owners and dates. Every slide has an action title that states its finding, so the titles read as the argument on their own.
Interview question: "What makes a chart slide good or bad?"
Good: the title states the finding, one colour highlights the bar that proves it, the bars carry direct labels, the axis starts at zero, and the source and definition are on the slide or in the notes. Bad: a topic title, six colours, a legend, 3-D, a pie with more than three slices, and a number nobody can reproduce.
Interview question: "Linked or embedded charts from Excel: which do you use?"
Linked with the destination theme for recurring packs, because Refresh Data updates the deck when the workbook changes and the file stays small. Embedded only for a deck that must travel on its own, knowing it carries a copy of the workbook. Picture for anything leaving the company. And I keep the deck and workbook in the same folder so links don't break.

Quick check

1. Where does the recommendation go in an SCQA deck for executives?

Executives read the first slides and skip. The answer goes up front and the evidence proves it; suspense is for films.

2. Which of these is an action title?

An action title is a sentence with a finding and usually a number. The other two name the topic and leave the analysis to the reader.

3. The monthly pack's charts must update when the workbook changes. Which paste option?

Only a linked chart refreshes from the source. Embedding copies the workbook at paste time; a picture never changes.

4. October 2025 revenue is 74% above October 2024, but the two-month festive window is up 29%. What do you put in the title?

The month comparison is distorted by the calendar. The window is the like-for-like number, and the note stops the "but October was up 74%" question before it starts.

Level 2 · Module 10 · about 60 min

Outlook and Teams: running the week

Your analysis is worth exactly what someone does with it. An email that gets read in eight seconds, a meeting invite that arrives with an agenda, a Teams thread that ends in a decision: these are analyst skills as much as SUMIFS is. This module is about the week around the workbook, and how a new analyst is judged on it before anyone has opened their Excel.

  • You'll write an email whose subject line carries the number and whose first line carries the ask, and you'll retire "please do the needful" for good.
  • You'll tame an inbox with rules, categories, flags and Quick Steps, and find any mail in ten seconds with search operators.
  • You'll schedule a meeting people can attend, with the Scheduling Assistant, a time zone you checked and an agenda in the invite.
  • You'll know what a team, a channel, a thread and a chat are, where the files really live, and when each one is the wrong tool.
  • You'll run one full "Monday review" week for the Analytics team: pack, invite, channel post, notes, follow-up.

Concept

Monday, 8:10 am

Vikram Shah pings you on Teams before you've sat down. "Nandini's review moved to 9:30. Send her the August pack and ask about the Kochi promo. And copy Arjun, he's asking about cancellations again." You have 80 minutes, one workbook, and three people who each read email differently. What you send in the next ten minutes decides whether the meeting is about the numbers or about finding them.

A new analyst produces perhaps two hours of analysis a day. The other six are spent asking for data, explaining results, chasing decisions and sitting in meetings. Most of that traffic flows through Outlook and Teams, and it leaves a trail. Managers form their opinion of you from that trail long before they audit a formula.

The good news is that the rules are few and learnable. Put the number in the subject. Put the ask in the first line. Say when you need an answer and what happens if you don't get one. Keep the detail below the fold, and put the file where people can find it next month. The diagram shows one email that does all five.

Why a manager cares

Nandini gets around 140 emails a day and reads most of them on her phone between store visits. A subject line that says "August numbers" gets opened tonight. A subject line that says "77% of target, decision by Wed" gets opened now, and forwarded to Meera with one line added. The analyst who writes the second kind gets invited to the meeting instead of being asked for the file afterwards.

How it works

Email that gets replies

Here is the same request twice. The first version is how most first-week emails look at an Indian company. The second is the one Vikram will forward without editing.

Before

Subject: Data

Dear Sir,
Hope you are doing well. As discussed, please find attached the August data for your kind perusal. Kindly go through the same and do the needful at the earliest. There are some issues in Kochi also. Let me know if any clarification is required.
Thanks & Regards

After

Subject: Aug revenue at 77% of target – Kochi promo: yes/no by Wed

Nandini, I need a yes or no by Wednesday 5 pm on pulling the Kochi promo forward to September. Kochi closed August at 8% of its target.
• Delivered revenue ₹12.5 lakh vs ₹16.3 lakh target (77%)
• Kochi ₹3,999 vs ₹50,000; every other store is within range
• 11 of 117 orders cancelled (9.4%)
Pack: Documents / Monday review / 2026-08_Monday-Review_v02.xlsx
If I don't hear by Wed 5 pm I'll plan on "hold".

"Please do the needful" is the tell. It means "I have not decided what I want you to do, so you decide." Nobody will. Every email you send should pass a three-second test: can the reader say, from the subject and first line alone, what you want, from whom, by when? If the answer is "read the attachment", rewrite it.

Weak subjectSubject that gets openedWhy
DataAug revenue at 77% of target – Kochi promo: yes/no by Wednumber, decision, deadline
MeetingMonday review 9:30 · agenda + pack link insidesays what's inside
QueryNeed: Kochi footfall counts, Apr–Aug, by Thu (for Nandini's review)the ask, the deadline, the reason
FYIFYI only: cancellations 9.4% in Aug, no action neededtells the reader they can skip it
Re: Re: Re: Fwd: Fwd: numbersDecision: Kochi promo goes ahead 15 Sep (was: Re: numbers)a thread that changed topic gets a new subject

Two more habits. Write the ask before the context, not after ("I need X by Thursday because…" rather than three paragraphs ending in a request). And when you send a file, send a link to the SharePoint copy, never an attachment of a live workbook; Module 01 explains why the attachment becomes a second, wrong version by lunchtime.

Outlook mechanics: rules, categories, flags, Quick Steps

An inbox with 3,000 unread items isn't a productivity problem, it's a filing problem. Rules file mail as it arrives. Categories colour it. Flags turn it into a task with a date. Quick Steps do three clicks in one.

  1. Home ▸ Rules ▸ Manage Rules & Alerts ▸ New Rule. Choose "Apply rule on messages I receive". You'll see a two-part builder: conditions, then actions.
  2. Condition: "from people or public group" ▸ pick the POS-export mailbox. Novamart's till system mails a CSV every morning at 6:05 with subject "Daily sales extract". You never want that in the inbox.
  3. Action: "move it to the specified folder" ▸ Data feeds. Add a second action, "mark it as read". Finish, and tick "Run this rule now on messages already in Inbox" to clear the backlog.
  4. Home ▸ Categorize ▸ All Categories ▸ New. Make four: Decision needed (red), Waiting on someone (yellow), Reference (grey), Monday review (blue). More than six and you'll stop using them.
  5. Right-click a mail ▸ Follow Up ▸ Custom. A flag with a due date puts the mail in To Do and on your Outlook task list. Flag the mail you sent to Nandini, due Wednesday 5 pm, so the chase happens even if you forget.
  6. Home ▸ Quick Steps ▸ Create New. Name it "To Vikram, filed". Actions: forward to Vikram Shah, move to folder Sent for review, mark as read. One click replaces three. Give it a shortcut, Ctrl+Shift+1.

Search is the other half. The search box at the top understands operators, and the difference between "scroll for four minutes" and "found it" is knowing five of them.

OperatorExampleFinds
from:from:nandinimail from anyone whose name or address contains "nandini"
subject:subject:"Monday review"the exact phrase in the subject; quotes matter
hasattachment:hasattachment:yes from:pos-exportonly mails with files, from the POS mailbox
received:received:last week · received:>=01/08/2026date ranges; "yesterday", "this month" also work
to: / cc:to:arjun cc:mewhat you were copied on that went to Arjun
category:category:"Decision needed"everything you tagged as waiting for a decision
AND / OR / NOTKochi AND (promo OR launch) NOT newsletterboolean logic, capitals required

Calendar: the Scheduling Assistant and Focus time

A meeting invite is a small contract. The other side agrees to give you an hour; you agree to make it worth it. Three things belong in every invite you send: a time everyone can actually make, an agenda in the body, and a Teams link if anyone is remote. The Scheduling Assistant handles the first.

  1. Calendar ▸ Home ▸ New Meeting. Title it like a subject line: "Monday review · Aug close and Kochi promo". Not "Meeting".
  2. Add required attendees, then Scheduling Assistant. The grid shows everyone's busy blocks side by side. Nandini is blocked 9:00–9:30 on Mondays, so the review starts at 9:30, not 9:00.
  3. Set Optional for people who need the notes, not the hour. Arjun's team can read the decisions afterwards. Optional attendees see the invite but the meeting doesn't show as "busy" for them by default.
  4. Recurrence ▸ Weekly ▸ Monday ▸ End after 26 occurrences. A recurring series with no end date outlives the project. Six months, then re-issue.
  5. Body: the agenda, three lines, with owners and minutes. "1. Aug close vs target (you, 10 min). 2. Kochi promo decision (Nandini, 10 min). 3. Cancellations follow-up (Arjun, 5 min)." A meeting without an agenda is a chat with a calendar entry.
  6. Teams meeting toggle on; Response options ▸ Allow forwarding off. Forwarded invites grow the meeting until nobody speaks.

Time zones bite twice a year and every time a vendor is abroad. File ▸ Options ▸ Calendar ▸ Time zones lets you show a second zone in the day view; for a one-off, the invite form has a time-zone picker next to the start time. Type the meeting in the other person's zone and let Outlook convert. And protect your own analysis time: Viva Insights ▸ Protect time, or just book yourself "Focus: pack build" on Tuesday and Thursday mornings and set it to show as Busy. A block on the calendar is the only thing the Scheduling Assistant respects.

Out of office is part of the same contract. File ▸ Automatic Replies (or Settings ▸ Accounts ▸ Automatic replies in new Outlook). Write two lines: when you're back, and who covers what. "For the Monday review pack, Vikram Shah. For data requests, the #data-requests channel." Set a time range so it switches itself off.

Teams: team, channel, thread, chat

Teams confuses people because four different things are called "Teams". A team is a group of people with a shared SharePoint site behind it. A channel is a topic inside a team, with its own folder in that site. A post in a channel starts a thread, and replies stay under it. A chat is separate from all of this: private, unfiled, and invisible to the team.

Some mechanics worth knowing on day one. @mention a person to notify them; @mention the channel only when everyone must read it. Reply under a post rather than starting a new one; a channel where every reply is a new post is unreadable within a week. The Files tab of a channel is a SharePoint folder, so a workbook you drop there gets versions, co-authoring and a link you can paste into email. Meetings held in a channel leave their recording and transcript in that channel; meetings started from the calendar leave them in the organiser's OneDrive. Collaborative notes (the Notes button in a meeting) are a Loop component: agenda, notes and tasks in one block that stays in sync wherever it's pasted. And your status is read literally; "Available" during your focus block means you'll be interrupted, so let the calendar set it to Busy.

Teams etiquetteDoDon't
Starting a topicone post with a subject line (Format ▸ Add a subject) and the ask"hi" … "are you there?" … "quick question" as three messages
ReplyingReply under the post; @mention the one person who must acta new post for every reply; @channel for a question one person can answer
Filesupload once to the channel Files tab, share the linkattach the same workbook to four chats
Decisionsre-post any decision made in chat or a call into the channel threadlet the decision live in a 1:1 chat nobody else can search
Meetingscamera on for small meetings; mute when not speaking; use the raise-handtyping loudly on an open mic; a 12-person meeting for a 2-person question
Hoursschedule send (Outlook and Teams both have it) for anything written after 8 pma 11:40 pm message that reads as an emergency

Teams, email or a meeting?

SituationUseBecause
A quick question with a quick answer, inside the teamTeams chat or channelfast, informal, and nobody needs it next month
A request to someone outside the team, or outside NovamartEmailit needs to be findable, forwardable and formal
A decision with a record, owners and a deadlineEmail (then a channel post with the outcome)email is the paper trail; the channel is where the team looks
Anything that has gone past three replies without resolvingA 15-minute callthe fourth email is always longer than the call
Bad news, disagreement, feedbackCall or in person, then a written summarytone doesn't survive text
A weekly status with numbersChannel post with the pack link; email only to people not in the teamone place, one version, searchable
Working the same document together, nowTeams meeting with the file shared, or co-author in the browseryou both see the same cells

Two apps in one paragraph, because you'll meet them. Bookings publishes a page where outsiders pick a slot in your calendar, useful when the CA's firm or a vendor needs to schedule with Arjun's team without six emails. Viva Insights sits inside Teams and Outlook and reports how much of your week is meetings, who you haven't replied to, and lets you book focus time in bulk; the numbers are private to you, and the "protect time" feature is worth switching on in week one.

Application: running the Monday review week

The Monday review is Nandini's weekly hour with the Analytics team and the store heads. Vikram owns the meeting; you own the pack and everything around it. Here is the whole week, built once so that it runs itself the following Monday.

Friday, 4 pm: the numbers

The pack is a workbook (Module 07); the email needs three figures from it. Compute them in a cell, then quote them, so the email and the pack can never disagree.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹12,48,348, which you'll write as ₹12.5 lakh. The email says "delivered" because that's the finance definition, and Arjun will check.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
    /SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08")

76.6%, so "77% of target" in the subject line. The target for the month is ₹16.3 lakh across the 13 rows on the Targets sheet.

=COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&DATE(2026,8,1),Orders!G:G,"Cancelled")
    /COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&DATE(2026,8,1))

11 of 117 orders, 9.4%, a touch above the long-run one-in-fourteen. Arjun asked; that's his line in the email.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!D:D,"Novamart MG Road Kochi")
    /SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08",Targets!B:B,"Novamart MG Road Kochi")

8% (₹3,999 against ₹50,000). That is the reason the email exists, so it goes in the first line, not the third bullet.

="Aug revenue at "&TEXT(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
    /SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026-08"),"0%")&" of target – Kochi promo: yes/no by Wed"

"Aug revenue at 77% of target – Kochi promo: yes/no by Wed". Keep this cell on the pack's cover sheet and copy it into Outlook every week; the subject can't drift from the data.

Friday, 4:30 pm: file, link, schedule

  1. Save the pack to the channel. Teams ▸ Strategy & Analytics ▸ # Monday review ▸ Files ▸ Upload, as 2026-08_Monday-Review_v02.xlsx. This is the SharePoint folder; the file now has version history and one address.
  2. Copy the link. On the file, ⋯ ▸ Copy link ▸ People in Novamart with the link ▸ Can view. Store heads read; they don't edit the pack.
  3. Write the email to Nandini, cc Vikram and Arjun. Subject from the cell above. First line, the Kochi ask with the Wednesday 5 pm deadline. Three bullets. Paste the link. Close with the default.
  4. Options ▸ Delay Delivery ▸ Monday 7:45 am. Nandini reads on the train at 8. A Friday-evening email is buried by Monday; a Monday-morning one is on top.
  5. Flag your own sent copy ▸ Custom ▸ due Wednesday 5:00 pm. If no reply lands, the flag turns red and you send a one-line chase: "Nandini, going with 'hold' unless you say otherwise by 5."

Monday, 9:30: the meeting

  1. Calendar ▸ the recurring "Monday review" series ▸ this occurrence ▸ edit body. Paste this week's agenda with owners and minutes. Send update to attendees only (Outlook asks).
  2. Join from the channel, not the calendar. A channel meeting leaves its recording, transcript and chat in # Monday review, where next month's you can find them.
  3. Notes ▸ Collaborative notes. A Loop component opens with Agenda, Notes and Follow-up tasks. Type decisions as they're made: "Kochi promo: pulled forward to 15 Sep. Owner Priya. Budget ₹2 lakh."
  4. Assign each follow-up task in the notes to a person with a date. They land in that person's To Do and Planner automatically; nobody has to be reminded to be reminded.
  5. Share screen ▸ the pack, not your desktop. Window sharing keeps your inbox out of the recording.

Monday, 3 pm: the follow-up

The meeting isn't over until the decisions are written down somewhere the whole team looks. Post in # Monday review, with a subject line, the three decisions and owners, and the link to the notes. Then send one email, to the people who were in the room but not in the team (the store heads), with the same three lines. Same words in both; the channel is the record, the email is the courtesy.

Friday afternoon, the calendar block "Weekly wrap, next agenda" is where you draft next week's three agenda lines and check that the Wednesday deadline was met. Then the Delay Delivery email goes out again. By week three, the whole loop is 40 minutes of your Friday, and Nandini has stopped asking where the file is.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askOutlook / Teams move
Finance"Month-end close: everyone's inputs by the 3rd."one email with a table of owner · input · due; a recurring reminder on the 1st; flags on each reply
Marketing"Get the Diwali creative approved by four people."a # Diwali-2026 channel, the files in its Files tab, one post per creative with @mentions; approvals in Module 12
Operations"Store managers need the audit schedule."a Teams meeting invite per store with the SOP link (Module 08) in the body; Optional for regional heads
HR"Onboard three interns next Monday."a shared mailbox hr-onboarding@, a rule that files replies, a Bookings page for the induction slots
Digital"Why did app cancellations jump?"a channel thread, not a 1:1 chat with Sameer; the answer is searchable when it happens again
Analytics"Stop people emailing me for data."a # Data requests channel with a pinned Forms link (Module 11); an Outlook rule that files "data request" mails to a folder

The HR one is worth a closer look. A shared mailbox is a mailbox nobody logs into; it's added to Kavita's Outlook and to yours, and a rule moves every reply with "onboarding" in the subject into a folder both of you see. The Bookings page lets each intern pick their own laptop-collection slot. Three interns, zero back-and-forth. The Excel part is a formula that tells Kavita how many working days are left before they start.

=NETWORKDAYS(TODAY(),DATE(2026,10,20))

37 working days. Put the same formula in the onboarding tracker and the number in the weekly HR email never has to be typed.

Practice

These are writing and set-up tasks, so the solutions describe what good looks like rather than a formula. Do them in your own Outlook and Teams if you have a work or university account; the muscle memory is the point.

Exercise 1 · Rewrite the needful

Rewrite this email from Rohan's buying team so that it passes the three-second test. "Subject: Inventory. Hi, hope you're well. As per our discussion kindly find the inventory file. There are many products which are below reorder level, 91 items showing zero stock. Please do the needful and revert. Regards."

Hint

What does Rohan actually want done, by whom, and by when? He hasn't said, so decide for him and make it easy to correct you.

What good looks like

Subject: 91 SKUs at zero stock – approve reorder list by Thu?

First line: "Rohan, please approve the attached reorder list (91 SKUs, ₹ value on the sheet) by Thursday 3 pm so POs go out Friday." Then three bullets: how many below reorder level in total, the three stores worst hit, the link to the Inventory workbook in the Merchandising channel. Close: "If I don't hear by Thursday I'll raise the POs for the top 30 by value only." Note the link, not an attachment, and the default action in the last line.

Exercise 2 · Three rules and a Quick Step

Set up the inbox for the Analytics role. Write the three rules and the one Quick Step you'd create in your first week, with the condition and action for each.

Hint

Think about what arrives every day without needing you (feeds), what arrives that you're only copied on, and what you send repeatedly.

What good looks like
  • Rule 1: from the POS export mailbox → move to Data feeds, mark read. The daily CSV never touches the inbox.
  • Rule 2: where my name is in the Cc box and not the To box → move to Cc, no notification. You read it once a day.
  • Rule 3: subject contains "Monday review" → assign category Monday review, so a category search rebuilds the whole history.
  • Quick Step "To Vikram, filed": forward to Vikram Shah, move to Sent for review, mark read, shortcut Ctrl+Shift+1.

Anything you'd need to re-read within the hour stays in the inbox; rules are for mail you need to exist, not to see.

Exercise 3 · Find it in ten seconds

Write the search string for each. (a) Everything Priya sent you last month with a file attached. (b) The mail where Arjun agreed the cancellation definition, sometime in 2026, subject contained "cancel". (c) All mail you tagged Decision needed that you haven't replied to.

Hint

Combine from:, hasattachment:, received:, subject: and category:. Outlook also understands isflagged:yes and read:no.

What good looks like
  • (a) from:priya hasattachment:yes received:last month
  • (b) from:arjun subject:cancel received:>=01/01/2026, then sort by date; add definition as a bare word if the list is long.
  • (c) category:"Decision needed" isflagged:yes; Outlook can't search "unreplied", so the flag you set when reading stands in for it.

Exercise 4 · The invite that gets a decision

Priya needs a decision from Nandini and Sameer on the Diwali app-only offer. Write the meeting title, the attendee list with Required and Optional, the recurrence (if any), and the agenda body.

Hint

One-off decisions don't recur. Who must be there for the decision, and who just needs to know it?

What good looks like

Title: Decide: Diwali app-only offer (₹ and dates) · 30 min. Required: Nandini Rao, Sameer Joshi, Priya Nair. Optional: Vikram Shah, you (for the numbers). No recurrence. Body: "Decision needed: run an app-only 10% offer 20 Oct–2 Nov? 1. Last year's Diwali app share and margin (you, 10 min). 2. Ops impact on store stock (Nandini, 10 min). 3. Decide and assign (Priya, 10 min). Pre-read: link to the deck." Scheduling Assistant to find a slot inside Nandini's Tuesday office day; Teams link on; forwarding off.

Exercise 5 · Which tool?

For each situation, choose email, Teams chat, channel post, or a call, and say why in one line. (a) Asking Sameer whether the app export includes cancelled orders. (b) Telling the 12 store heads the audit schedule. (c) Vikram has disagreed with your Kochi number twice by email. (d) Recording that Nandini approved the promo. (e) A vendor in Singapore wants a slot with Arjun.

Hint

Use the decision table. Ask: who needs to find this later, and does tone matter?

What good looks like
  • (a) Channel post in # Data requests (not a chat): the answer will be needed again by the next analyst.
  • (b) Email with a table, plus a calendar invite per store; store heads aren't in the Analytics team.
  • (c) A 15-minute call with the workbook shared, then one email summarising the agreed definition.
  • (d) Post in # Monday review with "Decision:" as the subject, linking the notes. A chat message would be lost.
  • (e) A Bookings page on Arjun's calendar, or an invite typed in Singapore time with the time-zone picker.

Exercise 6 · The follow-up post

The Monday review has ended. Decisions: Kochi promo moves to 15 Sep (owner Priya, ₹2 lakh budget); Sameer to explain online cancellations by Friday; the September targets to be re-cut for Kochi (owner Vikram). Write the channel post and the email to the store heads.

Hint

Same three lines in both. Subject line, owners, dates, link to notes. Nothing else.

What good looks like

Channel post, subject Monday review 31 Aug · decisions: "1. Kochi promo pulled forward to 15 Sep, @Priya, budget ₹2 lakh. 2. Online cancellation root cause by Fri 4 Sep, @Sameer. 3. Kochi Sep target re-cut by Wed, @Vikram. Notes and recording: [link]." Email to store heads, subject Monday review 31 Aug: three decisions (Kochi promo 15 Sep), the same three lines, no @mentions, the pack link. Flag the Friday and Wednesday items on your own calendar so the chase is yours, not luck.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

Reply All to a 40-person thread with "Thanks!" is the first-week mistake everyone remembers. Before you hit Reply All, ask whether every name in the To and Cc boxes needs your sentence. Usually one does. And never, ever send a live workbook as an attachment to a group; within a day there are five versions with five different Kochi numbers, and yours is the one that gets blamed.

Pro habit

Write the subject line last. Draft the body, find the one number and the one ask, and then write the subject from them. The subject is the summary of an email that already exists, not a placeholder you fill in first and forget.

  • One ask per email. Two asks get one answer. If you need three things, send three short emails or one email with a numbered list and a deadline per item.
  • Say the default. "If I don't hear by Wednesday I'll do X" turns silence into a decision. It also gets you replies, because people would rather choose than be chosen for.
  • Links, not attachments, for anything that changes. A PDF of the signed contract can be an attachment. The pack is a link.
  • Reply in the thread; re-title the thread when the topic moves. "Re: Re: numbers" that is now about a promo date should become "Decision: Kochi promo 15 Sep (was: numbers)".
  • Chats are for now; channels are for later. Anything you'd want to find in a month goes in a channel, even if it was decided in a chat.
  • Protect two mornings. Without blocks on the calendar you will be booked solid by Wednesday of week two, and the pack will be built at 11 pm.
  • Schedule send. Writing at 10 pm is fine; sending at 10 pm sets an expectation for everyone else.

Note

Meeting recordings and transcripts are searchable and kept for a period your IT team sets. Assume anything said in a recorded Teams meeting can be quoted back. That's a reason to be precise, not a reason to be silent.

On the job

Nobody hires an analyst for their email. But everyone forms an opinion of a new analyst from it, and in weeks one to four that opinion is the only data your manager has.

WeekWhat your manager is watchingWhat "good" looks like
1Do your messages have a subject line and an ask? Do you reply within the day?every email answers "what, from whom, by when"; you acknowledge within hours even if the answer takes days
2Do you put things where the team can find them, or in chats and attachments?files in the channel, decisions in threads, a link in every email
3Can you run a meeting? Invite, agenda, notes, follow-up.the follow-up post is out the same afternoon, with owners and dates
4Do people have to chase you, or do you chase yourself?flags and calendar blocks mean deadlines arrive with a reminder attached; nobody has asked "any update?"

In the assessment test

Some analyst assessments end with a written task: "Here are the numbers; write the email to the COO." The graders are looking for a subject line with a number, the recommendation in the first sentence, a deadline, and three bullets in order of importance. Many candidates write a page. Write eight lines and you'll stand out. If the test gives you a pack of data and a case, the email is where the case is decided.

First 90 days

Set the rules, categories and two focus blocks in week one. Volunteer to own the notes in the first recurring meeting you attend; the person who writes the decisions down is the person the decisions go through. By day 90, one recurring review should run on your calendar, your pack link and your follow-up post, without anyone asking.

"How do you make sure a stakeholder actually reads your analysis?"
I write the conclusion in the subject line and the ask in the first sentence, with a date. The detail is three bullets and a link to the workbook, so a manager can act from their phone and dig in later if they want. I state what I'll do if I hear nothing, which turns silence into a decision.
"When would you use email rather than Teams?"
Email for anything that needs a record, goes outside the team or the company, or carries a decision with owners and dates. Teams channels for working conversations the team needs to search later; chat for quick questions with no shelf life. And after three rounds of back-and-forth in any of them, a 15-minute call.
"A senior manager keeps asking you for files you've already sent. What do you do?"
Stop sending files. I'd put the pack in the team channel's Files tab, which is a SharePoint folder with one address, and send the same link every week with the same subject line format, so their search for "Monday review" finds every edition. Then I'd pin the folder in the channel.

Quick check

1. Which subject line follows BLUF?

The number, the decision and the deadline are all visible before the email is opened. The other two tell the reader nothing they can act on.

2. Where does a file uploaded to a Teams channel's Files tab actually live?

Every team has a SharePoint site; each channel is a folder in it. The Files tab is a view of that folder, which is why versions and links work.

3. Nandini approved the promo in a 1:1 Teams chat with you. What's the right next step?

Chats are private and unsearchable by the team. A decision needs to live where the team looks and where it can be found next month.

4. What does an Outlook rule do that a category doesn't?

Rules run on arrival and take actions; categories are labels you (or a rule) apply; flags are what add a due date.
