Level 3 · Module 11 · about 60 min

Forms, Lists and Planner: capture and track

Half the data an analyst is asked about was never in a system. It was in a WhatsApp group, a paper checklist at the Kochi store, or a manager's memory. Forms captures it, Lists holds it in a shape you can filter, and Planner turns what needs doing into cards with names and dates. Three small apps, and together they replace the spreadsheet-that-everyone-edits.

  • You'll design a Forms survey with the right question types, branching that skips what doesn't apply, and settings that stop duplicate answers.
  • You'll open the live results workbook and compute an NPS score, promoter and detractor shares, and a year-on-year trend from the NPS sheet.
  • You'll build a Microsoft List with typed columns, views and a rule that emails the right person when a row changes.
  • You'll run a Planner board with buckets, labels, assignments and the Charts view for a festive-season launch.
  • You'll know how the three connect, and where Power Automate (Module 12) fits between them.

Concept

Tuesday, 11:20 am

Priya Nair drops a screenshot into the Analytics chat. It's a Google Form her intern built in 2024, 400 NPS responses, exported once to a CSV nobody can find. "Can you tell me if NPS is going up or down? And Nandini wants the store audits off WhatsApp; the Kochi manager sends photos of a paper checklist." Two asks, both about the same problem: data that was captured badly is data you can't analyse.

Capture, store, act, see. That's the chain. A Forms survey captures one response per customer with the question types you chose, so the score is always a number and the reason is always one of six choices. The responses land in an Excel workbook or a List, where every column has a type and every row is a record. From there, the things that need doing become Planner tasks with an owner and a date. And all of it sits inside a Teams channel where the team already is.

Why a manager cares

Priya's 2024 intern typed "9/10" and "nine" and "9 (delivery late)" into a text box, and the NPS was computed by hand, once. A Rating question makes the score a number every time, and the results workbook updates while the survey is live. Nandini's audits on WhatsApp mean she has a hundred photos and no count of which stores failed the fire-exit check. A form with a Choice question gives her that count in a pivot by lunchtime.

How it works

Forms: question types and branching

A form is a list of typed questions, and choosing the type is most of the design. The rule is simple: never use Text where a Choice, Rating or Date will do, because you'll pay for every free-typed answer later, in cleaning.

Question typeUse it forWhat lands in the results column
Choiceone of a fixed set (reason for a low score, store name)the label text; enable "multiple answers" and you get a semicolon-separated cell
Rating / NPSscores; the NPS type is a fixed 0–10 with the standard wordinga number, which is what you want
Textcomments, order IDs; use the "Restrictions" option to force a number or a rangewhatever they typed
Dateaudit date, visit datea real date
Likerta grid of statements against Agree–Disagreeone column per statement
Ranking"order these five features"a semicolon-separated list in rank order
File uploadthe shelf photo from a store audit (form must be in your organisation)a link to the file in the form owner's OneDrive or the group's SharePoint
Sectionpages; branching jumps between themnothing; it's structure

Branching is the difference between a survey people finish and one they abandon. A customer who scored 10 should never be asked "what went wrong". The branch is set on the question: ⋯ ▸ Add branching, then for each answer pick the question or section it jumps to.

Settings live under ⋯ ▸ Settings at the top right. The ones that matter: Who can fill out this form (anyone with the link, for customers; people in Novamart, for the store audit, which also records their name and enables file upload); One response per person (only for people in the organisation); Start and end date; Shuffle questions (off for surveys, on for quizzes); the thank-you message. A form made from a Team or group (Forms ▸ New group form) belongs to the group, not to you, and its results workbook lives in the group's SharePoint; a personal form's workbook lives in your OneDrive and leaves with you. For anything Novamart will keep, make it a group form.

The Responses tab shows a summary of every question, and Open in Excel gives you the workbook. For a group form it's a live workbook in SharePoint that keeps filling as responses arrive; for a personal form the newer "sync" option does the same, and the older download is a one-off copy. Either way the first sheet is a Table with one column per question plus ID, Start time, Completion time, Email and Name. That Table is what Module 05's pivots and this module's formulas point at. Quizzes are the same app with points per question and automatic marking; the HR team uses one for the induction test, and the results sheet has a Total points column.

Lists: a table with types and rules

A Microsoft List is a SharePoint list with a friendlier face. Think of it as an Excel Table where every column enforces its type, several people can edit rows at once without a lock, each row has its own form and version history, and a rule can send an email when something changes. Start one from Lists ▸ New list ▸ Blank / From Excel / Template; the "Issue tracker" template is close to what the store issues list needs.

Column typeUse forNote
Title (text)the one-line description of the rowalways present; make it a sentence someone can act on
ChoiceStore, Issue type, Priority, Statusset the default; tick "can add values" only if you enjoy cleaning
Date and timeReported on, Due, Closed ondate-only unless the time matters
PersonReported by, Ownerpulls from the directory, so names are never misspelt
Number / CurrencyEstimated cost in ₹two decimals, no thousands separator issues
Yes/NoPhoto attached, Customer affecteda real boolean, filterable
LookupStore, taken from a separate Stores listthe List version of XLOOKUP; keeps store names identical everywhere
Hyperlink / Imagelink to the audit response, the shelf photoImage shows a thumbnail in gallery view

Views are saved filters and layouts: a List view grouped by Store, a Board view by Status, a Calendar view by Due date, a Gallery view for the photos. Rules (Automate ▸ Create a rule) are four sentences: when a column changes, when a new item is created, when a column value is set, when a date arrives, then email a person. "When Priority is set to High, email Nandini Rao" is a rule, and it takes a minute. Anything more than one condition and one email is a Power Automate flow.

From Excel is the shortcut most people need: New list ▸ From Excel, pick the workbook, pick the Table, then confirm each column's type. If the Excel column has "Delhi" in 40 rows and "delhi" in 3, the Choice column will have both; fix that in Excel first with Power Query, not afterwards in the list.

Planner: buckets, cards, labels, views

A Planner plan is a board. Buckets are columns (by workstream, by phase, by week). Cards are tasks, each with an owner, a start and due date, a priority, a checklist, notes, attachments, comments and up to 25 coloured labels. The board is one view; Charts shows tasks by status, bucket, priority and person, and Schedule puts the due dates on a calendar. A plan created inside a Teams channel (+ ▸ Planner) belongs to that team and appears as a tab.

To Do is the personal side of the same system. Every Planner task assigned to you, every flagged email in Outlook and every task ticked in a Loop component appears in To Do, under "Assigned to me" and "Flagged email". You plan your day there; the team plans the project in Planner. Neither replaces the other.

Application: the NPS survey, the store audit and the launch board

Build 1: the NPS survey

  1. Teams ▸ Marketing & CRM ▸ # NPS ▸ + (add a tab) ▸ Forms ▸ Create a shared form. Name it Novamart NPS · Sep 2026. Shared means the results workbook lives in the Marketing team's SharePoint, not in your OneDrive.
  2. Add new ▸ Net Promoter Score. The wording comes pre-set ("How likely are you to recommend…"). Mark it Required.
  3. Add new ▸ Section three times: Detractor, Passive, Promoter. Inside the first, a Choice question "What went wrong?" with six options and an "Other" text; then a Text question "Tell us more" (Long answer). Inside Passive, one Text question. Inside Promoter, a Choice "What did we do well?" and a Yes/No "May we quote you?".
  4. On Q1 ▸ ⋯ ▸ Add branching. Scores 0–6 go to the Detractor section, 7–8 to Passive, 9–10 to Promoter. Each section's last question goes to End of form.
  5. Add a Text question "Order ID" before the score, with Restrictions ▸ Number ▸ Between 10001 and 13000, so the response can be joined to the Orders sheet.
  6. Settings. Anyone can respond (customers have no Novamart login). Start date today, end date 30 Sep. Thank-you message: "Thanks. If you asked us to get in touch, someone from Novamart will within two working days."
  7. Collect responses ▸ Link ▸ Shorten URL, and the QR code for the delivery slip. Preview on mobile before you send anything; most customers answer on a phone.

Build 2: the store audit form

  1. Forms ▸ New group form (Store Operations group) ▸ Monthly store audit. Group form, because Nandini's team owns it and you'll leave one day.
  2. Choice "Store" with the 12 store names typed exactly as on the Stores sheet, and a Date "Audit date".
  3. Likert "Checks" with rows: fire exits clear, price tags match POS, promo signage up, trial rooms clean, billing queue under 5 min; columns Pass / Fail / N/A. One question, five typed answers.
  4. File upload "Photo of the promo wall", images only, max one file, 10 MB. Uploads go to the group's SharePoint under a folder named after the form.
  5. Branching on each Fail: a Text question "What's wrong, and by when will it be fixed?" only for a Fail. Passing stores finish in 90 seconds.
  6. Settings ▸ Only people in my organisation ▸ Record name. The manager's name lands in the results without a question; one response per person is off, because one manager audits one store every month.

Build 3: the "Store issues" List

  1. Lists ▸ New list ▸ Issue tracker template ▸ name Store issues ▸ save to the Store Operations team site. The template gives you Title, Priority, Status, Date reported, Issue source. Keep those.
  2. Add column ▸ Choice "Store" with the 12 names, Choice "Issue type" (Stock-out, Pricing, Signage, Facilities, Staffing, IT), Person "Owner", Date "Due", Currency "Est. cost ₹", Yes/No "Customer affected", Image "Photo".
  3. Create view ▸ Board ▸ organise by Status for the weekly review, and Create view ▸ List ▸ group by Store ▸ filter Status ≠ Closed for Nandini's store visits.
  4. Automate ▸ Create a rule ▸ "When a column value is set" ▸ Priority ▸ High ▸ email Nandini Rao. Test it by creating one High row; the mail arrives in under a minute.
  5. Add the list as a tab in # Store ops (+ ▸ Lists ▸ Add an existing list) so nobody has to find it.

Build 4: the festive-launch Planner board

  1. Teams ▸ Festive 2026 team ▸ General ▸ + ▸ Planner ▸ Create a new plan ▸ Festive Launch 2026.
  2. Buckets: Buying, Stores, Marketing, Digital, Analytics. By workstream, because each has one head who owns the bucket. Phases (Plan / Build / Live) would be the other choice; pick one and don't mix them.
  3. Labels: one per function, plus "Decision needed" and "Blocked". Labels cut across buckets; a Buying card can carry "Blocked" without moving.
  4. Cards, one per deliverable, each with an owner (one person; shared ownership means nobody), a due date, a checklist for the sub-steps, and the Form or List linked in Attachments. "Confirm TV stock for 12 stores · Rohan · 15 Sep" is a card. "Buying stuff" is not.
  5. Charts view every Monday. Tasks by bucket and by person, with the Late count at the top. That chart is slide 2 of the launch review.
  6. Schedule view for the last three weeks before Diwali, so the store audits, creative approvals and the app offer don't all land on the same Friday.

Reading the results: the NPS sheet

Priya's 400 responses are on the NPS sheet: one row per response, score in column E, survey date in D, an optional comment in F. This is exactly the shape the Forms results workbook has, so every formula below works unchanged on a live survey. Start with the three counts NPS is built from.

=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9")

164 promoters.

=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6")

122 detractors. Passives (7 and 8) are the remaining 114; they count in the denominator and nowhere else.

=COUNTA(NPS!E:E)-1

400. COUNTA counts the header cell too, hence the minus one; COUNT(NPS!E:E) would skip it because it only counts numbers, and either is fine as long as you know which you used.

=(COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9")-COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6"))/(COUNTA(NPS!E:E)-1)

0.105, so 41.0% promoters minus 30.5% detractors: an NPS of +11 when you round it the way the industry does (to a whole number, no percent sign). For an Indian retailer that's ordinary rather than alarming; Priya's question was the direction, not the level.

=AVERAGEIFS(NPS!E:E,NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2025,1,1),NPS!D:D,"<="&DATE(2025,12,31))

7.05 for 2025, against 6.90 for 2024 and 6.94 for 2026 so far. Averages hide the shape, though: the same 7.0 can be all 7s or half 10s and half 4s, and NPS was invented to tell those apart.

=SUMPRODUCT((YEAR(NPS!D2:D401)=2025)*NPS!E2:E401)/SUMPRODUCT((YEAR(NPS!D2:D401)=2025)*1)

7.05 again. SUMPRODUCT needs bounded ranges (whole columns would multiply a million rows), and it lets you use YEAR() directly instead of two date bounds. Use AVERAGEIFS when it fits; reach for this when the condition isn't a plain comparison.

=(COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9",NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2026,1,1))-COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6",NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2026,1,1)))
    /COUNTIFS(NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2026,1,1))

0.058, an NPS of +6 on 120 responses. Run the same formula with 2024's bounds and you get +14; 2025 gives +11. So the answer to Priya's question is "down, from +14 to +11 to +6", and the reason is on the next line.

=FILTER(NPS!F:F,(NPS!E:E<=6)*(NPS!F:F<>""))

82 comments spill down the column; 40 detractors left the box empty. Multiplying the two conditions is how FILTER does AND. Six distinct reasons appear, and counting one of them is one more COUNTIFS.

=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6",NPS!F:F,"Delivery was very late.")

19 of the 82 commented detractors, and the count by year runs 4, 8, 7. "Wrong item delivered." is next at 16, then "Received a damaged item." at 14. Three of the top three are logistics. That's the slide.

=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6",NPS!D:D,">="&EDATE(TODAY(),-3))

14 of the 46 responses since 31 May 2026. EDATE(TODAY(),-3) moves with the calendar, so this cell is right every Monday without editing.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askTool and shape
Marketing"Is NPS up or down, and why?"Forms NPS question with a branched Choice reason; COUNTIFS on the results Table
Operations"Get the audits off WhatsApp."group form with Likert checks and file upload; a Store issues List for the Fails
HR"Track the 40 induction tasks for three interns."a Planner plan with one bucket per intern, a checklist per card; the induction quiz in Forms
Finance"Collect month-end inputs from seven departments."a List with one row per department and a Yes/No "Submitted"; a rule that emails Arjun when all seven flip
Merchandising"Which returns reasons are growing?"the Returns sheet already has a typed reason column; COUNTIF by reason, then a pivot by month
Digital"Beta testers for the new app checkout."a Forms sign-up with a Choice for device, one response per person; a Planner card per bug

The Merchandising one shows why typed capture matters. The Returns sheet's Reason column has five values and no free text, so the count is a single function. Had it been a text box, you'd be writing wildcards for "late", "Late delivery", "delayed" and "didn't arrive".

=COUNTIF(Returns!E:E,"Late delivery")

41 of the 263 returns, the single biggest reason. A typed column also means the same idea appears in the NPS survey (Choice "late") and the returns log (Reason "Late delivery"), and Rohan and Priya are for once arguing about the same thing.

Practice

Three formula exercises on the NPS sheet, three design exercises. For the formulas, say what the denominator is before you write it; NPS mistakes are almost always denominator mistakes.

Exercise 1 · Promoter share

What share of all 400 responses are promoters? Return a fraction.

Hint

Numerator is a COUNTIFS; the denominator is the response count from the Application section.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9")/(COUNTA(NPS!E:E)-1)

0.41, so 41% promoters. Detractors are 30.5%; the gap between the two is the NPS.

Exercise 2 · NPS for 2025

Compute the NPS for calendar 2025 only, as a fraction. Dates are in column D.

Hint

Every COUNTIFS needs both date bounds. The denominator is the count of responses in 2025, not 400.

Show solution 
=(COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9",NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2025,1,1),NPS!D:D,"<="&DATE(2025,12,31))
    -COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6",NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2025,1,1),NPS!D:D,"<="&DATE(2025,12,31)))
    /COUNTIFS(NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2025,1,1),NPS!D:D,"<="&DATE(2025,12,31))

0.1097, an NPS of +11 on 155 responses. Dividing by 400 instead gives +4 and a wrong slide.

Exercise 3 · Late-delivery detractors this year

How many detractors in 2026 wrote "Delivery was very late." as their comment?

Hint

Three criteria: the score band, the exact comment text, and a lower date bound. The data ends today, so no upper bound is needed.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6",NPS!F:F,"Delivery was very late.",NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2026,1,1))

7 in eight months of 2026, against 8 in all of 2025 and 4 in 2024. The rate is rising, which is what Priya takes to Nandini.

Exercise 4 · Fix the intern's form

The 2024 form had these questions, all Text: "Your score out of 10", "Your order number", "Why did you give this score?", "Would you recommend us? (yes/no)". Redesign it: list each question with its type and any branching.

Hint

Which answers do you want to count? Those need Choice or Rating. Which questions shouldn't be asked of everyone?

What good looks like
  • Order number: Text with Restrictions ▸ Number ▸ Between 10001 and 13000, Required.
  • Score: the NPS question type. Drop "Would you recommend us?" entirely; the score already answers it.
  • Reason: a Choice with six options plus Other, shown only to 0–6 via branching. A second Choice, "what did we do well?", only for 9–10.
  • Free text "Tell us more": optional, Long answer, on every branch, last.

Four questions become three per respondent, and every countable answer is typed.

Exercise 5 · Columns for the Store issues list

Nandini wants to answer three questions from the list without opening Excel: which store has the most open issues, what the open issues will cost, and who is late. Name the columns and types that make each question a view, and the rule you'd add.

Hint

Every question maps to a column with a type and a view with a group or filter. "Late" needs a date and a status.

What good looks like
  • Most open issues by store: Choice "Store" + Choice "Status"; a List view grouped by Store, filtered Status ≠ Closed, with the group counts showing.
  • Cost of open issues: Currency "Est. cost ₹"; same view with Totals ▸ Sum on that column.
  • Who is late: Date "Due" + Person "Owner"; a view filtered Due < [Today] and Status ≠ Closed, grouped by Owner.
  • Rule: when Priority is set to High, email Nandini. Anything fancier (overdue reminders, weekly digests) is Module 12.

Exercise 6 · Buckets or phases?

Rohan wants the festive board's buckets to be Sep / Oct / Nov. Priya wants them to be Buying / Stores / Marketing / Digital. Kavita wants Not started / In progress / Done. Who's right, and what do the other two get instead?

Hint

Buckets are the one grouping you can't change with a click. Which of the three groupings does Planner already give you for free?

What good looks like

Priya. Progress (Kavita's ask) is a built-in field, and Group by ▸ Progress shows it as columns any time; making it a bucket means dragging cards to update a field that already exists. Months (Rohan's ask) are due dates; Group by ▸ Due date and the Schedule view cover that. Workstream is the one grouping Planner doesn't know unless you tell it, so it should be the bucket. Add a label per function too, so a card that spans two teams can carry both.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

A personal form's results workbook lives in the creator's OneDrive. When the intern's account was closed, the 2024 NPS data went with it. Anything Novamart will need next year goes in a group form, created from the team or in Teams, so the results sit in SharePoint and survive people leaving. The same is true of Lists (save to a site, not "My lists") and Planner plans (create them in a team).

Pro habit

Test the form with three fake responses before you share it, then delete them from the results (Responses ▸ ⋯ ▸ Delete all responses before going live, or filter them out by the Email column). Check on a phone. Check that the branching sends a 10 past the "what went wrong" question. Every survey that goes out with a broken branch teaches a few hundred customers not to answer the next one.

  • Type everything you'll count. Choice, Rating, Date, Yes/No. Text is for what you'll read, never for what you'll add up.
  • Denominators. NPS divides by responses in the period, not all responses. Say the denominator out loud before you write the formula.
  • Store names must match the Stores sheet exactly. A Choice option "Kochi" in the form and "Novamart MG Road Kochi" in the workbook means an XLOOKUP that fails on every row. Copy the names, don't retype them.
  • One owner per card. Planner lets you assign several people; it also lets a task belong to nobody. Assign one, and add the others as followers in the comments.
  • Lists aren't Excel. No formulas across rows, no pivot. When you need analysis, Export ▸ Export to Excel (a live query, refreshable) or connect Power Query to the list.
  • Rules are one condition, one email. The moment you want "and only on weekdays" or "post to Teams as well", stop and build a flow.
  • Don't ask what you won't use. Every extra question drops completion. The NPS survey is three questions for a reason.

On the job

In the assessment test

NPS appears in analyst tests as a formula question: "here is a column of 0–10 scores, compute the NPS". The expected answer is promoters minus detractors over total, with COUNTIFS, and the two classic wrong answers are averaging the scores and forgetting the passives in the denominator. If the test adds a date column, the period filter goes on every count. A follow-up often asks for the most common reason among detractors; that's a COUNTIFS with two criteria or a pivot.

First 90 days

You'll inherit at least one survey with free-text answers and one tracker that is a shared workbook with 14 tabs. Rebuild the survey as a group form with typed questions, move the tracker into a List with views, and put the follow-up in a Planner plan in the team. Then show your manager the Charts view. Nobody has ever been asked to change that back.

"How would you compute NPS in Excel, and what could go wrong?"
Count scores of 9–10 and scores of 0–6 with COUNTIFS, subtract, divide by the total number of responses, and report it as a whole number. What goes wrong: averaging the scores instead, dropping passives from the denominator, and mixing periods so the numerator and denominator cover different months.
"When would you use a Microsoft List instead of an Excel sheet?"
When several people add or edit rows at the same time, when columns need enforced types like Person or Choice, and when a row change should trigger something, like an email. I'd keep Excel for analysis, and connect it to the list with Export or Power Query rather than maintaining two copies.
"Design a survey question to find out why customers give low scores."
A Choice question with five or six specific reasons and an Other, shown only to respondents who scored 0–6 via branching, followed by an optional free-text box. The Choice makes the reasons countable; the branch keeps promoters from seeing a question that doesn't apply to them.

Quick check

1. 164 promoters, 114 passives, 122 detractors. What is the NPS?

Passives don't count in the numerator but they do in the denominator. 42 ÷ 400 = 10.5%, reported as +11.

2. Where does a group form's results workbook live?

That's the reason to use a group form for anything the company will keep: the data survives the creator leaving.

3. Which question type should "What went wrong?" be, if you want to count the reasons later?

Countable answers need a fixed set of values. A free-text box can follow it for the detail.

4. A List rule can do which of these?

Rules are one condition and one email. Teams posts and Planner tasks need a Power Automate flow, which is Module 12.

Level 3 · Module 12 · about 75 min

Power Automate: the work that does itself

Every Monday someone opens the NPS workbook, scrolls to the bottom, copies the new low scores into a Teams message, and forgets one. Every discount above 20% waits in Rohan's inbox behind forty other emails. Every weekly digest is typed by hand from numbers that already exist in a sheet. Power Automate is how an analyst makes those three things happen without a person, and this module builds all three.

  • You'll read any flow as trigger, conditions and actions, and know which of the three kinds of cloud flow a job needs.
  • You'll build the Forms → Excel Table → Teams pipeline that feeds capstone 07, with the exact connector actions.
  • You'll build an approval flow with two branches and see how "Start and wait for an approval" pauses a flow for days.
  • You'll schedule a Monday digest that reads an Excel Table and mails a summary, and write the expressions that format its dates and text.
  • You'll test a flow, read its run history, handle the step that fails, and know when not to automate at all.

Concept

Thursday, 5:50 pm

A customer in Jaipur scored Novamart 2 on the NPS survey on Friday, with the comment "Wrong item delivered". Nobody saw it until Wednesday, because the intern who checks the results workbook was on leave. Priya, to Vikram: "I want a Teams message the minute a low score lands. And I want the Monday digest to send itself; I'm tired of chasing it." Vikram, to you: "That's a flow. Two flows. Build them before Monday."

A flow is a short program you assemble from blocks instead of writing. It has exactly one trigger, the event that starts it: a form response arrives, a file lands in a folder, a clock strikes 8 am, someone presses a button. It has zero or more conditions, which split the path into Yes and No. And it has actions, the things it does: add a row, send a mail, post a message, wait for an approval. Each action's output becomes dynamic content the later actions can use, which is how the score from the form ends up in the Teams message.

Why a manager cares

The Jaipur customer waited five days for a reply that a flow would have triggered in a minute. A discount request that sits two days in an inbox is a sale lost to Amazon. A digest typed by hand is a digest that arrives late and occasionally wrong. Managers don't care about flows; they care that the alert, the approval and the summary happen without anyone remembering. The analyst who can wire that up in an afternoon is the one whose team looks organised.

How it works

Three kinds of cloud flow

KindStarts whenNovamart example
Automatedsomething happens in a connected servicea Forms response arrives; a row is added to the Store issues list; a file lands in a SharePoint folder
Instanta person presses a button (in the app, in Teams, on a selected Excel row)"Request discount approval" on a row of the price list
Scheduleda clock: every Monday 8:00 IST, every hour, the 1st of the monththe weekly digest; a month-end reminder to seven department heads

Desktop flows are a fourth kind and get their own paragraph at the end. You create any of them at make.powerautomate.com ▸ Create, or from inside Teams (Apps ▸ Power Automate), or from a form (Responses ▸ ⋯ ▸ Create a flow), which is the shortcut most people find first.

The connectors that matter

A connector is the plug into one service; each has triggers and actions. You'll use about eight of the thousand available, and the names below are the ones you'll pick from the search box, spelled the way the builder spells them.

ConnectorTrigger you'll useActions you'll use
Microsoft FormsWhen a new response is submittedGet response details (always the first action; the trigger only gives you an ID)
Excel Online (Business)none worth using; Excel isn't event-drivenAdd a row into a table · List rows present in a table · Get a row · Update a row
SharePointWhen an item is created or modified · When a file is created in a folderCreate item · Update item · Get items · Create file
Office 365 OutlookWhen a new email arrives (V3)Send an email (V2) · Send an email from a shared mailbox · Create event
Microsoft TeamsWhen a new channel message is addedPost message in a chat or channel · Post adaptive card and wait for a response
ApprovalsnoneStart and wait for an approval · Create an approval (non-blocking)
OneDrive for BusinessWhen a file is createdGet file content · Create file
PlannerWhen a task is completedCreate a task · Update task details
Schedule (built in)RecurrenceDelay · Delay until
Data Operation (built in)noneCompose · Select · Filter array · Create HTML table

Watch out

The Excel connector only sees Tables, and only in workbooks stored in OneDrive for Business or SharePoint. A plain range, however tidy, does not appear in the "Table" dropdown, and a workbook on someone's laptop doesn't exist as far as the flow is concerned. Before you build, open the workbook, select the data, Ctrl+T, and name the table (Table Design ▸ Table Name) something like tblNPS. Module 02 is the reason this matters; this module is where you pay for skipping it.

Dynamic content and expressions

When you click into an action's field, a panel offers dynamic content: every output of every earlier block, by name. "Score" from Get response details, "Response Id" from the trigger, "Outcome" from the approval. Most flows need nothing else. When you do need to change something, format a date, join two strings, turn text into a number, you switch the panel to Expression and type a function. The syntax is its own small language, close to Excel's but not the same: single quotes for text, no =, functions all lower-case.

formatDateTime(utcNow(),'dd-MMM-yyyy')

utcNow() is UTC, five and a half hours behind Gurugram. A digest that runs at 8 am IST and prints utcNow() will print 2:30 am. Convert first.

convertTimeZone(utcNow(),'UTC','India Standard Time','dd-MMM-yyyy HH:mm')
concat('NPS alert: score ', string(outputs('Get_response_details')?['body/r8f2a1c']),
       ' from order ', outputs('Get_response_details')?['body/r3c9d0e'],
       '. Comment: ', outputs('Get_response_details')?['body/r5e7b2f'])

The r8f2a1c codes are how Forms names its questions internally; you never type them, you pick the field from the dynamic content panel and the expression editor writes the reference. What you do type is the concat around them. A few more you'll reach for:

ExpressionDoes
addDays(utcNow(),-7,'yyyy-MM-dd')a date a week ago, formatted; also addHours, addMinutes
int(…) · float(…) · string(…)type conversion; the form's Score arrives as text, and a Condition comparing text "10" to number 6 gives nonsense
formatNumber(209226.3,'N0')"209,226"; use 'C0' with a locale for currency
if(lessOrEquals(int(x),6),'Detractor','OK')an inline condition, for a single field rather than a whole branch
empty(x) · coalesce(x,'none')test for blank; replace blank with a default
length(body('List_rows_present_in_a_table')?['value'])how many rows an Excel action returned
triggerOutputs()?['body/…']reach into the trigger's outputs directly

Conditions, loops and scopes

A Condition block takes a value, an operator and a value, and gives you an "If yes" and an "If no" lane; add rows with And/Or for compound tests. An Apply to each appears by itself whenever you use an output that is a list (the rows from List rows present in a table, say); everything inside it runs once per item. A Scope is just a box that groups actions so you can handle their failure as one, which is the next topic.

Testing, run history and the step that fails

  1. Save ▸ Test ▸ Manually, then submit a real form response (or press the button, or wait for the schedule). The designer switches to the run view; every block turns green or red, and clicking a block shows its inputs and outputs. That is where you learn the score arrived as the text "2" rather than the number 2.
  2. My flows ▸ the flow ▸ 28-day run history. Every run, with status, start time and duration. A red run opens to the failing block and its error message, which is usually clear ("Table not found", "The response is not JSON", "Access denied").
  3. On any action ▸ ⋯ ▸ Settings ▸ Retry policy. The default retries transient failures four times. Leave it.
  4. On the action after a risky one ▸ ⋯ ▸ Configure run after. Tick "has failed" (and "has timed out"). Now that action runs only when the previous one fails, so make it "Send an email (V2)" to yourself with result('Scope_name') in the body, and the flow tells you it broke instead of silently stopping. Put the risky actions in a Scope and configure the email to run after the Scope fails, so one handler covers them all.
  5. Flow checker (top right) before you turn it on. It catches empty required fields and unused Apply to each loops.

Ownership matters. A flow you build runs as you, with your permissions, and stops when you leave. For anything that outlives the project, Share ▸ add a co-owner (Vikram), or build it as a team flow from inside Teams; and use a shared mailbox for outgoing mail so it doesn't come from your name.

Limits, licensing, desktop flows, and when not to

The Microsoft 365 licence Novamart already pays for includes Power Automate for the standard connectors used here (Forms, Excel, SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, Approvals, Planner). Premium connectors (SQL Server, Dataverse, HTTP, most third-party SaaS) need a per-user or per-flow plan, and the builder marks them with a diamond. Each user gets a daily API request allowance; a flow that loops over 6,000 Excel rows every hour will hit it, and the fix is to filter in the action (List rows has a Filter Query field) rather than loop. A run can take up to 30 days (which is what lets an approval wait), and an Apply to each runs up to 5,000 iterations by default.

Desktop flows are the RPA half of the product: a recorder that drives a Windows application by clicking and typing, for systems with no connector, like the old billing software at the Dehradun store. They need Power Automate for desktop installed on a machine that stays on, a premium licence for unattended runs, and far more maintenance than a cloud flow, because a UI change breaks them. Use one when there is truly no API, and say so in the README.

When not to automate. If the job happens once a quarter, a checklist beats a flow. If the input is messy (free-text emails, PDFs of handwritten forms), fix the capture first with Forms; a flow on bad input just delivers bad output faster. If the process isn't agreed (who approves discounts above 20%? Rohan says him, Arjun says Finance), automating it freezes the argument into the flow. And if a List rule (one condition, one email) covers it, use the rule; it's simpler to hand over.

Application: the customer feedback pipeline

This is capstone 07 in three builds. Together they take an NPS response from the customer's phone to a row in a Table, a Teams alert for low scores, an approval path for the goodwill discount that follows, and a Monday summary nobody has to write. The flowcharts show the three side by side; the steps below are the exact clicks.

Build 1: new NPS response → Excel Table → Teams alert

  1. Prepare the workbook. In SharePoint, Marketing & CRM / Documents / NPS / NPS-responses.xlsx, with a Table named tblNPS and columns ResponseID, OrderID, SurveyDate, Score, Reason, Comment, Email. Same shape as the Lab's NPS sheet, so every Module 11 formula works on it.
  2. make.powerautomate.com ▸ Create ▸ Automated cloud flow ▸ name NPS response to Excel and Teams ▸ trigger "When a new response is submitted" (Microsoft Forms). Pick the form Novamart NPS · Sep 2026.
  3. + New step ▸ "Get response details" (Microsoft Forms). Form Id: the same form. Response Id: the dynamic content chip from the trigger. Without this step you have an ID and nothing else.
  4. + New step ▸ "Add a row into a table" (Excel Online (Business)). Location: SharePoint site Marketing & CRM; Document Library: Documents; File: NPS/NPS-responses.xlsx; Table: tblNPS. The column fields appear; fill each from dynamic content: ResponseID ← Response Id, Score ← the NPS question, Reason ← the "What went wrong?" choice, SurveyDate ← Submission time.
  5. + New step ▸ Condition. Left: Expression int(outputs('Get_response_details')?['body/…']), picking the score chip inside the int(). Operator: is less than or equal to. Right: 6.
  6. In "If yes" ▸ "Post message in a chat or channel" (Microsoft Teams). Post as: Flow bot. Post in: Channel. Team: Marketing & CRM. Channel: # NPS-alerts. Message: "Low score: [Score] on order [Order ID]. Reason: [Reason]. Comment: [Comment]. Owner: @Priya." Leave "If no" empty.
  7. Save ▸ Test ▸ Manually ▸ submit a response with score 3. Watch the run: four green blocks, a row in the Table, a message in the channel. Submit a 10 and check that the Teams step is skipped, not failed.

A quick sanity check on the Table, once the flow has been running: the alert count and the detractor count in Excel must agree. On the Lab's NPS sheet, the last seven days look like this.

=COUNTIFS(NPS!D:D,">="&(TODAY()-6),NPS!E:E,"<=6")

3 of the 9 responses since 25 August. Three alerts in the channel, three rows with a score of 6 or under in the Table; if those two numbers differ, the flow has a failed run in its history.

Build 2: discount approval with two branches

Store managers may give up to 20% off a returned-and-repurchased item on their own authority; anything above needs Rohan. Today that's a WhatsApp to Rohan and a wait. The flow makes it a form, an approval card in Rohan's Teams, and a row in a Table that Finance can audit.

  1. Forms: Discount request, people in the organisation only, record name. Questions: Order ID (Text, number restriction), Store (Choice), Discount % (Text, number 0–50), Reason (Choice: goodwill after complaint / price match / damaged packaging / other), Notes (Text).
  2. Automated cloud flow ▸ "When a new response is submitted" ▸ "Get response details" as before.
  3. + New step ▸ "Start and wait for an approval" (Approvals). Approval type: Approve/Reject – First to respond. Title: concat('Discount ', [Discount %], '% on order ', [Order ID], ' (', [Store], ')'). Assigned to: Rohan Desai. Details: the reason and notes. The flow now stops here, for up to 30 days, until Rohan responds in Teams, Outlook or the Approvals app.
  4. + New step ▸ Condition ▸ Outcome (from the approval) is equal to Approve.
  5. If yes ▸ "Add a row into a table" ▸ tblDiscounts in Finance's workbook, with Order ID, Store, Discount %, Approver (Responder display name), Approved on (Completion date), Comments. Then "Send an email (V2)" to the requester (Responder's email from Get response details): "Approved. Apply [Discount %]% at the till; reference [Response Id]."
  6. If no ▸ "Send an email (V2)" to the requester: "Not approved. Rohan's note: [Comments]."
  7. Test with a 25% request. The approval card lands in Rohan's Teams activity feed (test with yourself as approver first). Approve it; check the row in tblDiscounts and the email. Reject one; check the other branch.

Only requests above 20% should reach Rohan, so add a Condition before the approval: Discount % greater than 20 goes to the approval; 20 or under goes straight to the Table row and the "Approved automatically" email. The Lab's Sales sheet shows how often this matters.

=COUNTIFS(Sales!O:O,">=25")

350 lines, against 808 at 20% or more. If a third of the deep discounts came through this flow, Rohan would see about ten approvals a month, which is a number he'll accept.

Build 3: the scheduled Monday digest

The digest has three numbers: last week's delivered revenue, the change on the week before, and last week's cancellation rate. The trick is that the flow never computes them. Excel does, in a small Table called tblDigest with columns Metric and Value, and the formulas are relative to TODAY() so the Table is always about the last full week (Monday to Sunday). Build the cells first.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,
    Sales!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6),
    Sales!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)),
    Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹2,09,226 for 24–30 August. WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2) returns 1 for Monday, so TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2) is always last Sunday and six days before it is last Monday. Run on any day of the week, it points at the same seven days.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6),Sales!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
    /SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-13),Sales!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-7),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")-1

−24.4%: the week before came to ₹2,76,869. One line in the digest, and Nandini will ask why; that is the digest doing its job.

=COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6),Orders!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)),Orders!G:G,"Cancelled")
    /COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6),Orders!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)))

3 of 26 orders, 11.5%. Small numbers, so the digest should print the count as well as the rate; a 1-in-9 week and a 3-in-26 week both look like "11%".

="Weekly digest · "&TEXT(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6,"dd-mmm")&" to "&TEXT(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2),"dd-mmm")
    &" · revenue ₹"&TEXT(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6),Sales!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"),"#,##0")

"Weekly digest · 24-Aug to 30-Aug · revenue ₹209,226". Put this in tblDigest as a row called Subject, and the flow's email subject is one dynamic content chip.

  1. Create ▸ Scheduled cloud flow ▸ Monday digest ▸ Repeat every 1 Week ▸ Monday ▸ 08:00. In the Recurrence block, open Advanced options and set Time zone to (UTC+05:30) Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai, New Delhi. Without this, 08:00 means 08:00 UTC, 1:30 pm in Gurugram.
  2. + New step ▸ "List rows present in a table" (Excel Online (Business)) ▸ the pack workbook ▸ Table tblDigest. Because the cells are formulas, the workbook must have been recalculated; Excel Online does this when the flow opens it, but a workbook nobody has opened in a month can return stale values. Adding "Get a row" for the Subject row first is a cheap warm-up.
  3. + New step ▸ "Create HTML table" (Data Operation). From: the value output of List rows. Columns: Automatic. This turns the Metric/Value rows into a small table for the email body.
  4. + New step ▸ "Send an email (V2)" (Office 365 Outlook). To: Nandini Rao; Cc: Vikram Shah. Subject: the Value of the Subject row (use Filter array on Metric equals "Subject", or simply Get a row with key Metric = Subject and use its Value). Body: two lines of text, then the Output of Create HTML table, then the SharePoint link to the pack. Tick "Is HTML" in advanced options.
  5. + New step ▸ "Post message in a chat or channel" (Teams) ▸ # Monday review, same subject line and the link. The channel post is the record; the email is for Nandini's phone.
  6. Wrap steps 2–5 in a Scope; add "Send an email (V2)" to yourself after the Scope, Configure run after ▸ has failed, has timed out. Body: result('Scope'). Now a Monday with a broken Table is a Monday you hear about at 8:01, not at 9:30 in front of Nandini.
  7. Test ▸ Manually. Don't wait for Monday. Check the email renders the table, the subject has the right week, and the Teams post has the link. Then turn it on and share it with Vikram as co-owner.

Pro habit

Keep the flow dumb and the workbook smart. A flow that computes revenue with expressions over 6,000 rows is slow, hits the API limit and can't be checked by anyone who doesn't build flows. A flow that reads five cells that Excel computed can be verified by opening the workbook. When the CFO asks "where does this number come from", the answer should be a cell, not a Compose action.

Use cases across the business

FunctionThe askTrigger → actions
Marketing"Alert me on every detractor."Forms response → Get response details → Add a row → Condition → Post message (build 1)
Merchandising"Approve discounts above 20% without WhatsApp."Forms response → Start and wait for an approval → Condition → row + email (build 2)
Operations"Every store-audit Fail becomes a task."Forms response → Condition on each Fail → Create a task (Planner) in the Store ops plan, assigned to the store's manager
Finance"Remind the seven department heads on the 1st, and me on the 4th about who hasn't submitted."Recurrence (monthly) → List rows on the inputs tracker → Filter array Submitted = No → Send an email per row
HR"When someone joins, create their induction checklist."When an item is created (SharePoint Joiners list) → Create a task ×12 (Planner) → Post message to the manager
Digital"File the daily app export the moment it arrives."When a new email arrives (V3), from the app vendor, has attachment → Create file (SharePoint, Data feeds) → Post message
Analytics"Tell me when the pack is edited by anyone but me."When a file is modified (SharePoint) → Condition Modified By ≠ me → Post message in a chat

The Operations one shows the pattern for "one form, many tasks": the Likert question produces one output per row, so the flow has five Conditions in parallel (or one Apply to each over a Select of the rows), each creating a Planner task only for a Fail. The task title is built with concat from the store name and the check, and the due date with addDays(utcNow(),7,'yyyy-MM-dd'). What the audit doesn't tell you is how many stores are running on empty, and that is a formula, not a flow.

=COUNTIFS(Inventory!E:E,0)

91 of 936 rows. That's the number a Monday digest for Rohan would carry, straight from the Inventory sheet, and a Condition of "greater than 50" on it is a reasonable reason to @mention him.

Practice

Four design exercises and two formulas. For the design ones, write the flow as a list: trigger, then each action with its connector in brackets, then the condition and the two lanes. That's how you'd describe it to Vikram before building it.

Exercise 1 · Audit Fail to Planner task

The store-audit form has a Likert question with five checks (Pass / Fail / N/A). Design the flow that creates a Planner task for each Fail, assigned to the store's manager, due in seven days.

Hint

One trigger, one Get response details, then one Condition per check. Where does the manager's email come from? The form records the responder.

What good looks like
  • Trigger: When a new response is submitted (Microsoft Forms) · Monthly store audit.
  • Get response details (Microsoft Forms).
  • Five parallel Conditions, each "[check] is equal to Fail". In each If yes: Create a task (Planner) in plan Store ops, bucket = the store name, title = concat([Store], ' · ', 'Fire exits blocked'), assigned to = Responders' Email, due = addDays(utcNow(),7,'yyyy-MM-dd'); then Update task details with the "What's wrong" text in Notes.
  • Outside the conditions: Post message in # Store ops summarising the audit with a link to the response.

A version with Apply to each over a Select of the five rows is neater but harder to read; five Conditions is fine for five checks.

Exercise 2 · Subject lines with expressions

Write the expression for an email subject that reads "Discount 25% on order 12345 (Novamart Kothrud) · 31-Aug-2026", using the form fields and today's date in IST.

Hint

concat for the joining, convertTimeZone for the date. Field references are chips you pick; write them as [Discount %] in your answer.

What good looks like 
concat('Discount ', [Discount %], '% on order ', [Order ID], ' (', [Store], ') · ',
       convertTimeZone(utcNow(),'UTC','India Standard Time','dd-MMM-yyyy'))

Single quotes around every literal, and the date converted before formatting. formatDateTime(utcNow(),…) alone would show the UTC date, which is yesterday for anything sent before 5:30 am.

Exercise 3 · The week before last

The digest compares last week with the week before. Write the formula for the week before last's delivered revenue (the second-to-last full Monday–Sunday week), relative to TODAY().

Hint

Last Sunday is TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2). The week before ends seven days earlier and starts thirteen days earlier.

Show solution 
=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-13),Sales!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-7),Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")

₹2,76,869 for 17–23 August. Put this in tblDigest as its own row and the flow can show both weeks, not just the percentage.

Exercise 4 · What happens when the Table is missing

Someone renames tblDigest to Table3. Describe what the Monday digest flow does on Monday, what the run history shows, and the two changes you'd make so that this fails loudly next time.

Hint

Think about which block fails, what "Configure run after" does, and who owns the workbook.

What good looks like

"List rows present in a table" fails with a "table not found" error; every block after it is skipped; the run shows red at that block in the 28-day history; Nandini gets nothing and nobody knows until 9:30. Change one: wrap the reading and sending steps in a Scope, and add "Send an email (V2)" to yourself and Vikram configured to run after the Scope has failed or timed out, with result('Scope') in the body. Change two: protect the Table name, by documenting it in a Readme sheet in the workbook and, better, by keeping the digest cells in a workbook only the Analytics team can edit, linked to the pack with formulas.

Exercise 5 · Two approvers

Arjun wants Finance to co-approve any discount above 30%. Redesign build 2 so that requests above 30% need both Rohan and a Finance approver, while 21–30% still need only Rohan.

Hint

The approval action has an "Everyone must approve" type. You'll need a Condition on the discount before the approval, and the "If no" lane still matters.

What good looks like
  • Condition A: Discount % greater than 30. If yes: Start and wait for an approval, type Approve/Reject – Everyone must approve, assigned to Rohan Desai; Finance approver. If no: Start and wait for an approval, First to respond, assigned to Rohan only.
  • After both lanes: a Condition on Outcome equal to Approve, then the same row-and-email branches as before. Use a Compose to hold the Outcome from whichever approval ran, so the later Condition has one thing to test.
  • Keep the earlier Condition for 20% or under, which needs no approval at all.

Three tiers, one flow, and the approval type does the "both must agree" logic for you.

Exercise 6 · Cancellations in the digest

Add the count of cancelled orders in the last full week to tblDigest, so the digest can print "3 of 26" rather than a bare percentage.

Hint

It's the numerator of the cancellation-rate formula from build 3, on its own.

Show solution 
=COUNTIFS(Orders!B:B,">="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)-6),Orders!B:B,"<="&(TODAY()-WEEKDAY(TODAY(),2)),Orders!G:G,"Cancelled")

3. With a second row for the order count (26), the flow can build "3 of 26 (11.5%)" with one concat, and Nandini can tell a bad week from a small one.

Pitfalls and pro habits

Watch out

A flow that posts to a channel, and a trigger on "When a new channel message is added" in the same channel, is an infinite loop, and it will run until someone notices the 4,000 messages or the API limit stops it. Any time a flow's action could fire another flow's trigger (a row added that triggers "when a row is modified", a file created that triggers "when a file is created"), add a Condition that checks who made the change and exits if it was the Flow bot.

Pro habit

Rename every block as you add it. "Get response details" is fine; "Condition 3" is not. Call it "Score 6 or under?" and "Post low-score alert". Six months later, in the run history, at 8:05 on a Monday, that's the difference between a two-minute fix and a rebuild. The names also make expressions readable: outputs('Get_NPS_response') beats outputs('Get_response_details_2').

  • Tables, not ranges, in SharePoint or OneDrive. The single most common "why can't the flow see my data" question.
  • Types. Form answers arrive as text. Wrap numbers in int() or float() before comparing, or "9" will be less than "10" and also less than "6" depending on the day.
  • Time zones. Every timestamp is UTC until you convert it. Set the Recurrence time zone; convert with convertTimeZone in expressions.
  • Test both lanes. A condition whose "If no" has never run has never been tested.
  • Handle failure on purpose. A Scope plus an email configured to run after failure, on every flow anyone depends on.
  • Co-own everything. A flow owned by one person stops when that person's account does. Add Vikram; better, build it in the team.
  • Don't loop over what you can filter. List rows has a Filter Query field (Score le 6) and a Top Count; use them before reaching for Apply to each over 6,000 rows.
  • Write the README. Trigger, what it does, which workbook and Table, who owns it, what to do when it fails. One paragraph, in the channel's Files tab.

On the job

In the assessment test

Power Automate rarely appears as a hands-on task in an analyst test; there's no sandbox. It appears as a design question: "A survey response should be recorded in a spreadsheet and the team alerted if the score is low. Describe how you would automate this." The grader wants the vocabulary in order: trigger (new response), actions (get details, add a row to a Table), a condition on the score, an action in the yes lane (Teams post), and one sentence on what happens when it fails. Mention that the Excel target has to be a Table and you're ahead of most candidates.

First 90 days

Find the one thing your team does by hand every week that involves copying from one place to another. Build the flow for it, in the team, with a co-owner and an error email, and a README. Show the run history at the next review. It's the fastest way a new analyst becomes the person the team can't do without, and it costs an afternoon.

"Walk me through a flow you've built."
An NPS pipeline: a Forms trigger, Get response details, Add a row into an Excel Table in SharePoint, then a condition on the score that posts to a Teams channel for six or under. I wrapped the actions in a scope with an error email configured to run after failure, and shared it with my manager as co-owner. The design choice I'd defend is keeping the numbers in Excel formulas rather than flow expressions, so anyone can check them.
"What's the difference between an automated, an instant and a scheduled flow?"
The trigger. Automated flows start on an event in a connected service, like a form response or a new file. Instant flows start when a person presses a button, including from a selected row in Excel or a message in Teams. Scheduled flows start on a recurrence. The actions available afterwards are the same.
"When would you not automate something?"
When it's rare enough that a checklist is cheaper, when the input is too messy to trust without fixing the capture first, or when the people involved haven't agreed the process; automating an argument just freezes it. And when a simpler tool, like a List rule or an Outlook rule, already covers it.

Quick check

1. The "Add a row into a table" action shows no tables for your workbook. Most likely cause?

The Excel connector addresses Tables by name and only reaches files in OneDrive for Business or SharePoint. Ctrl+T and a name fixes it.

2. What does "Start and wait for an approval" do to the flow?

The run stays open at that block. The Outcome, comments and responder then become dynamic content for a Condition.

3. A scheduled flow set to 08:00 with no time zone chosen runs at what time in Gurugram?

Recurrence times are UTC unless you set the time zone in the block's advanced options. IST is UTC+5:30.

4. What does "Configure run after ▸ has failed" on an email action achieve?

By default an action runs only after success. Changing it to "has failed" turns that action into the error handler.
