    SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,s,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,9,1),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31)),
    SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!B:B,s,Targets!C:C,">=2025-09",Targets!C:C,"<=2026-08"),
    XLOOKUP(s,Stores!B:B,Stores!H:H)))

Thirteen rows. Andheri West leads the physical stores at ₹8.05 lakh, Rajpur Road brings up the rear at ₹62,051 against a ₹7 lakh target, and the last cell of the online row is blank, which is exactly what you want to see before you divide by it.

Watch out

Three things in this data will quietly wreck a naive scorecard. Kochi's targets start in April 2024, its opening month, at ₹50,000, and its delivered revenue that month was ₹2,664 because the first sale landed on 28 April; its 2024 total is ₹49,494 for nine partial months, so any "2024 vs 2025" growth line for Kochi is meaningless. Novamart.in has a blank SqFt, and dividing revenue by SqFt returns #DIV/0! there — wrap it in IF(SqFt="","n/a",…), never IFERROR(…,0), which would rank the biggest store last. And 62 of the 263 rows in Returns sit on orders whose status is still Delivered, worth ₹1,85,192 in refunds; your "delivered revenue" is gross of those partial returns unless you say otherwise. Check the first one yourself: =SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,"Novamart MG Road Kochi",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-04").

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Store-Scorecard_v01.xlsx: source sheets untouched; a Scorecard sheet with the PivotTable, slicer and colour scale; a Check sheet where the SUMIFS version of every column reconciles to the pivot; an Assumptions sheet naming the window, the status rule and the Kochi handling.
  • Store-Capex-Memo.docx: one page to Nandini with the ranking table, the shortlist, and the store that gets a business review instead of money, with the reason in one sentence.
  • README.md with a paragraph headed "What would change my answer", for example store-level rent, which you do not have.

Stretch goals

  • Add revenue per active store employee from Employees (E Store, H ExitDate blank) as a second productivity measure, and say which of the two you would present and why.
  • Build the twelve-month window from a single as-of cell with EDATE so the scorecard rolls forward when the month changes.
  • Add a "months since last target hit" column per store using MAXIFS on the months where delivered revenue met target.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Metric definition20%Window, status rule and the two denominators written down before the pivot exists, and used consistently in every column.
Workbook correctness25%Pivot and SUMIFS agree to the rupee on all thirteen stores; online store shows "n/a" not zero on revenue per square foot; Kochi flagged as partial in 2024.
Trap handling20%Kochi, the blank SqFt and partial returns each handled and the size of the error each would have caused stated in the README.
Recommendation20%A named shortlist, a named store for review, and one sentence on what would change the answer.
Presentation and reproducibility15%One page, colour scale that reads without a legend, workbook refreshes cleanly on another machine.

Monthly Sales Pack: what happened in August, and can we produce this every month in under an hour?

Brief from the CFO

Arjun gets a "monthly pack" on the fifth working day, and every month it arrives late with a different layout. "I want one Excel file and one deck. Same six charts every month, same order, numbers linked so nobody retypes them. Build August 2026 and prove it will take you forty minutes to do September."

The brief

A monthly pack is a factory, not a report. The value is not in August's numbers; it is in the fact that September's numbers will drop into the same cells and the same charts will update without anyone opening PowerPoint and typing. That means the workbook needs a single "reporting month" cell that every formula reads, Tables that expand when new rows arrive, and charts in the deck that are linked, not pasted.

August 2026 has a story in it. Delivered revenue was ₹12.48 lakh, up 36 per cent on July and 81 per cent on August 2025. Electronics carried more than half of it. The app did less than it did a year ago in absolute rupees. Arjun will want all three of those on slide two, and he will want to know which of them survives once you look at what "August" actually contains.

Because that is the second thing a monthly pack has to be honest about: the latest month is never finished. Orders placed in the last week are still Processing, and returns on August orders will mostly be booked in September. A pack that compares an unfinished August with a finished July is comparing two different things.

The data

Sales (C Month, K Category, G Channel, P LineRevenue, Q Status), Orders (B OrderDate, G Status, J OrderValue) for order counts, Targets for the attainment line, Returns (D ReturnDate, F Refund) for the lag. Start from files/cap02-monthly-sales-pack-starter.xlsx, which has a Control sheet with the reporting-month cell and an empty Pack sheet; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. For the reporting month: delivered revenue, delivered orders, average order value, and the same three for the prior month and the same month last year, all driven from one cell holding 2026-08.
  2. Revenue by category and by channel for the month, with month-on-month and year-on-year change.
  3. A thirteen-month trend of delivered revenue against target, ending in the reporting month.
  4. How much of the month's revenue is still Processing, how much was Cancelled, and how do August's booked returns compare with July's?
  5. Six charts in a deck, each linked to the workbook, each with an action title ("Electronics carried August", not "Revenue by category").
  6. Change the control cell to 2026-07. Does every number and chart update? Time yourself.

Starter

=LET(cat,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!K2:K6315)),
  HSTACK(cat,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!K:K,cat)))

Six rows: Electronics ₹6,43,784, Home & Kitchen ₹3,11,834, Fashion ₹1,57,568, then Sports, Beauty and Grocery at ₹67,022, ₹52,154 and ₹15,985. In the real workbook, replace "2026-08" with a reference to the control cell so September is a one-cell change.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")
 /SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-07",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered")-1

0.361, a 36 per cent jump on July's ₹9.17 lakh. Before that goes on a slide, look at the "Watch out" box.

Watch out

August is not closed. Thirteen orders worth ₹47,101 are still Processing, all placed on or after 24 August, so the month's "all statuses" revenue of ₹13.70 lakh contains money that has not been earned yet; check it with =SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!C:C,"2026-08",Sales!Q:Q,"Processing"). The bigger distortion runs the other way: returns land a median of nine days after the order (maximum eighteen), so August shows only ₹19,118 of Returned lines against July's ₹73,915. That is not a quality improvement, it is a calendar. Either report returns one month in arrears or label the latest month "provisional" in the pack, and do the same for the Targets line, where the ₹16.3 lakh August target against ₹12.48 lakh delivered gives 76.6 per cent attainment that will move as Processing orders clear.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Monthly-Pack_v01.xlsx: a Control sheet with the reporting month, a Pack sheet with every table driven from it, Tables (Ctrl+T) over the source so new rows are picked up, a Checks sheet where category and channel totals reconcile to the month total.
  • 2026-08_Monthly-Pack.pptx: eight slides — cover, headline numbers, six linked charts with action titles, and a "provisional items" slide naming Processing and returns lag. Speaker notes on every chart slide.
  • README.md with the forty-minute runbook for next month: which cell to change, which Table to extend, which links to refresh, in order.

Stretch goals

  • Add a returns-in-arrears line: refunds from Returns by the month of the original order, not the return date, and show how it changes July.
  • Build the deck from the workbook with a linked Camera-tool picture of the headline table so it updates like the charts do.
  • Add a store-level page driven by a dropdown, and time a full refresh with all thirteen.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Single point of control25%One cell drives every number and chart; changing it to 2026-07 updates the whole pack with no manual edits.
Workbook correctness20%Category, channel and store cuts each reconcile to the month total; prior-month and prior-year cells computed, not typed.
Trap handling20%Processing orders and the returns lag both identified, quantified and labelled "provisional" in the pack.
Deck quality20%Charts linked not pasted, action titles, one message per slide, consistent layout from the slide master.
Runbook15%A stranger could produce September from the README alone, and the timed run is under an hour.

CRM Lead Clean-up: how many real people are in this export, and can the telecallers dial it on Monday?

Brief from the Head of Marketing & CRM

Priya has 150 leads exported from the website form, an event stall and three Instagram campaigns, all in one sheet, and a telecalling team starting Monday. "Before anyone dials, tell me how many real people are in here, give me a clean list, and tell me what went wrong so I can fix the form. And do it in a way that works again next month, because there will be a next month."

The brief

This is the project that most resembles a real first week on the job. The Leads sheet has names in capitals, names with trailing spaces, four date formats in one column, email addresses missing their @, phone numbers in five shapes, Bengaluru spelled five ways and Dehradun two, and the same person entered twice with different casing. None of it is a puzzle. All of it is work, and the point of doing it in Power Query rather than by hand is that next month's export runs through the same steps untouched.

Two outputs are needed and they serve different readers. The clean contact list is for the telecallers and should be conservative: flag fields rather than delete rows, because a lead with a broken email may still have a perfectly good phone number. The scorecard is for Priya and should name the source of each problem, so the web form gets a dropdown for City and a validation rule for Email.

The judgement calls matter more than the transforms. Is a lead the same person because the email matches, or the phone, or both? Different rules give different counts. Whatever you choose, write the rule at the top of the README and show the count under the other rules too.

The data

Leads (B FullName, C Email, D Phone, E City, F Source, G CreatedAt as text, H Status) and Customers (C Email, D Phone) for the cross-check. Start from files/cap03-leads-raw.csv, which is the same 150 rows as the sheet but as a CSV so you practise Get Data from a file; the full workbook is files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Profile the raw file first, with formulas on a sheet you keep: blanks per column, emails without @, distinct emails before and after lower-casing and trimming, city and source spelling variants, and how many rows each date format covers.
  2. In Power Query: trim and proper-case names, lower-case and trim emails, strip phones to their last ten digits, and map cities and sources to a canonical list using a lookup table you build as a second query.
  3. Parse CreatedAt into a real date. There are four formats; state which one is ambiguous and what you assumed.
  4. Remove duplicates on your chosen key and keep the most complete row. How many distinct people are in the 150? Show the count under email-only, phone-only and combined keys.
  5. Score every lead 0–100 on contactability (valid phone, valid email, known city, has a status, created in the last 60 days) and load the clean Table sorted by score.
  6. Match the clean list to Customers on normalised email and on the ten-digit phone. How many leads are already customers, and what does that say about how the form is wired?
  7. Drop a fresh CSV with the same columns into the folder and click Refresh All. Does everything survive?

Starter

=ROWS(UNIQUE(FILTER(Leads!C2:C151,Leads!C2:C151<>"")))
 -ROWS(UNIQUE(LOWER(TRIM(FILTER(Leads!C2:C151,Leads!C2:C151<>"")))))

4 — there are 132 distinct email strings among the 143 non-blank ones, but only 128 once you lower-case and trim, so four "different" leads are the same person typed twice. MOHIT.RAO84@GMAIL.COM in row 3 is the first of them.

=HSTACK(COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"????-??-??"),COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"????-??-?? ??:??"),
    COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"??/??/????"),COUNTIF(Leads!G:G,"??-???-????"))

59 ISO dates, 31 ISO with a time, 41 slashed dd/mm/yyyy, 19 like 21-Aug-2026. That is all 150, so four rules parse the column. The slashed ones are the ambiguous set.

Then the first three Power Query steps, which the Lab does not run.

  1. Data ▸ Get Data ▸ From Text/CSV. Pick cap03-leads-raw.csv, click Transform Data, and immediately change every column's type to Text so Power Query does not guess dates for you.
  2. Transform ▸ Format ▸ Trim, then Capitalize Each Word on FullName; Format ▸ Lowercase then Trim on Email. Check the Applied Steps pane: each click is a step you can rename.
  3. Add Column ▸ Custom Column named Phone10 with Text.End(Text.Select([Phone], {"0".."9"}), 10). Then Home ▸ Remove Rows ▸ Remove Duplicates on Email and Phone10 together.
= Table.AddColumn(#"Trimmed", "Created", each
    let t = Text.Trim([CreatedAt]) in
    try Date.From(Text.Start(t, 10), "en-GB")            // 2026-07-20 and 2026-08-19 14:28
    otherwise try Date.FromText(t, [Format="dd/MM/yyyy"])  // 13/07/2026
    otherwise Date.FromText(t, [Format="dd-MMM-yyyy"]),   // 21-Aug-2026
    type date)

Watch out

The dedupe key decides the answer, so never quote one number. Email-only gives 128 distinct people but drops the 7 leads with no email at all; the ten-digit phone gives 120 distinct phones among the 140 non-blank ones; combined keys give something in between. Sixteen emails have no @ (joseph.gupta21outlook.com in row 9 is a person, not junk), so flag them and keep the row. The dates hide a real ambiguity: 04/05/2026 in row 10 is 4 May under day-first and 5 April under month-first, and nothing in the file tells you which; the form was built in India, so assume day-first, and write that assumption down. Verify the broken-email count: =COUNTIFS(Leads!C:C,"<>",Leads!C:C,"<>*@*"). And 28 rows have a blank Status — those are usually the newest leads, not lost ones.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Leads-Clean_v01.xlsx: the raw query loaded as connection only; a CityMap and SourceMap Table; the clean query loaded as a Table with a flag column per problem and the contactability score; a Profile sheet of formulas on the raw data that a reviewer can read top to bottom.
  • Lead-Quality-Scorecard.docx: one page to Priya with the counts under each dedupe rule, the top three form changes, and the customers-already-in-CRM overlap.
  • README.md stating the dedupe key, the survivorship rule, the date assumption and how to refresh next month.

Stretch goals

  • Add fuzzy matching: same ten-digit phone, different spelling of the name, and decide whether they are one person; count how many the rule catches.
  • Parameterise the query on a folder path so a new monthly CSV dropped in the same folder is picked up by Refresh All.
  • Build the contactability score as a second query that merges back, and compare with doing it in a Table column.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Profiling before cleaning15%Every problem counted with a formula on the raw sheet before any transform; counts quoted in the scorecard.
Query correctness25%Steps named, types set explicitly, four date formats parsed, mapping tables used instead of hard-coded replaces; Refresh All works on a new CSV.
Judgement on rules20%Dedupe key, survivorship and the day-first assumption stated, defended, and the count shown under the alternatives.
Conservatism20%Rows flagged not deleted; raw columns preserved beside cleaned ones; nobody with a good phone number is lost over a bad email.
Scorecard for the form owner20%Three specific form changes, each tied to a count of the rows it would have prevented.

Management Dashboard: can Meera see the whole business on one screen every Monday?

Brief from the CEO

Meera opens four different files before the Monday review and none of them agree. "One sheet. Revenue against target, by store and by channel, with the trend, and a way to click on a region and see only that. I should be able to read it on my laptop without scrolling. And when I ask why a number moved, the answer should be on the same screen."

The brief

A dashboard is a layout problem and a denominator problem wearing the same shirt. The layout part is well known: headline KPIs across the top, a trend in the middle, a breakdown and a ranked table below, one colour plus one highlight, nothing 3-D. The denominator part is where most student dashboards fail, because the moment you add a slicer, every KPI has to be a formula that respects it, and every percentage has to know what it is a percentage of.

Dynamic arrays are the engine. UNIQUE builds the list of stores, SUMIFS against that spill builds the numbers, SORTBY ranks them, FILTER pulls out the ones below target, and a chart pointed at the spill redraws when the list changes. No PivotTable refresh, no helper columns hidden in grey. The trade-off is that slicers only attach to Tables and PivotTables, so you will build the slicer's selection into a cell and read that cell in your formulas, or run a PivotTable alongside and reconcile the two.

The story the dashboard has to tell for 2026 to date: the chain is at 65 per cent of target, the online store is at 88 per cent and carrying more than half the revenue, and seven physical stores are below half their target. Meera will look at that and ask one question. Make sure the answer is on the screen.

The data

Sales (D Store, F Region, G Channel, C Month, P LineRevenue, Q Status), Targets, Stores (E Region, F Type). Start from files/cap04-dashboard-starter.xlsx, which has a Dashboard sheet with the grid laid out and named ranges for the selector cells; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Four headline KPIs for the year to date: delivered revenue, target attainment, delivered orders, app share of revenue, each with the same figure for the prior year beside it.
  2. A monthly trend of delivered revenue against target for the last thirteen months, as a combo chart with a line for target.
  3. A ranked bar chart of stores by year-to-date attainment, built from a SORTBY spill so it re-ranks when the region selector changes.
  4. A FILTER list of stores below 50 per cent of target, with the rupee gap, that shrinks to "none" cleanly when the selection is healthy.
  5. A region selector (data validation list or a slicer on a helper Table) that every number on the sheet respects, including the KPIs.
  6. Conditional formatting: a colour scale on attainment, an icon set on month-on-month change, and a formula rule that highlights any store whose latest month was zero.
  7. Fit it on one screen at 100 per cent zoom on a 13-inch laptop. Print it to one page. Both.

Starter

=LET(s,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!D2:D6315)),
     att,SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,s,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2026*")
        /SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!B:B,s,Targets!C:C,"2026*"),
  SORTBY(HSTACK(s,att),att,1))

Rajpur Road at 7.7 per cent, Gomti Nagar at 21.6, Kochi at 23.3, up to Andheri West at 81.7 and Novamart.in at 88.3. Point a bar chart at this spill and it re-ranks itself.

=FILTER(Stores!B:B,
   SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!D:D,Stores!B:B,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2026*")
   <0.5*SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!B:B,Stores!B:B,Targets!C:C,"2026*"),"none")

Seven stores — T. Nagar, Kothrud, SG Highway, Malviya Nagar, Gomti Nagar, Rajpur Road and Kochi. Add a rupee-gap column with HSTACK and this becomes the "why did the number move" panel.

Watch out

Region is blank for every online line, and Novamart.in is 54 per cent of delivered revenue. Build a PivotTable by Region and ₹1.29 crore of delivered revenue (₹1.48 crore across all statuses) lands in a row labelled "(blank)" at the bottom, which a reader will skip. Prove it: =SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!F:F,"",Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered"). Either add "Online" as a fifth region on a helper column, or make the region selector explicitly include a "Digital" option, and never let the four physical regions add up to a total that is not the total. Second trap: a slicer on a Table filters the Table, not your dynamic-array formulas, so a KPI built with SUMIFS on the whole column ignores the slicer silently; read the selector into a cell and put that cell in your criteria. Third: Rajpur Road delivered nothing in February 2026, and a line chart draws that as a plunge to zero rather than a gap. That one is real, and the dashboard should say so instead of smoothing it.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Management-Dashboard_v01.xlsx: a Dashboard sheet that fits one screen, a Calc sheet with every spill formula labelled, an Assumptions sheet with the as-of month and the status rule, and a Checks sheet where the four regions plus online reconcile to the chain total.
  • A one-page PDF export of the dashboard for the Monday pack, plus a 60-second screen recording (Teams or PowerPoint) showing the region selector changing every number.
  • README.md with the design decisions: why these four KPIs, why this chart type for each panel, and how online is treated in the region cut.

Stretch goals

  • Add a "same period last year" toggle so every panel can show 2025 to date beside 2026 to date.
  • Replace the region dropdown with a slicer on a one-column helper Table and read the selection with a SUBTOTAL-based visible-row formula.
  • Add a sparkline column to the store table and decide whether it earns its space on a one-screen layout.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Design20%One screen, KPIs top, trend middle, breakdown and table below, one colour plus one highlight, action titles on every chart.
Formula engine25%All panels driven by dynamic arrays from one selector cell; no hidden helper columns; no hard-coded store names.
Trap handling20%Online handled explicitly in the region cut, slicer-versus-formula scope understood, the Rajpur Road zero shown honestly.
Reconciliation15%Every breakdown adds to the chain total on a Checks sheet, and a PivotTable built alongside agrees with the formulas.
Communication20%A reader who has never seen Novamart can say what the business's problem is within thirty seconds of opening the sheet.

Campaign ROI Tracker: what did we get for ₹1.7 crore of marketing?

Brief from the Head of Marketing & CRM

Priya is defending next year's budget to Arjun and he has asked, reasonably, what the last ten campaigns returned. "Build me a tracker: one row per campaign, budget, orders we can trace to it, revenue, return per rupee. Then tell me honestly how much of that ranking I can stand behind, because he will ask."

The brief

Attributed revenue divided by budget is a two-line calculation and a five-paragraph caveat. An order carries a CampaignID in Orders!E when something in the checkout credited a campaign, which is last-touch attribution: whoever was standing closest when the customer bought gets the credit. Television campaigns do not stamp an ID on anything, so the two Diwali TV campaigns — ₹1.1 crore of the ₹1.7 crore total — will always look worst on this measure whether or not they worked.

So build a second view alongside it. Compare chain-wide revenue during each campaign window with an equally long window immediately before it. It is crude, it is contaminated by seasonality, and it is still more informative than the tagged number alone because it does not depend on the tagging. Both views need XLOOKUP to pull the campaign's dates and budget from Campaigns, and SUMIFS with date-range criteria against Orders.

The third section of the tracker is the honest one: what this workbook can and cannot prove about causation. Write it before you build the ranking, so the ranking does not seduce you.

The data

Campaigns (A CampaignID, B Campaign, C Channel, E Start, F End, G Budget), Orders (B OrderDate, E CampaignID, F Channel, G Status, J OrderValue), and Customers (K SignupDate) for the acquisition question. Start from files/cap05-campaign-roi-starter.xlsx, which has a Tracker sheet with the ten campaign IDs in column A; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. One row per campaign: name, channel, budget, tagged non-cancelled orders, attributed revenue, revenue per rupee. Every cell a lookup or a SUMIFS off the ID in column A, so adding campaign 11 is one new row.
  2. Chain-wide non-cancelled revenue during the campaign window and during the equally long window before it, with the percentage change.
  3. Roll both views up to channel with a PivotTable. Which of Search, Paid Social, Influencer, TV and Email looks best on each view, and do they agree?
  4. How many orders carry a CampaignID at all, and what share of all orders is that? What does that share do to your confidence in question 1?
  5. Do tagged orders have a different average order value from untagged orders in the same window?
  6. For App Launch Bonanza 2026, count app-channel orders in January, February and March. Did the launch month do what a launch month should?
  7. Write the section titled "What this tracker cannot prove" and make it specific to these sheets.

Starter

=SUMIFS(Orders!J:J,Orders!E:E,10,Orders!G:G,"<>Cancelled")
 /XLOOKUP(10,Campaigns!A:A,Campaigns!G:G)

0.135 — App Launch Bonanza 2026 brought back ₹2.02 lakh of tagged order value against a ₹15 lakh budget. In the tracker, the 10 is a reference to column A.

=SUMIFS(Orders!J:J,
    Orders!B:B,">="&XLOOKUP(10,Campaigns!A:A,Campaigns!E:E),
    Orders!B:B,"<="&XLOOKUP(10,Campaigns!A:A,Campaigns!F:F),
    Orders!G:G,"<>Cancelled")

₹7,33,116 across all of February 2026 — three and a half times the tagged figure, which is the gap between "orders we can trace" and "orders that happened while the campaign ran".

=HSTACK(Campaigns!B2:B11,
    COUNTIFS(Orders!E:E,Campaigns!A2:A11,Orders!G:G,"<>Cancelled"),
    SUMIFS(Orders!J:J,Orders!E:E,Campaigns!A2:A11,Orders!G:G,"<>Cancelled")/Campaigns!G2:G11)

Winter Warmers 2025, an email campaign with a ₹2 lakh budget, tops the table at 0.77 rupees back per rupee; Republic Day Sale 2024 sits at the bottom on 0.015 with three orders. Nothing returns more than it cost, which is the first thing to explain in the memo.

Watch out

Only 135 of the 3,000 orders carry a CampaignID, 4.5 per cent, and five of those were cancelled; every ranking you build rests on 130 orders spread across ten campaigns. Republic Day has three. The two TV campaigns have 13 and 15 tagged orders against budgets of ₹50 lakh and ₹60 lakh, so their 0.026 and 0.017 return per rupee measures the tagging, not the television. The window comparison has its own problem: Big Diwali Dhamaka 2025 ran 10–25 October and chain revenue in that window was ₹4.61 lakh against ₹5.83 lakh in the sixteen days before, a 21 per cent fall — during a Diwali campaign — because Diwali 2025 fell on 20 October and the pre-festival shopping peak sat in the "before" window. Check it: =COUNTIFS(Orders!E:E,"<>") gives the 135. And the app launch: app orders were 24 in January, 19 in February (the launch month) and 27 in March. Say that plainly rather than hiding it under the campaign's ₹2 lakh of tagged revenue.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Campaign-ROI-Tracker_v01.xlsx: a Tracker sheet with one formula row copied down ten times, both views side by side, a Channel PivotTable, and a Checks sheet showing tagged orders sum to 135.
  • Campaign-Review.docx: two pages to Priya — the ranking, the window comparison next to it, and a clearly separated section on what the numbers do not establish, plus which campaigns to repeat, which to test properly, and what test to run.
  • README.md stating the attribution rule, the cancelled-order treatment and the "before window" construction.

Stretch goals

  • Check whether campaign windows overlap any other campaign, and decide how you would split credit where they do.
  • Compare each window against the same calendar window a year earlier instead of the weeks before, and say which comparison is less contaminated by season.
  • For the three acquisition campaigns, count customers whose SignupDate falls inside the window and who ordered at least once.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Tracker mechanics25%Every cell a lookup or SUMIFS off the campaign ID; adding a row extends the tracker; dates compared with real date criteria, not text.
Two views, kept apart20%Attributed and window-based views built separately, never averaged, each with its stated weakness.
Trap handling20%The 4.5 per cent tagging rate, the TV blind spot, the Diwali-in-the-before-window problem and the app-launch order count all surfaced with numbers.
Honesty section20%"What this cannot prove" is specific: last-touch, no holdout, seasonality, small counts. Names a test that would fix it.
Recommendation15%Repeat, test, or stop, per campaign, with the reason in one line each.

Inventory Reorder Model: what do we order, where, and what happens if the lead time slips?

Brief from the Head of Merchandising

Rohan has a purchase order to sign by Friday and a stock file that says 235 store-product lines are below their reorder level. "I am not ordering 235 things. Tell me which ones matter, how much to order, and what the bill is if the vendor's lead time goes from two weeks to four. And if I only have ₹25 lakh, what do I drop?"

The brief

Inventory is a snapshot and sales are a flow. Inventory is one reading of stock on hand and reorder level for every store and product as at 31 August 2026; Sales tells you how fast each product moves. Every interesting question here comes from putting the two together with XLOOKUP and SUMIFS, and every trap comes from forgetting that they are measured on different scales.

The model has three layers. First, the flag: which lines are below reorder level, and of those, which products actually sold in the last ninety days. Second, the quantity: a reorder quantity per line that depends on a daily sales rate, a lead time in days and a safety-stock multiplier, all sitting on an Assumptions sheet so Rohan can change them. Third, the What-If: Goal Seek to find the lead time at which the order bill hits ₹25 lakh, a Data Table showing the bill across lead times of 7 to 42 days, and, for the stretch, Solver choosing which lines to fund under the cap.

Rohan will sign a shorter list than 235. The model's job is to make the cut defensible: this line is out because the product is discontinued, this one because it has not sold since June, this one because the store already has 400 days of cover.

The data

Inventory (A StoreID, C ProductID, E StockOnHand, F ReorderLevel, G LastRestock), Products (F UnitCost, I Active), Sales (J Product, M Qty, B OrderDate, Q Status). Start from files/cap06-inventory-reorder-starter.xlsx, which has an Assumptions sheet with lead time, safety factor and budget cap cells already named; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Flag every inventory line below reorder level. How many are there by store, and how many of them are on products that sold at least once chain-wide in the ninety days to 31 August?
  2. Add a column that looks up Active from Products. How many flagged lines are on discontinued products, and what would ordering them have cost at unit cost?
  3. Compute a chain-wide daily sales rate per product from the last ninety days, and from it a reorder quantity per line: rate × (lead time + safety days) − stock on hand, floored at zero, allocated to stores by their share of that product's sales.
  4. Total the order bill at unit cost. Use Goal Seek to find the lead time at which the bill equals ₹25 lakh.
  5. Build a one-variable Data Table of order bill against lead time from 7 to 42 days in 7-day steps, and a two-variable one adding the safety factor.
  6. Compute days of cover per product (stock ÷ daily rate). Why can you rank on it but not quote it?
  7. Stretch: with Solver, choose which flagged lines to fund under a ₹25 lakh cap, maximising ninety-day revenue covered. State the constraints you used.

Starter

=SUMPRODUCT(--(Inventory!E2:E937<Inventory!F2:F937))

235 of 936 store-product lines, which is Rohan's starting number and the one the model has to shrink honestly.

=SUMPRODUCT((Inventory!E2:E937<Inventory!F2:F937)
   *(XLOOKUP(Inventory!C2:C937,Products!A:A,Products!I:I)=FALSE))

51 — more than a fifth of the flagged list is stock nobody should reorder. That single XLOOKUP is worth more than the rest of the model.

=SUMIFS(Inventory!E:E,Inventory!D:D,"Orbit Wireless Mouse")
 /(SUMIFS(Sales!M:M,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!B:B,">"&DATE(2026,6,2),Sales!J:J,"Orbit Wireless Mouse")/90)

2,452 days. Read the "Watch out" box before you put that in front of anyone.

The What-If steps, which the Lab does not run.

  1. Data ▸ What-If Analysis ▸ Goal Seek. Set cell: the order bill total. To value: 2500000. By changing cell: the lead-time cell on Assumptions. Read the answer, then put the lead time back to what the vendor actually quoted.
  2. Data ▸ What-If Analysis ▸ Data Table. Lay out lead times 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42 down a column, the bill formula in the cell above and to the right, select the block, Column input cell = lead time. Chart the result.
  3. Data ▸ Solver. Objective: revenue covered, Max. Variables: a 0/1 column per flagged line. Constraints: bill ≤ 2500000, variables binary, discontinued lines forced to 0. Solving method: Simplex LP.

Watch out

Four of the 72 products are discontinued — Nimbus Lite 5G Smartphone, Pulse Fit Smartwatch, Aurelle Block Heels, Loom & Light Wall Clock — and Inventory still carries a row for each at all thirteen locations, 52 rows in total, of which 51 are below reorder level. Reorder off the flag alone and you order ₹3,25,315 of stock at cost for products that sold zero units in the last ninety days. Check: =SUMIFS(Sales!M:M,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!J:J,"Nimbus Lite 5G Smartphone",Sales!B:B,">"&DATE(2026,6,2)). The second trap is scale: Inventory holds 47,942 units at full-chain scale while Sales is a sample, so days of cover comes out in the thousands for nearly everything (the mouse above: 790 units on hand, 29 sold in ninety days). Use it to rank, never to quote, or a reviewer who knows retail stops reading. Third: StoreID 13 is Novamart.in, and it holds 72 inventory rows like everyone else — that is the warehouse, and its "store" sales are the online channel. And LastRestock runs only from 1 June to 31 August 2026 with no history, so "how long has this been empty" is not answerable from this file.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Inventory-Reorder_v01.xlsx: Assumptions (lead time, safety factor, budget cap, as-of date), Flags with the lookups and exclusion reasons, Order with quantities and the bill, WhatIf with the Goal Seek result recorded and both Data Tables, and a Checks sheet.
  • Purchase-Order-Note.docx: one page to Rohan with the recommended list length, the bill, the lead-time sensitivity chart, and the exclusion rules stated as three sentences.
  • README.md with every assumption and the direction each would move the bill if wrong.

Stretch goals

  • Build an ABC classification of products by ninety-day revenue and cross it with the flag, so the note separates "out of stock on an A item" from noise.
  • Add a service-level input: how much extra stock would the chain hold to keep A items above reorder level, at unit cost?
  • Rebuild the allocation to stores using each store's own ninety-day sales of that product, with a floor for stores that sold none.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Model hygiene20%No hard-coded numbers in formulas; inputs on Assumptions, colour-coded; every exclusion has a reason column.
Lookup and rate logic20%Active flag, unit cost and sales rate all looked up correctly; allocation to stores sums to the chain quantity.
Trap handling25%Discontinued lines excluded and costed, the scale problem stated, days of cover used as a rank only, the warehouse row understood.
What-If tools20%Goal Seek result recorded with the input restored, Data Tables correct and charted, Solver constraints stated (stretch).
Recommendation15%A list Rohan can sign, a bill, and the sentence that explains why it is shorter than 235.

Customer Feedback Pipeline: can a complaint reach the right person the same day, without anyone forwarding an email?

Brief from the Head of Digital

Sameer has 400 survey responses in a sheet that someone exports monthly, and a Teams channel where store managers occasionally paste screenshots of angry WhatsApp messages. "I want one form. Customer fills it, the answer lands in Excel on its own, anyone scoring six or below pings the store manager in Teams within a minute, and I get an NPS number every Monday that I did not have to ask for."

The brief

This is a plumbing project with an analytics tail. The plumbing is Forms → Power Automate → Excel Online (Business) → Teams, and each joint has a rule that will bite you: the flow can only write to an Excel Table, not a range; the file has to live on OneDrive or SharePoint, not a desktop; the Teams action needs the channel to exist before you build; and the form's question types decide what arrives in the spreadsheet, so a "score 0–10" question built as free text gives you the word "ten".

The analytics tail is NPS, which is not an average. Promoters (9–10) minus detractors (0–6), as a percentage of all responses. The 400 historical responses in the NPS sheet average 6.97 out of 10, which sounds like a B grade; their NPS is +10.5, which for a retailer is weak. Sameer's Monday number needs to be the second one, computed with COUNTIFS off the same Table the flow writes to, so the historical rows and the new ones sit in one place.

Design the form to fix what is wrong with the existing data before you copy it. A third of the 400 comments are blank. Four in five responses come from store or website orders; the app has 77 of the 400. Ask yourself what a branching question could do about each of those.

The data

NPS (B CustomerID, C OrderID, D SurveyDate, E Score, F Comment), Orders (F Channel, G Status, D StoreID) via lookup on OrderID, Stores for the manager routing. Start from files/cap07-feedback-form-spec.docx, a one-page spec template for the form's questions, branching and the Table schema; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Design the form: score (0–10 rating), order number (text with validation), store (dropdown of the thirteen), one branching follow-up for scores of 6 or below, comment. Write the spec before you build.
  2. Build the Excel destination: a Table named Feedback on a workbook in SharePoint, with the 400 historical rows loaded into it and a Channel column filled by XLOOKUP against Orders.
  3. Build flow 1: new response → add a row to Feedback → if score ≤ 6, post an adaptive card to the store's Teams channel mentioning the store manager, with the comment and order number.
  4. Build flow 2: every Monday 08:00, read the Table, compute last week's NPS and response count, post to the leadership channel. Do the arithmetic in the flow or in a cell the flow reads; either is fine, but say which and why.
  5. Compute NPS from the historical 400 by channel and by year. Which channel is weakest, and is 2026 better or worse than 2024?
  6. Compare responses on Returned orders with Delivered ones. What does that do to the routing rule?
  7. Test with ten fake submissions, then check the run history. What happens when the order number does not exist in Orders?

Starter

=(COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,">=9")-COUNTIFS(NPS!E:E,"<=6"))/COUNT(NPS!E:E)*100

+10.5 — 164 promoters, 122 detractors, 114 passives who count in the denominator and nowhere else. The average score of 6.97 is on the same sheet and tells a different, wronger story.

=(SUMPRODUCT((NPS!E2:E401>=9)*(XLOOKUP(NPS!C2:C401,Orders!A:A,Orders!F:F)="App"))
  -SUMPRODUCT((NPS!E2:E401<=6)*(XLOOKUP(NPS!C2:C401,Orders!A:A,Orders!F:F)="App")))
 /SUMPRODUCT(--(XLOOKUP(NPS!C2:C401,Orders!A:A,Orders!F:F)="App"))*100

+6.5 on 77 responses, against +10.5 for store and +12.9 for online. The app is the weakest channel and the one with the fewest answers, which is a form-design finding as much as a product one.

The first three build steps, which the Lab does not run.

  1. forms.office.com ▸ New Form. Add a Rating question (0–10, numbers not stars), a Text question for the order number with a "number" restriction, a Choice question for store with all thirteen names, then a Rating follow-up that appears only when the score is 6 or below using … ▸ Add branching.
  2. Excel ▸ Insert ▸ Table on a new workbook saved to the team's SharePoint library, columns exactly matching the form, name it Feedback in Table Design. Paste the 400 historical rows in. Power Automate will not see a range, only a Table.
  3. make.powerautomate.com ▸ Create ▸ Automated cloud flow. Trigger: Microsoft Forms "When a new response is submitted". Action 1: Forms "Get response details". Action 2: Excel Online (Business) "Add a row into a table", picking the SharePoint file and the Feedback Table. Action 3: Condition on score ≤ 6, then Teams "Post card in a chat or channel".
int(outputs('Get_response_details')?['body/r1a2b3c4'])
formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'dd-MMM-yyyy HH:mm')

Watch out

Small numbers. The 400 responses span 32 months and 200 distinct customers, so a typical month has 14 to 17 answers; August 2026 has 14, and one response moves that month's NPS by seven points. July 2026 came out at exactly 0 and August at +7.1, and neither is a trend. Check: =COUNTIFS(NPS!D:D,">="&DATE(2026,8,1),NPS!D:D,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31)). Sameer's Monday post has to carry the response count next to the score or it will be read as a movement. Second: 26 of the 400 responses sit on orders whose status is Returned and they average 5.0 against 7.1 for Delivered orders, so a routing rule that pings the store manager for every detractor will page them for returns the store did not cause — route by channel and status, not just by score. Third: 137 comments are blank, so any "theme analysis" is on 263 rows; "deliver" appears in 80 of them and "late" in 47, which points at logistics rather than stores.

The deliverable

  • The live pipeline: a Form (share link in the README), the SharePoint workbook with the Feedback Table and an NPS sheet of COUNTIFS by week, channel and store, and two flows exported as .zip packages into the folder.
  • Feedback-Pipeline-Spec.docx: the completed form spec, the Table schema, a diagram of the flow, the routing rule, and a test log of the ten fake submissions with what happened to each.
  • README.md with the NPS definition, the by-channel and by-year findings, and the "read the count before the score" rule for the Monday post.

Stretch goals

  • Add a third flow: a weekly digest of all comments containing "late" or "deliver" to the logistics channel, with the order numbers.
  • Compute NPS by store for the store channel only, and say which stores have enough responses for the number to mean anything.
  • Build the Monday post as an adaptive card with the last eight weeks as a sparkline image generated from the workbook.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Form design15%Question types chosen so the Table receives numbers as numbers; branching used for the detractor follow-up; spec written before building.
Flow correctness25%Both flows run without failures in the test log; Table not range; condition uses a typed score; card names the manager and quotes the comment.
NPS analytics20%NPS not average; by channel, year and status; historical rows and new rows in one Table so the Monday number covers both.
Trap handling20%Response count posted with every score; returns routed differently; blank-comment share stated before any theme claim.
Documentation20%A colleague could rebuild the pipeline from the spec and the exported flows without asking you anything.

Festive Season Review deck: did Diwali 2025 beat Diwali 2024, and what do we do differently this year?

Brief from the CEO

Meera presents to the board in three weeks and wants ten slides on the festive season. "Last year against the year before, by category, by channel, by store. What worked, what did not, and three things we change for Diwali 2026. Not a data dump — a story. And every number linked to the workbook, because the last deck had a typo on the revenue slide and I found out from a board member."

The brief

A board deck is an argument with exhibits, not a tour of the data. The storyline comes first: situation (festive season is a quarter of the year), complication (growth depends entirely on how you define the season), question (what actually changed?), answer (electronics and the app carried it; fashion was flat; one store fell off a cliff). Ten slides, one message per slide, every title a sentence a board member could repeat in the corridor.

Then the mechanics. A slide master with Novamart's colours and fonts so nothing is formatted by hand. Charts pasted from Excel as linked objects, so a corrected number in the workbook flows to the slide. Speaker notes that say what you will say, not what is on the slide. Sections in the deck so you can jump to the store slide when the COO asks.

The analytical spine is one workbook sheet called Festive: October and November of each year, delivered revenue by category, channel and store, with 2025 against 2024 and the change. Every chart in the deck points at that sheet. Build the sheet before you open PowerPoint.

The data

Sales (C Month, B OrderDate, K Category, G Channel, D Store, O DiscountPct, P LineRevenue, Q Status), Campaigns (E Start, F End for the two Diwali TV campaigns). Start from files/cap08-festive-review-deck-starter.pptx, which has a slide master in Novamart's theme and ten empty layouts with placeholder titles; the numbers come from files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Define "festive season" in writing. Calendar months (Oct+Nov)? A fixed window around the festival date? The campaign window? Compute delivered revenue under all three for 2024 and 2025 before you pick one.
  2. By category: which grew, which did not, and what share of the season's growth came from Electronics alone?
  3. By channel: how much did the app's festive revenue grow, and what was its share of the season in each year?
  4. By store: which stores grew and which shrank, and is there one that needs its own slide?
  5. Discounting: what was the average discount per line in September, October and November 2025, and did the deeper festive discount buy proportionately more revenue?
  6. Build the SCQA storyline as ten action titles before any chart exists. Then build the charts to match the titles, not the other way around.
  7. Three recommendations for Diwali 2026, each tied to one exhibit, with the date Diwali 2026 falls on written on the slide.

Starter

=(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2025-11"))
 /(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-11"))-1

+33 per cent: ₹21.05 lakh against ₹15.82 lakh. That is the headline if you define the season as October plus November. Now try the other two definitions.

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2025-10")
 /SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-10")-1

+67 per cent. Same business, same two years, twice the growth, because Diwali fell on 20 October in 2025 and on 1 November in 2024, so October 2025 contains the festival and October 2024 does not.

=LET(cat,SORT(UNIQUE(Sales!K2:K6315)),
  HSTACK(cat,
    SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-10",Sales!K:K,cat)+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2024-11",Sales!K:K,cat),
    SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2025-10",Sales!K:K,cat)+SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2025-11",Sales!K:K,cat)))

Electronics went from ₹6.68 lakh to ₹9.89 lakh, Home & Kitchen from ₹2.86 lakh to ₹4.58 lakh, and Fashion stayed flat at just under ₹3 lakh. Two categories are the whole story; that is slide four.

The first three deck steps, which the Lab does not run.

  1. View ▸ Slide Master. Set the theme colours (one brand colour, one highlight, greys), the fonts, and edit the Title and Content layout so the title box holds two lines of 28-point text. Close Master View and never format a title by hand again.
  2. In Excel, select the chart ▸ Ctrl+C. In PowerPoint, Home ▸ Paste ▸ Paste Special ▸ Paste link ▸ Microsoft Excel Chart Object. Change a number in the Festive sheet and watch the slide update after File ▸ Info ▸ Edit Links to Files ▸ Update now.
  3. Home ▸ Section ▸ Add Section four times: Situation, What changed, Where, What we do. Then View ▸ Notes Page and write the sentence you will say on each slide before you touch a chart's formatting.

Watch out

Diwali moves. It fell on 1 November 2024, 20 October 2025, and falls on 8 November 2026, so any comparison built on calendar months compares different amounts of festival. October-on-October says +67 per cent; October-plus-November says +33 per cent; a fixed four-week window centred on the festival (18 Oct–15 Nov 2024 against 6 Oct–3 Nov 2025) says −6.6 per cent, ₹8.20 lakh against ₹8.78 lakh. Three defensible definitions, three different headlines, one of them negative. Check the window version: =SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,10,6),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2025,11,3)). Pick one, put the definition on slide two, and show the other two in the appendix — a board member will ask. Second: the 2025 TV campaign window was 10–25 October, which ended before the festival, while 2024's ran 20 October to 5 November and straddled it; the campaign slide has to say that. Third: Rajpur Road took ₹66,228 in the 2024 season and ₹1,633 in 2025, and that store deserves its own slide, not a footnote.

The deliverable

  • 2026-09_Festive-Review.pptx: ten slides plus appendix, built on the starter master, every chart linked to the workbook, action titles throughout, speaker notes on every slide, four sections, exported also as PDF.
  • 2026-09_Festive-Review-Data_v01.xlsx: the Festive sheet with all three season definitions computed, the category, channel and store cuts, and a Checks sheet where the cuts reconcile to the season total.
  • README.md with the storyline in ten sentences, the season definition chosen and why, and the three recommendations with the date of Diwali 2026.

Stretch goals

  • Add a slide on discount depth: average DiscountPct per line by month for September to December in both years, and whether the deeper festive discount bought proportionate revenue.
  • Build a Morph transition between the 2024 and 2025 category charts so the change is animated, and decide whether it helps or distracts.
  • Produce a two-slide executive summary version of the same deck for the pre-read email.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Storyline25%SCQA visible in the section structure; ten action titles read as an argument on their own with the slides hidden.
Season definition20%All three definitions computed, one chosen and stated on slide two, the moving-Diwali problem explained in one sentence.
Mechanics20%Master and layouts used, no hand-formatted titles, every chart linked and updating, sections and notes present.
Analysis20%Category, channel, store and discount cuts each reconcile; Electronics and app share quantified; Rajpur Road surfaced.
Recommendations15%Three, each tied to an exhibit, each with an owner and a date, and the 2026 festival date on the slide.

Store Audit SOP and mail-merge letters: can every store be audited the same way, and can seventeen vendors get a personal letter by Friday?

Brief from the Head of Merchandising

Rohan has two Word problems and one afternoon. "The store audit checklist is a Word file that each store manager has edited into a different shape; I want one SOP with a table of contents that Nandini can sign. And I need a letter to each of our seventeen brand vendors before the festive buy — same letter, their name, their products, their numbers — and I am not typing seventeen letters."

The brief

Both halves are about Word doing the work instead of you. The SOP is a styles problem: Heading 1, 2 and 3 applied properly give you a navigation pane, an automatic table of contents, cross-references that survive edits, and a document that a reviewer can comment on with Track Changes and send back. A document formatted by hand with bold 14-point text has none of that, and the moment Nandini asks for section 4 to move above section 3, you are retyping.

The letter is a mail-merge problem, and the interesting part is upstream in Excel. One row per vendor with everything the letter needs: brand name, active product list as a single text field, delivered revenue for the last twelve months already formatted with a ₹ and Indian commas, units on hand, lines below reorder level. UNIQUE, TEXTJOIN, FILTER and TEXT build that from Products, Sales and Inventory; the merge just reads it.

What separates a good submission is what the letter says. "Your products did well" is filler. "Your six lines took ₹19 lakh with us in the last twelve months and we would like to discuss the festive order" is a letter a vendor answers.

The data

Products (B Product, E Brand, I Active), Sales (J Product, P LineRevenue, Q Status, B OrderDate), Inventory (C ProductID, E StockOnHand, F ReorderLevel). Start from files/cap09-store-audit-sop-starter.docx, the hand-formatted SOP as the stores currently use it, and files/cap09-vendor-letter-mergelist.xlsx, which has the seventeen brand names and a contact name and email per vendor in a Table; the numbers come from files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Rebuild the SOP with real styles: Title, Heading 1–3, a Normal body style, a numbered checklist style. Insert an automatic TOC, page numbers, a header with the document code and version, and a sign-off table with cross-references to the sections it approves.
  2. Add a section "Stock count procedure" that states the as-of data honestly: 91 store-product lines were at zero on 31 August 2026, between 4 and 9 per store, and the count has to reconcile to Inventory. Cross-reference the count sheet as a caption.
  3. Turn on Track Changes, make five edits a reviewer would make, add three comments, and save as a second version. Then use Compare to produce the change summary.
  4. Build the merge list: brand, active products as a comma-separated field, product count, twelve-month delivered revenue as formatted text, units on hand, lines below reorder level, contact name, email.
  5. Write the letter with merge fields, a conditional paragraph (IF the vendor has a discontinued product, mention it; else omit), and a date field that prints as 5 September 2026 not 9/5/2026.
  6. Merge to seventeen individual PDFs, then merge to email as a test to yourself. Check the ₹ figures and the "&" in Loom & Light survived.

Starter

=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,FILTER(Products!B:B,(Products!E:E="Nimbus")*(Products!I:I=TRUE)))

"Nimbus Fold Smartphone, Nimbus Power Bank 20000mAh" — two products, not three, because the Nimbus Lite 5G is discontinued and the festive letter should not ask for it. Drop the Active condition and the Lite comes back.

=TEXT(SUMPRODUCT(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",
    Sales!B:B,">="&DATE(2025,9,1),Sales!B:B,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31),
    Sales!J:J,FILTER(Products!B:B,Products!E:E="Nimbus"))),"₹#,##,##0")

A text string with the rupee sign and Indian grouping already in it, so the merge field prints it as-is. Merge the raw number and Word prints 1116411.2 with no thousands separator unless you add a \# switch to the field — and Word's switch does not know about lakhs.

=LET(b,SORT(UNIQUE(Products!E2:E73)),
  HSTACK(b,COUNTIF(Products!E:E,b),COUNTIFS(Products!E:E,b,Products!I:I,TRUE)))

Seventeen rows. Four vendors — Aurelle, Loom & Light, Nimbus, Pulse — have one product fewer in the third column than the second, and those four get the conditional paragraph.

The first three Word steps, which the Lab does not run.

  1. Home ▸ Styles ▸ right-click Heading 1 ▸ Modify. Set font, size, spacing and "Style for following paragraph" once. Then select each hand-formatted heading in the starter SOP and click the style. Open View ▸ Navigation Pane and check the outline reads correctly.
  2. References ▸ Table of Contents ▸ Automatic Table 1. Then Insert ▸ Page Number and Insert ▸ Header with the document code. After any edit, right-click the TOC ▸ Update Field ▸ Entire table.
  3. Mailings ▸ Start Mail Merge ▸ Letters, then Select Recipients ▸ Use an Existing List and pick the Table in cap09-vendor-letter-mergelist.xlsx. Insert Merge Fields where the brand, products and revenue go; Rules ▸ If…Then…Else for the discontinued paragraph; Preview Results and page through all seventeen before Finish & Merge.

Watch out

Three traps, one in the data and two in the tools. In the data: four of the seventeen brands carry a discontinued product, so a merge list built with TEXTJOIN over all products asks Nimbus to restock a phone Novamart has stopped selling; the starter formula's Active filter is the fix, and =COUNTIFS(Products!I:I,FALSE) confirms there are exactly four. In Excel: PROPER is not safe on store names — =PROPER("NOVAMART MG ROAD KOCHI") gives "Novamart Mg Road Kochi", so if you proper-case a list for the SOP's store table, check it by eye. In Word: a merged date field prints in the machine's locale (9/5/2026 on a US-set laptop), so put a \@ "d MMMM yyyy" switch on it, and a merged number loses its formatting entirely, which is why the revenue column is pre-formatted text. Also watch the ampersand: "Loom & Light" merges fine into a letter but breaks if you ever push the same list through a URL or an email subject line without encoding it.

The deliverable

  • SOP-STO-004_Store-Audit_v02.docx: styled, with TOC, page numbers, header, captions, cross-references, a sign-off table, and alt text on any image; v02-tracked.docx with the Track Changes and comments; the Compare output as a PDF.
  • 2026-09_Vendor-Letter-Merge_v01.xlsx with the completed merge Table and a Checks sheet where the seventeen revenue figures sum to the chain total for the window; Vendor-Letter-Template.docx with the fields and rule; a folder of seventeen PDFs.
  • README.md with the style map (which heading is which), the merge-field list, and the two formatting rules for dates and rupees.

Stretch goals

  • Add a second merge for the twelve store managers: a store-specific audit letter listing that store's zero-stock lines from Inventory.
  • Turn the SOP into a .dotx template with Quick Parts for the store name and audit date, and produce two audits from it.
  • Merge to email through Outlook with a personalised subject line, and check how the ₹ figure and the ampersand survive.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Styles and structure25%No direct formatting on headings; navigation pane shows the outline; TOC, captions and cross-references update on F9.
Review loop15%Tracked version with meaningful edits and comments; Compare output attached; version naming follows the convention.
Merge list in Excel25%Built entirely by formula from the source sheets; active-only products; pre-formatted rupee text; totals reconcile.
Merge execution20%Conditional paragraph works for the four vendors; date switch applied; seventeen PDFs with no field codes showing.
Letter quality15%The letter asks for something specific, quotes the vendor's own numbers, and fits on one page.

Budget vs Actual Variance Model: where is the money going, and what does the rest of the year look like under three scenarios?

Brief from the CFO

Arjun has a board pack due and two unrelated variance questions in it. "Revenue against target for the year so far, by store, with the gap in rupees. Payroll against each department's budget. Then give me September to December three ways — base, best, worst — with the assumptions on one sheet where I can change them and watch the total move. And I want to see how attainment reacts if growth and discounting both change, on one grid."

The brief

A variance model is where model hygiene stops being a nicety. Every input on an Assumptions sheet, colour-coded blue; every formula black; no number typed inside a formula; a Checks sheet where the parts add to the whole and any mismatch turns a cell red. Arjun will open this on a Sunday night without you in the room. If a number is wrong he needs to find out where in under a minute.

Two variances, two different kinds of honesty. Revenue against target is straightforward arithmetic with an uncomfortable finding underneath it: the chain has hit its monthly store target in 28 of 413 store-months since January 2024, about 7 per cent, and 2026 attainment to date is 65 per cent. That is not thirteen underperforming stores. That is a target-setting problem, and the memo has to say which one it is. Payroll against department budget is the opposite: payroll is only 40 per cent of the ₹26.2 crore of department budgets in total, which means the budgets cover things this workbook cannot see, and comparing the two as if they were like-for-like would be a mistake.

Then the forecast. Scenario Manager holds three sets of inputs — growth on last year's September to December, average discount, cancellation rate — and a summary report shows the four-month total under each. A two-variable Data Table shows full-year attainment across a grid of growth against discount. Both are built from one base formula that reads the Assumptions sheet, which is the whole point.

The data

Sales (C Month, D Store, P LineRevenue, Q Status, O DiscountPct), Targets, Employees (C Department, G HireDate, H ExitDate, I MonthlySalary), Departments (B Department, C AnnualBudget). Start from files/cap10-budget-vs-actual-starter.xlsx, which has the Assumptions and Checks sheets laid out with named cells and the colour convention; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Revenue variance, January to August 2026, by store: actual delivered, target, gap in rupees, attainment. Which stores account for most of the ₹36.9 lakh shortfall?
  2. Target history: how many store-months hit target in 2024, 2025 and 2026, and what is chain attainment each year? Is the target too high, or is the chain underperforming? Argue it.
  3. Payroll variance by department: annualised payroll of active staff as at 31 August against AnnualBudget, with the ratio. Say why the ratio is not "budget utilisation".
  4. Build the base forecast for September–December 2026: last year's same months × (1 + growth) × (1 − discount change) × (1 − cancellation rate), per month, reading every input from Assumptions.
  5. Scenario Manager: base, best and worst with the three inputs. Produce the Summary report and rewrite it into a three-row table Arjun can read.
  6. A two-variable Data Table: full-year 2026 attainment (actual to August + forecast) across growth from −10 to +30 per cent and discount from 4 to 12 per cent. Colour it.
  7. What target would you set for Q4 2026, and how would you explain the change from the current one?

Starter

=SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!C:C,"2026*")-SUMIFS(Targets!D:D,Targets!C:C,"2026*")

−₹36,92,931 — delivered ₹68.67 lakh against a ₹1.056 crore target for January to August, 65 per cent. The wildcard on the Month column works because it is text; on a real date column you would use two date criteria.

=SUMPRODUCT(--(SUMIFS(Sales!P:P,Sales!Q:Q,"Delivered",Sales!D:D,Targets!B2:B414,Sales!C:C,Targets!C2:C414)
   >=Targets!D2:D414))

28 of 413. A target that is met 7 per cent of the time is not a target, it is a wish, and that sentence belongs on page one.

=LET(d,SORT(UNIQUE(Employees!C2:C86)),
  HSTACK(d,
    SUMIFS(Employees!I:I,Employees!C:C,d,Employees!H:H,"",Employees!G:G,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31))*12,
    XLOOKUP(d,Departments!B:B,Departments!C:C)))

Sales & Store Operations runs ₹3.71 crore of payroll against a ₹9.5 crore budget; Marketing ₹92 lakh against ₹4.2 crore, because the other ₹1.7 crore of campaign spend in Campaigns sits in that budget too. The Executive Office is at 90 per cent, which is what a two-person department with a CEO in it looks like.

The What-If steps, which the Lab does not run.

  1. Formulas ▸ Define Name for each input on Assumptions: Growth, DiscountPct, CancelRate. Write the forecast formula once using the names, so the Scenario Manager can change them.
  2. Data ▸ What-If Analysis ▸ Scenario Manager ▸ Add. Three scenarios, changing cells = the three named inputs. Enter values, then Summary with the four-month total as the result cell. Copy the summary onto a clean sheet and label it.
  3. Data ▸ What-If Analysis ▸ Data Table. Growth values across the top row, discount values down the first column, the attainment formula in the corner cell. Row input cell = Growth, Column input cell = DiscountPct. Apply a colour scale.

Watch out

Two employees on the sheet have not started yet: hire dates of 29 September and 4 December 2026, after the as-of date. Leave them in and annual payroll reads ₹10.79 crore instead of ₹10.56 crore, a ₹23.04 lakh error for people who have not been paid a rupee; the HireDate <= as-of criterion in the starter is what removes them, and =COUNTIFS(Employees!G:G,">"&DATE(2026,8,31)) proves there are two. Second: Targets ends in August 2026, the same month as the data, so there is no target to look up for September to December; your full-year attainment denominator has to be built from an assumption you state, not read from the sheet. =COUNTIFS(Targets!C:C,"2026-09") returns zero. Third: department budgets are annual and include far more than salaries, so a "payroll is only 39 per cent of budget" line about Sales & Store Operations says nothing about whether the department is under-spending. Present it as payroll share of budget and stop there.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Budget-vs-Actual_v01.xlsx: Assumptions (blue inputs, named), RevenueVar, PayrollVar, Forecast, Scenarios (the summary, cleaned), DataTable, and Checks with red flags for any mismatch.
  • Board-Variance-Note.docx: two pages to Arjun — the revenue gap by store, the target-setting argument, the payroll table with its caveat, the three-scenario table and the grid, and a recommended Q4 target.
  • README.md listing every assumption with its source, the as-of handling, and what would change the recommended target.

Stretch goals

  • Add a monthly seasonal index from 2024 and 2025 and use it to shape the September–December forecast instead of a flat growth rate.
  • Build a per-store version of the Data Table for the three largest stores and say whether the data is deep enough for it.
  • Add a one-line check that reproduces August 2026 from data to July with your method, and report the error.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Model hygiene25%Inputs named and colour-coded, no hard-coded numbers in formulas, Checks sheet with visible pass/fail, opens clean on another machine.
Variance correctness20%Store gaps sum to the chain gap; payroll excludes leavers and not-yet-joiners; department names reconcile to Departments.
Trap handling20%Future hires removed and costed, missing Q4 targets stated as an assumption, the payroll-versus-budget caveat written plainly.
What-If tools20%Scenario summary rebuilt into a readable table, Data Table correct on both axes, both driven by the same base formula.
Judgement15%Takes a position on the target-setting question with the 28-of-413 evidence and proposes a Q4 number with its reasoning.

Workforce Analytics: where are we losing people, is pay fair within a role, and is anyone managing too many?

Brief from the Head of HR

Kavita is preparing a people review for the executive committee and she wants it built once, not rebuilt every quarter. "Three questions: where are we losing people, is pay fair for the same job title, and does anyone have more direct reports than they can manage? Put it in the Data Model so I can slice it by department and store without asking you, and give me the revenue-per-head number the CEO keeps asking for, with whatever warning it needs."

The brief

This is the Power Pivot project. Employees, Departments, Stores and Sales go into the Data Model as Tables, related on Department name and Store name, and the measures are written once in DAX: headcount as at a date, exits in a period, attrition rate, average and median salary, span of control, revenue per active store employee. A PivotTable on the model with slicers for department and store answers Kavita's questions, and next quarter's refresh is a Refresh All.

The analytical judgement is about small numbers. Eighty-five rows, seven exits in total, every one of them in Sales & Store Operations, six of them Sales Associates. Six departments have an attrition numerator of zero, and "0 per cent attrition in Finance" from a base of six people is arithmetic pretending to be insight. The review should describe the seven exits individually and compute a rate only where the base can stand it.

Pay equity is better supported. Twenty-four Sales Associates earn between ₹25,000 and ₹32,000 a month, median ₹28,000, and a two-line correlation shows tenure explains some of the spread while rating explains none of it. Span of control needs one self-lookup: ManagerID against EmpID, and one person on the sheet carries seventeen direct reports.

The data

Employees (all columns), Departments, Stores, Sales (D Store, P LineRevenue, Q Status, B OrderDate). Start from files/cap11-workforce-analytics-starter.xlsx, which has the four sheets already converted to Tables named tEmployees, tDepartments, tStores, tSales and an empty Model sheet; the full data is in files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Load the four Tables to the Data Model and create the relationships. Draw the diagram and note which direction each one filters.
  2. Write measures for headcount as at 31 August 2026, exits all time, exits in the last twelve months, and attrition (exits ÷ average headcount). Show them by department, and say in the review which cells are not meaningful.
  3. Pay by job title: count, minimum, maximum, median and spread. For Sales Associates, does tenure or rating explain who sits below the median?
  4. Span of control: direct reports per manager via a lookup of ManagerID to EmpID. Who has the most, how many managers have exactly one, and who has none recorded?
  5. Revenue per active store employee for the twelve months to August 2026, as a measure. Present it with the warning it needs.
  6. Park Street changed store manager on 1 April 2025. Compare the store's monthly revenue before and after, indexed against the chain over the same months.
  7. Build the one-screen PivotTable with slicers for department and store, and a PivotChart of headcount by department, on the model.

Starter

=HSTACK(COUNTIFS(Employees!H:H,"",Employees!G:G,"<="&DATE(2026,8,31)),
    COUNTIFS(Employees!H:H,"<>")-1)

76 active and 7 exits. The -1 removes the header row, which "<>" counts because it is not blank; in the Data Model version the measure will not need it.

=LET(m,SORT(UNIQUE(FILTER(Employees!K2:K86,Employees!K2:K86<>""))),
     n,COUNTIF(Employees!K:K,m),
  TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(XLOOKUP(m,Employees!A:A,Employees!D:D),n),n,-1),5))

The Head of Sales & Store Operations has 17 direct reports, all thirteen store managers among them; the CEO has 7; nobody else has more than 5. That is one slide on its own.

=CORREL(FILTER(Employees!I2:I86,(Employees!D2:D86="Sales Associate")*(Employees!J2:J86<>"")),
        FILTER(Employees!J2:J86,(Employees!D2:D86="Sales Associate")*(Employees!J2:J86<>"")))

−0.04, so no. Swap the second argument for days since hire and it comes to +0.38: tenure moves pay a little, performance does not move it at all. Kavita will want to know that before the next review cycle.

Headcount := CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(tEmployees),
                 tEmployees[HireDate] <= DATE(2026,8,31),
                 ISBLANK(tEmployees[ExitDate]))
Exits 12M := CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(tEmployees),
                 tEmployees[ExitDate] >= DATE(2025,9,1),
                 tEmployees[ExitDate] <= DATE(2026,8,31))
Revenue 12M := CALCULATE(SUM(tSales[LineRevenue]),
                 tSales[Status] = "Delivered",
                 tSales[OrderDate] >= DATE(2025,9,1), tSales[OrderDate] <= DATE(2026,8,31))
Revenue per Head := DIVIDE([Revenue 12M], [Headcount])

Watch out

All seven exits are in one department, so attrition by department is a column of zeros with one number in it — describe, do not divide. Check it: =COUNTIFS(Employees!C:C,"Sales & Store Operations",Employees!H:H,"<>") gives 7 and every other department gives 0. Second: Rating is blank for 7 rows, 5 of them active staff with no completed cycle plus the 2 not-yet-joined, and AVERAGE skips blanks silently, so an average rating rests on fewer people than the headcount. Third, and the one that bites revenue per head: Andheri West shows one active employee on the sheet, its store manager, so revenue per head there is ₹8.05 lakh against ₹2–4 lakh elsewhere — not productivity, a staffing record gap. Verify with =COUNTIFS(Employees!E:E,"Novamart Andheri West",Employees!H:H,""). Fourth: Park Street has two Store Manager rows, one exited 31 March 2025 and one hired 1 April 2025, so a naive count of managers per store double-counts it, and the before/after comparison has no control unless you index against the chain.

The deliverable

  • 2026-08_Workforce-Model_v01.xlsx: four Tables in the Data Model with relationships, the measures above plus attrition, median pay and span, a Review sheet with the slicer-driven PivotTable and PivotChart, and a Checks sheet where the formula versions agree with the measures.
  • People-Review.pptx: six slides — the department snapshot, the seven exits described, pay spread by title, the span-of-control list, revenue per head with its warning, and the Park Street mini-case as a caution about before-and-after comparisons.
  • README.md with the relationship diagram, each measure's definition in a sentence, and a paragraph on why attrition rates were not published by department.

Stretch goals

  • Add a headcount-by-month series from January 2024 with a date spine, counting anyone hired by the month end and not yet exited.
  • Write a DAX measure for median salary by title using MEDIANX and compare with the Excel MEDIAN on the Checks sheet.
  • Walk the reporting chain from the CEO down with repeated XLOOKUP on ManagerID and report the organisation's depth.
CriterionWeightWhat full marks looks like
Data Model25%Four Tables related correctly, measures not calculated fields, slicers filter every visual, Refresh All works.
Measure correctness20%Headcount excludes leavers and future hires; exits windowed; revenue per head uses the same window in numerator and denominator.
Small-number judgement20%No attrition percentages on bases under twenty; exits described individually; averages carry their n.
Trap handling20%Blank ratings, the Andheri West staffing gap and the Park Street double row each identified with their effect quantified.
Review quality15%Six slides Kavita could present without you; the span-of-control recommendation names the role to split.

Project Launch Hub: can the Diwali 2026 launch run in Teams without a single status email?

Brief from the COO

Nandini ran Diwali 2025 out of a WhatsApp group, an email thread with 140 replies and a spreadsheet nobody could find. Diwali 2026 falls on 8 November, sixty-nine days from the end of August. "One place. Everyone knows what they own and when it is due. Store managers, merchandising, marketing and logistics see the same plan. I get a status I did not have to chase. And when I ask why last year's campaign ended before the festival, someone can show me."

The brief

This is the project that ties the non-Excel half of the course together. A Team with a channel per workstream, its Files tab pointing at a SharePoint library with a folder structure that follows the naming convention, a Planner plan with buckets per workstream and tasks with owners and dates, a Loop component in the channel holding the weekly status so it is edited in place rather than re-sent, and two Power Automate flows: one that posts overdue Planner tasks to the channel every Monday, and one that turns a Forms "issue report" from a store into a Planner task in the right bucket.

What separates a hub from a folder is the plan inside it, and the plan has to be built backwards from a date that moves. Diwali 2025 was 20 October; the TV campaign that year ran 10–25 October and the pre-festival window was over before it ended. Diwali 2026 is 8 November, nearly three weeks later in the calendar, so a plan copied from last year's dates would have the campaign, the stock and the store displays ready for a festival that had not arrived. The data in the workbook shows what the season is worth: October and November were 23 per cent of 2025's delivered revenue.

Nandini's status should be readable in under a minute: on track, at risk, blocked, by workstream, with the next milestone and its date. Build the Loop template so that is all it can hold.

The data

Campaigns (E Start, F End for campaigns 4 and 8), Sales (C Month, P LineRevenue, Q Status) for the season's value, Inventory (E StockOnHand, F ReorderLevel) for the stock workstream's opening position, Stores (B Store, C City) for the store-readiness checklist. Start from files/cap12-launch-hub-brief.docx, the one-page project brief with the four workstreams and the milestone list to be dated; the numbers come from files/novamart-m365.xlsx.

The questions

  1. Build the milestone plan backwards from 8 November 2026 on a sheet: campaign live date, stock-in-store date, vendor order date, creative sign-off, store display audit. Use WORKDAY for each offset and put the offsets on an Assumptions sheet.
  2. Create the Team and channels (General, Merchandising, Marketing, Logistics, Stores), set up the SharePoint folder structure and pin the plan workbook in each channel's Files tab.
  3. Build the Planner plan: one bucket per workstream, every milestone as a task with an owner, a due date from your sheet, a label for the store group, and a checklist for the store-readiness items across the twelve physical stores.
  4. Post a Loop component in General with the status table — workstream, RAG, next milestone, date, owner — and show that editing it in Teams updates it everywhere it is embedded.
  5. Flow 1: every Monday 08:00, list Planner tasks past due, post them to the owning channel with @mentions. Flow 2: a Forms "store issue" submission creates a Planner task in the Stores bucket and replies to the submitter.
  6. Run the first weekly review from the hub: invite with agenda, the Loop status as the only document, decisions captured in the meeting notes, follow-ups as Planner tasks. No email.
  7. Write the one-page "what went wrong in 2025" note from the campaign dates and the season revenue, and pin it in the channel.

Starter

=NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2026,8,31),DATE(2026,11,8))
